20012-the-hawarden-visitors-hand-book-re:
The Hawarden Visitors' Hand Book, in its revised 1890 edition, guides guests through a Welsh village. Hawarden was W. E. Gladstone's home, and visitors came in numbers. Two crosses once stood in the churchyard, the Upper and the Lower. Both were destroyed in 1641, during the civil wars. A lime tree planted in 1742 marks the Lower Cross's site. The parish stocks stood near that eastern end too.

Gladstone's retirement made Hawarden a place of pilgrimage. The handbook serves sightseers touring his church and castle grounds. Local history fills it more than politics does. Crosses, stocks, and trees carry a thousand years of parish life. Such handbooks were the apps of the excursion age. This one preserves Gladstone's village as visitors saw it.
21590-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, the London comic paper, opens its January 18, 1890 number among amateur actors. The Thespian Perambulators stage Heads or Tails? at the Theatre Royal, Blankbury. Lady Surbiton and Mrs Gagmore take their stalls seats as the house fills.

A sketch mocks a manager who insists a parrot belongs in a drawing-room scene. Lady Surbiton lends hers, since it scarcely ever talks. Jokes at critics, proud amateurs, and fond relations fill the piece. The whole number, volume ninety-eight, gives a week's worth of Victorian wit, sketches, verses, and drawings at the height of Punch's fame.
21596-the-american-architect-and-buildin:
Volume twenty-seven of the American Architect and Building News covers January to March 1890. Ticknor and Company issued the weekly from Tremont Street, Boston. Its index alone runs to hundreds of entries, from abbeys to accidents.

Reports treat the fall of a hotel in Sydney and of a St Louis music hall roof. Other items cover aluminium from bauxite, American bricks, and faulty gutters on the Albany Capitol. A design contest for a new White House, under a travelling scholarship, draws note. Architects of the day kept such volumes as a working record of their fast-changing craft.
22051-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, the London comic weekly, had mocked British life since 1841. This single issue, volume 98 for February 1, 1890, shows the paper at its Victorian height. Verse, jokes, dialogues, and cartoons fill its pages. One poem teases a hostess about a guest whose lyric theories threaten everything she cares for.

Politicians, fashions, and drawing-room manners all take their turn under the lash. Punch's writers assumed readers who followed Parliament and the season alike. A lone issue like this one freezes a week of London talk. It also shows the house style that made "Mr. Punch" a national institution for a hundred years.
aphorismi-urbigerani-or-certain-rules-cl:
Aphorismi Urbigerani, printed in 1690, sets out one hundred and one aphorisms by Baro Urbigerus. The rules claim clearly to demonstrate the three infallible ways of preparing the grand elixir, the circulatum majus of the philosophers. Along the way they promise to discover the secret of secrets and to detect the errors of vulgar chymists in their operations.

An engraved allegorical frontispiece by William Faithorne opens the book. Bound within it, with its own title page, stands the Circulatum Minus Urbigeranum, the philosophical elixir of vegetables, extending the system from minerals to plants. The aphorism form packs Urbigerus's whole doctrine into short numbered rules, a portable summa of the elixir art for English readers.
arxiv-2510-00190:
Narges Ahmadi and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on labeling regions of near-Earth space automatically. NASA's Magnetospheric Multiscale mission streams data as its craft cross five distinct plasma regions. Sorting those regions by hand is slow, so the team trained a hybrid machine learning model. One part reads ion energy spectrograms as images, using a convolutional network.

A random forest handles the simpler scalar inputs, such as field strength, ion temperature, and position. Together the two parts classify solar wind, magnetosheath, inner magnetosphere, plasma sheet, and lobe samples. The combined model reached about ninety-nine percent accuracy on held-out test data. It labels the region every three minutes of mission data. The authors note the light design needs little hand labeling and could transfer to other magnetosphere missions with similar instruments.
arxiv-2510-00290:
Hsueh-Yung Lin and Evgeny Shinder wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on invariants of birational maps in algebraic geometry. Birational maps reshape varieties without changing their core function field. The authors define new horizontal and vertical motivic invariants for maps between rational maps. They first study the basic properties these invariants must obey.

One application shows the usual motivic invariants vanish for birational automorphisms of threefolds over suitable fields. The new invariants behave very differently in higher dimensions, the authors prove. For projective spaces of dimension at least four, they form no bounded family. The same holds for many other cases, even after enlarging the field. A corollary says those groups are not generated by maps preserving nice fibered structures. Their abelian forms also fail to stabilize, adding algebraic evidence of wildness.
arxiv-2510-00590:
Natsuki Hayatsu and twelve colleagues published this 2025 astronomy paper on a galaxy so dusty that optical telescopes miss it entirely. Such hidden galaxies still forged a real share of the early universe's stars. The team stumbled on one behind a quadruply lensed quasar while observing something else. Carbon monoxide emission lines pinned its redshift precisely at about three point four.

The galaxy holds roughly a hundred billion solar masses of molecular gas. Its central black hole weighs in near a hundred million solar masses, judged from archival X-ray data. Total infrared luminosity reaches several trillion times the Sun's output. Those numbers paint a gas-rich system caught mid-transformation. The authors suggest it is transitioning from furious starburst toward quasar activity. It offers a rare laboratory for watching galaxies and black holes grow up together under heavy dust.
arxiv-2510-00690:
Wang and eight co-authors introduce ACPO in this 2025 arXiv paper, a reinforcement learning method for aligning vision-language models on hard reasoning tasks. Standard training tools such as PPO use fixed schedules and one rigid clipping limit for every update. The authors argue those fixed choices waste samples and can destabilize training on complex visual problems.

ACPO adapts in two ways during training. Its curriculum slowly shifts from fresh on-policy samples toward reusing past samples more often. Its clipping rule also sets bounds per token, based on how promising that token looks. On MathVista, LogicVista, and MMMU-Pro, the authors report that ACPO beat strong baselines such as DAPO and PAPO. They also report faster convergence and steadier training runs across their benchmark suite.
arxiv-2510-00890:
Yin and Wang present Sci-SpanDet in this paper, published in the journal Knowledge-Based Systems, on detecting AI-written scientific text. As language models spread through scholarly writing, journals worry about authorship integrity. Most detectors label a whole document at once or lean on shallow statistical cues, so they cannot point to the exact passages in question. They also calibrate their confidence poorly and fail across new fields or new generator models.

Sci-SpanDet instead locates AI-generated spans inside a paper, using section-aware style modelling and multi-level contrastive learning. A sequence labelling layer with pointer-based boundary decoding marks precise start and end points. On a new dataset of one hundred thousand samples from several model families, it led all baselines on the main detection scores. It also stayed resilient when text was adversarially rewritten.
arxiv-2510-00990:
Fracaro and four co-authors, at the Universities of Padova, Örebro, and Tuscia, measure how album cover design evolved over seventy-five years in this 2025 arXiv paper on cultural analysis. Album covers sit where art meets commerce, and studies found simplification trends in music itself. The authors assembled covers across eleven genres and scored them with a battery of complexity measures. Object recognition tools added a view of what the covers depict.

The trend runs toward minimalism in most genres, echoing the simplification seen in songs and lyrics. Metal and hip hop break the pattern, and experimental genres grow more complex through abstraction. The variance across covers keeps rising, intricate designs never disappear. Covers that show the artist's face score low on complexity, which the authors link to promotion. They frame the cover archive as a quantifiable record of cultural history in the platform era.
arxiv-2510-01090:
Andrews and five co-authors describe how two stratifications interact on a unitary Shimura variety, in this 2025 arXiv paper on arithmetic geometry. The variety parametrizes five-dimensional abelian varieties in characteristic p with an action of signature (3,2) from an imaginary quadratic field. Researchers sort its points two ways: the Ekedahl-Oort stratification by the p-torsion subgroup scheme, and the Newton stratification by the p-divisible group's isogeny class. On modular curves the two sorts agree, but in higher dimensions their interaction is subtle.

The main theorem lists exactly which Ekedahl-Oort strata sit inside which Newton strata. Five named strata lie inside the supersingular Newton stratum, and one more lies inside a second Newton stratum. A stratum meets both of those Newton strata, splitting across them. Two further strata sit inside a third Newton stratum, and the last Ekedahl-Oort stratum equals the mu-ordinary Newton stratum outright.
arxiv-2510-01190:
Ouermi and co-authors, based at the University of Utah and Oak Ridge National Laboratory, visualize how uncertain a flow field's divergence really is. Divergence flags sources and sinks in fluid data, but noisy measurements can fake both. The classical sampling approach converges slowly and scales badly to large fields.

Assuming each vector carries independent Gaussian error, the team derives the divergence uncertainty in closed form. The formula replaces thousands of simulation samples with direct computation. A parallel implementation inside a standard visualization library keeps big datasets interactive. Scientists can finally see flow features and their trustworthiness in one picture. Sources glow positive and sinks negative in the divergence map. Closed form beats sampling when every grid point needs an error bar. Viskores supplies the parallel engine under the visualization. Uncertainty becomes a visible picture, not a footnote. Trust gets drawn too.
arxiv-2510-01290:
Ramachandran and co-authors squeeze the memory of long reasoning sessions down to a twentieth of its size without dulling the model. Extended chains of thought balloon the key-value cache until graphics memory chokes. Their insight is that attention patterns reveal which thoughts matter and which are filler.

A hybrid scheme stores important thoughts at higher precision and progressively evicts the rest. A custom kernel reuses freed memory slots inside paged attention, avoiding costly reshuffles. Across mathematics and coding benchmarks, accuracy stayed near-lossless at extreme compression. Throughput climbed several-fold over the strongest existing baselines. Reasoning, execution, and transition segments receive different treatment under the scheme. DeepSeek and AceReason models supplied the test subjects. Evicted slots return to service without compaction pauses. Long outputs are the feature that created the problem. Thought-aware compression respects what the cache is for.
arxiv-2510-01790:
Ammad and Ling propose a faster way to evolve shapes given as point clouds in this 2025 numerical methods paper. Their setting tracks points that lie on smooth surfaces, called manifolds, as the shapes move. Standard radial basis function methods recompute interpolation often, which gets expensive. The authors instead use B-splines as the local basis for interpolation.

B-spline coefficients carry direct geometric meaning, unlike opaque fit parameters. They can be shifted like points, so the interpolant updates rapidly after each move. Adding or removing points becomes seamless, even where point density changes sharply. Normals and curvature still come out of the same local fits. Numerical tests confirmed that these geometric quantities converge as expected. The team also simulated curvature flows driven by coupled reaction-diffusion systems, which form patterns on the evolving curves.
arxiv-2510-01890:
Irbäck, Knuthson, and Mohanty fold a toy protein on a packed grid in this 2025 paper. Their model protein is a chain that must fill every site of a minimal lattice, leaving no gaps. Dense packing makes ordinary chain methods clash and stall. Finding the lowest-energy fold is a hard optimization problem, akin to tough scheduling puzzles.

The authors recast the search as a quadratic binary optimization problem, a form both classical and quantum solvers accept. Simulated annealing solved chains of length forty-eight swiftly and consistently in that form. A hybrid quantum-classical annealer on a D-Wave system needed only about ten seconds for the same task. Linear and quadratic programming worked for a simpler lattice gas, but they struggled with the chain rules. Exact enumeration checked every claim at high cost. The encoding now opens dense multi-chain systems to similar treatment.
arxiv-2510-02290:
Midha and Zhang sharpen a workhorse approximation for tensor network calculations. Their 2025 physics paper studies belief propagation, a message passing method. Tensor networks compress huge quantum and statistical problems. Contracting them exactly on messy graphs is often impossible. Belief propagation gives fast estimates, but its error was poorly understood. The authors build a theory that explains that error. Their cluster expansion adds corrections group by group. They prove the corrections shrink fast when loop effects fade with loop size. A simple algorithm computes the expansion to any order.

They test the method on the two dimensional Ising model. The corrected results beat plain belief propagation clearly. They also beat older fixes like loop series methods. A rigorous error bound comes with the improvement. Quantum error correction decoding uses such contractions daily. A systematic accuracy ladder helps that field directly.
arxiv-2510-02390:
Li shows that careful settings let an old diffusion model rival new distilled ones. His 2025 paper skips retraining entirely. Distilled models generate images in few steps but cost extra training. Li analyzes the truncation error of diffusion equations instead. That analysis guides a training free sampling algorithm. The method tunes step schedules and guidance scales directly. It also adjusts skip connections at the right moment. Decoder traits of the latent model get used deliberately. Small leftover noise is ignored to reschedule the steps.

The algorithm draws sharp images in about eight steps. It handles both standard and large image sizes. At large size, its quality matched the latest distilled model. At standard size, it beat a leading solver using twenty steps. Five and six step runs also stayed competitive. Hyperparameter craft can replace expensive distillation pipelines.
arxiv-2510-02890:
Balbiani, van Ditmarsch, and Lerouvillois extend a logic of knowledge and messages. In their logic, an announcement is sent at one moment. Each agent may receive it at a later moment. Statements are judged against a world plus a history of past events. An earlier axiom system covered only the empty history. It worked by reducing each claim to a plain knowledge claim.

Their new system, marked with a star, covers every history. It lists the claims that hold after any sequence of sends and receives. The system is infinitary, using rules with endless premises. It is not a reduction system like the older one. Some old truths also lapse once a history exists. For instance, it is no longer valid that no one has received anything. Private messages and forgetting are also on the list. The logic suits distributed systems with no global clock.
arxiv-2510-03690:
Azizpour and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper teaching graph learning methods to notice when a data set mixes several kinds of networks. Graph collections often blend populations generated by random mechanisms, yet contrastive learning and mixup usually assume one distribution. The authors model each population with a graphon, a generative template. Motif densities, the frequencies of subgraph patterns, fingerprint which graphon made a graph. Clustering those fingerprints separates the mixture before learning begins.

Their mixup variant interpolates within a shared model, reaching top accuracy on six of seven supervised benchmarks. Their contrastive variant restricts negative examples to graphs from other models, cutting false negatives. It took the top average rank across eight unsupervised data sets. A theorem tightens the link between graphon distance and motif similarity. Mixture awareness is free once the clustering is done. Social, biological, and wireless graph collections all hide mixtures, so the upgrade should travel well.
arxiv-2510-03990:
Gao and Aragam wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on the limits of picking the right variables in regression. Analysts want the small subset of variables that truly drives the outcome. The classic method, best subset selection, tries combinations directly but is slow. Faster methods exist, yet it was unclear whether they match the classic method's quality when variables are correlated.

The authors compute the exact minimum sample size that variable selection needs under a general covariance design. Best subset selection reaches that optimum, both when the number of true variables is known and when it is not. They then prove no fast algorithm can reach the same optimum, under standard complexity assumptions. The gap between the two hinges on a quantity called the restricted eigenvalue. The results separate what is statistically possible from what is computationally feasible. That separation matters wherever high-dimensional data guides real decisions.
arxiv-2510-04290:
Wu and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on ChronoEdit, an image editing framework that borrows the physical knowledge embedded in video generators. A text instruction can change an object's pose, but a still-image editor may produce a result that looks locally while violating how bodies and objects can actually move. ChronoEdit treats the source and target images as the first and last frames of an imagined video. A pretrained video model supplies motion priors and temporal consistency that constrain the transformation.

At inference, a reasoning stage jointly denoises the target frame with reasoning tokens for several steps. These tokens sketch a plausible editing trajectory before being dropped, avoiding the expense of rendering the whole video. ChronoEdit surpassed leading baselines in visual fidelity and physical plausibility on that benchmark.
arxiv-2510-04390:
Xuehai He and six coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on building virtual worlds for robots. Good world models let researchers train robots and test them in a safe, repeatable setting. Video generators make nice moving scenes, but they show one flat view and allow little control. The team built MorphoSim, a system that makes four dimensional scenes from plain language commands. The scenes change over time and stay consistent when seen from many angles.

Inside a MorphoSim scene, a user can steer an object, change its color, or remove it. Edits apply at once, without rebuilding the whole scene from scratch. The system guides motion with set paths and spreads scene features so views stay aligned. Tests showed high scene quality along with strong control and editing power. Such tools could speed up robot training and give planners a flexible test ground.
arxiv-2510-04490:
Akshay Srinivasan, Vikas Dwivedi, and Balaji Srinivasan wrote this 2025 paper on fast neural solvers for hard equations. Physics informed neural networks solve equations without a mesh, but training them is slow. A shallow variant replaces slow gradient training with a single least squares solve. The team tested that variant on the biharmonic equation, a fourth order equation used in flow and plate problems. Two benchmark cases measured speed, size, and accuracy.

On a lid driven cavity flow case, the shallow solver trained about 350 times faster than deep networks. It also used more than ten times fewer parameters for similar accuracy. Its error on that case came out lower as well. On a wavy manufactured solution, accuracy dropped as the waves grew more extreme. Even with that speed, the method still trailed mature mesh based solvers overall. The team released their code for others to extend.
arxiv-2510-04590:
Torbjörn Sjöstrand wrote this 2025 paper on a bump in top quark production near threshold. The CMS and ATLAS experiments saw more top and antitop pairs just below the energy where pairs should appear. Many read the excess as toponium, a bound state of the pair. Sjöstrand revives a modeling approach from 1989 that already treated this region with quantum chromodynamics Green functions. He implements those formulas in the Pythia event generator.

Gluon exchange between the slow pair reshapes the cross section near threshold. A color singlet pair gains cross section, while a color octet pair loses it. The shares of the two color states differ between gluon and quark driven production. Above threshold, the modeling is direct and safe. Below threshold, the virtual states need care, and the paper tests its prescription against simpler ones. Cross sections and properties for the region come out of the generator runs.
arxiv-2510-04690:
Christian Berg and Ryszard Szwarc wrote this 2025 mathematics paper continuing their study of a special operator. The paper concerns the Jacobi operator tied to an indeterminate moment problem. In such problems, many measures share the same list of moments. The operator domain is subtle, and work left open which vectors fill it densely. The authors exhibit countable sets of vectors inside the domain, whose span reaches every vector.

Their example sets are built from the orthonormal polynomials of the problem. Two auxiliary functions from the classical Nevanlinna theory shape the construction. The sets are optimal in a sharp sense. Remove one vector, and the span no longer fills the space. The results close gaps left by an earlier paper in this series. They give analysts dense sets to use in proofs about these operators. Moment problems appear in probability, physics, and signal analysis, so the tools travel.
arxiv-2510-04890:
Shihan Fang and Wenxin Zheng wrote this 2025 paper on helping compilers use the wide vector units in modern chips. Vector instructions run one operation on many data items at once, which can speed code. Compilers like LLVM and GCC often miss chances to vectorize. Their passes are disjoint, and flow tangles hide the patterns they seek. The authors retrofit the compiler intermediate code with two extensions.

One extension stores level structure of the program flow. The other spells out instruction dependencies found by data analysis. With dependencies explicit, vectorization passes can share information and search a space of matching instructions. The framework stays flexible, so passes can plug into the code form. In tests the pipeline beat the compilers by margins. Speedups reached about half again the LLVM speed and a bit more over GCC. Faster automatic vectorization helps every program the compiler touches, from science codes to media tools.
arxiv-2510-04990:
Narda Cordero-Michel and Mika Olsen study how colorings of directed graphs can change step by step in this 2025 arXiv paper. A dicoloring assigns colors so that no directed cycle is all one color. The recoloring graph links two colorings when they differ on just one vertex. The question is whether that graph stays in one connected piece.

The authors first prove a negative result about all directed graphs at once. No formula based only on the dichromatic number can guarantee connectedness for large color counts. They then study two infinite families of circulant tournaments in detail. For the seven-vertex Paley tournament, the recoloring graph is connected whenever at least three colors are used. Its diameter, the longest shortest path, is exactly 8 in that case.
arxiv-2510-05290:
Manuel Eppler and four co-authors show how one bad frame can wreck a factory network in this 2025 arXiv paper. Time-Sensitive Networking schedules periodic traffic with a time-aware shaper on Ethernet. Schedules assume every talker sends exactly on time. Real frames arrive early, late, missing, or duplicated.

The authors build minimal examples on a single link showing how a faulty frame corrupts the schedule. Simulations then show one slightly delayed frame causing packet loss across multiple links. Longer transmission slots, or none at all for top traffic, soften the failures. Full protection needs per-stream filtering plus frame isolation in the schedule. Current hardware cannot yet filter every stream reliably, a blocker for industrial deployment.
arxiv-2510-05390:
Felicity Anderson, Julien Sindt, and Neil Chue Hong profile the people who build research software in this 2025 arXiv paper. Research software engineers contribute in wildly different patterns. Personas built from data turn raw activity into readable archetypes. Some fix one typo and vanish, while others organize whole projects. Knowing the common patterns helps teams credit work and spot skill gaps.

The authors mined GitHub interactions across 1,284 research repositories. Their data covered more than 115,000 contributors sampled from Zenodo records. Clustering the interaction patterns produced seven distinct personas. They range from the Ephemeral Contributor to the Project Organiser and the Active Contributor. The method characterizes contributors despite huge differences in domains, project management, and backgrounds.
arxiv-2510-05590:
Badza and colleagues hunt for the hidden order inside turbulent convection. In Rayleigh-Bénard convection, a fluid layer heated below forms ridge networks of rising hot fluid. These patterns steer how much heat crosses the layer. Their 2025 study extracts the patterns with a data-driven operator method.

The inflated generator framework lifts the transfer operator into space-time. Its leading eigenvectors reveal families of almost-invariant sets that evolve slowly. Applied to three-dimensional turbulent flow data, the method isolates transient heat transfer patterns. The layer is cooled from above and heated uniformly from below. Some families contribute least to the convective heat flux. The analysis centers on a field coupling vertical velocity with temperature fluctuation. Such sets explain how superstructures organize transport despite small-scale chaos. Knowing the least-contributing patterns sharpens theories of turbulent heat transport.
arxiv-2510-06090:
Hansen and co-authors release a public heart imaging dataset in a 2025 medical paper. The dataset centers on the left atrial appendage, a small pouch of the heart where clots can form before a stroke. Good outlines of this pouch are hard to produce, and most earlier collections stayed private and small.

The team built the labels on ImageCAS, a public set of 1,000 cardiac CT angiography scans. A specialist network, trained on 980 hand-annotated scans from a Copenhagen population study, produced detailed appendage outlines for every scan. Whole-heart labels came from the TotalSegmentator tool, and the coronary artery and pulmonary vein labels were corrected for anatomical consistency. The release even lists scans with flaws such as step artefacts or cut-off anatomy. Researchers can now study appendage shape and blood flow at a scale that private data never allowed.
arxiv-2510-06390:
Carrington and four co-authors push proper-time expansions further into glasma dynamics in a 2025 nuclear theory paper. The glasma is the dense gluon system formed in the first instants of a heavy ion collision. Its evolution obeys classical Yang–Mills equations, which admit early-time solutions as proper-time expansions.

The catch is reach: the expansion parameter is time itself, and computing beyond eighth order is impractical. Reliable results previously stopped near five hundredths of a femtometer over c. The authors explore several methods for extending that horizon. Depending on the quantity, the reliable window grows by roughly a factor of one and a half. Results now stay trustworthy to about eight hundredths of a femtometer over c. The gain is modest absolutely but significant proportionally. Early glasma evolution sets initial conditions for everything after, so extra trustworthy time improves the whole modeling chain.
arxiv-2510-06490:
Akhtiamov, Ghane, and Hassibi derive exact asymptotic formulas for randomized singular value decomposition error in a 2025 numerical analysis paper. The randomized algorithm approximates large matrices at low rank without a full decomposition. Practitioners knew its error only through upper and lower bounds. Those bounds leave a theory-versus-practice gap.

The authors close it with precise asymptotic expressions. Their formulas describe the error as dimensions grow without bound. The error depends only on the matrix's singular values. They evaluate the expressions for two spectral families. Power-law spectra cover smoothly decaying singular values. Bilevel spectra cover sharp two-tier structures. The analysis extends to polynomial-filtered algorithm variants. Its characterizations yield insight into optimal filter choice. The program replaces worst-case guarantees with exact characterizations of actual performance. Anyone compressing huge matrices can now predict the method's accuracy, not merely bound it.
arxiv-2510-06790:
Tavish McDonald and four colleagues at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory study how extra thinking time protects models. Their 2025 paper builds on a finding. Models that reason longer at test time follow safety specifications better and resist jailbreaks. That benefit seemed to fade when attackers could see model gradients or use images.

The authors propose a hypothesis they call RICH, short for Robustness from Inference Compute Hypothesis. Attacked inputs are built from familiar parts that appeared in training. A model that understands those parts can apply its safety rules to the whole. Extra inference compute then pays off, provided the training data covers the parts. They show reasoning strategies raise robustness in models never trained for reasoning. Benefits appear for open-source models and against white-box vision attacks. A trick follows from the hypothesis. Light fine-tuning on attacked data improves the rate of return on extra compute.
arxiv-2510-07090:
Marcella Palese, a single author, rebuilds a family of water-wave models from a variational principle. The 2025 paper works in Lagrangian field theory on fibered manifolds. The targets are modified Boussinesq-type systems in two space dimensions. They model long waves in shallow water and related media.

Palese derives the two-dimensional systems as coupled Euler-Lagrange laws for two fields. The tool is a recursive formula built on integration by parts. It produces Lepage equivalents of the Lagrangians, of Krupka-Betounes type. From those equivalents, the systems drop out as one component of a differential. The main result is a set of new modified Boussinesq-type equations. They come in fourth-order and sixth-order versions with mixed terms in both space variables. A side result gives a variational form for a stationary reduction of the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation. Invariant Lepage equivalents yield conserved charges through Noether's theorem.
arxiv-2510-07190:
Zhi and co-authors present MV-Performer, a system that re-films a human performer from every angle. Their 2025 conference paper starts from one ordinary video of a full body. From that one view, the system must imagine the back and sides in motion. Prior video models handled small camera moves well, but full turns broke them. The team aims for synchronized videos from many viewpoints at once.

Geometry hints guide the generation. Surface direction maps, rendered from partial 3D point clouds, mark which body parts the camera could actually see. A multi-view diffusion model blends the source video, these hints, and the target angles. A robust inference routine cleans up flaws from imperfect depth estimates in casual footage. Tests on three data sets beat prior methods by a wide margin. Such tools could serve film and games, where reshoots from new angles are costly.
arxiv-2510-07290:
Liu and co-authors study why language models get morally better answers when simply told to improve them again. Their 2025 paper examines intrinsic self-correction, where no detailed feedback is given. The model must spot its own flaws from a general instruction. The team tracks what happens over many rounds of correction. They focus on moral questions, where the effect is easy to measure.

Performance rises over rounds and then settles at a stable level. The authors find the cause inside the model. Each repeated instruction switches on moral concepts more strongly. As those concepts stabilize, the model's uncertainty about the answer falls. Steadier concepts produce the converged scores seen in the experiments. The mechanism suggests self-correction is not magic but repeated activation of relevant knowledge. Designers can schedule correction rounds until answers stop changing.
arxiv-2510-07690:
Singh and fourteen coauthors wrote this 2025 instrumentation paper on X-ray detectors for large spectrometers. Modern experiments pack hundreds or thousands of cryogenic detectors onto one focal plane. Each absorber needs wiring to its readout circuit, and bulky bonds waste area. The team works with transition edge sensors, which are sensitive superconducting thermometers. Their readout uses microwave SQUID multiplexers, which let many signals share one line.

The authors report the first chip that builds both parts in one fabrication flow. Detector and multiplexer circuits are patterned first and shielded, then the sensors and connecting wires are added. Printed wiring replaces wire bonds and flip-chip bonds. The finished multiplexers worked with reasonable yield, and the process adds no heat steps that could harm the sensors. The approach promises denser detector arrays for X-ray astronomy. It could also serve gamma-ray detectors and cosmic microwave background telescopes.
arxiv-2510-08090:
Banerjee and Mishra wrote this 2025 particle physics paper using a rare nuclear decay to probe a supersymmetric left-right model. Neutrinoless double beta decay would prove neutrinos are their own antiparticles. The left-right model restores parity at high energies through a breaking scale. The authors formulate the decay amplitude with effective field theory, separating long-range and short-range contributions.

Their analysis forces the parity-breaking scale above one teraelectronvolt. Future experiments could push the bound beyond four to five teraelectronvolts. The model's dark matter candidates also matter: the lightest neutralino and sneutrino contribute significantly to the predicted half-life. A tabletop nuclear measurement thus constrains both high-scale symmetry breaking and supersymmetric dark matter. The study shows how a low-energy process can carry indirect hints about very high energy scales. Upcoming decay searches will sharpen these constraints.
arxiv-2510-08390:
Shunhong Deng and co-authors build a unified catalog of Cepheid stars in open clusters in a 2025 arXiv paper. Classical Cepheids are pulsing stars whose brightness cycles reveal their true luminosity. Cepheids inside open clusters are precious, since cluster ages and distances can be pinned down independently. Distant, long-period cases are scarce, and known samples need sharper physical values.

Using Gaia Data Release 3, the team combined position-based and brightness-based membership checks. They identified one hundred ten Cepheids tied to one hundred two clusters. Of these, forty-one Cepheids in thirty-seven clusters counted as confirmed cluster members. Four of the confirmed ones are newly reported in this work. With hand-fitted cluster ages, they refined the period-age relation linking pulse period to stellar age. They also recalibrated the period-Wesenheit relation, a brightness rule used for cosmic distances.
arxiv-2510-08490:
Zijian Wang and co-authors test how noise that couples to charge density harms fractional quantum Hall states, in a 2025 arXiv paper. These states are prized for topological quantum computing, since they store information in global properties that local noise cannot easily erase. The team studies two paradigms: the Laughlin state and the non-abelian Moore-Read state. Density decoherence couples local charge to non-thermal noise around it.

They identify a critical filling factor above which encoded information stays fully recoverable under arbitrarily strong decoherence. Both flagship states sit safely above that threshold in filling. Below it, a Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition pushes states into a critical decohered phase. There, Laughlin ground-state information degrades gradually with noise strength. Moore-Read fusion-space information, by contrast, remains fully recoverable beyond the transition. The contrast strengthens the case for non-abelian states in quantum computing.
arxiv-2510-08590:
Yaxin Shi and a large team recast evolutionary computing as a natural form of generative AI in a 2025 arXiv paper. Today's generative AI learns from fixed training sets, guided by local gradient signals. Its outputs often stay close to what it has seen, more copied than truly new. Evolution-based search takes a unlike path: it explores far beyond the data it starts from.

The authors call this view Natural Generative AI, where search under natural selection does the creating. Classic evolution with parent-like operators mirrors today's generative models, they show. Bold, disruptive operators instead make sharp leaps to out-of-sample outputs in just a few rounds. Mixing traits across domains, and letting odd new solutions survive, keeps the search fresh over time. They argue these two forces, bold change and mild selection, drive real creativity in such systems.
arxiv-2510-08890:
Qin proves sharp, fully explicit versions of a classic family of inequalities for holomorphic functions, in this 2025 arXiv paper in complex analysis. Holomorphic functions are the smooth, rigid functions of complex variables. Carleman-type estimates bound a function's size inside a region by its size on the boundary. Earlier forms often hid their constants, which limits their use in precise work.

Working over bounded domains in several complex variables, Qin first proves a Sobolev-type inequality for the Laplace operator with every constant made explicit. That yields quantitative estimates for holomorphic functions. He then lifts the results to holomorphic sections, functions valued in bundles of vector spaces, under stated limits on the bundle's curvature. Careful tracking of constants runs through the proofs. He also estimates a boundary smoothness quantity from how fast the boundary's outward direction can turn.
arxiv-2510-09390:
Mert İnan and five co-authors study unclear user requests in a 2025 arXiv paper on data visualisation code generation. A user describes a chart in words, and a model writes the code, but vague wording can yield a chart that looks right while missing the user's intent. The authors use this setting to catalogue how ambiguity creeps into human and machine communication.

They build a taxonomy of ambiguity types for the task and propose metrics to measure each type. On chart problems from the DS-1000 dataset, their metrics matched human judgements better than uncertainty-based baselines. The team then tests dialogue strategies drawn from three theories of conversation, including Gricean cooperativity. In a simulated user study, pragmatic multi-turn dialogue reduced ambiguity and improved code accuracy, showing the value of letting the model ask before it draws.
arxiv-2510-09690:
Morteza Sargolzaei Javan, the sole author, builds a semantic model for auditing cloud systems in a 2025 arXiv paper. Cloud computing underpins modern digital infrastructure, yet no unified framework ties its architecture to its compliance rules, which hampers interoperability, auditability, and security. The paper answers with a formal, machine-readable model centred on cloud engines.

The model merges the architectural taxonomy of one ISO cloud reference standard with the security and compliance controls of two others, including ISO/IEC TR 3445 from 2022. It decomposes cloud systems into four canonical interfaces, for control, business, audit, and data, and adds a security ontology mapping mechanisms such as authentication and encryption to specific controls. Written in RDF and Turtle notation, the model supports automated compliance checks. Case studies on OpenStack and Amazon Web Services, with validation workflows in SPARQL and SHACL, demonstrate its practical use for vendor-neutral design.
arxiv-2510-09790:
Michael Freenor and Lauren Alvarez find geometry inside language embeddings in a 2025 arXiv paper. Old word embeddings famously allowed analogy sums, like king minus man plus woman giving queen. Modern text embeddings are far richer, and whether they hold a similarly readable geometric structure was unclear.

The authors introduce RISE, short for Rotor-Invariant Shift Estimation, which treats meaning-and-grammar changes as steady rotations in embedding space. A change such as negation becomes a turn of the whole vector, riding on the curved structure of modern embeddings. They test RISE against two baselines on three embedding models, three datasets, and seven languages from five language families. RISE mapped discourse-level changes with clear grammar features across languages and models, and it worked across both without losing performance. The authors present it as first proof that such sentence-level changes act as steady geometric operations, backing the linear representation hypothesis.
arxiv-2510-09990:
Reza, Lifan Wang, and Lei Hu identify Type Ia supernovae from light alone in this 2025 arXiv paper in astronomy. These exploding stars are key tools for big cosmic questions, from the Hubble tension to the nature of dark energy. Modern surveys mostly record brightness over time, not spectra, so clean samples must be picked photometrically.

The authors build an ensemble learning framework, combining several models, boosted by functional principal component analysis. That technique compresses each light curve, the record of brightness over time, into its main patterns of variation. Feeding those patterns to the ensemble sharpens the sorting of true Type Ia events from impostors. A cleaner sample strengthens every cosmic measurement built on it.
arxiv-2510-10190:
Beyraghi and co-authors automate the placement of reconfigurable intelligent surfaces in this 2025 arXiv paper on wireless networks. A reconfigurable intelligent surface is a panel of tunable elements that can steer radio reflections to boost coverage. Deciding where to deploy many of them across a cellular network is a large planning problem.

The authors present a fully data-driven framework for that deployment at scale. It uses measured network data rather than idealized propagation models to judge candidate sites. Automation matters because manual planning cannot search the huge space of placements. Better surface placement can lift signal quality in weak zones without new base stations, a cheaper path to denser coverage.
arxiv-2510-10390:
Muhamed and co-authors present RefusalBench in this 2025 arXiv paper on language model safety. Retrieval-augmented systems answer from supplied documents, and they should refuse when the context is flawed. That selective refusal is critical for safety, yet the authors' large-scale study finds it is a major failure point.

Even frontier models struggle: refusal accuracy drops below half on multi-document tasks, and models show dangerous over-confidence or over-caution. RefusalBench evaluates this skill generatively, testing whether models refuse for the right reasons. A model that answers from bad context spreads errors, while one that refuses too much is useless. The benchmark measures the balance directly.
arxiv-2510-10590:
Jianfeng Hou and four co-authors settle a question about how dense a hypergraph can be while avoiding a given pattern, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Turán density measures the most edges a large hypergraph can have without containing a forbidden configuration. Sidorenko showed in 1989 that every hypergraph with three edges, where each edge has r vertices, has Turán density at most one half. For even r, that bound is achieved.

The authors prove that for odd r, the bound of one half is never attained. This answers a question posed by Keevash and reveals a basic difference between hypergraphs of odd and even uniformity. Their result also implies that expanded triangles form the unique class of three edge hypergraphs whose Turán density reaches one half. Such parity effects are rare in extremal combinatorics, so a clean odd versus even split stands out.
arxiv-2510-10690:
Abdurakhmon Sadiev, Peter Richtárik, and Ilyas Fatkhullin study optimization when the noise has heavy tails, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Heavy tailed noise, where extreme values appear often, pervades modern machine learning through messy data and outliers. Second order methods, which use curvature information, converge fast under tame noise but can be brittle here. The team takes a first step toward a theory of such methods in this regime.

They assume the random gradients and Hessians have only bounded moments of low order. First, they establish tight lower bounds on the sample complexity of any second order method, the number of samples any algorithm must use. They then design a variant of normalized stochastic gradient descent that reaches those bounds. A further algorithm clips both gradients and Hessians to tame large deviations, with high probability guarantees that nearly match the fundamental limits.
arxiv-2510-10890:
Yu Chao and nine co-authors present a modular agent system that writes in depth research surveys interactively, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their system, LLM×MapReduce-V3, builds on an earlier version. Each functional component, such as initializing the survey skeleton, building digests of sources, and refining the skeleton, runs as an independent server under the Model Context Protocol. These atomic servers can be aggregated into higher level servers, forming a hierarchy.

A high level planner agent orchestrates the work. It picks modules based on their tool descriptions and the execution history. Because the pieces are modular, users can intervene mid process, steering the research perspectives through multi turn interaction. The system first nails down a comprehensive skeleton, then develops it into a full survey. In human evaluations, the system surpassed representative baselines in both content depth and length.
arxiv-2510-11190:
A multimodal model answering factual questions should stay literal, but the same model writing stories should make loose, creative associations. Shengming Yuan and co-authors tackle that tension in this 2025 arXiv paper on multimodal large language models. Existing methods cannot adjust how strongly a model associates, so the authors first probe where associative behavior lives inside the model.

They find that the middle layers shape the model's associative tendencies, and that editing representations in those layers regulates the strength of association. Their framework FlexAC, which needs no training, builds steering vectors from hallucination-guided representations and calibrates their strength for each task. It also derives task-specific vectors from a few target-domain examples. FlexAC improved creativity up to 5.8 times on the Creation-MMBench benchmark while cutting the hallucination rate by 29 percent on CHAIR, beating existing baselines at both ends of the trade-off.
arxiv-2510-11390:
Doctors may soon rely on language models, yet nobody knows where inside these networks the medical knowledge actually sits. Razvan Marinescu, Victoria-Elisabeth Gruber, and Diego Fajardo map that internal geography in this 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. They apply four interpretability techniques to five large language models: projections of intermediate activations, gradient-based saliency, layer removal, and activation patching.

The resulting knowledge maps show where information about patient age, symptoms, diseases, and drugs is stored and processed. In Llama3.3-70B, most medical knowledge is processed in the first half of the layers. The team also found that age is often encoded nonlinearly and sometimes discontinuously. Disease progression is represented in a non-monotonic, circular way at certain layers. Drugs cluster by medical specialty rather than by mechanism of action. In Gemma3-27B and MedGemma-27B, activations collapse at intermediate layers but recover by the end.
arxiv-2510-11590:
Predict-then-optimize pipelines fail: a forecast can be accurate on average yet lead to bad decisions, because the loss never knew what the decision cost. Zihao Zhao, Christopher Yeh, Lingkai Kong, and Kai Wang bring diffusion models into decision-focused learning in this 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. Instead of a single point prediction of uncertain parameters, their model learns the whole distribution, and decisions are optimized against samples drawn from it.

Their first formulation trains the diffusion model end to end through the optimization using the reparameterization trick, which is heavy because gradients flow through sampling. They therefore derive a lightweight score function estimator that needs only a few forward diffusion passes and no backpropagation through sampling. They justify it by showing the full gradient can be approximated in weighted score form. In experiments it consistently beat strong baselines on decision quality.
arxiv-2510-11690:
Boyang Zheng, Nanye Ma, Shengbang Tong, and Saining Xie rethink a core part of image-generating AI. Their 2025 arXiv paper concerns diffusion transformers, models that build images by gradually removing noise. These models usually work in a compressed space made by an old-style autoencoder. The authors argue that this encoder limits quality. Its space is small, and it learns only to rebuild pixels.

They replace it with encoders borrowed from strong vision models such as DINO, SigLIP, and MAE, paired with freshly trained decoders. They call the result a representation autoencoder. Because the new spaces are much larger, the team first studies why diffusion struggles there. They then offer fixes grounded in theory. Their model converged faster than the standard design and needed no extra alignment losses. On ImageNet it reached image-quality scores that rival the best published diffusion results, at two different image sizes.
arxiv-2510-12490:
Reis and colleagues run hospital intake interviews with a language model steered by formal medical algorithms, in a 2025 arXiv paper published in Biomedical Informatics. Emergency departments face high patient volumes. Rushed history taking produces incomplete or clashing data that harms diagnosis. Their system aims to make interviews faster, adaptable, and complete.

The dialogue follows a directed acyclic graph of medical questions. A pipeline converts medical rules and guidelines into a question corpus. Layered clustering generates good opening questions with no prior patient information. An expand and prune step branches or backtracks as answers arrive, and ending logic stops the interview once enough information is gathered. The system then writes a structured, doctor friendly report. Five doctors evaluated both applications with standard workload and usability instruments. Both scored low workload and high usability and satisfaction. Latency and the small, non diverse sample limit the conclusions.
arxiv-2510-12690:
Crosta and a large team create quantum light sources inside silicon by gently bombarding it with light ions, in a 2025 arXiv physics paper. Atomic scale defects in silicon can emit single photons and fit with existing photonic tech. But controlled creation of near infrared color centres for long distance quantum links remains challenging. The team used hydrogen and helium ions to generate emitters in a crystalline silicon matrix.

Temperature dependent readings show optically active defects whose glow matches the primary telecom window, where optical fibers lose least signal. Time resolved readings reveal long lived excited states lasting microseconds. They confirm the emitters are interstitial oxygen carbon complexes known as C-centers. They also show controlled irradiation methods that create C-centers in germanium on silicon heterostructures, an advanced platform for built in quantum photonics. The work maps practical routes toward silicon quantum light sources that can be built.
arxiv-2510-13190:
Ren, Dras, and Naseem add a safety front-end to vision-language models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Large vision-language models reason across images and text, but that breadth expands the attack surface: adversaries hide harmful goals inside benign-looking prompts or pictures. Binary moderators that simply allow or block are too blunt for the range of attacks.

Their framework, SHIELD, is a lightweight preprocessing layer that works with any model without retraining. A fine-grained safety classifier first categorizes the input, then category-specific guidance composes a tailored safety prompt, and an explicit action follows: block, reframe, or forward. Across five benchmarks and five representative models, SHIELD consistently lowered jailbreak success and instruction non-following rates while preserving normal utility. The authors emphasize negligible overhead and easy extension to new attack types, calling it a practical safety patch for both weakly and strongly aligned models.
arxiv-2510-13990:
G. Pagnini and co-authors hunt for the scattered remains of the dwarf galaxy that once hosted Omega Centauri, the Milky Way's most massive globular cluster, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Omega Centauri is widely believed to be the stripped core of an accreted galaxy, and a family of clusters dubbed Nephele may share that origin. Finding their debris would reveal how the Milky Way assembled.

Using chemical abundance data from the APOGEE survey, the team applied a statistical clustering method in an eight-dimensional abundance space to find field stars matching Omega Centauri's chemistry. They found 470 such stars, including 58 rich in aluminum, a marker of stars born inside clusters. A second test on orbital motion found six stars matching the predicted Omega Centauri stream, plus stars tied to streams of five other Nephele clusters. The combined evidence supports a common, now-disrupted progenitor.
arxiv-2510-14190:
Ruchi Sandilya and co-authors introduce ConDA, a method that reorganizes the hidden space of diffusion models so content becomes interpretable and controllable, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Diffusion models generate images well, but their latent spaces are large and messy, so users cannot steer outputs along factors such as time or stimulation levels.

ConDA applies contrastive learning, training that pulls related examples together and pushes unrelated ones apart, to diffusion latents using extra signals like facial action units or stimulation levels. The learned low-dimensional embedding aligns its directions with the factors driving the system. Simple trajectories through it support smooth blending and counterfactual editing. Images still render in the original diffusion space, through a decoder that keeps neighborhoods intact. Across fluid dynamics, neural calcium imaging, medical stimulation, facial expressions, and motor cortex activity, ConDA produced clearer structure that is easier to steer than traversals and baselines.
arxiv-2510-14690:
Fang, in a 2025 arXiv paper, works on complex Hessian equations, a family of nonlinear equations for functions on Hermitian manifolds. Such equations generalize the famous Monge-Ampère equation and appear in geometry when one prescribes curvature-like quantities. The hard part is controlling solutions: before proving a solution is continuous, one must bound it, and the bound must survive rough right-hand sides.

Fang derives an a priori estimate that caps the size of any bounded solution. The estimate holds when the right-hand side lies in a certain Orlicz space, a flexible scale of function spaces, and its weight satisfies a condition named after Kołodziej. Building on that cap, the paper then proves existence: under the stated assumptions, the complex Hessian equation admits continuous solutions on a compact Hermitian manifold. The result extends the known theory for these equations to weaker, more realistic hypotheses on the data.
arxiv-2510-15790:
Chirag Pabbaraju, Gregory Valiant, and Rishi Verma present a proof in a 2025 paper. It is a simpler proof of a classic statistics result. The problem is deciding a coin's bias. The goal is to use as few tosses as possible. The coin is known to lean one of two symmetric ways. Wald's test is known to be optimal here. It stops once the evidence crosses a threshold. Standard proofs are analytical and non-constructive.

The authors recast the problem geometrically. It becomes a biased random walk. The walk runs on a lattice of heads and tails counts. Their argument is discrete and self-contained. It shows directly why no stopping rule can beat the test. This covers both expected sample size and error probability.
arxiv-2510-16190:
Zhicheng Chen, Elizabeth Denne, Kyle Patterson, and Timi Patterson study knots tied from a flat strip of ribbon. Fold a strip into a knot, join the ends, and press it flat: that is a folded ribbon knot. The key measure is ribbonlength, the knot's length divided by the strip's width, and the hunt is for its lowest possible value.

With new ways to fold, the team lowers the best known upper bounds for whole families of knots and links. Their twist knots reach a ribbonlength of the twist count plus six. For the figure-eight knot that gives eight, which they conjecture is the true floor. The gains give the best bounds yet for small knots in these families and fresh targets for proof.
arxiv-2510-16290:
Yue Zheng and three co-authors build Cerberus, a fast guard for spotting odd events in video feeds. Vision-language models can spot trouble in new settings with no retraining. But they run too slowly and ground their gaze poorly for live use. Cerberus splits the job: a light filter screens frames, and the big model reasons only over flagged ones.

Two ideas drive the gains. Motion mask prompting steers the big model's eye toward the parts of the scene that move. Rule-based checks flag acts that break learned norms of normal behavior, instead of listing every odd thing that could occur. Across four data sets, Cerberus runs at about fifty-eight frames per second. That is more than one hundred fifty times faster than plain model use. Its accuracy stays near the best reported, making live video watch with smart models practical.
arxiv-2510-16490:
Reza Naserasr and Huan Zhou colour signed graphs in their 2025 maths paper. A signed graph marks each link as plus or minus. A circular colouring maps each point to a spot on a ring. Plus links and minus links each set a least gap rule. The least ring size that works is the circular chromatic number.

Brooks' classic theorem caps colour needs by the top degree of a graph. Past work settled the cap for even top degree in signed graphs. The odd case is harder, and this pair take the first step. For top degree three, they cap the ring size at ten-thirds. One signed form of the famed Petersen graph shows the cap is tight. The result guides more work on the odd case.
arxiv-2510-16590:
Alan Kai Hassen leads five co-authors in a 2025 study on language models that reason about molecules. Drug work lacks cheap labelled data, which caps trained tools. Their frame needs no task training at all. It anchors the model's step-by-step thoughts to the molecule's own atoms. Each atom gets a unique tag the model can cite.

Step one asks the model to tag key parts and their change class, cold. Step two, if used, shows a few class cases for the final call. The test task is retrosynthesis, the plan of how to build a target molecule. Hit rates were high for sites, classes, and final reactants. The frame gives a broad plan for data-poor chemistry work.
arxiv-2510-16690:
Anna L. F. Lucchi and three co-authors build a single framework that ties together divergences, generalized free energies, generalized Fokker-Planck equations, and the H-theorem. These tools describe how systems settle over time, including systems that defy standard statistical mechanics. The Fokker-Planck equation tracks how a probability distribution drifts and spreads.

Starting from a free energy that includes potential energy gives a direct link between that energy and the final steady state. Starting from a divergence as the free energy removes the potential from the equation, so an extra relation must be added to restore it. The authors apply both routes across several cases, showing old and new results from one viewpoint.
arxiv-2510-16890:
Jiří Klepl, Martin Kruliš, and Matyáš Brabec write about supercomputer programming in a 2025 paper. Programs on many machines pass messages using a standard called MPI. That standard still uses an old C interface from decades ago. It lacks the type checks and flexible tools of modern C++.

The team built a new layer on top of a C++ library called Noarr. Their design treats data layout as a separate, changeable choice. Programmers can then swap layouts without rewriting message code. A shared matrix multiplication program tests the idea in practice. It runs about as fast as the best existing C++ bindings. At the same time, the code stays easier to reshape for new machines.
arxiv-2510-17290:
Qihao Peng and six co-authors put atomic quantum receivers on satellites for direct ground links in this 2025 article. Ground to satellite links face long paths, weak signals, and tight gear limits. Crowded airwaves add noise that old radio fronts handle poorly. The authors swap the front for atoms that turn radio into light.

The receiver uses a clear-atom effect to read fields with sharp tone choice. Its cell is tiny, at the scale of a few millimeters. A hybrid atom and circuit design lifts rate, reach, and sense truth. It beats old radio fronts on those counts in the authors' model. The piece maps fit steps and open tasks for flight use.
arxiv-2510-17590:
Mir Nafis Sharear Shopnil, with Sharad Duwal and two co-authors, built a fake news checker in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their system, called MERIT, checks posts that mix images and text. It splits the job among four parts that each handle one kind of check. One part inspects the image for tampering. Another checks whether image and text match.

A third part searches the web to test the claim itself. A fourth part weighs all the evidence and gives a final call. On a standard test set, MERIT scored about 82 percent on a balanced accuracy measure. That beat all prior no training baselines. Removing any part hurt mainly its own check type. The system also gives reasons linked to sources for human review.
arxiv-2510-17990:
Antoni López-Martínez, writing alone, studies fuzzy dynamical systems under a distance called the endograph metric. A system here is a set with a map that moves its points, lifted to fuzzy sets by a standard extension. The question is which lively behaviors survive that lift and how the metric choice changes the answer.

Transitivity, recurrence, chaos, and the specification property are all examined. Under this metric the lifted system behaves much like it does under three better-known metrics. The results settle open questions in the area and add new ones on point-level transitivity. Specialists in topological dynamics get a cleaner map of when the metrics agree.
arxiv-2510-18090:
Lucas Teinturier, Benjamin Charnay, Aymeric Spiga, and Bruno Bezard use a full climate model to show that clouds drive the color changes of brown dwarfs. These heavy objects sit between stars and planets, and their shift in color across the L/T boundary has long lacked a settled cause. Air flow and clouds were both candidates.

With cloud forming, moving, and radiating inside the model, the simulated dwarfs varied in light, place, and time much like real ones. Cloud heating stirred convection, and waves ruled low latitudes while eddies ruled higher ones. The work makes clouds the lead suspect in dwarf weather.
arxiv-2510-18190:
Zhanhong He, Hanyu Meng, David Huang, and Roberto Togneri read piano dynamics and meter from audio in one compact network. Loudness shaping and beat structure together form the metrical skeleton of a score, yet they are usually estimated apart. The shared network predicts dynamic levels, change points, beats, and downbeats from one latent core.

A loudness feature matched to human hearing shrinks the model hugely against the usual spectral input, allowing minute-long windows. On a public mazurka data set the model set new best scores on all tasks. Music analysis readers get a small, strong tool for expressive performance study.
arxiv-2510-18390:
Ryuichiro Kitano and his four co-authors examine what a proposed collider with two beams of positively charged muons could reveal about heavy neutral leptons. Such particles may help explain why neutrinos have mass. The machine, nicknamed muTRISTAN, would collide same-sign muons at energies around ten trillion electron volts, creating chances to see rare processes that present machines cannot reach.

Two signals anchor the study. One changes lepton flavor, producing a tau particle alongside other products, and the other breaks lepton number, a pattern that would strongly point to neutrinos being their own antiparticles. The authors compute how sensitively the collider could detect the mixing of heavy neutral leptons with muon and tau neutrinos. Over a wide mass range, the reach passes current limits from precision measurements, improving by about tenfold for the heaviest cases studied.
arxiv-2510-18790:
Kevin Michalewicz and his six co-authors introduce a protein design method that loosens a stubborn trade-off. Designers often need many varied versions of a functional protein motif, the small structural piece that does the biological work. The standard diffusion-based approach varies a motif only slightly before its geometry breaks and the function is lost.

Their framework, PGEL, learns a rich embedding of the target motif, capturing both its sequence and its structure inside the representation space of a frozen diffusion model. Controlled nudges in that embedding space then generate diversity while design metrics stay satisfied, in effect relaxing raw geometric constraints in favor of learned ones. On three test cases, a single protein, a protein-protein interface, and a cancer-related transcription factor complex, PGEL produced structures more diverse than partial diffusion while scoring better on designability and self-consistency.
arxiv-2510-19290:
Sehyun Park and four co-authors introduce Gaussian distillation, a way to compress a deep ensemble's uncertainty into a single student model. Ensembles give the most reliable uncertainty estimates, but they are heavy in compute and memory, which blocks use on small devices and in fast applications.

Ordinary distillation shrinks models yet tends to flatten the very variation that carries uncertainty. Gaussian distillation instead fits a distribution over the ensemble using a deep latent factor model, a special Gaussian process, then teaches the student that distribution. Preserving honest uncertainty in a compact model matters wherever a wrong, confident answer is costly.
arxiv-2510-19390:
Max O Al-Hasso and Marko von der Leyen test probabilistic computing. They aim it at the closest vector problem. That problem asks for the lattice point nearest a target. It underpins lattice cryptography. A famous factoring method also reduces to it. Breaking RSA-style systems is at stake.

Recent studies tried quantum methods for a heuristic refinement step. This work tests probabilistic hardware instead. Such hardware runs randomized optimization in a natural way. The authors weigh how well these machines handle the refinement. An emerging classical accelerator is set against quantum proposals, at a key bottleneck for cryptography.
arxiv-2510-19490:
Jasem Hamoud and three co-authors study how irregular two families of trees can be, using measures from chemical graph theory. Trees here are branching networks, and caterpillar trees, where vertices hang off a central spine, often model molecular chains. The team works with trees whose degree sequences, the lists of connections per vertex, are fixed in advance.

They derive a closed-form expression for the Albertson index of caterpillar trees and set extreme-value bounds for both the Albertson and sigma indices across the tree families considered. Together the results give one framework for comparing the linear and quadratic irregularity measures. The findings add structural insight for chemical graph theory and extremal graph analysis.
arxiv-2510-19590:
Elias Stenhede, Agnar Martin Bjørnstad, and Arian Ranjbar built an open-source system that converts paper electrocardiograms into digital signals. Millions of clinical ECGs survive only as paper scans or photographs, locked away from modern automated analysis. Their fully automated framework handles the artifacts typical of scanned tracings.

Validation covered more than thirty-seven thousand ECG images, including a hospital collection from Akershus University Hospital in Norway, plus a large public dataset with wrinkled, stained, and distorted pages. The method reached a strong signal-to-noise ratio on scanned papers and beat the previous state of the art in every subcategory of the public set. The team hopes the tool opens old ECG archives to research and AI-based diagnostics.
arxiv-2510-19790:
Philippa Helen McGuinness and fourteen co-authors pin down what drives the charge-density-wave order in the kagome metal CsV3Sb5, a material where that order coexists with superconductivity. The kagome family AV3Sb5 has raised basic questions about how its intertwined phases form. The team combined high-resolution inelastic X-ray scattering with first-principles calculations.

Guided by the scattering patterns, they found a soft phonon mode running between two high-symmetry directions, strongest at the L point, exactly where elastic scattering grows fastest on cooling. Calculations including lattice anharmonicity and electron-phonon coupling reproduce the observations, establishing a softened-phonon instability as the mechanism behind the charge order. The result highlights lattice dynamics as central to kagome metals.
arxiv-2510-19890:
Jan Zelinka, Oliver Kost, and Marek Hrúz train deep sequence models to detect spoofing attacks on satellite navigation signals. Spoofed GNSS signals can mislead receivers about their position, so detection matters for safety-critical users. Because real attack data are scarce, the authors first built a generator that simulates attacks and scatters the scenarios randomly around the world.

LSTM networks and transformer-inspired architectures were trained on the generated data for online detection. Both families learned to separate spoofed from genuine signals with high accuracy. The best results came from transformer-style models that fuse their inputs early, reaching an error rate well under one percent. The study suggests learned detectors can guard navigation receivers in real time.
arxiv-2510-19990:
Zachary Horvitz and six co-authors explore reasoning in masked diffusion language models, which fill in blanked parts of a sequence rather than predicting one token at a time. They introduce reasoning-as-infilling, a prompting method that marks out separate regions for reasoning and for the final answer before generation begins. That layout makes answer probabilities directly readable during generation.

Because the answer region is explicit, the model can stop early when it is already certain. The same setup can also create reasoning traces after an answer is known, a task that is hard for standard models. Fine-tuning on those traces improves GSM8K accuracy and gives step scores that track correctness well.
arxiv-2510-20090:
R. A. Tonacatl-Monez, R. Heid, and O. De la Peña-Seaman use first-principles calculations to study how magnetism and lattice vibrations interact in cubic FeGe under pressure. They use a spin-scaling approach that adjusts the magnetic moment and the energetics of the ferromagnetic phase with one parameter. That adjustment brings the predicted critical pressure in line with the measured value.

Under the adjusted scheme, a strong softening and broadening of the lowest acoustic phonon branch near one point in momentum space becomes milder. As pressure rises toward the critical value, the anomaly fades, tracking the shrinking magnetic moment. Comparisons show the pattern follows the electron-phonon coupling itself, unlike related compounds where nesting dominates.
arxiv-2510-20590:
Simon Schindler and three co-authors ask how machine learning ops, or MLOps, can fit the work frames of plant tech, called OT. MLOps use grows in plants, but its match with OT frames brings hard blocks. The team rates two set frames for the fit: RAMI 4.0, the Industry 4.0 arch model, and ISA-95, a plant norm from the ISA.

A full map ties MLOps life steps to RAMI 4.0, shown by a real plant case. Stock MLOps ways can not be moved to OT as they stand, the marks show. But a shaped fit through set frames gives a clear path. The team gives that path as a guide for plant teams who add learning to live lines.
arxiv-2510-20690:
Kushal Chakrabarti and Nirmal Balachundhar argue that false outputs from language models can be cut by keeping parallel inner representations less alike, a trait they call neural diversity. Larger models and more data alone have not removed made up answers, so a different lever is needed.

The pair give formal bounds on false output chances for grouped models and frame the issue as a reliability problem tied to spread, not just average accuracy. Their ND-LoRA method trains side by side adapters with a decorrelation push and cuts false outputs by up to about a quarter while holding general accuracy. Tests show the two parts help each other, and the best diversity level varies by task.
arxiv-2510-20790:
Louise Wolswijk leads fourteen co-authors on a tutorial review of how labs trap, steer, and probe ultracold atoms for quantum science. Cooled near absolute zero, atoms share phase and act as one quantum system, enabling precise measurement, simulation, and early information tasks.

The review walks newcomers through laser cooling, magnetic and optical traps, optical lattices, and fine tweezers for single atoms. It then covers control of inner and outer atomic states, atom interferometry, and tuning of interactions between atoms. Detection methods close the tour, from absorption and glow imaging to state selective readout, correlation checks, non destructive measures, and high resolution imaging, giving a full map of the standard toolkit.
arxiv-2510-20890:
Sheng-Jie Huang leads three co-authors on hybrid lattice surgery, a route to non Clifford gates in surface codes using non Abelian code patches. Non Clifford gates are essential for universal quantum computing, but in many codes they devour space and time resources.

Standard lattice surgery merges and splits code patches, and the hybrid version lets those moves run across different topological code types. The authors build non Clifford operations in the standard surface code on this hybrid machinery. Simpler, cheaper logical gates would ease the path to large fault tolerant machines, where gate overhead dominates cost.
arxiv-2510-20990:
Ian Anderson leads five co-authors on phononic frequency combs made in lithium niobate acoustic resonators, bringing comb behavior from optics into compact mechanical devices. Optical combs power precision timing and ranging, while microwave combs usually rely on electronic nonlinearity.

Acoustic wavelengths are far shorter, so a mechanical comb could shrink the hardware greatly. Using thermal nonlinearity in high quality overmoded thin film resonators, the team generates an evenly spaced microwave spectrum. The demonstration opens a route to chip scale stable signal sources built from sound rather than light or circuits.
arxiv-2510-21190:
Mingrui Liu leads three co-authors on TrojFill, a black box jailbreak framework that bypasses language model safety filters through template filling and unsafety reasoning. Safety alignment is the main control against harmful outputs, yet it remains brittle under crafted prompts.

White box attacks need gradients that commercial services hide, while many black box attacks produce unnatural or non transferable prompts. TrojFill targets a fundamental weakness in how filters judge filled templates, aiming at prompts that read naturally and transfer across models. Published attack research of this kind pressures providers to harden alignment before hostile users find the same routes.
arxiv-2510-21290:
Juan Esteban Suarez Cardona, Holger Boche, and Gitta Kutyniok ask a basic question about partial differential equations, the equations behind much of physics. Which of them can a digital computer actually solve, and at what cost in effort? The answer separates equations with workable numerical methods from those hiding impossible demands.

Their framework recasts each equation as a least-squares problem and follows the downhill flow of that problem step by step toward an answer. Traits of the equation, such as how strongly it pushes solutions back toward balance, then translate into limits on computing effort. They give conditions where good approximations run in reasonable time, and others where even reasonable inputs force effort that grows far faster, offering guidance for building sound numerical methods.
arxiv-2510-21390:
Laura Selicato, Flavia Esposito, and Andersen Ang present Binno, a method for two-level optimization problems. In these problems, neither level is smooth or convex. Such problems appear in machine learning and engineering. Their jagged shape breaks many standard solvers. It also leaves the theory thin.

Binno updates each level in turn with proximal gradient steps. Those steps handle kinks by mixing a move with a penalty. The method then blends the two results.
