The key notion is optical layer intelligence: doing computing at the scale of a lightpath, where paths crossing the same node can interact. A case study on optical aggregation shows how this differs from today's optical bypass designs, which only route light through. The authors give a mathematical formulation for optimal aggregation enabled networks. On the realistic NSFNET topology, their design beats the bypass model, promising more capacity from less spectrum.
arxiv-2512-15490:
Valentin Haberl, Piotr Szewczak, and Lyubomyr Zdomskyy bound the size of universally meager sets in certain set theory models in a 2025 paper. Universally meager sets of reals are small in a strong sense that survives many mappings. The question is how large such sets can be forced to remain in specific models of set theory.

Working in the Miller model and in a model built by Goldstern, Judah, and Shelah, the authors prove all universally meager sets have size at most the first uncountable cardinal. The same limits follow for Rothberger and Hurewicz spaces with no copy of the Cantor set. In the Miller model, strong measure zero sets obey the same bound.
arxiv-2512-15590:
Cesar Venegas and Helbert Venegas survey the Zariski cancellation problem through locally nilpotent derivations in a 2025 paper. The cancellation problem asks whether adding a trivial factor to an algebra can hide a real difference between two algebras. Derivations that become zero after repeated application give a key invariant for attacking it.

The survey unifies cancellation results across commutative algebras, noncommutative algebras, and skew Ore type extensions. It stresses rigidity and the Makar Limanov invariant, which collect what these derivations see. The method detects cancellation well in rigid settings. Its limits also show clearly, above all in the skew case, where Makar Limanov stability fails.
arxiv-2512-15790:
Akhil Sharma and co authors present XAMT, a framework for covert memory tampering attacks on mixed multi agent systems, in a 2025 paper, dated December 15. Modern agent systems blend reinforcement learning agents, which share an experience replay buffer, with language model agents that draw on a shared knowledge base. That shared memory is a common weak point.

XAMT frames attack design as bilevel optimization: the upper level keeps changes tiny for stealth, while the lower level pushes system behavior toward an attacker chosen target. Tests use SMAC and SafeRAG benchmarks at poison rates at or below 1 percent for the learning agents and 0.1 percent for the retrieval agents. The work defines a threat class meant to guide intrinsic defenses.
arxiv-2512-15890:
Jiyuan Fang, Qicheng Tang, and Xueda Wen uncover universal maximal entanglement swapping in fermionic Gaussian states in a 2025 paper. Entanglement swapping transfers entanglement through a joint measurement, and how much survives non unitary steps is a basic question. Fermionic Gaussian states, common in free fermion physics, are the setting here.

Take two decoupled, half filled copies of a free fermion system and perform projective Bell measurements on half the matching sites. Remarkably, the post measurement state factors into a product of Bell pairs, giving maximal interlayer entanglement regardless of the starting Gaussian state. The authors derive the state exactly for particle number conserving cases, with simulations as checks.
arxiv-2512-15990:
Arpan Akash Ray and Boris Skoric wrote this quantum communications paper, uploaded to arXiv in 2025. Quantum key distribution lets two parties share secret keys whose safety rests on physics, not on hard math problems. The continuous-variable kind uses standard telecom gear, but over long distances the signal is weak and error correction becomes slow and heavy.

The authors propose a random codebook method for fixing errors in these weak signals. It scores blocks by likelihood ratios and rejects bad blocks by a threshold rule, and it can run in parallel for real-time use. Under cautious assumptions about computing power, they predict a key rate of at least 8 percent of the theoretical Devetak-Winter value. That beats existing correction schemes for long links.
arxiv-2512-16090:
Huali Zhang opens a new line of analysis in this 96-page 2025 paper on arXiv. The relativistic Euler equations describe fluids moving near light speed, as in astrophysical jets. The Cauchy problem asks whether starting data evolves into a unique solution, and the hard part is allowing rough, low-regularity starting data.

Zhang rewrites the two-dimensional system using good variables: a rescaled velocity, a logarithmic enthalpy, and a carefully defined vorticity. That turns the equations into a coupled wave-transport system open to modern tools like Strichartz estimates. Well-posedness is proved at lower regularity than before for general pressure laws. In the stiff special case, where the acoustic metric becomes flat, even weaker data works, and small irrotational flows are shown to exist globally. The work adapts famous methods from non-relativistic fluid theory.
arxiv-2512-16190:
Sahil Kalra and Niraj K Shukla revive a classic number tool in their arXiv paper from 2025, accepted by a harmonic analysis journal. Ramanujan sums, introduced by the famous mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan, extract periodic parts from a signal. Filter banks built on them split signals into channels for analysis and recovery.

The authors prove these filter banks can reconstruct signals perfectly and study how robust they are when some channels are erased. Non-uniform versions fix limits of the uniform design. Using the uniform banks, they prove an uncertainty principle for a tight frame built from shifted Ramanujan sums, with recovery conditions stated through Euler's totient function. Exploiting a signal's known periodicity improves recovery algorithms in practice, raising signal-to-noise ratios and sharpening reconstructions after data loss or noise.
arxiv-2512-16690:
Justus Teller and coauthors report how to best make stencil masks for Josephson junctions, devices at the heart of superconducting circuits. Stencil lithography builds the junctions in place, in vacuum, and is now used for junctions with many terminals.

The team made and checked 270 mask designs under a scanning electron microscope. They report yield, the smallest safe sizes, and how results shift as terminal count grows. The verdict is that the method is reliable for multi-terminal junctions, with side sizes down to about 40 nanometers on average. The data give builders concrete design rules for a method with few other guides.
arxiv-2512-16790:
Aaron Imani, Mohammad Moshirpour, and Iftekhar Ahmed probe how large language models use code comments when they do software tasks. Comments do not run, yet models lean on them for completion, translation, and code fixes, and no one knew where that lean lives inside the model.

Using concept activation vectors, the team shows models store comments as distinct inner concepts, split by type such as Javadocs, inline, and multiline notes. Turning those concepts up or down shifted task scores from minus 90 percent to plus 67 percent, by model and task. Across ten tasks, code summarization lit the comment concept most, and completion least, opening a path to tools that steer inner concepts.
arxiv-2512-16890:
Jason Aebischer, Luigi C. Bresciani, and Nudzeim Selimovic complete the one-loop anomalous dimensions for general effective gauge theories, covering the fermionic sector. Combined with their past bosonic results, the work closes the leading renormalization group equations for such theories.

On-shell methods drive the derivation, with renormalization effects kept at order one over the new physics scale squared, for both renormalizable and higher couplings. The template equations include mixing between operators of unlike dimension and hold for any gauge group, with scalar and fermion fields present. Such templates let model builders evolve couplings from high scales to lab scales without redoing loop math per model.
arxiv-2512-17590:
Malak Sadek, Loraine Clarke, Stefania Forlini, and Uta Hinrichs ask what gets lost when a rare book becomes a flat scan on a screen. Library closures during COVID pushed readers online, where digital collections are easy to search yet strangely lifeless: no weight, no paper feel, no browsing by hand. The team invited creative professionals and collection experts to imagine richer ways in.

Their answer is digital bricolage, a design stance borrowed from making do with materials at hand. Interfaces, they argue, should let readers handle digital objects playfully, shuffling, juxtaposing, and poking around, much as hands do in a reading room. Such handling invites the casual, curious wandering that keyword search tends to kill. The paper offers speculations and prompts for designers, not a finished product.
arxiv-2512-17790:
Jasmin Katz, Xiaopan Lian, Alexandru Malekshahian, and Andrey Shapiro work in Ramsey theory, which asks how big a structure must be before a pattern is forced to appear. They color the edges of a large complete graph with labels from a group. They ask when a given graph must show up with edge labels that add to zero.

The team proves the size needed grows only in a straight line with the graph's vertex count, as long as each vertex touches few edges. The bound holds for any finite abelian group whose size divides the graph's edge count. A linear bound is far stronger than the loose bounds known for many such problems.
arxiv-2512-17890:
Callum Deakin and Xi Chen study a new way to shape light signals for very fast fiber optic links. The usual method mixes signal parts with electronic parts that have speed limits. Their method passes light through a chain of phase shifters and spreaders, which in theory wastes no light and dodges those limits.

The pair maps out the trade offs: how many stages are needed, how much spread, and how much power. Fewer than six stages can still reach the clean signal quality that links above 200 gigabaud demand. They also measure how small errors in phase, strength, or spread would hurt the signal, which guides real builds.
arxiv-2512-18090:
Benjamin Xiao and Dong Ye settle a question about packing tight clusters into a network. A clique is a set of points all linked to each other. They ask how large a share of a graph can be covered by cliques that stay separate, for graphs that avoid a certain dense pattern called a K4 minor.

Their proof shows the best share is exactly one half, which closes two conjectures posed by Biró, Collado, and Zamora. The same one half value holds for graphs where each point has at most three links. Clean cut values like this give network designers a firm rule for dividing such graphs into dense blocks.
arxiv-2512-18390:
Vassilis Digalakis and three co-authors ask a management question with a statistical core. When a company gains a new data source, when should it replace its working prediction model? The replacement, a challenger, would be trained on the richer data. The catch is that the challenger can only train on new data, which piles up slowly, while retraining again and again costs money.

Their framework links learning curves, which chart how a model improves with more data, to the economics of switching. They show the best moment to test the challenger grows as a power of the total time horizon. They also give an evaluation algorithm that needs no knowledge of the curve in advance. A real credit-scoring study shows the method performs near the level of an all-knowing oracle. It beats both greedy checks, which quit too early, and one-shot tests.
arxiv-2512-18590: Tenglin Hu of the Chinese Academy of Sciences computes the mapping class group for a family of seven dimensional manifolds. Each space is the total space of the sphere bundle of a three dimensional real vector bundle over the complex projective plane, with first Pontryagin number 8n + 5. The family includes the Milnor hypersurface and its generalizations M_k for odd k. Knowing this group catalogs the essentially distinct symmetries of these spaces, a basic step in understanding their geometry.
arxiv-2512-18690:
Lijuan Liu and Hanzhao Yang report a possible warning sign before big solar flares in this 2025 study. Magnetic field changes at the Sun's surface during eruptions are well known, but changes just before them are rarely documented. Using fast vector field data from the HMI instrument on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, they analyze an X1.8 class flare and find the horizontal field weakening beforehand along the flaring polarity inversion line.

Over the 30 minutes before the flare, the horizontal field dropped by about 100 gauss in a coherent patch, with no matching flux emergence or cancellation. Images show the erupting filament rising slowly at the same time and place. The authors propose that the rising filament stretched the loops above it upright, cutting the horizontal field at their feet, making the dip a genuine eruption precursor.
arxiv-2512-19090:
Fan Yu, Tao Wang, You Wu, and Lin Zhu present JoyVoice, a model that synthesizes long conversations with up to eight speakers. Most speech systems handle one voice reading short lines, or two voices taking turns. JoyVoice aims for flowing group talk that sounds human.

One end-to-end design joins a transformer with a diffusion stage, instead of chaining separate parts. A custom tokenizer packs both meaning and sound into a low-rate code, and training with perturbed text data hardens the front end. Tests report top results for speech in Chinese, English, Japanese, and Korean, plus strong zero-shot voice cloning from a sample.
arxiv-2512-19190:
Marios Thoma, Zenonas Theodosiou, Harris Partaourides, and Vassilis Vassiliades built PEDESTRIAN, a first-person video dataset for spotting obstacles on sidewalks. Blocked pavements endanger walkers, and phone-style egocentric vision could warn of hazards in real time. Good detectors need balanced training data, which did not exist for this task.

The set holds three hundred forty videos shot on phone cameras from a walker's viewpoint. Twenty-nine common obstacle kinds appear, from parked scooters to broken paving. The authors also train several modern deep learning detectors on the data as a starting benchmark. The dataset is meant to seed safer navigation aids.
arxiv-2512-19590:
Bernd Schroers, Martin Speight, and Thomas Winyard map the full phase diagram of planar chiral magnets. In these materials, ordinary exchange and a magnetic field push toward uniform order, while the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction twists it, and the contest can even favor negative-energy ground states. Parameter choices change the winner in tangled ways.

The study allows arbitrary spiralization tensors for the twisting term and any field direction. Ground states are sorted by symmetry into ferromagnetic sheets, one-directional spirals, and skyrmion lattices. Analytic and numerical methods together give, the authors state, a complete description of the phase diagram for this whole class of theories.
arxiv-2512-19690:
Chun Wang Chau, Robert-Jan Slager, and Wojciech Jankowski show that a magnet can expose hidden order in a material. Some materials carry multiband topology, a global twist in their electron waves. Normal band tests miss that twist. Orbital magnetization is the magnetic response from electrons moving in orbits. The authors say it holds clear traces of the twist. The trick is to split that response into an energy part and a quantum-shape part.

The split works when the energy spectrum of the material is known. The team shows it on models with multiband Euler topology. They find the same marks in models of strontium ruthenate. That is a much-studied material with odd traits. New lab tests that vary doping could check the claim in practice. The scheme gives multiorbital materials a fresh probe for topology.
arxiv-2512-19890:
Xuanhe Li and Tal Cohen unify the physics of how plastics cure. Curing turns a monomer mix into a cross-linked network. The reaction shifts temperature, density, and stiffness at once. That can bake in stress and warping. Plants cure parts two ways. One is bulk curing, fed by outside energy. The other is frontal curing. There, a self-feeding heat wave sweeps through the part. All the coupling is packed into a narrow zone.

Their framework covers both modes in one set of laws. The reaction rate depends on stress. The stress-free shape evolves as curing goes on. A narrow-zone shortcut in one dimension gives clear calls. It predicts front speed, stress growth, and stability. A stability rule extends the classic Zeldovich number. It adds heat loss and load. The end result is a phase diagram with stable, unstable, and quenched spread.
arxiv-2512-20490: Callum Deakin, Zichuan Zhou, Ronit Sohanpal, and Zhixin Liu show a light-based trick to catch very high-frequency radio signals. Their dual optical comb system down-converts any narrow signals from the D-band, the short-wave range between 110 and 170 gigahertz, straight to baseband. The shift needs no filter and no tuning of optical or radio parts, and it works with low-frequency radio components, which keeps the receiver fairly simple.
arxiv-2512-20790:
Thales Azevedo, Humberto Gomez, and Renann Lipinski Jusinskas study a newly found pattern in scattering amplitudes, the numbers that predict how particles and strings collide. At tree level, amplitudes can split into two parts in a clean way. Until now that splitting was written using currents with one leg off shell, meaning slightly outside physical conditions.

The authors show how to rewrite the split amplitudes using only on-shell, fully physical quantities in several theories. They also find the same two-split behavior in gauge and gravity theories with higher-dimensional operators. That wider reach supports the idea that the pattern is universal. Along the way, they extend transmuting operators to higher-derivative theories.
arxiv-2512-21190:
Qaasim Shafi and Calla Tschanz construct the first good type III degenerations of hyperkahler varieties beyond dimension two. Hyperkahler spaces are prized geometric objects. A degeneration is how one can collapse into a singular special fibre. Type III is the most complex collapse pattern, long missing explicit models in higher dimensions. Their cases arise as moduli spaces parametrizing finite clusters of points. The points sit on an expanding family built from a degenerating K3 surface, using logarithmic Hilbert scheme tools.

Projectivity of the expanded degenerations is proved, which keeps the moduli spaces inside well-behaved algebraic geometry. For two concrete degenerations of hyperkahler fourfolds, the authors compute the dual complex. That is a combinatorial shadow that tracks how the special fibre's pieces intersect. They match its simplices to the fibre's geometric strata. Degeneration theory gains reference cases where abstract predictions can finally be checked.
arxiv-2512-21290:
Ang Li, Christoph Paus, and four co-authors blueprint the flagship Higgs measurement of the proposed FCC-ee collider. The goal is the rate for producing a Z boson together with a Higgs, measured without assuming how the Higgs decays. The recoil-mass trick delivers that independence: reconstruct the Z from its muon, electron, or hadronic decay products, and whatever recoils against it must be the Higgs, seen or unseen. Runs at 240 and 365 GeV are analyzed under one workflow.

The projected precision is striking. Combining leptonic and hadronic channels gives a relative uncertainty near three tenths of one percent at 240 GeV. At 365 GeV it is about half a percent. That is the most precise expectation among future lepton colliders. Tests verify the promised model independence at that level. Since the ZH rate directly measures the Higgs coupling to the Z, collider planners gain a benchmark for the Higgs program.
arxiv-2512-21590:
Yun Gao revisits Macaulay's theorem, a classic result constraining Hilbert functions in commutative algebra. The Hilbert function counts the dimension of each graded piece of a polynomial ring or its quotient by an ideal. Macaulay's theorem limits how fast that count can grow from one degree to the next.

Textbooks usually quote the theorem for the quotient ring, in a form whose combinatorics depends on the degree. Gao points out that Macaulay's original statement concerns the ideal itself, and its combinatorics involves the number of variables instead, not the degree. He gives an elementary proof that the two versions are equivalent. The original version fits problems about sums of squared polynomial norms better. Motivated by Hilbert's seventeenth problem and mappings between unit balls, he uses the theorem to derive new inequalities. They link the number of variables, an exponent, and the signature and rank of certain Hermitian polynomials.
arxiv-2512-22090:
Quentin Michaud and four co-authors survey Trusted Execution Environments, the protected areas inside processors that shield code and data from the operating system and other untrusted software. Because each vendor's design differs, they examine the abstraction layers meant to hide those differences. Their goal is to judge how far such layers can carry confidential computing toward everyday use.

The survey first sorts the main environment designs by their key choices, then reviews the abstraction layer built around each choice and how it works. The authors find clear room to improve current layers. They single out WebAssembly as the approach supporting the widest set of features, and they close by sketching how future layers may evolve.
arxiv-2512-22490:
Yao-Bei Liu and Stefano Moretti calculate how well future electron-positron colliders could find vector-like leptons, proposed heavier cousins of the electron. They study pair production of first-generation, weak-isosinglet versions of these particles, folding in beam polarization options and full detector sims. The particles would decay into electrons or neutrinos plus Z or W bosons, giving two multilepton patterns to hunt.

With optimized cuts separating signal from background, the authors map what could be excluded or found across the mass spectrum. At the studied energies and luminosities, the mass range within reach stretches to roughly 490, 740, and 1440 GeV for the three collider settings. Those reaches improve by far on current hadron collider limits for these particles.
arxiv-2512-22590:
A team of eleven authors led by A. Paz Jalca measures how the electrical resistance of iron-cobalt alloy films responds to magnetic fields, and how that response depends on crystal direction and temperature. Their epitaxial Fe65Co35 films were grown in the [001] orientation. The anisotropic magnetoresistance ratio differed clearly by current direction, reaching higher values along the magnetic hard axis than along the easy axis at room temperature.

Cooling the films to eighty kelvin shrank the ratio at different rates for the two directions. Fitting the magnetization reversal curves with the Stoner-Wohlfarth formalism extracted cubic and uniaxial anisotropy constants, and the cubic constant's sign flipped compared with iron-richer compositions. The authors argue such tunable, direction-sensitive response suits magnetic sensor design.
arxiv-2512-22690:
Poojan Vanani and ten co-authors present Mesquite, an open-source motion capture system meant to escape the expensive laboratory. Optical mocap is costly and complex. Their alternative is a body-worn network of fifteen inertial sensor nodes. The nodes stream orientation data over a low-power wireless link to a USB dongle. A hip-worn Android phone handles position tracking. Everything runs in a browser, using WebGL rendering, WebXR for simultaneous localization, and web standards for device communication.

Against a commercial optical system, Mesquite's mean joint-angle error was two to five degrees, at roughly five percent of the cost. It sustains thirty frames per second with latency under fifteen milliseconds indoors. Hardware designs, firmware, and software are released openly for entertainment, healthcare, and virtual reality uses.
arxiv-2512-22890:
Sosuke Ito and four co-authors extend a geometric way of splitting information flow to systems described by overdamped Langevin dynamics. Those are the noisy diffusion equations of statistical physics. Information thermodynamics studies how information between subsystems modifies the second law for each part. A recent decomposition for jump processes separates information flow into excess and housekeeping parts, and this work carries it to diffusion.

For Langevin systems the decomposition connects directly to optimal transport, through the Wasserstein distance between the two subsystems, and the result is simpler than in the jump-process case. Features special to diffusion, including Koopman mode expansions and links to the Fisher information matrix, fit. The authors generalize the second law with the split flows. They define excess and housekeeping versions of Maxwell-style demons. They derive an uncertainty relation and a speed limit that use the excess flow, shown on Gaussian examples.
arxiv-2512-22990:
Soham Dutta and four co-authors built a low-cost drone pipeline that inspects apple orchards using an ordinary color camera. Growers need diseased leaves spotted early, fruit freshness judged, and apples counted for yield estimates, but existing drone systems treat these jobs separately and often depend on expensive multispectral sensors. The unified pipeline splits the work among three proven neural networks.

A ResNet50 model classifies leaf disease, a VGG16 model judges apple freshness, and a YOLOv8 model detects and locates fruit in real time. Everything runs offline on an ESP32-CAM and a Raspberry Pi carried with the drone, so no cloud connection is needed in the field. Reported accuracy reached about ninety-nine percent for disease classification and about ninety-seven percent for freshness, with a solid detection score for apples. The authors offer the setup as an accessible route to precision agriculture on cheap hardware.
arxiv-2512-23090:
Armin Berger and co-authors report a cautionary result about using reinforcement learning to train medical vision-language models. Their model, ChexReason, reads chest X-rays. It was trained with an R1-style recipe, supervised fine-tuning followed by GRPO reinforcement learning, on a budget of a few thousand examples and one graphics card. Benchmark scores then told two opposite stories.

On CheXpert, the dataset family it trained toward, reinforcement learning recovered performance, improving results by about a quarter. On the NIH dataset, a different institution's data, the same training degraded transfer by about a fifth. The pattern matched a larger high-resource model, suggesting the cause lies in the reinforcement learning paradigm itself rather than scale. Notably, the purely supervised checkpoint transferred best, as if teacher-guided reasoning kept more institution-agnostic features. The authors argue curated supervised training may beat aggressive reinforcement learning for clinical deployment.
arxiv-2512-23490:
Radio telescopes produce huge data sets, and calibration requires storing predicted model signals that can be far larger than the original observations. A. R. Offringa and R. J. van Weeren present Sisco, a compression method for these noiseless simulated signals. Lossy compression, which works fine on noisy real data, corrupts the calibration step when applied to model data.

Sisco predicts each visibility value by polynomial extrapolation over time and frequency, then compresses only the leftover differences. Linear and quadratic prediction together worked best, shrinking model data to about a quarter of its original size on average across LOFAR, MeerKAT, and MWA data. Built as an open-source storage manager, Sisco drops into existing workflows without changing formats.
arxiv-2512-23590:
Karlo Lelas and Robert Pezer look for pencil-and-paper formulas describing a damped harmonic oscillator when the damping is nonlinear. Exact solutions rarely exist once friction depends on velocity in nonlinear ways, so engineers rely on approximations. Their method starts from a trial solution: a slowly decaying amplitude multiplied by an oscillation with the undamped frequency but a shifted initial phase.

The amplitude's decay law follows from energy balance, matching the dissipation rate to the power of the damping force. Part one of the series treats damping quadratic in velocity, dry Coulomb friction, and their combination. Against numerical solutions, the formulas are excellent for weak to moderately strong quadratic damping, and with improved variants they track Coulomb-type motion accurately until the oscillator's final swings. A later part will take up damping that also grows in step with speed.
arxiv-2512-24190:
Himanshu Mishra and Anubhab Roy watch a small particle sink through surface waves. The particle is anisotropic, longer in one direction than another. A neutrally buoyant spheroid in such waves settles into a preferred orientation. That orientation depends only on its aspect ratio. The authors ask what changes when the particle actually sinks.

They compare sinking speed with wave speed and wave steepness. Weak settling keeps the aspect-ratio-driven orientation. Strong settling makes the outcome depend on the starting state. Translation and orientation are coupled throughout. Fluid inertia adds a torque that Stokes flow lacks. That torque drives the particle toward broadside alignment. The authors use the orientation dynamics to predict sideways drift. Finite-size effects are checked as well. A large spheroid drifts differently, and the small-size approximation holds near the wavelength limit.
arxiv-2512-24290:
F D Amaro and a large collaboration shrink data from a rare-event detector. The CYGNO chamber is an optical time projection chamber. It produces megapixel images rich in track detail. Rare-event searches need that detail. The image size overwhelms real-time data selection, though. Most of each frame is empty noise.

Their method learns the noise itself. A convolutional autoencoder trains only on pedestal images, frames with no signal. It learns the detector's noise morphology without labels or simulation. On real frames, reconstruction errors then flag particle structures. Thresholding and clustering carve out compact regions of interest. The best setup kept nearly all signal intensity. It discarded nearly all of the image area. Inference took about twenty-five milliseconds per frame on a consumer graphics card.
arxiv-2512-24490:
Veronika Hubeny and Massimiliano Rota settle a question about holographic entropy. Entropy vectors list the entanglement entropies of a multipartite system. Graph models from holography can realize some of them. A recent paper found a necessary condition for realization by simple tree graphs. The condition is chordality of an associated structure.

This paper proves the condition is also sufficient. The proof is constructive. An algorithm from a companion work builds the tree graph model whenever the condition holds. It always succeeds, for any number of parties. The result matters beyond holography. Entropy vectors from graph models can be matched by stabilizer states, at least approximately. Tree data may thus encode the holographic entropy cone's essential structure. The authors state that conclusion with a conjecture in view. Its strong form would make all holographic vectors tree-realizable.
arxiv-2512-24590:
Jozsef Solymosi and Chi Hoi Yip study two-distance sets over finite fields. A two-distance set is a point set whose pairs realize only two distances. The setting is a standard quadratic space in d dimensions. Euclidean intuition comes from the Larman-Rogers-Seidel bound. Finite fields break that intuition in instructive ways.

In characteristic three, the authors build sets reaching the full classical bound. Blokhuis's Euclidean bound need not hold in this world. A rank-sensitive replacement measures exactly where positive definiteness fails. Attainability gets a complete answer too. The Blokhuis bound is reached over some finite field for every dimension except six. Dimension six is exceptional. Its exact maximum is twenty-seven points. The paper mixes construction with sharp counting in finite geometry.
arxiv-2512-24690:
Gautami Bhowmik and Masao Tsuzuki count maximal lattices over p-adic fields and the rationals using Hecke series for reductive groups. Local factors of the counting series are treated through theory developed by Andrianov and Hina-Sugano. Their Euler factor calculations produce zeta functions of classical groups, objects earlier reached through p-adic cone integrals.

Where their series matches known zeta functions, old results are recovered more simply. New zeta functions appear for non-split even and odd orthogonal groups. Number theory readers get both a cleaner method and fresh cases. Lattice counting connects local arithmetic data to global analytic functions in a precise way.
arxiv-2512-24890:
Martinelli, Elancheliyan, and Scotti probe dense suspensions of ultra-low crosslinked microgels, soft particles that form supercooled and glassy states. Small-angle X-ray scattering and dynamic light scattering reveal microscopic structure and motion across length scales and effective volume fractions. The particles act as fragile glass formers whose dynamics depend only on volume fraction.

Structure, by contrast, depends on the specific mix of particle number density and swelling state, so dynamics and structure partly decouple. A superposition across time and length scales organizes the dynamics. Soft matter readers get a clean glassy system where one variable controls motion while structure remembers more history.
arxiv-2512-24990: Cristian Rios and Eric Sawyer prove a smooth Alpert testing profile of convolution type for the Fourier extension conjecture on paraboloids. The Fourier extension conjecture concerns bounding an extension map tied to curved surfaces such as paraboloids, a central open problem in harmonic analysis. Testing terms reduce checking an map trait to checking it on special Alpert functions. Their result further extends earlier characterizations of convolution type for this conjecture. Analysis readers get a sharper testing test, since full bounds are hard to check while ordered tests are tractable.
arxiv-2601-00090:
Anne Harrington works with four co-authors to fight mode collapse in text-to-image diffusion models, where repeated sampling with one prompt yields near-identical pictures. Their 2026 study takes a different route from guidance steering or generating huge candidate pools. Instead they optimize the starting noise itself, using a simple objective that spreads generations out while keeping the base model's image quality.

The team also studies the frequency makeup of that noise, showing that starting points with different frequency profiles can improve both the optimization and the search for diverse outputs. Experiments report better generation quality and diversity than rival approaches. The appeal is practical: the trained model stays untouched, so the method can in principle be layered onto existing systems. For creative tools, more varied samples from the same prompt mean users see real options instead of slight copies.
arxiv-2601-00290:
Sixue Xing leads six coauthors in redesigning failed clinical trials with a team of self evolving agents. Trials are vital, slow, and hugely costly per drug. Their protocols are long, complex language documents. Older AI tools can predict trial failure well. They stop short of saying how to fix the plan. This system treats redesign as an optimization task.

Agents diagnose why a protocol likely failed first. Safety aware edits then reshape the protocol text. A predictor model scores each new candidate cheaply. That loop gives dense rewards for steady improvement. A layered memory stores lessons within one trial. It also distills patterns that transfer across trials. Over half of failed protocols flip to predicted success. The cost per trial stays near zero. Case studies match real expert edits closely. Failed plans become drafts worth a second look.
arxiv-2601-00490:
J. Sumaya-Martinez and E. Torres-Garcia tackle photon-efficient fluorescence lifetime imaging, a microscopy method that times how long molecules glow after excitation. The glow fades fast, photons are scarce, and the total light dose is fixed, so when each photon arrives matters. Their framework uses Fisher information, a measure of how much data reveal about a quantity, to choose the timing of measurements.

They derive the relevant quantities for two hardware styles, photon-counting histograms and programmable time gates, while allowing for messy realities like unknown background light and instrument blur. In simulations, timing plans chosen by their criteria consistently beat uniform sampling, and plans that account for uncertain nuisance settings stay robust. The payoff is clearer lifetime images from fewer photons.
arxiv-2601-00890:
Zheshu Song, Lu Wang, Wei Deng, Zhuo Yang, and Yong Wu present Index-ASR, a large speech recognition system built on a language model backbone. Such systems transcribe impressively on public benchmarks, yet two weaknesses persist in real use. They hallucinate, producing long repetitive text not grounded in the audio, and they offer little control for recognizing specific names or terms a user cares about.

Index-ASR attacks both problems by integrating the language model with large-scale training data enriched with background noise and contextual information. Robustness improves because the model learns to transcribe through messy audio rather than clean studio speech. Contextual customization, including hotword recognition for chosen terms, is built into the design rather than bolted on, and experiments are reported to support the claims.
arxiv-2601-01190:
Diogenes de Jesus Ramirez and three co-authors propose a better yardstick for choosing among statistical models when the data come in groups or mixtures. The classic Bayesian Information Criterion penalizes complex models, but it treats all complexity alike. Their modified version adds information about the curvature of the likelihood surface, drawn from a matrix of second derivatives.

That curvature gives a finer penalty, since a model whose fit bends sharply is more constrained than one that bends gently. Theory and extensive simulations, on both plain and mixed linear models, show the new criterion beating the classic criterion, the Akaike criterion, and related variants. The gains are clearest with small samples and with useless noise variables in the mix. Better selection matters wherever nested data arise, from school studies to hospital trials, because the wrong model can bend every conclusion drawn from it.
arxiv-2601-01290:
Harshita Narnoli and Mihai Surdeanu probe how in-context learning works, the trick where a language model learns a task from examples placed in its prompt. They ask whether the model behaves like a plain classifier trained on those examples. If so, which kind fits: one that learns by gradient steps, or one that copies nearest neighbors?

Using text classification across six data sets and three models, they find the behaviors line up when the examples are relevant to the task. On average, the model's choices sit closer to the neighbor method than to the gradient method. That hints that attention acts more like neighbor matching than like training. When examples are weakly relevant, the model does better than both classifiers. It can fall back on knowledge stored in its weights, an option the simple classifiers lack.
arxiv-2601-01490:
Junichiro Niimi tests whether making a language model reason step by step actually makes it more truthful. The test is strict: recommend peer-reviewed computer science journal articles, with no outside tools or browsing allowed. Two commercial models were compared in reasoning and non-reasoning modes.

A troubling trade-off appeared in both. Non-reasoning models broke the constraints often, in about two thirds to three quarters of cases, but kept their facts straight. Reasoning models broke the rules far less, yet they bent known facts to fit the constraints and invented more articles outright. The pattern held across both architectures. Niimi argues the distortion is worse than the violation, because a bent fact is harder to spot than a broken rule. The study challenges the common assumption that more reasoning always means more reliability, at least inside closed systems.
arxiv-2601-01590:
Beck and Schneider hunt for repeating flow patterns hidden inside high-dimensional chaos. Such patterns, unstable periodic orbits, are thought to be the basic building blocks of turbulent flow. Finding them is hard. Chaos magnifies errors, and fluid models carry huge numbers of variables. Their method works inside a learned low-dimensional map of the chaos instead.

A loop-closing algorithm searches that small map directly, skipping step-by-step time marching that lets errors explode. Math links through the learned map keep the small-space physics faithful in a statistical sense. Tests on a model equation and on two-dimensional fluid flow show matching orbits in both spaces, opening a route to study turbulence from its skeleton.
arxiv-2601-01990:
Running many quantum gates in parallel is essential for large quantum computers, but crosstalk between neighboring qubits corrupts simultaneous operations and makes full-system control design impossibly expensive. Xiaodong Yang, Ran Liu, and Jun Li cut the problem down: optimize control only over small, constant-sized subsystems in a crosstalk-robust way.

The reduction cancels the leading crosstalk-induced errors, turning noise growth for parallel single-qubit gates from exponential to linear in system size, with an order-of-magnitude gain for multi-qubit gates. Validation spans nitrogen-vacancy centers, a nuclear-spin processor, and superconducting arrays up to two hundred qubits, without needing crosstalk strengths or a specific lattice geometry. The framework targets genuinely large architectures.
arxiv-2601-02090:
Storm surge flooding is forecast with physics-based models that are accurate but heavy. Nils Melsom Kristensen and four co-authors present Flo. It is a machine learning surge model for the North, Norwegian, and Barents seas. It is built on the Anemoi framework. That framework is used for AI weather forecasting.

The graph neural network predicts the non-tidal water level driven by wind and pressure at four-kilometer, hourly resolution. Training used forty-three years of reanalysis weather and a numerical surge hindcast. More than ninety coastal gauges served as checks. Against them, Flo's hindcasts matched the numerical model's quality. Key physical processes were reproduced. Flo is a foundation for faster, observation-friendly surge forecasting rather than a replacement that beats physics outright.
arxiv-2601-02390:
Alex Thornton, Ian Halliday, Harry Saxton, and Xu Xu modify the unscented Kalman filter. So it can estimate all ten parameters of a lumped parameter model of the human cardiovascular system from only four measured outputs. The model is nonlinear and stiff. The standard filter suffers rank deficiency here. That normally means only a small subset of parameters can be estimated, and the rest must be fixed by guesswork.

Because parameter estimation, unlike live control, does not need a fresh control action at each step, that constraint can be dropped, and their changes exploit the freedom. The modified filter proves robust under heavy noise, difficult disease states, and no prior knowledge of parameter values. Bringing even weakly influential parameters into the estimate matters for clinical use of such models.
arxiv-2601-02490:
Arash Azizi offers a way to rescue the Unruh effect from the noise that usually buries it. An accelerated detector should respond as if it sat in a warm bath, but that response is swamped by plain spontaneous emission, described by Wigner Weisskopf theory. Azizi uses interference between several detectors to cancel the noise rather than fight it head on.

Three entangled Unruh DeWitt detectors are put in a set W state, a shared entangled state of one set form. In that state the emission channels going both ways can be made to interfere destructively and vanish at once. The cancellation needs one unique entangled state whose coefficients are set by a geometric rule based on sines of logarithms of detector accelerations. The work presents multi detector entanglement as a sharp tool for silencing noise in relativistic quantum tests.
arxiv-2601-02590:
Loïc Herviou, Elodie Campan, and Pierre Nataf study a Fermi Hubbard model where each fermion carries one of many degenerate orbital types, called colors. They work on a short chain with few sites, in the limit of many colors and particles. For an attractive local interaction the model was known to break a cyclic symmetry tied to the number of sites. The new work extends that result to chains of three or more sites and to positive temperatures.

Several methods are combined, exact diagonalization respecting the full symmetry, a generalized Holstein Primakoff transformation, Hartree Fock theory, and a large color saddle point approximation. At zero temperature the ground state becomes degenerate, one state per site, once attraction passes a threshold that shrinks as colors grow. At positive temperature the transition temperature grows with both color count and attraction, favoring large color systems.
arxiv-2601-03090:
Rocio Mexia Diaz, Yasmin Greenway, and Petru Manescu present LesionTABE, a framework meant to make skin lesion AI fairer across skin tones. Diagnostic models for skin disease are known to do worse on darker skin. That gap has slowed their use in clinics. LesionTABE pairs adversarial debiasing, a training trick that removes tone-based shortcuts, with features from a foundation model built for skin medicine.

Tested across several datasets, on both cancerous and inflamed conditions, the framework improved fairness metrics by more than twenty-five percent over a strong ResNet-152 baseline. It also beat other debiasing methods. At the same time, it raised overall diagnostic accuracy. The authors argue that debiasing large foundation models, rather than small task models, is a practical step toward fairer clinical AI.
arxiv-2601-03290:
Hema Hariharan Samson surveys lightweight transformer architectures designed to run on edge devices. These are the phones, embedded boards, and appliances where real-time AI must live within tight power and memory budgets. The survey reviews how model compression, quantization, pruning, and knowledge distillation shrink big transformers for such hardware. It examines prominent small variants, including MobileBERT, TinyBERT, DistilBERT, EfficientFormer, EdgeFormer, and MobileViT.

Performance benchmarks span standard datasets for language and vision. The analysis covers industry adoption across hardware platforms, such as NVIDIA Jetson and Apple Neural Engine. It also covers deployment frameworks, such as TensorFlow Lite and ONNX Runtime. The results show modern lightweight transformers can keep roughly seventy-five to ninety-six percent of full-model accuracy. They cut model size several-fold, and latency substantially.
arxiv-2601-03390:
Daniel Qian and six co-authors present Aspen, a Byzantine fault tolerant protocol that keeps its fast path fast even under concurrent load. No such protocol can commit faster than one round trip, and leaderless speculative designs approach that bound by letting clients broadcast directly to replicas. The catch is fragility: concurrent requests arrive at replicas in different orders, states diverge, and the protocol falls into expensive recovery.

Aspen adds a tiny waiting delay, sized by loosely synchronized clocks and network delay estimates, to give requests a tentative shared order before execution. It also fields extra replicas, so the fast path survives a bounded number of diverged replicas instead of collapsing. The design makes near-optimal two-message-delay commits practical for real, messy networks rather than only quiet ones.
arxiv-2601-03590:
Zhongbin Guo and eight co-authors ask whether language models can understand space from words alone, without any picture. Most spatial intelligence research uses vision models, leaving open whether the skill comes from seeing or from reasoning. Their benchmark, SiT-Bench, converts scenes into coordinate-rich text descriptions and asks models to reason over them symbolically.

The set holds more than thirty-eight hundred expert-checked items across five categories and seventeen subtasks, from navigation and viewpoint changes to robot manipulation details. Top models handled local semantic tasks well but showed a clear spatial gap in global consistency. Explicit spatial reasoning steps helped a great deal. The results matter for robots and assistants that receive the world as text, sensors, or maps rather than images.
arxiv-2601-03890:
Harishwar Raman and seven co-authors experimentally study how active Janus colloids, tiny spheres half-coated in platinum, gather into clusters. These chemically powered swimmers are a model system for non-equilibrium self-organization, with lessons for programmable materials and synthetic assemblies. Most earlier work stopped at pairs or small groups, while this team followed clusters as large as nine particles in a regime where clusters constantly form, dissolve, and merge.

The clusters travel in circular paths, and both their translation and rotation can be predicted directly from the orientations of their member particles. Formation also changes mechanism with size: small clusters assemble through chemical interactions, while larger ones form mainly through steric effects, simple physical blocking. The switch arises from a motility mismatch between incoming swimmers and the cluster, a detail modelers of active matter must include.
arxiv-2601-04090:
Jiaxin Huang and five co-authors present Gen3R, a system that makes three-dimensional scenes while also rebuilding them. Good scene generation needs both the strong priors of reconstruction models and the imagination of video diffusion models. Gen3R joins the two instead of choosing one.

The team adapts the VGGT reconstruction model so its tokens become geometric latents, trained to line up with the appearance latents of a pre-trained video diffusion model. Generating both kinds of latents together yields colour videos plus matching geometry: camera poses, depth maps, and a global point cloud. Tests show leading results for scenes guided by one or several images. Generation also steadies reconstruction in return, which shows the benefit runs both ways.
arxiv-2601-04190:
Juan F. Gutierrez, Nhung Nguyen, Jesus M. Quintero, and Andres Gomez build a wireless node that runs on light alone and also receives data by light. Their target is the Internet of Things, where batteries limit where nodes can go. A solar panel does double duty, harvesting energy and acting as the antenna for signals from LED sources.

A light analogue front end cleans and digitises the signal for a small eight-bit processor, which wakes the main processor only when stored energy allows. Reception is timed to the harvester's open-circuit phase, which cuts interference and sharpens the signal. The prototype decodes short frames reliably at the stated rate, uses only a few millijoules per frame, and sleeps at very low power, the four authors report.
arxiv-2601-06790:
Bowen Shen and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers SecMoE. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Privacy-preserving Transformer inference has gained attention due to the potential leakage of private information. Despite recent progress, existing frameworks still fall short of practical model scales, with gaps up to a hundredfold.

A possible way to close this gap is the Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture. Which has emerged as a promising technique to scale up model capacity with minimal overhead. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-06990:
Carl Johan Casselgren and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers single conflict coloring and palette sparsification of uniform hypergraphs this paper is partially. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The authors introduce and investigate single conflict coloring in the setting of r r -uniform hypergraphs. We establish some basic properties of this hypergraph coloring model and study a probabilistic.

Model of single conflict coloring where the conflicts for each edge are chosen randomly. In particular, we prove a sharp threshold-type result for complete graphs and establish. A sufficient condition for single conflict colorability of r r -uniform hypergraphs in this model. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07190:
Nikhil Verma and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with active context compression. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Large Language Model (LLM) agents struggle with long-horizon software engineering tasks due to “Context Bloat.” As interaction history grows.

Computational costs explode, latency increases, and reasoning capabilities degrade due to distraction by irrelevant past errors. Existing solutions often rely on passive, external summarization mechanisms that the agent cannot control. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07690:
Davide Catta, Rustam Galimullin, and Munyque Mittelmann study logics for agents who can rebuild their own world. Their 2026 preprint, On Angels and Demons, concerns strategic reasoning about agents that modify a model's structure. Such logics suit systems that evolve over time. Examples include communication networks, security protocols, and multi-agent planning. The paper is an extended version of a conference paper for AAMAS 2026.

The title's angels and demons suggest builders and destroyers acting on dynamic models. Formal tools must track both what agents know and what they can change. Ordinary strategic logics usually hold the model fixed. Letting agents construct or deconstruct parts of it adds real expressive power. The work speaks to scholars in logic, verification, and multi-agent systems.
arxiv-2601-07990:
Lulu Zhang and colleagues find signs of feedback in the centers of faint active galaxies, using JWST spectra. The team analyzed infrared spectra from about three to twenty-eight micrometers. The spectra come from the central regions, within 150 parsecs, of four low-luminosity active galactic nuclei. Instruments were JWST's NIRSpec and MIRI spectrographs. The work extends the Galaxy Activity, Torus, and Outflow Survey. Their 2026 preprint is presented as a letter.

Feedback means the central black hole pushes back on its host galaxy's gas. Low-luminosity nuclei are the quiet majority, so their feedback is easy to overlook. Infrared spectroscopy can see through dust to the gas motions involved. Evidence of outflows there would widen feedback's known reach. The paper serves astronomers studying galaxy evolution. It shows space-based spectroscopy opening a regime ground telescopes cannot reach cleanly.
arxiv-2601-08290: Prosanta Pal and three co-authors flag a loophole in Bell tests run on superconducting quantum processors. Their 2026 arXiv paper questions a quiet assumption behind CHSH tests. Analysts usually assume repeated circuit runs sample one stationary preparation ensemble. The authors show this assumption can be violated on current hardware. If preparations drift between runs, reported Bell violations need fresh interpretation. The finding matters for teams that use processor Bell tests as evidence of quantum behavior or device quality.
arxiv-2601-08390: Estrid Buhl Naver and co-authors report direct hydrogen detection pointing to a crustal water reservoir on early Mars. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks ahead to returning Martian samples to Earth. Getting the most science from those samples needs non-destructive methods first. Such methods allow early three-dimensional study of sample interiors before any cutting or crushing. Hydrogen signals can reveal water held in crustal materials. A macroscopic early reservoir would reshape accounts of how Mars gained and lost its water over time.
arxiv-2601-08590:
Amin Coja-Oghlan and four co-authors study a classic model of tiny magnets on a random net. Each magnet can point up or down, and near pairs like to point the same way. The net here is a random graph where links form by chance. The team looks at the free energy of this system, a key count of its state.

They ask how much that count swings from one random net to the next. Such swings tell us how much a single net can stand for the whole class. The work uses a net with a fixed mean count of links per point. A reader in math physics gets new bounds on those swings. The bounds help judge when mean field claims are safe to trust.
arxiv-2601-08690:
Shubham Kulkarni and three co-authors evaluate AI-human dialogue by required phases and their order. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that conversational AI now supports real clinical work. Most evaluation methods miss how compliance depends on the full course of a conversation, though.

Their method, OIP-SCE, checks whether every required clinical obligation is met. It also checks that obligations are met in the right order. Clear evidence is kept for clinicians to review afterward. A system that gathers required information out of order can still harm care. Phase-level evaluation brings dialogue checks closer to how clinical protocols actually work.
arxiv-2601-08790:
Lei Tan and three co-authors build a tool to spot fake images made by AI. New image tools can make false scenes that look real. A spot tool trained on one maker tends to fail on the next maker. It learns marks of that maker, not marks of fakeness as such. The team seeks cues that hold across makers.

Their net is called MCAN. It joins more than one type of cue in one net. Each cue expert looks at a distinct sign, such as edge flaws or odd light. The net then weighs the cues as a group. A reader who must check images gets a tool built for broad use. It aims to keep its skill when a new image maker shows up.
arxiv-2601-09090:
Christopher Blake and three co-authors study a Bitcoin form that uses more than one hash type to link blocks. A hash is a short print of a block. Work proofs rest on how hard it is to find a block with a good print. One may guess a multi hash chain is safe if and only if each hash type holds a most share guard.

They prove that guess is false. The safe zone is not a plain and of all hash guards. They then give a form called Merged Bitcoin, where links can use mixed hash types. A reader in crypto work gets a warn and a build. More hash types do not add safety in the plain way one may hope.
arxiv-2601-09190:
Takahito Kashiwabara proves a strong solve for a class of flow type rules with a bar. The rules mix a two way flow term of Navier-Stokes type with a bar term set by a convex sum. Such mixes model flow with a yield point or a cap. He works in a broad space frame that fits more than one real case.

He uses Rothe's method, which steps time in cuts and solves each cut. He shows a strong solve lives for a short time span near the start. Strong here means the solve has the rates the rules ask for, not just a weak mean sense. A reader in flow math gets a base step for harder global asks.
arxiv-2601-09790:
Gonzalo Herrera, Shunsaku Horiuchi, Xiaolin Qi, and Ian M. Shoemaker argue that the cosmic neutrino background is nearly within reach. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies relic neutrinos boosted to high energies. Cosmic rays crossing the universe can scatter off the faint neutrino sea and kick its particles upward.

Earlier work covered one channel: cosmic-ray protons bouncing off relic neutrinos in neutral-current hits. Boosted relic neutrinos would be far easier to detect than the cold originals. Future neutrino telescopes might catch them. A detection would open a direct window on the first second of the universe and on how neutrinos shaped what came after.
arxiv-2601-10190:
Zhiwen Lin, Ke Li, and Kun Fang study how fast error falls when pure quantum links are made. Labs can make rough pairs of linked qubits. A pure step cleans many rough pairs into fewer clean pairs. The best yield of that step is well known.

Past work took the start state as known in full. The team ask a new ask. How fast does the error of the clean step fall as pairs grow? That rate is named the reliability function. It holds when the rate sits below the best yield. The work gives a math form for that fall off.
arxiv-2601-10390:
Pham Duy Khanh, Vu Vinh Huy Khoa, and Tran Hong Mo prove swap rules for cone based plans. Such plans seek the best point in a cone in a vector space. The space can be vast, with no fixed dim. A Farkas rule says when a set of bounds has no point at all.

The team prove pure algebra forms of that rule. They then prove strong swap rules for the same plans. Swap rules say the best primal and dual values match. Their proofs use facts about how the value bends when the plan is nudged. The work needs no shape or space caps.
arxiv-2601-10590:
Zhangyi He, Feng Yu, Suzie Cro, and Laurent Billot write about group sequential designs, a common plan for clinical trials. Such designs let a trial stop early at planned checks while keeping the false-positive rate in bounds. In the classic frequentist style, O'Brien-Fleming bounds stop trials only with great care at first, then loosen as data build up.

The paper follows the move from bold early stopping to cautious early stopping in Bayesian versions of these designs. It looks at how prior beliefs shape when a trial may end. The topic guides trial designers who must weigh speed against proof. Early stops save time and spare patients, but weak early proof can mislead.
arxiv-2601-10690:
Andrew F. Ilersich, Kevin Course, and Prasanth B. Nair build faster stand-ins for complex systems that change over time. Full simulations of such systems under many settings can be too slow to use. Reduced-order models shrink the math to a size that runs fast. But many shrink methods stumble on random dynamics and give no sense of their own error.

The authors present data-driven reduced models for stochastic, parametrized systems. Their models aim to track random behavior while also stating prediction uncertainty. Knowing the error bars matters when models guide real decisions. The work targets engineers who need quick forecasts they can trust, with honest bounds on what the forecast might miss.
arxiv-2601-10790:
Luca Brunelli, Filippo Revello, and Gonzalo Villa classify the gravitational wave output of cosmic string networks whose tension varies. Cosmic strings are thin relics that some early-universe theories predict. A scaling network of them hums with waves across many frequencies. In string compactifications, the tension can change with time as moduli fields move.

The authors work out the full range of behaviors and compute the spectral indices of the wave backgrounds. The index tells how wave power tilts with frequency. Observatories read that tilt to tell one source from another. A complete map helps future detections point back to the physics that made the strings, or rule whole families out.
arxiv-2601-10890:
Amílcar Branquinho, Ana Foulquié-Moreno, and Manuel Mañas extend spectral theory for a broad class of Markov chains. A recent spectral Favard theorem covers bounded banded matrices with a positive bidiagonal factorization. The authors apply it to Markov chains whose transition matrices are banded and factor the same way. The class reaches beyond the classic birth-and-death chains.

In the finite case, they derive the Karlin-McGregor spectral representation. That formula expresses chain dynamics through orthogonal polynomials. Spectral views let analysts read a chain's long-run behavior from its spectrum. The work widens the family of chains with a full spectral toolkit, useful in queueing, biology, and random walks.
arxiv-2601-10990:
Xinpo Li and Jingtao Shi work on a hard control task in this 2026 preprint. The system they study is ruled by a random differential equation. Its delays mix three forms at once. They are a point delay, a spread-out delay, and a noisy memory term.

The model is broad by design. The mixed delays show up in all the terms of the system. They affect the noise term and the final cost as well. Work of this kind aims at best control choices for systems with long memory. Such systems arise when past states and past inputs still shape what happens now.
arxiv-2601-11190:
Laura Menotti, Stefano Marchesin, and Gianmaria Silvello work on reading facts from long texts. Their 2026 preprint deals with relation extraction at the scale of whole documents. The task is hard for two main reasons. Facts often span more than one sentence in a text. And most relation types are rare, with few training cases.

Their frame, DOREMI, works in rounds to lift the rare types. Each round adds a small set of hand-checked notes by design. The notes are picked to help the weak types most. The work has been accepted by the journal Knowledge-Based Systems. It aims at strong gains for rare links at low cost in human time.
arxiv-2601-11390:
A. Filippi reviews what is not known about antineutron interactions. The 2026 report looks back at tests done at CERN's LEAR. Antineutrons are the antimatter twins of neutrons. Low-energy beams of them probed strong-force physics for years.

Most such tests ran up to the 1990s at LEAR. Many questions stayed open when that program ended. Filippi lists those open issues in a clear survey. He also hints at new tests for a future facility. An upgraded antiproton decelerator complex could host them. Fresh beams could open new areas of physics to study. The report is a map for where the field could go next.
arxiv-2601-11490:
Melvyn Nathanson runs races between sumset sizes in this 2026 preprint. The setting is a locally compact abelian group with Haar measure. Sumsets add one set to another, element by element. Their size, or measure, is a core topic in additive combinatorics.

Nathanson fixes counts n at least 2 and H at least 2. He takes tuples of exponents from the natural numbers. For any such choice, measurable sets can be built to order. The tuple of measures of scaled sumsets then follows a set pattern. In effect, the race order between sumsets can be prescribed. Such freedom results show how wild sumset growth can be. They bound what any general sumset law could claim.
arxiv-2601-11590:
Fan Bai and nine coauthors serve multimodal models with a split design. Their 2026 preprint names the system EPD-Serve, built for Ascend. Large models now process text, image, audio, and video. Real applications increasingly demand all of those at once.

Most serving systems use a monolithic architecture today. Encode, prefill, and decode stages stay tightly coupled there. They also run on homogeneous hardware, one kind only. EPD-Serve disaggregates those three stages from each other. Each stage can then sit on hardware that fits it best. Flexible splits can raise throughput and cut waste. The system targets the Ascend platform by name.
arxiv-2601-11690:
Yakov Mandel unifies two routes to gravitational baryogenesis in one frame. The 2026 preprint asks why matter beat antimatter in the cosmos. Baryogenesis is any process that tips that balance. Gravity-based versions tie the tip to spacetime itself.

The first mechanism is an entropy-clock source term. Irreversible entropy production sets a sign-definite chemical potential. That potential favors matter over antimatter as entropy grows. The second is CP violation from a gravitational theta term. That term mirrors the QCD vacuum angle in form. Joined, the two may yield the seen baryon surplus. The frame gives theorists one stage for both effects.
arxiv-2601-12290:
Avijoy Chakma, Adity Khisa, Soham Khisa, Jannatun Noor, and Sharifa Sultana study a Chakma language revival effort in the Chittagong Hill Tracts of Bangladesh. Indigenous tongues face strong pressure from state languages, most of all in the Global South. Chakma speakers face mixing of their tongue into Bengali.

Their six-month study used interviews and focus groups with language learning stakeholders. It found social and economic blocks, plus resilience tactics in the community. They call for digital tools grounded in Chakma culture. The work joins language rights to tech design.  Stakeholder views drive their call for new tools.
arxiv-2601-12490:
Gian Parusa, Sotirios Fragkos, Samuel Beaulieu, and Michael Schuler present a way to simulate photoemission spectra. The method is called ARPES, and it maps the electronic states of a material. One step theory of photoemission has a long, strong record in this field. Past codes for it are often tied to special electronic structure formalisms, which limits their use.

The team compute photoelectron states directly as scattering solutions of the Kohn Sham equation. Scattering boundary conditions match the physics of an electron leaving a surface. Their framework is first principles and aims to be both exact and efficient. A portable, fast ARPES simulator would help many groups read their spectra. It would also ease tests of new materials for electronics and quantum devices.
arxiv-2601-12690:
Caleb Wohn and five co authors study stereotypes in AI advice given to autistic users. Autistic people sometimes disclose their autism when asking language models for social advice. They hope disclosure brings more personalized responses. They also know these systems may reproduce stereotypes, so the risks and benefits of disclosure are unclear.

The team run a mixed methods study on this question. One part is a large scale audit experiment on model outputs. The other part is interviews with eleven autistic participants. The title quotes a telling line about advice fit for a fictional alien logician. Findings here can guide safer design of advice systems. Their paper was set for a 2026 human factors venue.
arxiv-2601-12790:
Yang Zhang and six co authors present FocusNav, a navigation framework for humanoid robots. Robust local navigation in unstructured, dynamic places remains a significant challenge for humanoids. A robot must balance long range targets with immediate motion stability. Tipping over while chasing a goal is a real risk for legged machines.

FocusNav uses spatial selective attention with waypoint guidance. It adaptively modulates the perceptual field of the robot based on intent and real time stability. In plain terms, the robot looks where it matters for the next step. Attention that shifts with stability could keep a humanoid upright in clutter. The work serves the push toward humanoids outside the lab.
arxiv-2601-12890:
Hang Gao and six co authors use graph guided language models for efficient code analysis. Language models have advanced code analysis tasks significantly in recent years. They struggle with malicious behaviors fragmented across files, though. Intricate dependencies get lost in a vast amount of benign code. A lone model reading files in order can miss the pattern.

The team propose a graph centric attention acquisition pipeline. A code graph maps dependencies between files and functions first. That graph guides the model attention toward the fragments that matter. Better localization of malicious behavior helps security audits scale. The work serves defenders who face codebases too large to read by hand.
arxiv-2601-13290:
Syed Akbar Hussain, Ali Jasem, and co-authors grow thin films in the uranium germanium pair to map its phase plan. Phase plans state which crystal forms live at which mix and heat. To map this pair, the team sprayed both parts at once onto three kinds of crystal base.

The bases were MgO, CaF2, and SrTiO3. Most films came out as a mix of two forms, UGe3 and UGe. Traces of a third form, UGe2, also showed. Each base bends which forms can grow in a thin film. Such maps guide the hunt for new acts in heavy fermion stuff, where uranium pairs are a rich source.
arxiv-2601-13390:
Rosa Orellana and Foster Tom prove fresh links among star coefficients of the chromatic symmetric function. That function codes how a graph can be coloured so no linked pair shares a hue. Its growth in a star basis yields counts called star coefficients.

The pair shows one such count holds a big fact. The count for a set star form tells if a linked graph is two connected. That is, it tells if the graph stays in one piece when one node is cut. They also prove new straight links among other star counts. Such ties turn a hard graph trait into a count that can be read off a known function.
arxiv-2601-14390:
S. Mahesh Chandran and Karthik Rajeev study entanglement in strong-field quantum physics in this 2026 paper. In quantum field theory, entanglement entropy under a spatial split is a sharp probe of quantum correlations. The team applies it to the Sauter-Schwinger effect. That effect is pair creation from a strong electric field, a nonperturbative process.

The authors present the first comprehensive numerical study of this kind for that setting. They track how entanglement entropy evolves in time. They also study its geometric scaling, how it grows with the size of the split region. Readers get a new window on how correlations build up when a strong field rips pairs from the vacuum.
arxiv-2601-14890:
Ahmed Saoudi sets out a new math transform and works out its basic rules. His 2026 arXiv paper joins the Fourier transform with Bessel functions, then adds a quadratic phase term. Transforms like this split a signal into parts that are easier to study.

Saoudi proves the first key facts about his transform. It is continuous, it can be reversed, and it keeps energy in the Parseval sense. He also states a Riemann-Lebesgue type lemma for it. He then sets up shift and convolution tools inside the same frame, plus uncertainty principles.
arxiv-2601-15290:
Hareeshwar Karthikeyan builds fake users who act like real people in test chats. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with testing conversational AI at scale. A good test needs users with diverse habits and goals, across many domains.

The author presents a multi-agent framework for user simulation. Two ideas drive it: persona control and task state tracking. Together they mirror how a person thinks through a goal-driven conversation. The simulation stays explainable, so testers can see why a fake user acted as it did. That clarity helps teams trust the tests they run at scale.
arxiv-2601-15690:
Jiaxin Zhang and six co-authors survey uncertainty methods for language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Large models show remarkable skill, but unreliability blocks high-stakes use. Uncertainty quantification, or UQ, measures how unsure a model is. The survey charts a shift in UQ's role. It began as a passive diagnostic metric, read after the fact. It is becoming an active control signal that steers behavior in real time.

That shift changes how systems are built. A live uncertainty signal can trigger caution, extra checks, or a handoff to a human. The authors trace this evolution across methods and uses. For teams deploying models in medicine, law, or finance, the survey maps the options. Knowing when a model doubts itself is a first step to trusting it wisely.
arxiv-2601-15890:
Nikolas Mählmann and Sebastian Siebertz work on logical encodings of sparse graphs in a 2026 arXiv paper. Monadic stability is a tameness notion in structural graph theory. It generalizes planarity, bounded degree, bounded tree-width, and nowhere density. The sparsification conjecture makes a bold prediction. It says the tame, possibly dense graph classes are exactly those encodable by first-order transductions of sparse nowhere dense classes. The authors study existential positive transductions of sparse graphs.

Transductions are logic-driven ways to build one graph class from another. Existential positive ones use a restricted, monotone logic. Results here test the conjecture's edges. Structural graph theory feeds algorithm design for huge networks. Knowing which dense classes hide sparse codes helps transfer fast algorithms to them.
arxiv-2601-16290:
Niklas Schmid and three coauthors lift the odds of reach and dodge goals for chance systems. Their 2026 preprint deals with linear systems bent by chance noise. The goal is to reach a set zone and dodge a bad zone. Past ways work for small systems or give loose, safe bounds. Loose bounds waste the true room to act in big systems.

The team joins choice frames that mix strict rules with free picks. That mix aims for high odds with less loose loss. High true odds count for safe drive and flight plans. The work seeks scale to big linear chance systems. It gives a new plan frame for such tasks.
arxiv-2601-16390:
Rhitabrat Pokharel, Ameeta Agrawal and Tanay Nagar steer acts across tongues in large models. Their 2026 preprint deals with gaps in skill by tongue. Top tongues score well while low tongues lag far back. Past work ties the gap to shared and tongue tied cells. Cells for each tongue fire in split ways in the model.

Cross tongue steer shifts acts from a strong tongue to a weak one. Shifts use the shared cell space to carry skill across. Gains would cut the gap with no fresh train cost. That path serves users of low stock tongues. The work tests steer as a fair tool.
arxiv-2601-16490:
Adam Alflahi and coauthors set a four stage plan for deals in NoSQL stores. Their 2026 preprint deals with stores that hold doc type data. Such stores scale well and bend to new data forms. They oft rest on weak deal rules that lag in trust. Firm deals are key for apps that move funds or stock.

Four stages split deal work to checks that can scale. Each stage has a clear role in the deal chain. The plan aims to keep scale while it gains firm deals. Tests check if deal truth holds through all stages. The work serves apps that need both scale and trust.
arxiv-2601-16690:
Xinze Li, Ziyue Zhu, Siyuan Liu, Yubo Ma, Yuhang Zang, Yixin Cao, and Aixin Sun build a test for AI memory. Agents that play or work over long spans must recall the past. Most tests ask set quiz items. Their 2026 preprint takes a fresh path. It builds quiz items from the agent's own trail in a game.

Each item has a truth that can be checked from game logs. Items span words and scenes on screen. Skills probed range from plain recall to time and place sense. Trick items test if agents fall for false cues. Such tests can push agent memory past short chats.
arxiv-2601-16990:
Mirko Lai, Salvatore Vilella, Federica Cena, and Giancarlo Ruffo share a Python kit for science-map work. Science maps track how fields grow and link. Plain counts miss the web of those links. Their 2026 preprint gives pyBiblioNet, a kit built on nets. It reads cite webs, co-author webs, and word webs in one place.

Such webs show which teams and themes rule a field. They also show how themes rise and fade. The kit is free for all labs to use. It cuts the code work for map tasks. Fields from drugs to code can chart their past with it.
