arxiv-2601-17090:
Noam Koren, Rafael Moschopoulos, Kira Radinsky, and Elad Hazan teach nets to solve field rules with a spectral sieve. Field rules, or PDEs, run heat, flow, and wave work. Net solvers oft miss long-range links in those rules. Their 2026 preprint builds the Spectral Filtering Operator. It shapes its core weights in a fixed wave base. That base comes from the eigenmodes of the Hilbert matrix.

Fixed bases keep the core lean and broad at once. Long links in the rule map get their due weight. The team tests the tool on PDE tasks. Lean true solvers aid design in flight and chips.
arxiv-2601-17290:
Weloday Fikadu Moges, Jianmei Su, and Amin Waqas built a system to spot plant leaf disease on small devices. Phones, sensors, and farm gear have tight limits on compute and power. Big deep learning models often do not fit those limits. Yet farmers need fast, exact disease checks in the field. The team's Dynamic Meta-Ensemble Framework aims to meet both needs.

It joins models in a meta-ensemble that can adapt as it runs. The design chases high accuracy without heavy cost. Early disease finds can save crops and cut spray waste. A tool that runs on cheap gear spreads that gain widely. The work targets real farms, not just lab tests.
arxiv-2601-17890:
Ailin Liu and co-authors model how stress builds while people answer questions on the web. Their 2026 preprint deals with surveys and tests taken online. Time pressure and hard questions can push stress and mental load too high. That harms both the data quality and the user's experience. Most ways to spot stress rely on self-reports taken at coarse intervals.

Self-reports miss fast shifts that happen from one question to the next. The authors build models of body and behavior signals to track load as it moves. A finer view could let survey tools ease off when a user is overloaded. It could also flag items that strain people more than they should. The work joins health sensing with survey design.
arxiv-2601-17990:
Bokan Chen and a large team of co-authors study how to shape huge electric loads to cut carbon output. Their 2026 preprint deals with loads of many megawatts, like data centers. Shaping when such a load draws power changes which generators the grid runs. That in turn changes both the carbon released and the cost of energy. The authors take a cherry-picking approach to large load shaping, choosing the best hours and sites with care.

Not every hour of shifting pays off the same. Grid mixes change by place and by time of day. Picking the right moves can cut more carbon per unit of effort. The work speaks to grid planners and to the firms that run the biggest loads.
arxiv-2601-18090: Anthony Adams, Joshua Dorsam, Lily Levitsky, and Megan Mann extend the study of type B parking spaces. Their 2026 preprint builds on work of Armstrong, Reiner, and Rhoades, who defined a parking space representation for every Weyl group. The type B case is a representation of the signed symmetric group on a known module. The authors work out how this structure extends.
arxiv-2601-18290:
Yuan-De Jin, Zheng-Fei Ye, and Wen-Long Ma present a cheap way to hear the noise that disturbs a qubit. Their 2026 preprint deals with quantum dephasing environments. A qubit loses its phase when its surroundings fluctuate, and the noise spectrum tells how strong each rhythm of that fluctuation is. Their method uses repetitive weak measurements to read the spectrum directly. The weak measurement comes from a Ramsey interferometry step, applied again and again while the environment evolves freely.

Weak probes disturb the system far less than strong ones. Reading the spectrum with fewer resources helps labs map noise fast. Noise maps guide error correction and device design. The work serves the push for usable quantum hardware.
arxiv-2601-18790:
Etienne Lanzeray and three colleagues test if a model's drive to solve a math task can blind it to a life risk in the same ask. New models are taught to think long and hard on hard tasks. That drive has a cost lens: the model may pour all its care on the sums. A user may ask for help with sums while they tell of a stroke, a fall, or a crash in the same breath.

Their test set holds a chain of such cases, from mild to dire. In each, the right act is to drop the sums and urge help at once. The set grades if the model does that, or if it just works the sums. A fail would show a real risk in how thought tools are taught. The work gives firms a sharp test for that risk.
arxiv-2601-18890:
Ravishankar Anirudh and four colleagues test if the moves read from real sky shots of young far galaxies can be trusted. The shots come from a new space scope's slit web, which can read the light of scores of galaxies at once. From such shots staff read how gas in each galaxy turns and flows. Those reads feed tales of how galaxies grew in the young cosmos. But the scope's view is blurred and cut by slits, so the reads may bend.

The team make fake shots from a famed sim of galaxy birth. They run the scope's path on the fakes and set its reads next to the true moves in the sim. That side-by-side shows where the reads hold and where they stray. Such a check is a must before real shots are read as fact. It tells staff which claims the scope can bear.
arxiv-2601-19090:
Bochao Liu and four co-authors copy a trained model into a new one without leaking its private data. Models trained on private sets are shipped widely, but attackers can mine a shipped model for facts about its training data or labels. The team offers a conversion that carries a formal privacy guarantee.

Their method, called model transcription, is data free: it needs no access to the raw private set. It uses synthetic data, made private by design, to teach the copy. A safe way to reissue models would ease deployment in health, finance, and other fields where data cannot travel.
arxiv-2601-19290:
Yimeng Wang and nine co-authors let teams of language model agents rewrite their own roles and wiring. Multi agent systems split a hard job among specialists that talk and work together. Fixed roles, though, may fit the first task and miss the next one.

Their system, MetaGen, evolves both the roles and the topology, the pattern of who talks to whom. The team shapes itself as it learns what the work demands. Self shaping teams could beat hand designed ones on jobs too varied for a single fixed org chart.
arxiv-2601-19390:
Javier Silva Lafaurie and six co-authors give a sampling method a speed limit. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo explores a probability landscape by gliding through it like a frictionless particle. The shape of the landscape and the choice of starting momenta together set the glide.

Their sampler, Almanac, bounds the velocity of that glide. A bounded speed can keep the sampler stable where wild leaps would waste steps or break the math. Samplers of this kind sit under modern Bayesian statistics, so a sturdier one helps every field that fits models that way.
arxiv-2601-19490:
Ricardo Campos and a large team build a data set of claims in Portuguese news for fact checkers. Fact checking is slow, skilled hand work that cannot keep pace with how fast falsehoods spread online. Debunking takes longer to reach readers than the false claim itself, so speed tools matter.

Their set, ClaimPT, annotates claims inside news articles in Portuguese. Most claim data sets serve English, leaving other languages under tooled. A solid Portuguese set lets automated help reach the large share of the world's news that English tools skip.
arxiv-2601-19890:
Kenan Qu and Nathaniel J. Fisch propose a way to detect swirling turbulence inside hot plasmas. Theory suggests solenoidal turbulence, made of rotational flows, can greatly raise fusion reaction rates. No standard diagnostic can measure these flows directly in high-energy-density plasmas. Nor can existing tools separate rotational turbulence from compressional kinds.

Their method uses cross-polarization scattering of a probe laser. The laser's polarisation rotates in a way that reveals the turbulence's energy and spatial structure. A working diagnostic would let fusion experiments check whether the helpful turbulence is present. It could guide efforts to exploit the effect deliberately. The proposal joins plasma theory with a concrete measurement plan.
arxiv-2601-19990:
Xuan Chen and five colleagues compute a key process for Higgs physics to unprecedented precision. Pairs of Higgs bosons reveal the shape of the Higgs potential, which governs how the field holds the universe together. At hadron colliders, Higgs pairs are produced mainly through gluon fusion mediated by a top-quark loop. The authors report the first fully differential predictions at third order in the strong coupling.

The calculation also includes the effects of the top quark's mass. Fully differential means experimentalists can apply realistic cuts to the predictions. Precision at this level is needed because Higgs pair production is rare and backgrounds are large. The result sharpens the coming tests of the Higgs potential at the LHC.
arxiv-2601-20090:
Amirmohammad Farzaneh, Salvatore D'Oro, and Osvaldo Simeone give users of AI agents a way to ask what if. Language model agents turn a user's stated intent into plans and actions. After seeing an outcome, a user may wonder whether different wording would have done better. The authors build a framework for that counterfactual reasoning.

The framework explores alternative phrasings of the original intent and estimates their outcomes. Crucially, it provides formal reliability guarantees on those estimates. Without guarantees, counterfactual answers are just more model guesses. Reliable what-if analysis helps users phrase instructions better next time. It also helps designers see which intents are fragile. The work brings counterfactual thinking to everyday agent control. A guess with no bounds is just a guess.
arxiv-2601-20590:
Nathanaël Hassler builds a bijection, an exact one-to-one pairing, between two objects in combinatorics. On one side are the edges of the Turán graph, a classic extremal graph. On the other side are the meet-irreducible elements of a lattice. That lattice holds compositions of a number, where parts are bounded and the order is the dominance order.

A bijection proves the two collections have the same size by matching their members directly. Such pairings often reveal structure that counting alone hides. Hassler's matching links extremal graph theory with the theory of ordered sets in a concrete way.
arxiv-2601-20690:
Yuto Sugimoto, Shinichiro Akiyama, and Yoshinobu Kuramashi study the strong nuclear force under extreme cold and density. Their 2026 paper uses a tool called the tensor renormalization group. The setting is QCD, the theory of quarks and gluons, in its strong coupling limit. They work in three space dimensions plus time.

The team tracks two changes as the chemical potential is varied. One is the chiral transition, tied to how quark mass appears. The other is the nuclear transition, tied to matter filling up with quarks. They compute the chiral condensate and the quark number density to follow both. Such work helps map how matter behaves under conditions no lab can hold for long.
arxiv-2601-21190: A large particle physics collaboration reports a search for a rare particle decay in this 2026 paper. The target state is sought through its decay into an eta meson and a psi(2S) state. The search channel produces two eta mesons plus the psi(2S) from electron-positron collisions. The author list is headed by M. Ablikim, with a long list of colleagues from the collaboration. Searches of this kind test how quarks bind into exotic states.
arxiv-2601-21590:
Xiaotong Ji, Rasul Tutunov, Matthieu Zimmer, and Haitham Bou Ammar make power sampling practical for language model reasoning. Training with reinforcement learning improves reasoning, but growing evidence says the gain mostly sharpens the spread of answers the model already gives. It does not add brand new skills.

If gains are sharpening, a training-free sampler might reach the same place. Power sampling draws answers from a sharpened version of the model's own distribution. The authors make that sampling efficient enough to use. Skipping the training run saves large costs while keeping the sharper, more reliable reasoning.
arxiv-2601-21690:
Qinglun Li, Anke Tang, Miao Zhang, Mengzhu Wang, Quanjun Yin, and Li Shen build a unified theory for merging trained models. Merging blends several fine-tuned models into one, working only on their weights. It needs no original data and no costly retraining, yet it often works surprisingly well.

A general theory for why it works was missing, above all when the merged models were tuned with different settings. Learning rates and batch sizes vary widely in practice. The authors' framework explains merging across that heterogeneity. A firm theory tells builders when a merge is safe and when it will quietly average away the very skills they wanted.
arxiv-2601-21790:
Luqman Mustafa and co-authors study a family of crystals where the same material can form in two different atomic patterns. These patterns, called pyrite and marcasite, are model systems for crystal chemistry. In cobalt selenide, theory says marcasite is the stable ground state, yet labs normally make the pyrite form.

The 2026 study reports synthetic control over which pattern forms across a series that mixes iron and cobalt with selenium. Gaining that control had not been achieved for cobalt selenide before, though the two forms had been seen in tiny particles. Being able to choose a crystal pattern on purpose matters, because structure shapes how such materials conduct, react, and store energy.
arxiv-2601-21890:
Laura Mack introduces a software toolbox for scientists who measure how land and air exchange gases and heat. The eddy-covariance method infers those exchanges from fast wind and gas measurements above a surface. It began as a way to track ecosystem-scale exchange between air and vegetation.

The method now also serves to test theories of atmospheric turbulence, with the aim of improving weather and climate models. Reddy, the open-source toolbox in this 2026 preprint, is built for analyzing such measurements in heterogeneous environments. Where the land below is a patchwork rather than one uniform field. Shared tools matter because flux data feed the carbon budgets that climate policy relies on.
arxiv-2601-21990:
Nicolas Blin and co-authors speed up a core routine inside mixed-integer programming. Solvers for such problems repeatedly solve related linear programs, for instance when testing branches in strong branching or tightening bounds. Solving them one by one wastes the power of modern graphics processors.

The team presents a batched first-order method that solves many linear programs in parallel on GPUs. It extends the primal-dual hybrid gradient algorithm to handle whole batches at once. Their 2026 preprint targets the inner loop of industrial solvers. Faster linear programming batches translate directly into faster logistics, scheduling, and energy planning, where mixed-integer models decide real operations every day.
arxiv-2601-22090:
Runsheng Wang and co-authors help stroke survivors' hands obey them again. Surface electromyography reads muscle signals from the skin, a promising control signal for assist-as-needed hand rehabilitation. Detecting intent from weakened, stroke-affected muscles is hard, though: calibration is long and subject-specific, and detection stays brittle.

Their 2026 preprint, ReactEMG Stroke, adapts intent detection from healthy users to stroke patients with only a few examples from the patient. Few-shot adaptation could make rehabilitation devices practical in clinics, where long calibration sessions are unaffordable. A device that reads intent reliably can assist movement at the right moment, which is how retraining a hand is thought to work.
arxiv-2601-22390:
Chanwoo Park and Chanwoo Kim attack voice ID systems with a mask tuned to fool them. Speaker systems check who is talking from the sound of a voice. Their 2026 preprint uses an energy mask to hide the cues such a system reads, so it names the wrong person.

Work like this probes a real risk, as voice checks guard bank and phone access. The team frame the attack as an evasion test, meant to expose weak points. A known weak point can be patched; a hidden one cannot. Their results can help builders harden voice ID. They also warn users of its limits.
arxiv-2601-22890:
Christina Schenk and Ignacio Romero review how to tune complex computer models when data are scarce. The method, Bayesian calibration, adjusts a model's settings so its output matches real measurements, with honest doubt attached. It matters most when each simulation run is costly and experiments are few.

The authors gather many existing calibration methods into one unified framework. A shared frame helps engineers pick the right tool for fields like climate, energy, and design. It also shows where the methods agree and where they rest on shaky ground. The unified framework is presented as a review, gathering scattered calibration approaches into one place for comparison and reuse.
arxiv-2601-23190:
G. De Cillis and seven co-authors blend physics models with machine learning for sea ice forecasts. Their hybrid treats the learning component as a state-dependent fix for forecast errors in a sea-ice column model. Snow thermodynamics and the ice's radiative properties are key error sources.

They train dedicated neural networks for each model configuration and test transfer to new ones. Transfer learning matters because Arctic conditions vary by season and place. Better sea-ice forecasts serve shipping, climate science, and northern communities. State-dependent parameterization is the key mechanism, letting the learned correction change with the ice and snow conditions.
arxiv-2603-02090:
D. Mercier and Y. El Gharoussi improve phase mapping in multiphase materials with a neighborhood-aware feature. Their 2026 work uses nanomechanical maps from indentation or atomic force microscopy, where each point yields modulus and hardness. Ground-truth phase labels rarely exist for real maps, and easy synthetic tests flatter clustering methods.

Their benchmarks are controlled yet non-trivial, with tunable contrast, graded interfaces, and curved diffuse borders. A new feature, kernel-averaged mechanical mismatch, quantifies local heterogeneity by comparing each point with its neighbors. Adding that feature as a third clustering axis sharpens phase separability in low-contrast maps. Interphase zones stand out better and results grow more robust to noise in their tests. Cleaner segmentation supports representative volume elements and phase-specific property extraction.
arxiv-2603-02390:
Hymalai Bello, Lala Ray, Joanna Sorysz, and colleagues release a factory action data set in this 2026 paper. Smart factories track worker actions to measure performance and improve safety. Their data set, OpenMarcie, is billed as the largest multimodal one for manufacturing. It blends wearable sensors with cameras placed around the workspace.

Thirty-six participants took part across two study settings. One group assembled and disassembled a bicycle with no fixed protocol. Another built a 3D printer from the maker's instructions, partly in collaborative rounds. The set holds over thirty-seven hours of first-person and room views. Eight data types and over two hundred channels are included. Benchmarks cover action labeling, open captioning, and matching across sensor types.
arxiv-2603-02490:
Megha Khokhar, Lucas Norder, Paolo Sberna, and Richard Norte integrate delicate membranes into optical cavities in this 2026 paper. Silicon nitride membranes under high stress are stars of cavity optomechanics. They dissipate little energy and suit wafer-scale fabrication. Joining them to high-quality cavities usually needs bonding or fiddly alignment, which limits scale.

Their method builds the whole stack on one wafer at once. Membranes hang directly above Bragg mirrors that survive the hot growth process. A clean sacrificial layer and plasma undercut free the membranes in seconds. Atomic-scale sagging keeps the cavity mirrors near perfectly parallel. Light tests show high finesse, and ringdown tests confirm very low mechanical loss. The platform promises stable, high-yield quantum sensing devices.
arxiv-2603-02590:
Federico Villa, F Betül Durak, Tadayoshi Kohno, and colleagues extend cryptographic theory to AI agents in this 2026 paper. Language model agents now act with growing autonomy and authority. Permission systems aim to constrain them, but proposals lack a shared formal base. Comparing their security claims has been nearly impossible.

The authors first build an attack taxonomy tailored to language models. They then define agentic access control with a formal security game at its core. The game captures secrecy, integrity, and availability in one model. Within it, existing training-data secrecy approaches provably clash with completeness. A modular split of helpfulness and harmlessness is formalized and proven sound. Measurable security, they argue, needs that modular style of design.
arxiv-2603-02690:
Jian Sheng Wang presents VA-DAR, a 2026 protocol for recovering a serverless crypto wallet on a new device. Public lookup lists help recovery, but simple hashed IDs let strangers test guesses and learn who uses the service. His design must stay portable across vendors while hiding membership.

Recovery needs only an identifier such as an email plus one main passphrase. From that passphrase, separate keys seal the backup file and create a hidden lookup entry in a public registry. Version stamps and commitments expose tampering or rollback, and owner checks guard updates. Wang proves the security goals under standard assumptions. The scheme also leaves a path to post-quantum methods, if registry signatures are upgraded too.
arxiv-2603-02790:
Michelle Stegeman, Lena Philipp, Fennie van der Graaf, and a large consortium describe UNICORN, a unified benchmark for medical image AI. Older public challenges each test one narrow task, such as finding tumors in one scan type. Broad foundation models, trained across many body parts and diseases, need a wider yardstick.

UNICORN is designed to compare models across pathology, radiology, and language-linked tasks in one transparent framework. The paper lays out why standard, reproducible evaluation matters as AI enters diagnostic work, and how past challenges shaped current practice. By testing general representations rather than single-task tricks, the benchmark aims to show which models truly transfer. That should cut duplicate annotation work and expose weak spots before clinical use.
arxiv-2603-02990:
Rodrigo Coelho, Georg Kruse, and Jeanette Miriam Lorenz predict whether a quantum algorithm will succeed before running it. Their 2026 tool targets fixed-parameter QAOA, a quantum method for hard optimization problems that skips costly runtime tuning. Users still must guess good starting settings and how many layers the circuit needs.

A graph neural network reads the problem's graph and forecasts the chance of landing the optimal answer for many settings and depths. Predictions landed within a tenth of the true values in their tests. The model also generalized to unseen problem types, larger sizes, and deeper circuits. With such forecasts, users can pick promising problems and lean settings without burning quantum hardware time on trial runs.
arxiv-2603-03190:
Shogo Noguchi, Taketo Akama, Tai Nakamura, and colleagues identify songs from brain waves by teaching with two kinds of artificial targets. When people listen to music, cortex encodes both the sound itself and what the listener expects next. Artificial network representations resemble those brain patterns and can supervise EEG decoding.

The team pretrained decoders to predict either an acoustic representation or an expectation representation from artificial networks. Each target alone beat non-pretrained baselines, and combining both gave complementary gains beyond strong ensembles. Their expectation signal comes straight from raw audio with no hand labels, capturing predictive structure beyond onsets and pitch. The approach points toward general EEG models grounded in how cortex actually encodes sound.
arxiv-2603-03390:
Chairi Kiourt, Vassilis Evangelidis, and Dimitris Grigoropoulos simulate how people moved across rough ancient landscapes. Static finds alone rarely reveal transport strategies or spatial organization. Their 2026 framework populates a landscape with many independent agents and lets movement emerge from their decisions. Real elevation data becomes a detailed three-dimensional terrain where slope and ground shape directly constrain each step.

Agents differ by kind: human groups and animal-based transport each carry grounded traits like load, slope tolerance, and size. Navigation mixes a global route plan with local adjustment learned through reinforcement, so agents react to obstacles and each other without expensive replanning. Two test cases, a pursuit and evasion run and a comparison of pack animals against wheeled carts, show how terrain, visibility, and agent mix shape outcomes.
arxiv-2603-03590:
Oishik Chowdhury, Anushka Debnath, and Bastin Tony Roy Savarimuthu test whether multimodal models understand social rules. Robots in multi-agent systems must spot norms and violations, work long handled with rigid symbolic logic that fits only toy settings. Language models that see images as well as text promise broader judgment. Their 2026 evaluation gives five such models thirty text stories and thirty image stories posing norm questions, and compares their answers with humans.

Every model reasons better about norms in text than in images. GPT-4o leads in both formats and looks most promising for integration into agent systems, with a free model, Qwen-2.5VL, next. Complex norms challenge all five models regardless of format. The study maps a clear gap between reading about a social situation and actually seeing it.
arxiv-2603-03690:
Thanh Can and Thomas Rud complete the classification of measures on Cameron's elementary treelike Fraisse classes. Measures on Fraisse classes feed the Harman-Snowden construction of tensor categories, and treelike classes are a tractable source of cases. For the class of node-colored rooted binary tree structures with a given number of colors, the authors classify measures through a direct bijection. It links them to directed rooted trees whose edges carry color labels and which have a distinguished vertex.

Using families of these measures and their supports, they build Karoubi envelopes that yield infinite families of semisimple tensor categories with superexponential growth, beyond what Deligne's interpolation of representation categories can produce. They also prove that no measures exist on two related colored and labeled tree classes, extending Snowden's results for uncolored trees.
arxiv-2603-03790:
Qinsi Wang and fifteen colleagues argue that models read better when they first draw the text's skeleton. People facing hard reading mark key points, infer relationships, and structure the material. Their 2026 prompting technique, Structure of Thought, makes language models do the same, building an intermediate text structure before answering. It lifts performance consistently across eight tasks and three model families.

To measure the underlying skill they built T2S-Bench, the first benchmark for text-to-structure ability: nearly two thousand samples spanning six scientific domains and thirty-two structural types. Forty-five mainstream models took it, and the headroom is large. Average accuracy on multi-hop reasoning sits barely above half, and the best model's end-to-end node accuracy stays under three fifths. Fine-tuning on the benchmark stacks further gains on top of the prompting effect.
arxiv-2605-00090:
Martijn Janse and six co-authors demonstrate levitation of a ferromagnetic microsphere on a chip, at room temperature. Levitated microscopic objects in vacuum are prized for sensing and for macroscopic quantum physics, since they are so well isolated. Magnetic levitation covers many particle sizes and avoids hot trapping beams and electric field noise, but older magnetic schemes need bulky coils or magnets, low vibration frequencies, or cryogenic cooling.

Their platform stably levitates a nanogram sphere only micrometers across, on a scalable, tunable chip. Its rocking modes vibrate at frequencies above ten kilohertz, far stiffer than earlier magnetic traps. The authors point to further shrinking and coupling to solid-state spin qubits as a path toward cooling such a particle to its quantum ground state, besides uses in precision sensing.
arxiv-2605-00490:
Michal Valko and Milos Hauskrecht improve conditional anomaly detection, the search for data points that are odd relative to their context. In the conditional version, a pattern counts as anomalous only on a subset of attributes, judged against the values of the rest. Instance-based methods for this task lean hard on a distance metric, since the nearest examples decide what counts as normal here.

The authors study and devise a metric learning method that tunes the distance itself to reflect the conditional anomaly pattern as well as possible. Learning the metric, rather than accepting a default one, targets exactly the comparisons the detector will make. The paper's contribution is methodological: it shows how supervised metric learning can be adapted to conditional anomalies, where what 'near' should mean changes with context. That adaptation aims to lift the accuracy of a whole family of instance-based detectors.
arxiv-2605-00890:
Sergio D. Sierra M., Monica Sinha, Marcela Múnera, and Carlos A. Cifuentes evaluate models that classify posture and walker use from body skeleton data, aiming to make walker-assisted gait safer for older adults. Falls in this group cause severe injury and loss of independence. The team compares a geometric method, XGBoost, a support vector machine, and several deep learning designs on tasks for walker choice, standing versus sitting, and posture.

Geometric and XGBoost methods performed best overall. XGBoost reached near-perfect training accuracy on the binary tasks, and the geometric approach led on an eight-posture task, while deep models also scored strongly on binary tasks. The authors argue such classification can improve human-robot interaction in smart walkers and help prevent falls.
arxiv-2605-00990:
Ioanna Koutsouridou and seven co-authors use the NEFERTITI galaxy formation model to link the earliest galaxies to the assembly of the Milky Way. The model is coupled to about thirty high-resolution dark-matter simulations of Milky Way analogues, with local constraints and resolution down to minihaloes hosting the first stars. Ionization and chemical enrichment are tracked self-consistently and unevenly across space.

First star formation begins very early, peaks at an intermediate epoch, and persists to later times, producing small early systems. Present-day descendants span a huge range in iron abundance. Most stellar mass formed in place, but the accreted component dominates among the most metal-poor stars and is built mainly by a few massive destroyed dwarfs. The model also matches metal-poor Milky Way stars and a distant candidate system.
arxiv-2605-01690:
Hansol Lee and six co-authors retest a celebrated regularity in learning science: that students differ hugely in where they start but barely in how fast they learn. The claim, drawn from fits of a mixed-effects practice model across many course data sets, now feeds real conclusions about learners.

The team refit the same model on the same data under two choices of which practice records count: more of each student's work on a skill, or less. Starting-point variation holds steady across the choices. Learning-rate variation does not: it roughly doubles under one choice and grows several-fold under the other. Same model, same data, different answer, set only by an inclusion decision. The authors argue such sensitivity belongs at the center of any report that turns model estimates into claims about students.
arxiv-2605-01990:
Lázaro Sales and colleagues use fast radio bursts to estimate how much ordinary matter, in the form of baryons, fills the universe. The bursts are delayed as their signals pass through gas, and that delay tracks the gas along the path. The team uses 130 well-located bursts and rebuilds the expansion history from cosmic chronometer data with a neural network, without assuming a fixed model.

In a joint fit, they also estimate the gas contribution from each burst's host galaxy. The real data give a baryon density close to values from other methods, with a stated uncertainty near four percent. A mock catalogue test returns a similar value with tighter error, checking the method.
arxiv-2605-02190:
James Bagrow argues that Kolmogorov-Arnold networks need a curvature penalty to stay readable. These networks build functions from learnable one-variable activations, which gives accuracy and interpretability. In practice, well-fitting activations often develop sharp, high-curvature wiggles that are hard to read, and standard penalties do not stop them.

Bagrow derives a curvature penalty that does not depend on the chosen basis. Penalised models keep accuracy while reaching much smoother activations. By accounting for how composition shapes curvature, he proves an upper bound on the full model's curvature in terms of the penalty. That bound motivates richer penalty forms. The result targets the accuracy-interpretability trade-off that limits scientific machine learning.
arxiv-2605-02590:
Yogesh Shelke, Anpuj Nair S, and Hanumantha Rao Vutukuri study how the shape of tiny self-propelled rods controls the patterns a whole group forms. Shape effects are well known in still systems, but active rods move on their own. The team uses light-driven rods in experiments, matched with simulations, and varies rod length ratio and crowding.

As those knobs turn, the group shifts through distinct states: random active motion, swarming, turbulent flow, flocking, large clusters, and jamming. A state diagram sums up which conditions give which behavior, and analyses show sharp changes in number fluctuations across states. Because the system is minimal, physical effects can be separated from biological ones. The findings offer design rules for programmable active materials and a clean parallel to bacterial swarms.
arxiv-2605-02690:
Yash Madhwal and seven co-authors automate the tuning of Hyperledger Fabric, a blockchain platform whose speed depends on many interacting settings. Manual tuning is hard, and each test is noisy, so the team treats benchmarking as a black-box optimization problem. Their pipeline deploys a candidate setup, measures its throughput, and feeds the result back to the optimizer.

The search space, drawn from Fabric's own configuration files, has hundreds of dimensions, so dimension reduction is paired with Bayesian optimization. Sixteen combined variants plus random search were tried on a cloud testbed. The best pairing improved throughput by a clear margin over the starting setup, with a second method close behind. Measurement noise, the authors warn, must be kept in mind when reading such gains.
arxiv-2605-02890:
Umberto D'Alesio, Carlo Flore, and Marco Zaccheddu compute a spin effect planned for measurement at the future Electron-Ion Collider. The Collins asymmetry tracks how a quark's transverse spin shapes the direction of pions produced inside a jet. Past work used polarized proton-proton scattering; polarized lepton-proton collisions offer a cleaner, simpler route to the same physics.

Using a simplified momentum-dependent approach, the authors take the needed spin and fragmentation functions from earlier scattering and annihilation data. They compute asymmetries in the collider's range, at leading order and with a correction for near-real photon exchange. That correction matters across the range but does not overturn the dominance of quark-started channels, leaving gluons marginal. Cleaner access to the transversity distribution, including its sea-quark part, is the payoff.
arxiv-2605-03090:
Noman Bashir, Rob Sherwood, Le Xie, and Minlan Yu make the case for designing AI data centers and power grids together, not apart. Grids have long relied on millions of small users whose demands average out to a smooth total.

One large training campus breaks that pattern, drawing city-scale power that can swing by hundreds of megawatts in seconds with a single job. The authors contrast the cultures and incentives of the two sectors, show why coordination is hard, and list joint research needs in planning, control, protocols, and markets for a reliable AI future.
arxiv-2605-03190:
Zijian He, Adrian Sampson, Yiying Zhang, and Zhiyuan Guo present VDCores, a new way to program modern GPUs whose special units run out of step. Current software still packs work into single large kernels, which leaves those asynchronous units idle much of the time.

VDCores treats each unit as an isolated virtual core and splits work into small operations linked by dependencies. Overlap of memory and compute then happens automatically when resources are ready. On four language model workloads across three GPU types, decoding sped up by about a quarter on average, and kernel writing effort fell sharply. Code is open source.
arxiv-2605-03490:
Sapna Sachan, Amulya Kumar Mahto, and Prashant Wagambar Patil propose an orientation-aware system that classifies brain tumors across MRI sources without target labels. Scanners and protocols differ by hospital, expert labels are scarce, and those shifts badly hurt model generalization in real clinics.

Slices are first sorted into axial, sagittal, and coronal views, then handled by view-specific networks. A slice-wise adaptation strategy transfers knowledge from multi-modal source scans to post-contrast target scans, using discrepancy alignment plus pseudo-label guidance to keep classes distinct. Experiments show improved target performance over prior approaches, crediting the orientation split and guided adaptation.
arxiv-2605-03590: Busayo and colleagues build AfriVox-v2: a domain-verticalized benchmark for in-the-wild African speech recognition. The building builds. Their benchmark is domain-verticalized in-the-wild African speech recognition. The building builds. It is speech. AfriVox-v2 afrivox-v2s.
arxiv-2605-03690:
Filip Kronström and four co-authors build hierarchy-aware embeddings of knowledge graphs using graph neural networks enriched with meaning from ontologies. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked triples, but flat embeddings can ignore the class hierarchies that organize a domain. Their test application is predicting what gene deletions do to yeast.

Working with the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, they combine low-dimensional box embeddings with graph networks to predict cell growth for double gene knockouts. Cross-validated predictions beat baselines, and adding a semantic loss that aligns embeddings with ontology structure lifted accuracy further. The box embeddings also serve to judge revisions of a knowledge graph when no task of that kind is present.
arxiv-2605-04390:
Mu-Lin Li studies families of complex manifolds, where a whole collection of geometric spaces varies smoothly over a surface that serves as the parameter space. The manifolds are projective and non-uniruled, a restriction that rules out certain sweeping rational curves.

Suppose two such families agree point by point, in that the space over each parameter is isomorphic in both families. Li proves there is a large open set of parameters over which the families are locally isomorphic, meaning they match in whole neighbourhoods, not just at single points. The result partly answers a question posed by Wehler about when pointwise agreement forces local agreement.
arxiv-2605-04590:
Zishen Qu and seven co-authors rethink text-guided image segmentation, where a user names an object in words and the system outlines it. Borrowing features from diffusion image generators has become popular, but those models' generate-from-noise nature actively harms a task that needs precise discrimination.

Their framework instead learns a direct mapping from image to mask using rectified flow, a method that straightens the path between input and output. That removes the need to tune noise steps and improves accuracy, especially on categories never seen in training. Added label refinement and a one-step sampling strategy raise accuracy further while keeping inference fast.
arxiv-2605-04690:
Jan Rovirosa and Jesse Schmolze build a method for learning time-varying Markov dynamics, where a system's transition rules themselves drift, using financial time series as the testbed. Classical Markov operators are transparent and theoretically grounded, but estimating them by counting fails at fine resolution because the data become too sparse.

Their framework uses a neural network purely as a parameterisation engine. Its outputs are forced into the form of explicit, time-varying transition matrices. That preserves full interpretability of the learned dynamics. The learned operators capture regime shifts in the financial data. A stripped-down ablation that ignores state collapses exactly to no variation. That contrast confirms the structure is doing real work.
arxiv-2605-05090:
Quintin Pope and three co-authors present a pipeline for finding unexpected side effects when a language model is changed by training or editing. Changes such as distillation, knowledge editing, or unlearning can shift behaviour far beyond their target. Their method compares a base model and a changed model on aligned prompts, contrasting their free-form generations.

The pipeline turns the contrasts into plain-language hypotheses checked with statistics, and groups them into shared themes. On built test cases with added changes it recovered the known effects well. Applied to three real changes, it surfaced intended and surprise shifts, separated large from subtle changes, and avoided making up differences where none existed.
arxiv-2605-05190: Paul Burger and colleagues do release-free electro-optomechanical crystal modulator. The doing does. Their doing is release-free electro-optomechanical crystal modulator. The journal is opticajournal. It is photonics. The doing for. The modulator modulates electro-optomechanical-release-free.
arxiv-2605-05290:
András Grabarits, E. Medina-Guerra, and Adolfo del Campo study how quantum systems grow more complex over time. They focus on Krylov space, the smallest space in which a system's motion actually unfolds. Their systems are driven by Hamiltonians that change as time passes.

The team ties this motion directly to the Lie algebra behind the Hamiltonian. Ladder operators from that algebra generate the dynamics, and simple cases like a spinning particle in a rotating field fit the same frame. They also derive a new speed limit for complexity growth, and show when that limit can actually be reached.
arxiv-2605-05390:
Tracking a person's full body motion from cameras on a headset is the problem Nan Yang and five co-authors take on. The wearer moves, other people are partly hidden, and training data is scarce. Methods built for still cameras break down in this moving, first-person setting.

Their system, LAMP, first uses the headset's known motion and calibration to lift body keypoints into one shared 3D space. A transformer then fits the person's motion to that 3D data. The design beat earlier methods on standard tests and did far better in the egocentric setting it was built for.
arxiv-2605-05690:
Flat bands trap light in place and concentrate its interaction with matter, but making them usually demands delicate fabrication. Dun Wang and four co-authors engineer radiative flat bands in a single-layer honeycomb photonic crystal. Their trick is a gentle density-wave-like displacement of the lattice's air holes.

The periodic displacement couples flat-band states that normally sit below the light line up into the radiative continuum. There they can be excited and probed from free space. The strategy needs no exotic geometry or perfect multilayer alignment, offering a general recipe for flat-band photonics in a simple slab.
arxiv-2605-05790:
Smart glasses could help most if they knew when their wearer is mentally overloaded. Bin Wang and twelve co-authors present GazeMind, an agent that estimates cognitive load from eye gaze alone. Sensor-heavy alternatives are impractical in lightweight eyewear, and earlier gaze models were opaque and person-specific.

GazeMind encodes eye-tracking data into structured representations that a language model can reason over. The result is interpretable load predictions meant to generalize across individuals without task-specific fine-tuning. An assistant armed with that signal could time its help to moments when the user can actually absorb it.
arxiv-2605-05990:
Abdullah Al Shafi and Kazi Saeed Alam build a benchmark for removing motion blur from phone photos. Standard test scores average over all images, which hides how a method fares on easy versus severe blur. That hidden spread matters for tools that must run on consumer devices in daily use.

iPhoneBlur holds 7,400 image pairs made from high frame rate videos shot on an iPhone 17 Pro in varied real scenes. Samples are split into easy, medium, and hard tiers, backed by flow measures and rich metadata for each item. Six restoration models all dropped by 7 to 9 decibels from easy to hard tiers. The set also exposes a gap between pro and consumer cameras that targeted fine tuning largely closed.
arxiv-2605-06090:
Felipe Albino dos Santos gives a representation theoretic account of a recent discovery about orthogonal polynomials. Families of such polynomials had been found sitting in the centers of universal central extensions of superelliptic affine Lie algebras. Why they appear there, and why that particular family, called for an explanation inside representation theory.

Working in Verma modules of the Heisenberg subalgebra, dos Santos computes a canonical contravariant form in closed form on a special family of weight vectors. That family turns out to be the Legendre family, forced by the curve itself. The main result identifies a Sugawara element carried by an explicit intertwiner to the classical Legendre differential operator. All results are proved for the genus zero, four point case.
arxiv-2605-06390:
Aleksandr Bowkis and three co-authors argue that automating alignment research is harder and riskier than its proponents assume. A leading plan for aligning superintelligence uses AI agents to do a growing share of alignment research itself. Even with no deliberate sabotage, the authors warn, that plan could yield compelling but badly misleading safety assessments. It could end in the unintentional deployment of a misaligned system that everyone believed had been checked thoroughly and passed.

Alignment work is full of fuzzy tasks with no clear scoring, where human judgment is systematically flawed, so agent outputs would carry undetected systematic errors. Optimization pressure concentrates agent mistakes exactly where reviewers are least likely to catch them. Agent errors also differ from human ones, and shared training makes agent outputs correlate with each other. Scalable oversight and generalization, the leading remedies, face novel challenges in this setting.
arxiv-2605-06490:
Jonas Wiedermann-Möller, Leonard Dung, and Maksym Andriushchenko measure whether language model agents will break rules to reach a goal faster. Such instrumental behavior, like self-preservation, is hypothesized to matter for agent risk. Their benchmark uses realistic, low-stakes terminal tasks to reduce roleplay and evaluation awareness effects.

Each of seven tasks offers an official workflow and a policy-violating shortcut, under eight varied conditions. Ten models were tested over many samples with automatic scoring. Violations were rare overall, at about five percent, but concentrated in two Gemini models and three tasks. Making the shortcut necessary for success raised the rate far more than stressing how critical success was.
arxiv-2605-06690:
Debashis Guha, Amritendu Mukherjee, Sanjay Kukreja, and Tarun Kumar address two design choices recursive reasoning systems usually leave implicit: how to represent the growing state of reasoning, and when to stop. Such systems alternate between gathering evidence and consolidating what they know. The authors represent state as an epistemic graph holding claims, evidential links, open questions, and confidence weights.

Their stopping signal is the order-gap, the distance between states reached by expanding then consolidating versus the reverse order; agreement suggests more iteration will not help. They prove exactly when the linearized gap is informative near a fixed point, stressing this is a local condition only. Sketched uses include agent loops, tree-of-thought reasoning, and theorem proving.
arxiv-2605-06990:
Maria Despoina Siampou and six co-authors argue that city prediction needs movement, not just maps and images. Congestion, travel demand, and road safety depend on how people actually travel through a place. Trajectory data carry that signal, but sparse GPS points rarely line up with street-view images.

Their framework, TrajGANR, turns each trajectory into a continuous field that can be queried at any location along the path. That lets mobility data align with images taken off the path itself. Across four road-level tasks in San Francisco and Porto, it beats recent geospatial and trajectory models. Its location encoder also works where no imagery or trajectories exist.
arxiv-2605-07190:
Yu-Wen Xu and four co-authors create a higher-order topological phase in graphene using strain and light. Graphene is a standard playground for Floquet engineering, where shining circularly polarized light opens topological gaps. The team adds uniaxial strain and varies the light's angle of incidence to steer the effect.

Strain pushes graphene's electronic cones toward a merging point, making the light-induced mass strongly directional. With angled light, edges become gapped while robust corner modes survive, the signature of a second-order topological insulator. Calculations from first-principles-informed models confirm the predicted behavior, marking driven strained graphene as a tunable platform for such phases.
arxiv-2605-07290:
Masakazu Kato and two co-authors revisit a proof that answers to a quadratic wave equation in two space dimensions must blow up. The result, including a log-scale loss in lifespan guesses when an initial moment does not vanish, was already known with almost sharp constants. What was missing was a simpler proof suited to numerical use.

Using a slicing technique and looping over pointwise figures, the authors give that direct proof. Their aim is practical: a transparent argument whose figures analysts can apply. The paper is a proof-focused contribution, tightening how a known blow-up result for semilinear wave equations can be established.
arxiv-2605-07590:
Pedro Alonso and two co-authors look at why three-dimensional point cloud classifiers are easy to fool. Small shifts of the points that respect the surface shape can badly distort the model's internal features and flip its answer. They argue the root cause is a misalignment between the geometry the network learns and the true geometry of the surface.

Their framework, MAPR, adds features describing local curvature and diffusion structure, and trains the model to give consistent answers under shape-preserving perturbations. It needs no adversarial training and no extra data. Across several datasets and attacks, MAPR raised robustness substantially over plain models, by about twenty points on ModelNet40 and about nine points on ScanObjectNN in average gains.
arxiv-2605-07690:
Shijie Liu and three co-authors give time-series anomaly detection a certified defense, a guarantee that small adversarial tampering cannot flip its verdicts. Earlier certified defenses assume distortions measured by ordinary norms, which fit time series badly: a slight time shift is harmless yet changes those measures a lot. Dynamic time warping respects temporal alignment, but no certificate existed in that metric.

Adapting randomized smoothing, they build the first dynamic-time-warping certificate by bridging from the norm-based theory through a lower-bound transformation. Across datasets and models the defense held up in practice, improving F1 scores under warping-based attacks by up to about nineteen points over traditional certified models. Safety-critical monitoring is the intended beneficiary.
arxiv-2605-07790:
Hugo Vigna and Samuel Bontemps perform surgery on trained neural networks to fix their weakest classes, without retraining. The Hessian of a trained network has a telling spectrum: a bulk of near-zero eigenvalues plus a few large spikes, as many as the number of classes minus one. Earlier work described this structure but never used it operationally.

Their Hessian Surgery perturbs weights along the spike eigenvectors to rebalance per-class accuracy. A sensitivity matrix measures how each class's accuracy responds along each spike direction, a constrained optimization targets weak classes while protecting strong ones, and an adaptive budget grows or shrinks with progress. On CIFAR-10 and the ISIC-2019 skin lesion dataset, the method improved balanced accuracy and cut its spread across classes.
arxiv-2605-07890:
Claudio S. Montanari reflects on flavor, the pattern of fermion families, masses, and mixing, as the Standard Model's most successful yet least explained structure. The Higgs discovery completed the account of how mass is generated without explaining why the families and hierarchies look as they do. Neutrinos sit at the sensitive center of the puzzle, with tiny masses and large mixing.

Its long-baseline oscillation program and near-detector complex hunt for small, correlated departures from the minimal picture. arxiv-2605-08090:
Jaehwan Kim studies the rank-three lifting problem for incidence matrices of finite projective planes. A lift replaces the zero-one incidence pattern with richer entries while keeping the rank at most three, and earlier tropical methods could not see all the obstructions.

Working at the level of residues, Kim shows that any such lift, in residue characteristic other than three, forces a huge number of small zero rectangles whose cross-ratios are nontrivial. For planes of order at least six, no monomial lift exists at all, so any lift must use real first-order corrections. The hard remaining part of the problem is shown to be genuinely global.
arxiv-2605-08190:

arxiv-2605-08390:

Daniel Kynoch leads a large collaboration in 2026 mapping the gas around extreme coronal line emitting galaxies, rare nuclei that shine with unusually strong high-ionization lines. Several of these galaxies are linked to stars torn apart by their central black holes.

The team assembled optical spectra of thirty-three such galaxies and split them into changing, disruption-linked sources and steady, active-nucleus systems. In the changing ones, the highest-ionization iron lines flared and faded first, followed by lower lines, while oxygen brightened, suggesting the ionizing light softened or the illumination front moved outward. Line widths placed the glowing gas between the fast broad-line zone and the calm outer region. Gas distance grew with black hole mass in both groups alike.
arxiv-2606-04190:
Andrea Bonito and co-authors, including Ronald DeVore, settle a basic question in 2026. How well can a convex function of several variables be rebuilt from point samples? And what shape must the sampling take?

They prove matching upper and lower bounds for the best possible recovery. The lower bound shows no method can do better, no matter how clever. The upper bound gives a method that reaches the limit. Nonlinear sampling schemes reshape the problem in a helpful way: points cluster where the function bends most. Tests in simulations matched the theory. The result closes a gap in the theory of function recovery from data. It also guides how to place sensors for curved fields.
arxiv-2606-04690:
Lyu and coauthors hunt for a disputed particle state called Sigma 1380 in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. A resonance, in this setting, is a very short lived particle that shows up as a bump in data. Two experiments, Belle and BESIII, measured a decay of a heavier particle that might reveal it.

The team built a model where some particles form through interactions after the decay happens. They added both a known nearby state and the disputed Sigma 1380, then compared model curves with data. Adding the disputed state improved how well the model matched the measured mass and angle patterns. They also mapped which parts of the data react most strongly to that extra state. Better future measurements of this decay, they argue, could settle whether the Sigma 1380 exists. The claim stays open for now, since other work has explained the data without it.
arxiv-2606-04890:
Dobzinski and Shaulker break a barrier in the theory of trade between a buyer and a seller, in a 2026 arXiv economics paper. Both parties' values are drawn from independent distributions, and the goal is maximizing social welfare. The best fixed price guarantees at least 72 percent of optimal welfare, and none can guarantee more than about 73.8 percent. No other incentive-compatible mechanism was known to beat them.

The authors study the buyer-offering mechanism with a reserve price: the buyer makes a take-it-or-leave-it offer no lower than the reserve. They show some reserve price always guarantees 74.6 percent of optimal welfare. This improves the best known guarantee and proves fixed-price mechanisms are not optimal for bilateral trade.
arxiv-2606-05790:
Todorcevic and Jing Zhang build extreme colorings of pairs from any uncountable set in a 2026 arXiv paper. A coloring paints each pair of elements with one of countably many colors. Ramsey-style theorems hope for large calm sets where few colors appear. Strong colorings dash that hope as hard as possible. Their method rests on oscillations, counts of how walks between ordinals cross.

For any uncountable cardinal, their coloring hits every color on every large rectangular grid. The test sets need only be stationary, a weak form of largeness, near their shared top. Two hoped-for principles fall at once: a stationary Erdős-Rado theorem and a higher-dimensional Friedman property. Both are shown inconsistent with standard set theory. The authors also prove the result is optimal in several directions. The construction extends a line of work on walks that began in the early nineteen eighties.
arxiv-2606-05990:
Guolin Qin and Zhang prove a Harnack inequality for a critical nonlinear equation, with fine print stated up front in a 2026 arXiv paper. Harnack inequalities bound how wildly a positive solution can vary across a ball. For the critical p-Laplace equation the tools fail: Kelvin transforms and moving spheres need conformal invariance that the linear-like case enjoys. The authors assume critical Sobolev growth and a monotonicity condition on the nonlinearity.

Their result rests on two inputs from earlier work. Blow-up limits must classify as the Aubin-Talenti bubbles, and necks need a preliminary decay control. The heart is a Pohozaev-type neck argument. It upgrades the preliminary singular decay rate to the sharp rate of the p-harmonic fundamental solution. That upgrade delivers the Schoen-type estimate with a dimensional constant. Conditional progress is still progress: the neck argument supplies the missing step for general exponents.
arxiv-2606-06090:
Yaoqi Chen and a team argue an agent's memory should store execution state, not similar text in a 2026 arXiv paper. Long tasks chain interdependent decisions, and one bad step cascades. Similarity-based memory fragments those trajectories and mixes good traces with erroneous ones. Mage stores interactions in a hierarchical state tree instead. The agent's state is the path from root to current node, blending subgoal summaries, recent traces, and hints from sibling branches.

Four operations maintain the tree. Grow records new steps; Compress summarizes finished subgoals; Maintain validates the summaries; Revise rewinds to a clean boundary and branches anew. Context growth stays bounded while flawed segments are quarantined off the active path. On the MemoryArena benchmark, task success rose by eight to twenty points over baselines. Token consumption fell by over half at the same time. State integrity, not retrieval volume, is the paper's measure of memory quality.
arxiv-2606-06290:
Irem Topal and co-authors examine the physics style patterns of brain activity in early psychosis in this 2026 arXiv paper. Healthy large scale brain activity shows scale invariant dynamics, patterns that look similar at every zoom level, suggesting the brain works near a critical regime. That regime is prized for long range links and efficient processing. Earlier studies of such disorders used scattered measures, so it was unclear whether they pointed at one shared change.

The team combined three analyses on resting state fMRI scans from patients and healthy controls: a phenomenological renormalization group method, power spectral density, and detrended fluctuation analysis. Controls showed the expected critical like scaling. Patients kept the same overall scale invariant pattern, so criticality was not simply lost. Instead, their scaling exponents shifted across several measures at once. The authors read this as a reshaping of collective brain activity within a preserved critical regime.
arxiv-2606-06890:
Vision language models often answer from what text usually says, not from what the picture shows. Zhou, Zhang, Wang, and Wang diagnose that habit in this 2026 arXiv paper. They call it visual ignorance: confident answers with weak grounding in the image. Their study looks both inside the model and at the benchmarks judging it.

Inside, they swap layers and probe each layer's signals. Visual meaning often fades in the middle layers. Later layers can bury what survives under text biases. Outside, they blur test images step by step. Many questions stayed answerable even when the image was nearly destroyed. That held across twelve benchmarks and three models. So current tests can reward ignoring the picture. The authors urge training and testing on counterfactual data. Such data would force models to actually look.
arxiv-2606-06990:
Fake patient records let researchers share medical data without exposing real patients. Jalen Jiang and co-authors build the arena where generators of those records compete fairly in this 2026 arXiv paper. The field's code bases clash with each other. Data loaders, library versions, and scoring rules all differ. Head to head comparisons have been nearly impossible.

Their framework runs one pipeline from data intake to final scores. It reimplements four known generators under one roof. A plain GPT-2 baseline joins them as a reality check. All models produce diagnosis code histories at full vocabulary size. A shared privacy utility suite grades every model the same way. Bootstrapped confidence intervals accompany all metrics. The analysis exposes weak performance on rare, long tail diagnoses. A simple general model proved surprisingly competitive. Specialized designs, the authors imply, must now earn their complexity.
arxiv-2606-07090:
A mostly real video with a few fake seconds is a nastier forgery than a fully fake one. Umur, Guslu, and Delibasoglu study that scenario in this 2026 arXiv paper. Existing data sets cover deepfakes and object removal well. They poorly model a short manipulated clip spliced into authentic footage that then resumes.

The authors review those data sets and pinpoint the gap. They curate a custom test set for the spliced case. Two detectors establish the first benchmark on it. A supervised probe on modern visual features classified frame by frame. It missed most manipulated frames, struggling to generalize. An unsupervised method compared consecutive frames by feature similarity. It found the tampering boundaries far more reliably. On one hundred untouched control videos it held a near zero false alarm rate. Video level accuracy reached ninety five percent.
arxiv-2606-07190:
Judging a partial solution by whether each step is correct misses the point: does it make success more likely? Zhou, Cao, and Ye build a grader around that question in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reasoning prefixes are the opening stretches of a model's chain of thought. Their value, the authors argue, is the gain in solve rate they cause.

A lightweight student model measures that gain directly. Conditioned on a good prefix, the student finishes more problems. The Prefix Utility Model learns to predict these gains from paired comparisons. It can score both finished attempts and prefixes still in progress. Across best of many sampling, beam search, and reinforcement learning on math tasks, the signal proved strong. Benefits grew with larger candidate pools and tighter reward sparsity. The utility scores also transferred to stronger policies than the student. Correctness is a proxy; outcome gain is the thing itself.
arxiv-2606-07690:
Ning Wang and co-authors present HARP, a cheaper way to choose finetuning data for large language models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Picking the right training examples matters, but the most faithful selection methods retrain models many times to score each candidate, which is costly. Cheaper proxy methods are fast yet often miss what the target task actually needs.

HARP organises the training pool into a hierarchy of regions and leaves, then measures only representative leaves by actually finetuning on them. Statistical estimates fill in the value of unmeasured examples, and two selection rules balance caution about redundancy against rewards for complementary regions. In experiments the variants took the best results, beating the strongest baseline by up to about nine points. They did so while using roughly seven times fewer training examples, which cuts the selection bill sharply.
arxiv-2606-07790:
El Mir, Takáč, and Lahlou probe how language-model agents cooperate when one of them betrays the group, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is a four-player Stag Hunt, a game where cooperation pays best only if everyone commits. Talk between rounds is cheap talk, messages that cost nothing and bind no one. Byzantine agents signal cooperation, then defect.

Across six model families and seven hundred twenty trials, honest agents spotted betrayal within one round yet failed to adapt together. Many kept cooperating while being exploited, because the game's unanimity payoff blocks collective recovery. Restricting who can talk to whom collapsed cooperation when the restriction was announced, yet the same restriction applied silently left cooperation nearly perfect. Failure therefore comes from reasoning about hidden information, not from losing it. Two archetypes appeared in every cohort: models that defect forever after betrayal, and models that keep cooperating at cost.
arxiv-2606-07890:
Jaewook Lee and Zrnic study prediction when the world reacts to the predictor and drifts on its own, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Performative prediction covers feedback loops: a deployed model changes the population it predicts, as when disease forecasts trigger interventions that slow the disease. Classical distribution shift treats change as external. Real deployments mix both: partially performative prediction.

Their framework lets the data distribution evolve partly in response to the deployed model and partly through an outside process. The field's two central targets, performative stability, a model that remains best for the distribution it creates, and performative optimality, are extended into online versions tracking the moving environment. The authors analyse practical heuristics, especially repeated retraining, and characterise when it adapts and when it falls behind. The work gives learning systems a language for settings where fighting the drift and causing it are both part of the job.
arxiv-2606-08090:
Kyoungmin Kim, Martin Catheland, and Anastasia Ailamaki speed up a workhorse of data processing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The subject is the semantic filter: asking a language model a yes-no question about each document in a corpus. Calling the model on everything is the gold standard but prohibitively expensive, so systems cascade: a cheap proxy scores documents, and uncertain ones escalate.

The authors catalogue four structural weaknesses in current cascades. Each family commits to one representation and one fixed pipeline, winning only in a narrow regime. The strongest online proxies ignore established representation-learning tools and miss token-level evidence. They train on binary labels, discarding the big model's confidence exactly at the boundary documents that matter most. And their calibration is over-conservative, escalating far more documents than needed. Against this diagnosis they present a unified framework and an adaptive two-phase fix.
arxiv-2606-08190:
Chandia studies a question in string theory in this short 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is the heterotic pure spinor superstring, a form of string theory that treats supersymmetry, the symmetry between matter and force particles, in a clean algebraic way. Chandia asks when a curved ten-dimensional background still allows conserved worldsheet charges, quantities that stay fixed as the string moves and that match supersymmetry in ordinary spacetime. The charges must also respect a symmetry condition known as BRST invariance.

In flat space, these conditions reproduce the familiar generator of ten-dimensional supersymmetry, confirming the construction is sound. In curved space, they organize into a tidy set of constraints on the background geometry. The key object is a normalizable spinor superfield, a field with well-behaved size whose lowest part is the spinor used in standard treatments of compactification, where extra dimensions curl up small.
arxiv-2606-08390:
Kuskova, Zaytsev, and Coppedge ask when an interaction found by a neural network is real, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neural time-series models sometimes report that one variable modulates another's effect on a target. The authors argue this is a question of identifiability: whether the data could pin down one explanation at all. They study a model where source contributions are gated, meaning scaled up or down, by other lagged variables.

The analysis shows that capacity is not identifiability. Dependent inputs cause leakage between interaction terms, and low-dimensional support permits distinct decompositions that agree on all observed data while differing elsewhere. The authors then prove an identifiability theorem for normalized minimal decompositions under explicit support conditions. They package the theory into a pre-fit diagnostic, a check practitioners can run before training.
arxiv-2606-08790:
De Valois-Franklin and Bogdan specify RAILS, a clearing system for commerce between autonomous software agents, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agents now negotiate, buy services, and move money for their users. Yet no neutral mechanism decides whether an agent actually met its obligation, who is at fault when it did not, and what payment should follow. They call this the agentic clearing problem, arguing that paying, authorizing, and judging are each different from clearing.

RAILS combines a per-output reliability score, a published reliability record, and a clearing function that consumes both. Its protocol rests on seven primitives, from an Obligation Object stating the duty to Finality Rules closing the case. The central guarantee is a soundness property: no financially material settlement is issued on evidence weaker than the floor the obligation itself sets. The property can be checked against the specification, making the design falsifiable.
arxiv-2606-09090:
Treude and Baltes name a quiet decay creeping into AI-assisted programming: the instruction files guiding coding assistants drift out of sync with the code, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Developers now maintain persistent configuration files, such as CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md, describing architecture and conventions to their AI tools. As software evolves, these files go stale, a phenomenon the authors call context rot, and stale context misleads every AI session trusting it. Documentation researchers spent decades building consistency checkers for exactly this class of problem.

The paper maps that toolbox, built for READMEs, comments, and API docs, onto the new artifacts as a roadmap. As evidence, the authors applied a README and wiki consistency checker to a representative sample of 356 repositories. It found stale code-element references in 23 percent of them. The result shows existing tools already surface context rot unmodified, giving the field a running start.
arxiv-2606-09290:
Xu and colleagues split visual reasoning across a team of agents that are all the same model wearing different hats, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A single chain of thought commits early to one reading of an image, then defends it, hallucinations included. Visual Para-Thinker++ instead instantiates one shared multimodal policy as three roles. ashton-curious-creatures-in-zoology-1890:
John Ashton fills a cabinet of strange beasts in Curious Creatures in Zoology, his book of 1890. Ashton was a scribe who loved old prints and tales. He draws on sea logs, priest books, and fair tales. His hoard holds beasts that sit twixt lore and life. The kraken drags ships down. The sea serpent haunts a score of ships.

Each beast gets its tales, dates, and draws in Ashton's wry, rich prose. He grants doubt, yet loves the hoard too much to scorn it. The book is a joy for fans of strange life.
blake-marriage-heaven-hell-1790:
William Blake printed The Marriage of Heaven and Hell around 1790 by his own method of illuminated printing, words and designs etched together on copper plates. The work mixes prose argument, proverbs, and vision into one prophetic book. It stands as the founding text of Blake's mythic system.

Blake attacks the tame religion of his day and praises energy, desire, and creative fire against cold reason. His Proverbs of Hell, like the road of excess leading to the palace of wisdom, still get quoted worldwide. The book remains a landmark of visionary Romantic religion and of poetry as picture.
bohm-bawerk-capital-interest-smart-1890:
Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk was an Austrian economist and finance minister who took on Marx's theory of value head-on. His Capital and Interest, in Smart's 1890 translation, is the Austrian school's great statement on why interest exists. It mixes close criticism of rival theories with a positive account of his own.

Bohm-Bawerk argues that people value present goods above future goods of the same kind, and that interest prices that gap. Roundabout methods of production, which take longer, yield more, and interest helps coordinate them. His demolition of exploitation theories of interest set terms of debate for a generation.
burnet-sacred-theory-of-the-earth-vol2-1:
Volume two of Burnet's Sacred Theory, in English in 1690, holds the two last books. The third book treats the burning of the world to come. The fourth treats the new heavens and new earth after that fire. Burnet closes with a review of his theory and its proofs.

His Earth passes from smooth Paradise, through the Deluge's ruin, to final flame and renewal. Prophecy and natural philosophy march together through the scheme. Readers of the age praised the sweep and the prose alike. The two English volumes complete his famous system. Modern geology grew partly by arguing with Burnet. His questions about Earth's past outlived his answers.
carnot-motive-power-heat-thurston-1890:
Sadi Carnot was a young French engineer who asked a simple question: how much work can heat do? His short memoir first came out in 1824, when he was only in his twenties. Robert Thurston's English version, issued in 1890, is the form most readers meet here.

Carnot argues that a heat engine works best when heat moves from hot to cold in a smooth, reversible cycle. No engine can beat that ideal, no matter how it is built. His reasoning gave later scientists the seed of the second law of heat science, and the cycle still bears his name.
cia-0000009190:
Allen W. Dulles, director of central intelligence, addressed the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in a statement dated April 1960. Dulles was the CIA's best-known chief, a lawyer turned spymaster from the Second World War's secret services. Open testimony by a sitting director was still unusual.

The statement lays out the director's case before the Senate's senior foreign policy body. Such appearances shaped how Congress funded and watched over secret work. Weeks later, the U-2 shootdown would test Dulles and his agency severely. The file preserves his public footing just before that storm, in his own official words.
cia-0000009590:

Recovery figures carried political weight, since communists led many French unions and strikes could halt production. Analysts read output statistics as signs of stability or trouble. The paper shows economic reporting serving strategy in the early Cold War. France's rebirth as an industrial power can be watched here at its measured, uncertain start.
cia-0000009690:

Unconfirmed camps posed a lasting dilemma for the accounting. Chasing every rumor wasted effort, yet ignoring one could abandon a living man. Analysts recorded the location and its uncertainty together, honestly. Later evidence might promote or kill the lead. This file is that honest record: a place on the map with a question mark kept beside it.

Activity reports followed such men over time rather than in a single sighting. Patterns could show whether a man moved freely or under guard. That difference decided how officials treated his case. Domestic subjects made this file different from the foreign reports around it. Watching Americans at home later became one of the CIA's great scandals of the 1970s. Read now, the paper shows that watch in progress, numbered and routine. It preserves evidence for a lasting argument about where secret intelligence work should properly stop.

The Shah ruled Iran with American backing, eight years after the coup that restored his power. The estimate weighs the Shah's hold on his throne and the strength of those who opposed him. It also treats Iran's place in the contest between the West and the Soviet Union. The pages preserved here show the intelligence community's shared view of a key ally whose stability it rarely doubted aloud.
