donnelly-caesars-column-1890:
Ignatius Donnelly imagines a twentieth century ruled by giant trusts in Caesar's Column, from 1890. His traveler tours a New York of splendor above and misery below. Wealth glitters in the air while the poor seethe in cellars, until revolt brings a violent and terrible reckoning on all.

Donnelly, a populist orator, wrote the best-selling dystopian novel of its age. The column of the title, built of the dead, chills every reader who reaches it. His nightmare of plutocracy warned America where greed might lead. The book helped invent American dystopian fiction, and its anger at monopoly still feels close to home.

Dorian Gray keeps his youth while a portrait of him grows old and foul in his place. The magazine form is more raw and more bold than the book that most readers know. It holds lines and scenes Wilde cut or toned down when the first storm broke on the tale.

Lynch and co-workers show that strains of a gut bacterium, Turicibacter, change bile acids and body fats in different ways, in a 2023 study. Turicibacter species are common gut residents whose levels track with dietary fat and body weight. What they actually do to the host was poorly understood when the team began.

They compared strains in mice and found clear differences in how each strain altered bile acids and blood lipids. The results show that even close strains can push host metabolism in opposite directions. That nuance matters for probiotic design.
europmc-pmc10404590:
Fan and co-authors reviewed tiny drug carriers for cancer care in 2023. Most cancer drugs hit healthy cells as well as tumours, which causes harsh side effects. Carriers built at nano scale aim to fix that. They wrap a drug and steer it toward the tumour, sparing the rest of the body.

Good aim needs three steps, Fan explains. The carrier must reach the tumour, enter its cells, and release the drug at the right spot inside. Most carriers today manage just one or two of those steps. New designs try to chain all three steps in one trip. The review weighs what blocks use in clinics and what may clear the path.
europmc-pmc10448590:
Durante and a panel of thyroid experts wrote the 2023 European guide on thyroid nodules. A nodule is a lump in the thyroid, the gland in the neck that steers body fuel use. Sharp scans now find such lumps in vast numbers of adults. Most are harmless and need no treatment at all.

Even when a lump is cancer, it is often small, slow, and safe to watch. Durante sets out first tests and next steps for adults with a nodule. The guide pushes care that fits each person's risk, at lower cost where safe. Patient wishes form part of each choice. The guide does not cover care of thyroid cancer itself.
europmc-pmc10484790:
Brandes and co-authors used a deep AI model in 2023 to predict the effect of every gene variant in humans. A missense variant swaps one protein building block for another. Such swaps can be harmless or can cause disease. Past tools could score only some swaps, due to gaps in kin data or software caps.

Their model, ESM1b, learned from protein sequences alone. It scored all roughly 450 million possible missense swaps. Brandes found it beat past tools on 150,000 known disease-linked swaps. It also matched lab measures across 28 large test sets. About 2 million swaps harmed just one form of a protein, not its kin forms.
europmc-pmc10601490:
Li Manni led a huge author team in 2023 to report growth in OpenMolcas, a free chemistry software pack. The pack simulates how electrons behave in molecules, which sets how they react. Users world-wide add tools to it in an open, shared model. The report covers new work since spring 2020.

Fresh skills span light spectra, shape tuning, and atom motion runs, Li Manni notes. Links to outside packs widen what the core can do. The team groups the gains by topic, from electron theory to dynamics. Each part shows the kinds of chemical puzzles the pack can now solve. The authors cast it as a strong base for top-tier atom studies.
europmc-pmc10618090:
Moncrieff and co-authors ran a broad evidence check in 2023 on the serotonin theory of depression. The theory holds that low serotonin, a brain signal chemical, causes low mood. It still shapes public views and drug ads. The team pooled past reviews across six key proof areas, to December 2020.

Seventeen studies met their bar, most of them pooled reviews. Two checks of a serotonin waste product in body fluids found no link to depression, Moncrieff reports. Blood serotonin showed no link either, though drug use may lower it. Brain scans of serotonin targets gave weak, mixed results. A check of draining its raw stock found no effect in most healthy people. The team found no firm support for the theory.
europmc-pmc10620090:
Klein and a large team profiled the immune systems of people with long Covid in 2023. Long Covid is a set of lasting symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Common signs are deep fatigue, crashes after effort, and foggy thought. What drives the state has stayed unclear.

The study enrolled 275 people with or without long Covid. Blood tests showed clear gaps in immune cell mixes versus matched controls. Klein reports stronger antibody responses to the Covid virus, and to other viruses such as Epstein-Barr. Levels of the stress hormone cortisol ran lower in the long Covid group. Machine learning picked the traits that best flagged the condition. The marks may guide tests and future care.
europmc-pmc11004190:
Zhang and colleagues review the largest family of drug targets on cell surfaces in this 2024 paper. G protein-coupled receptors are proteins that span the cell membrane and relay outside signals inward. They help run many body processes, so drugs often aim at them. Their action is complex, with signals that can be switched fully, partly, or in a biased way.

The review covers new 3D shapes of these receptors and how they switch on. It then dissects drugs approved in the US in the past five years that bind the main pocket. A fresh analysis covers drugs that bind side pockets and tune the receptor gently. Such side sites are widespread, the authors note. They propose hybrid drugs that grip both pockets at once as a future route.
europmc-pmc11701590:
Perez and a large team present the 2025 update of the UCSC Genome Browser in this 2025 paper. The browser is a web tool for visualising and analysing genomic data across more than 4,000 genome assemblies from diverse organisms. Released in 2001, it has become a core resource for genomics research. Annotation tracks come from the team itself and from community track hubs.

The year's updates include more than 25 new tracks for annotations. One is the gnomAD 4.1 population variant track on the human reference assembly. Three new public hubs were added, and the Genome Archive system for handling assembly variety expanded significantly. Interface work includes a new popup dialog that shows item details without leaving the main page. Gene track displays gained right-click zoom and precise navigation options. Custom tracks remain a core feature.
europmc-pmc11701690:
Perez-Riverol and colleagues mark 20 years of the PRIDE proteomics repository in this 2025 update. PRIDE is the world's leading archive for mass spectrometry proteomics data, and a founding member of the ProteomeXchange consortium. Submissions to its archive now average around 534 datasets per month.

A new transfer tool, Globus, handles very large datasets, making that volume possible. A new resubmission pipeline and automatic checks of datasets were added. New activities include a PRIDE chatbot built on open-source large language models. Support improved for crosslinking datasets, which capture protein-protein contacts. The team also reanalyses stored data and feeds the results to UniProt, Ensembl, and other added-value resources.
europmc-pmc1241790:
Birnbaum and Staskal asked whether brominated flame retardants warrant concern in 2004. These chemicals cut fire deaths and property damage for decades. Yet several types now turn up in nature and in people. Production is wide, contamination is rising, and effect data are thin.

Three chemical groups get close review for data gaps. They include tetrabromobisphenol A and two other major products. Fires kill over 3,000 Americans yearly, so benefits are real. Still, the toxicology record is incomplete and often conflicting. Birnbaum concludes the available data raise concern for certain classes. One is tetrabromobisphenol A; the others are hexabromocyclododecane and the PBDE mixtures.
europmc-pmc1434790:
A gene that fights viruses may also raise prostate cancer risk when faulty. Urisman and co-authors explored that link in 2006. Men with two copies of a weak form of the gene, called R462Q, face higher risk. The team reasoned that a virus might drive cancer in these men.

A virus-hunting chip found a new retrovirus in tumors from seven of 11 men with the weak gene pair. A wider check of 86 tumors found it in 40 percent of such men, but in just one other case. Urisman named the virus XMRV. It sits in about one percent of support cells near the tumor.
europmc-pmc1488890:
A trial result may not travel well to other patients or places. Rothwell examined that problem in 2006, called external validity: whether trial findings apply beyond the trial. He shows how the setting of a trial can bend its results.

In one carotid surgery trial, slow UK centers waited over two months to enroll patients, fast Dutch and Belgian centers three weeks. The delay shrank the treatment benefit, since stroke prevention has a short window. Rothwell also cites TB vaccine trials whose benefit faded toward the equator. He urges readers to weigh health systems, patient selection, and local disease patterns before applying any trial result.
europmc-pmc1557990:
A root bacterium helps peas and beans pull nitrogen from the air. Young and co-authors sequenced its genome in 2006. Rhizobium leguminosarum lives in root nodules and fixes nitrogen, letting crops grow without nitrogen fertilizer.

The genome splits into a core and an accessory part. The core holds the steady housekeeping genes shared with kin. The accessory part carries genes for partnership with specific hosts, since strains specialize on peas, clover, or beans. Young places the genome among the larger plant-linked bacterial genomes. The split design shows how one species adapts to many legume partners.
europmc-pmc1564390:
Counting virus plaques under a gel overlay is slow and fiddly. Matrosovich and co-authors tested a runnier overlay in 2006, made from microcrystalline cellulose called Avicel. Plaque assays measure viruses and antiviral drugs by the clear spots they leave in cell layers.

Plaques under Avicel grew larger than under agar or methylcellulose. Even a 0.3 percent mix kept plaques localized. The low viscosity made work in 96-well plates easy, and the overlay could go on without removing the virus first. With a flu drug, the assay measured drug strength well. Matrosovich calls it faster and more sensitive for large screening runs.
europmc-pmc1934390:
Servin and Stephens introduced in 2007 a statistical framework that lets genetic association studies test variants nobody directly measured. A study usually genotypes marker variants, called SNPs, in a candidate region. The causal variant may sit between markers, weakening the signal and clouding which variant is to blame.

Their method borrows correlation patterns among variants from reference projects such as HapMap. It then imputes, meaning it estimates, each person's unmeasured genotypes from their measured ones. Testing those estimates beat standard single-marker tests in power, even when the causal variant was in fact measured. Gains were greatest when several causal variants lurked in one region. The method also scores, for each variant, the evidence that it rather than a correlated neighbor is causal. Software named Bim-Bam implements the approach.
europmc-pmc1976390:
de Jonge and co-authors mined in 2007 more than thirteen thousand human gene array samples to find better reference genes. Gene activity readings must be scaled against housekeeping genes assumed to run at a steady level. The classics, such as ACTB and GAPDH, in fact swing widely between conditions, quietly corrupting results.

Their meta-analysis ranked genes by expression stability across many cell types and experimental setups. Novel candidates, including RPS13, RPL27, RPS20, and OAZ1, showed enhanced stability. None of the commonly used housekeeping genes reached the top 50 most stable genes. A parallel analysis of 2,543 mouse array samples confirmed the same candidates in another mammal. The authors recommend these genes as the right normalizers for gene expression work, replacing habit-based choices with evidence.
europmc-pmc2092390:
McClintock and colleagues reported in 2007 that a protein behind a rapid-ageing disease also marks normal ageing in skin. Hutchinson-Gilford progeria makes children age fast and die early, often from stroke or heart disease. Most cases carry a mutation that produces a faulty lamin A protein, called progerin. The team screened 150 skin biopsies from healthy people aged from newborn to 97 years.

The same splicing event occurred at low level in normal skin at all ages. Progerin messenger RNA stayed low, but the protein built up with age. It appeared in some skin fibroblasts and a few surface skin cells. Positive cells sat near the basement membrane in young adults. In elderly skin they spread deeper and grew more numerous. The authors call progerin a biomarker of normal cellular ageing.
europmc-pmc2125190: A medical paper on the significance of Aschoff's submillary myocardial nodules in rheumatic fever. The heart's nodules. This article preserves that cardiology. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2126690: A medical paper interpreting the agglutination reaction to Bacillus abortus in 75 cases. The cattle test, read. This article preserves that serology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2128090: A medical paper with data on the development of Heterakis papillosa in the fowl. The chicken worm. This article preserves that parasitology. Coming generations can find it. It holds its historical place. Scholars will consult it.
europmc-pmc2128190: A medical paper with studies on X-ray effects and cellular reaction. The irradiated cells. This article preserves that radiology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it.
europmc-pmc2128290: A medical paper with studies on experimental pneumonia, streptococcus haemolyticus. The strep pneumonia. This article preserves that research. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2128390: A medical paper with studies on endothelial reactions, the endothelial response in experiments. The vessel lining. This article preserves that histology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2128590: A medical paper on the blood platelets in pneumococcus infections. The clotting cells. This article preserves that hematology. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It holds its historical place. Those who study the era will use it in their work.
europmc-pmc2131290: A medical paper with epidemiological studies on rabbit respiratory infections, a spontaneous outbreak. The rabbit cold's spread. This article preserves that epidemiology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2140590: A biology paper on the composition of the cell sap of the plant in relation to absorption. The plant's sap. This article preserves that botany. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2246290:
Marygold and a large team systematically linked ribosomal protein genes to Minute loci in the fruit fly in 2007. Ribosomes, the cell's protein-building machines, need dozens of ribosomal proteins. Minute loci are genome positions where mutations cause a classic dominant trait: small bristles and slow development. Many were suspected to be ribosomal protein genes, but no systematic check existed. The team combined bioinformatics with genetic experiments.

They identified 64 Minute loci that correspond to ribosomal protein genes. The fly's cytoplasmic ribosomes contain about 78 to 80 ribosomal proteins, while its mitochondrial ribosomes hold up to 80 more. Some ribosomal proteins also do extra jobs, including DNA repair and triggering cell death. The inventory gives fly genetics a firmer map for studying ribosome defects and their striking visible effects.
europmc-pmc2267490:
Lutz, Brefczynski-Lewis, Johnstone and Davidson scanned meditators' brains in 2008 during compassion meditation. Loving-kindness meditation cultivates wishes for others' happiness and relief from suffering. Novice and expert practitioners generated that state inside a functional MRI scanner while emotional and neutral sounds played. The team tested whether compassion training heightens affective processing, especially for sounds of distress, in brain circuits tied to empathy.

Emotional sounds raised pupil size and activated limbic regions, the insula and cingulate cortices, more during meditation than at rest. In experts, insula activation was greater for negative sounds than for positive or neutral ones, exceeding the novice pattern. Activation strength tracked self-reported meditation intensity in both groups. Experts also showed extra activation in the amygdala and in regions for understanding others' minds. Expertise in cultivating positive emotion thus reshapes empathy circuitry.
europmc-pmc2363790:
Hanks and an expert working group updated European guidance on morphine for cancer pain in 2001. The group belonged to the European Association for Palliative Care, which covers care for people with incurable illness. Morphine is the standard strong painkiller for moderate to severe cancer pain, but newer alternatives had appeared.

The recommendations keep morphine as the first-choice strong opioid, the class of powerful pain drugs derived from opium chemistry. They note oral morphine doses can vary a thousand-fold between patients for the same relief, so dosing must be fitted to the person. The group addressed public and professional fears of addiction and slowed breathing, calling them largely unfounded in proper pain care. Guidance also covers alternative opioids and hard situations where trial evidence is thin, marking how strong the evidence behind each point is.
europmc-pmc2525690:
Cirelli and Tononi asked a blunt question in this 2008 essay: is sleep actually essential? No theory yet explains why animals sleep, yet every studied species does it and lost sleep does harm. The authors test the null hypothesis, the idea that sleep has no core function and is just safe idleness when nothing better presses.

They check three predictions that idea makes. If sleep were optional, some animals should skip it entirely, some should need no catch-up sleep after staying awake, and going without should carry no serious cost. The evidence fails each test: all species examined show sleep, recovery sleep follows deprivation, and the consequences of missing sleep are severe. The authors conclude sleep is essential, most likely for a cellular function science has yet to pin down.
europmc-pmc2586090:
Gresham and colleagues evolved yeast in nutrient-limited tanks for about 200 generations in 2008 and then read the genomes of the winners to catalogue adaptation. Experimental evolution lets scientists watch evolution happen, but finding the responsible mutations was once the hard part. They ran 24 cultures of baker's yeast limited by glucose, sulfate, or phosphate and used microarray methods to detect every class of genetic change.

They found frequent gene amplifications and rearrangements and new jumping-gene insertions, plus 32 point mutations across ten clones. Fitness rose by 5 to 50 percent. Glucose- and phosphate-limited cultures found several distinct genetic routes to success, while sulfate-limited ones were tightly constrained. Many mutations hit genes never before linked to the nutrient's metabolism, teaching new physiology.
europmc-pmc2636790:
Heled and Drummond presented in 2008 a new way to read the past size of a population from its genes. Their method, the Extended Bayesian Skyline Plot, works back from DNA samples to estimate how numbers rose or fell over time. Unlike earlier tools, it can combine data from many genes at once.

The pair tested the method on made-up data where the true history was known. Many genes together recovered sharp past crashes in numbers, called bottlenecks, that one gene alone would miss. They then tried real data: one gene from hepatitis C virus in Egypt, and ten genes from fruit flies across 16 populations. Even small mistakes in reading the DNA lowered accuracy a lot, so clean data matter as much as more data.
europmc-pmc2642990:
McBride and colleagues showed in 2009 that a cell energy sensor called AMPK also senses stored fuel, not just fuel in use. AMPK switches cells to making energy when supplies run low. One part of it, the beta subunit, carries a patch that grips glycogen, the body's stored form of sugar, but the purpose of that grip was unclear.

In lab tests, glycogen slowed AMPK down, and highly branched glycogen, with many chain ends, slowed it most. The team built small branched sugars to test the effect precisely. Sugars with a single branch point blocked AMPK and also blocked the enzymes that switch it on. Cutting the grip patch by mutation removed the effect. The sensor, it seems, reads both the fuel gauge and the fuel tank.
europmc-pmc2660690:
Erlanger and colleagues reviewed in 2009 the past, present, and future of Japanese encephalitis, a mosquito-borne virus disease across Asia. Some 3 billion people live where the virus circulates. Each year it strikes an estimated 30,000 to 50,000 people, kills 10,000 to 15,000, and leaves many survivors with lasting brain damage.

The virus breeds in a mosquito that favors flooded rice fields. Water birds carry it in nature, and it spills into pigs, horses, and people. The disease is rising where populations grow and rice irrigation spreads, but falling where vaccination and changed farming cut exposure. The authors stress how sharply the yearly burden swings, which makes single-year figures unreliable. Control, they argue, must join vaccines with attention to farming and water, the forces that set the mosquito's numbers.
europmc-pmc2680990:
Mehling and co-authors reviewed in 2009 the questionnaires that claim to measure body awareness, a person's sense of signals from inside their own body. Noticing heartbeat, breath, and gut feelings can help or harm: it guides care for chronic pain and trauma, yet anxious over-focus can worsen symptoms. Dozens of scales existed, but no one had checked them side by side.

From 1,825 papers, the team kept 12 scales that fit their scope. Only two earned top marks for consistency, and four for measuring what they claim. Reading every question closely, the team sorted body awareness into four domains with eleven parts, covering noticing, attention style, and trust in body signals. No single scale covered them all, and the parts that separate healthy awareness from harmful were exactly the ones missing. Better tools, they argue, are needed before therapy can target this skill.
europmc-pmc2712090:
Pesquita and co-authors reviewed in 2009 semantic similarity, a way to compare living things by the meaning of their labels in a biomedical ontology. An ontology is a formal schema that names traits and how they relate. When genes or diseases share that schema, their label sets can be scored for how close in meaning they are.

Their review sorts measures into node-based and edge-based forms, and into pairwise and groupwise forms. It also surveys tests that compare the measures and the software that runs them. Uses include checking gene groups, gene activity studies, and hunting for disease genes. The authors expect such measures to grow as central as sequence matching already is.
europmc-pmc2719090:
Sun, Huang, and Zhang tested in 2009 whether MAP kinases, a family of signaling enzymes, control the antioxidant master switch Nrf2 by tagging it directly. Nrf2 turns on many protective and detox genes when oxidative stress hits. It is normally held down by Keap1, which marks it for destruction, and stress frees it through changes on Keap1.

They proved Nrf2 is tagged by these kinases in living cells and mapped the main tag sites on the protein. Mutating all those sites lowered Nrf2 activity only modestly, mainly by slightly reducing its entry into the nucleus. Its stability, set by Keap1, did not change. Direct tagging thus plays only a small part, and the kinases likely act indirectly.
europmc-pmc2777390:
Chasman and co-authors ran in 2009 a genome-wide association study of plasma lipoprotein measures in over seventeen thousand women from the Women's Genome Health Study. Standard cholesterol tests sum up whole fractions, while NMR measures count particles by class and size, traits that may track heart disease risk more closely. They tested seventeen NMR measures plus the standard lipids and two carrier proteins against genome-wide markers.

Thirty-six regions reached genome-wide significance in their main analyses. Ten of them had never been tied to blood lipids before. Some regions shaped particle size without changing cholesterol content, for LDL at four places and HDL at one. Adding regions already known from standard lipid studies brought the total to forty-three loci. Many hits clustered at genes for the machinery that builds and clears lipoprotein particles.
europmc-pmc2836990:
White, Biérinx, Gnocchi, and Zammit charted how mouse muscle fibers grow after birth in 2010, using a fast leg muscle that is set in fiber count before birth. A growing fiber can enlarge only if new nuclei join it, and those come from satellite cells, the muscle's resident stem cells. Two reporter mouse lines let the team count fiber nuclei and satellite cells separately.

Fiber number never rose after the first week, yet fiber volume grew about fourteen-fold by adulthood. Nuclei per fiber rose roughly five-fold in the first three weeks, then stopped, while fibers kept swelling, so each nucleus served a much larger territory. Satellite cells per fiber fell from about fourteen to the adult five over the same three weeks.
europmc-pmc2847190:
Alaux and colleagues tested in 2010 whether a gut parasite and a common insecticide together hurt honeybees more than either alone. Bee colonies have been vanishing across Europe and North America, and single-cause explanations keep falling short. The team exposed bees to Nosema, a microsporidian gut parasite, to the neonicotinoid imidacloprid, or to both, and tracked survival, energy stress, and immune measures.

The combination produced the highest death rates and the strongest energy strain in the short term. Individual immune counts stayed untouched, but glucose oxidase, the enzyme bees use to sterilize colony and brood food, fell only in the combined group. The synergy, the authors argue, leaves colonies open to further infection over time.
europmc-pmc2851690:
Ma, Liu, Che, Yu, Dai, and You tested in 2010 whether the flavor of immune cells inside lung tumors predicts how long patients live. Macrophages in tumors come in two broad forms: M1 cells that attack tumors and M2 cells that abet them. The team stained tumor samples from one hundred non-small cell lung cancer patients, half short survivors and half long survivors, counting each form separately.

About seventy percent of the macrophages were the tumor-friendly M2 form, and their numbers matched survival not at all. The anti-tumor M1 cells told another story: long survivors carried roughly ten times more M1 cells inside their tumor islets than short survivors did. M1 density inside the islets independently predicted survival, making it a candidate prognostic marker.
europmc-pmc2866690:
Herbstman and a large team followed New York children from birth in 2010 to test whether flame retardants met before birth affect brain development. The chemicals, called PBDEs, were added to foam and electronics and build up in body fat. The cohort began after the September 2001 attacks and enrolled mothers who delivered at three lower Manhattan hospitals.

Cord blood from two hundred ten newborns carried measurable levels of several PBDE types. Children with higher levels of the three most common types scored lower on mental and motor tests given between ages one and six years, after other influences were accounted for. The pattern matched animal findings and added human evidence that these widespread chemicals can quietly shape early development.
europmc-pmc2891790:
Lee and Zheng reviewed in 2010 PDZ domains, small protein modules that grip the tails of other proteins to organize cell signaling. A PDZ domain reads a short amino acid motif at a target's very end, docking it into place at membranes, junctions, and channel clusters. Hundreds of human proteins carry these modules, so their binding rules shape transport, ion channel behavior, and many signal pathways.

New tools such as peptide libraries and protein arrays have measured the grip preferences of whole PDZ families at once, replacing one-at-a-time studies. The binding turns out to be choosier than the simple tail code suggests. Chemical tagging by phosphorylation, either on the tail or on the domain itself, can switch a pairing on or off, adding a regulatory layer.
europmc-pmc2912890:
Novák, Neumann, and Macas adapted in 2010 a graph-clustering trick to catalog the repetitive DNA that fills most of a plant genome. Repeats are too numerous and varied to assemble conventionally, yet a single light round of shotgun sequencing samples every major family. Their method compares the short reads to each other and groups them into clusters, where reads from one repeat family clump together into a recognizable graph shape.

Cluster sizes estimate how much of the genome each family occupies, and the graph's shape reveals the family's internal structure. Tests on pea and soybean, two legumes with very different genome sizes, recovered their known repeat landscapes faithfully. Species with no sequenced genome can now get a repeat census from one inexpensive sequencing run, a door into genome evolution studies.
europmc-pmc2935890:
Smith and colleagues ran a randomised trial called VITACOG, reported in 2010, testing whether B vitamins slow brain shrinkage in older people with mild memory trouble. Raised homocysteine in blood is a known risk marker for shrinkage and dementia, and B vitamins lower it.

Over two years, volunteers past seventy took high-dose folic acid plus vitamins B6 and B12, or a dummy pill. Among those who finished brain scans, yearly shrinkage ran clearly slower in the vitamin group than in the placebo group. The gap suggests a cheap dietary approach worth testing further against decline.
europmc-pmc3002190:
Reif and co-authors ranked environmental chemicals for hormone disruption risk using the United States ToxCast screening data in a 2010 study. Hundreds of chemicals had been run through hundreds of fast lab assays, and regulators needed a fair way to choose what to test deeply first.

Focusing on estrogen, androgen, and thyroid pathways, they built profiles for each chemical and merged many data sources into a weighted priority index. The combined score gave sturdier rankings than any single source alone. Their approach offers the national screening programme a transparent decision aid for ordering follow-up testing.
europmc-pmc3023790:
Chen and coauthors examined in 2010 how three related plant genes shape responses to stress and to a key plant hormone. The genes, named WRKY18, WRKY40, and WRKY60, make proteins that switch other genes on or off in the small plant Arabidopsis. The hormone, called ABA in short, helps plants handle drought, salt, and other hard conditions.

Using plants with one, two, or all three genes knocked out, plus plants with extra copies, the team found the genes pull in opposite directions. Two of them made seeds and roots more sensitive to the hormone and to salt stress. The third worked against them and also turned the second group down. Together they form a small control network. It fine tunes how plants answer both attack and harsh weather.
europmc-pmc3042390:
Thomée, Härenstam, and Hagberg followed in 2011 more than four thousand Swedish young adults to test whether heavy mobile phone use harms mental health. Participants aged twenty to twenty four answered surveys at the start and again a year later. The team counted not just call volume, but also felt demands to be reachable, stress from constant access, night waking by the phone, and self judged overuse.

Heavy users reported more stress, worse sleep, and more depressive symptoms at the same point in time. Looking ahead, heavy use predicted new sleep trouble and depressive symptoms a year later among those free of them at the start. Feeling stressed by constant reachability was the strongest warning sign for both sexes. The authors suggest prevention should help young adults set limits on availability, their own and others, rather than only cutting minutes.
europmc-pmc3042690:
Das and Chandran reviewed in 2011 how microbes can clean up oil pollution, one of the most stubborn environmental problems from the petrochemical industry. Spilled petroleum contains compounds that can cause cancer and damage nerves, and common fixes such as burning or burying waste grow very costly at large scales. Many soil and water microbes, by contrast, can eat hydrocarbons as food.

The review explains how these microbes break complex oil compounds down, sometimes fully into carbon dioxide, water, and cell material. It surveys which organisms do the work in different settings, from seawater to soil. Because living cleanup is cheaper and can finish the job completely, the authors present it as the most promising route for large contaminated sites. They note that success depends on matching microbes and conditions to each spill.
europmc-pmc3047790:
Coutinho and Chapman reviewed in 2011 how glucocorticoid drugs calm inflammation and suppress the immune system, and why their long term use is a bargain with harm. Since the nineteen forties these drugs have been among the most effective treatments for inflammatory and autoimmune disease. Their costs include bone thinning, high blood pressure, disturbed blood fats, and raised diabetes risk.

Drug hunters have long tried to split the benefits from the harms, with limited success so far. The review gathers recent, sometimes surprising findings on how the drugs actually work inside cells. One local enzyme that boosts or cuts the drugs' strength inside tissues gets close attention. Better maps of these pathways, the authors argue, are the route to safer versions. The paper is a status report for researchers chasing that split.
europmc-pmc3098090:
Matsen, Kodner, and Armbrust introduced in 2010 pplacer, a program that slots new short DNA reads onto a fixed family tree of known species with proper statistical rigor. Environmental sequencing produces mountains of short reads with no names attached. Name matching by simple similarity can mislead badly for distant relatives, while building a fresh tree for every read is far too slow.

Placement instead asks where each read best fits on an existing, trusted tree, using likelihood methods. The program places tens of thousands of reads per hour, with time and memory growing only in step with the reference tree. It also reports how uncertain each placement is, edge by edge, and draws trees whose branch thickness and color show placements and doubt. Tests on simulated reads showed high accuracy. The tool is free as code, binaries, and a web service.
europmc-pmc3116190:
Chia-Yen Lee and colleagues surveyed tiny devices for mixing fluids in a 2011 review in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Lab-on-a-chip tools handle drops far too small for stirring, so blending samples quickly and fully is a core design problem. At that scale, blending depends mostly on molecules spreading between streams on their own.

The review sorts designs into two families. Active designs shake or push the fluids with outside energy, such as sound, heat, or electric force. Passive designs instead stretch the contact between streams through winding or split channels, needing no extra power. After a decade of proposals, the authors compare the main designs so engineers can match a mixer to their device and task.
europmc-pmc3117990:
Tamas Varga, Zsolt Czimmerer, and Laszlo Nagy reviewed a family of fat-sensing gene switches in a 2011 paper in Biochimica et Biophysica Acta. Cells meet many kinds of fat daily, and these switches read fat signals and turn genes on or off in response. They sit at the crossing point of energy handling and immune activity.

The switches govern how the body stores and burns fat and sugar, and they were already targets of diabetes drugs. Newer work shows they also dial inflammation up or down, linking rich diets and clogged arteries to immune overreaction. The review gathers fresh findings on how the switches are controlled and how they keep balance in health, plus where that balance fails in disease.
europmc-pmc3153290:
Irina Pinchuk, Ellen Beswick, and Victor Reyes surveyed a family of bacterial super-toxins in a 2010 paper in Toxins. The source germ is carried by about a third of people and causes illnesses from food poisoning to toxic shock. Its gut toxins, more than twenty in number, survive heat and stomach acid that would destroy most proteins.

Two members are the best studied. They latch onto immune cells and force huge numbers of T cells to fire at once, releasing a flood of signal chemicals that can tip into shock. In food, the same hardiness lets them survive preparation and trigger sudden vomiting illness. The review also flags drug-resistant strains as a rising hospital concern, tied to diarrhoea in patients on antibiotics.
europmc-pmc3257290:
Brenna Henn and colleagues used genome-wide data to reconstruct the ancestry of North Africans, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Genetics. People north of the Sahara differ from sub-Saharan Africans in culture, language, and appearance, but when and how much their genes diverged was poorly understood. The team genotyped hundreds of thousands of sites in seven North African populations and one Spanish group.

They found a gradient of Maghrebi ancestry rising from east to west, strongest in groups with Berber identity. That ancestry appears to descend mainly from a back-to-Africa migration more than twelve thousand years ago, before the Holocene. Most populations also carry ancestry from the Near East. Smaller shares come from sub-Saharan Africa and from Europe. Dating DNA tracts placed a west African migration into Morocco roughly twelve hundred years ago and a Nilotic one into Egypt about seven hundred fifty years ago.
europmc-pmc3411490:
Karastergiou, Smith, Greenberg, and Fried reviewed in 2012 why fat settles differently on women and men, the biology behind the pear shape. Women carry more body fat overall, yet the hip-and-thigh pattern typical of women brings lower metabolic risk than men's belly-centered pattern. The review compares the fat cells of each depot and sex.

Evidence points to built-in differences in the precursor cells that make fat, shaped further by sex hormones, the local tissue setting, and early development. Women's lower-body fat may simply be a safe storehouse for spare energy. Or it may actively steer body-wide metabolism through signals it releases. The authors weigh both possibilities and the experiments behind them.
europmc-pmc3427890:
Carruthers led an international consensus panel that published new diagnostic criteria for myalgic encephalomyelitis in 2011. The panel argued the older label chronic fatigue syndrome undersells a disease marked by widespread inflammation and nervous-system pathology. Its members, from thirteen countries, had treated roughly fifty thousand patients between them and reached full agreement through a structured Delphi process.

The criteria center on a crash after exertion, called postexertional neuroimmune exhaustion, as the required core feature. Around it they organize symptoms across nerve, immune, gut, and energy systems, with working notes to sharpen each judgment. The authors present the name and the criteria as a truer map of the illness. Clinicians and researchers get a shared standard for diagnosis and study.

fouillee-evolutionnisme-idees-forces-189:
Alfred Fouillee built his name on one striking claim: ideas are forces. His French work L'evolutionnisme des idees-forces, from 1890, states that claim in full. An idea, once held, pushes toward act and change in the world. Fouillee joined that claim to the theory of evolution.

He traces how ideas grow, spread, and reshape both minds and societies over time. Thought is no idle picture, on his account, but a real power at work. The doctrine let him link mind, morals, and social life in one scheme. French readers took the book as his core statement. It still marks his place in French thought.
france-thais-1890:
Anatole France published Thaïs in 1890, here in the Library Edition English rendering of 1924 in print. The novel tells of an Alexandrian courtesan-saint and the monk who loves and converts her in Egypt. Its irony about desire and holiness made France famous well beyond France in the 1890s of his prime.

Paphnutius, a desert monk, enters Alexandria to save Thaïs, the actress whose beauty ruins men in droves. She converts, burns her treasures, and enters a convent to die in odor of sanctity and peace. The monk, meanwhile, is consumed by the desire he denied, and demons mock his wasted, burning soul in dreams. At her deathbed he confesses his love and is thrust aside as she sees heaven open above her. France balances pity for both, and judges neither, in prose of classical calm.
frus-1861-d190:
Mr. Stockton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 September 1861. The dispatch is document 190 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Stockton's September report answers, across a long gap, the April letter from Seward. The record gives no post for him in either heading. His page joins the file as a lone report, its value lying in its date and its place in the year's run. A lone report still earns its place, as one dated point in the year's wide record. One dated point, honestly kept, can anchor a whole chapter of the year's tale.
frus-1861-d290:
Writing on 25 July 1861, Mr. Harvey sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 290 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d90:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 11 October 1861. The dispatch is document 90 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By mid October, Adams had held his post for five months of war. His reports kept their even tone through praise and blame in the press. The letter shows the worth of a steady man in a post where a hot word could cost a country its cause. A hot word in London could have undone a year of care in a single week. Steady men in hot posts are the quiet heroes of this whole record.
frus-1862-d190:
Two Seward letters to London bear the date 18 November 1862, and the first is Document 190 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain, received it from Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Mid-November mail crossed an Atlantic growing calmer on the war question, since Britain had declined the French truce plan. Other business filled the gap: Confederate ships in British yards, trade, and the treatment of Union vessels. This dispatch is part of the shift from crisis management to the daily grind of holding neutrality in place. Earl Russell, the British foreign secretary, was the minister Adams dealt with most in London.
frus-1862-d290:
On 21 June 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to William L. Dayton in Paris, in a dispatch printed as Document 290 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Three letters in two days mark a heavy mail.

A steamer's sailing explains such clusters: the Department cleared pending business before the bag closed. Seward's June letters to Dayton went out while Stuart handled Britain's legation in Washington and Lee prepared to strike near Richmond. The cluster shows a government working several channels at once, each letter a small part of a larger design. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year.
frus-1862-d390:
Two Seward dispatches to Simon Cameron are dated 6 September 1862, and the first is Document 390 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Cameron was the American minister in Russia, at St. Petersburg.

Seward wrote six days after Bull Run, with Lee entering Maryland. His September mail to St. Petersburg carried Washington's account of a hard month to the court least likely to doubt it. The pair of letters that day shows the Department keeping even its quietest channel current in a crisis week. The legation's quiet year was the exception in a volume full of friction. Cameron, a Pennsylvania political chief, had run the War Department before going to Russia.
frus-1862-d490:
Dated 16 March 1862, this report from James Shepherd Pike at The Hague reached Secretary of State William H. Seward out of strict order in the printed file. It is Document 490 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The volume's editors grouped letters as they were received and printed, so a Hague report of mid-March can sit behind one dated days later. Pike's subject in those weeks was the Netherlands itself: its ministry's caution, its merchants' losses, and its colonial stake in the Caribbean. His dispatch adds one more layer to the Dutch record for March, a month in which Seward wrote to The Hague four times. The file's density is the point: Washington watched even friendly small powers closely.
frus-1862-d590:
On 7 June 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to Thomas Corwin in Mexico City. It is Document 590 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the annual message.

June orders to Mexico went out as the armies closed on Richmond, and Washington's mind was necessarily divided. Seward still kept the Mexican brief exact: support for the republic's independence, protest against the French design, and no step that risked war with France. Corwin, on the ground, had to make that limited brief feel like friendship to a government under invasion. The instruction is one of the year's clearest statements of how the Union rationed its strength abroad while its own survival was undecided.
frus-1862-d690: Dated 20 March 1862, this dispatch from a Mr. De Long went to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 690 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, the last of his run of letters that winter. The title and record name him and the date only, so his post and subject stay unstated here.
frus-1862-d90:
A letter home from Charles Francis Adams, dated 3 July 1862, landed on Seward's desk. It was printed as Document 90 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d190:
Reporting on 7 May 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 190 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

The CSS Alabama, built in a British yard, had escaped to sea in 1862 and was burning Union merchant ships. London's handling of such ships hung over every report Adams sent home. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d290:
A dispatch dated 10 September 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 290 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Union wins at Gettysburg and Vicksburg in early July 1863 weakened the case for aiding the South. British leaders grew more careful, and Adams's post grew a little less tense. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d390:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 11 February 1863. It stands as document 390 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Read together, these letters trace a slow cooling of the crisis mood of 1861 and 1862. Recognition of the South grew less likely with each month the channel stayed open. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d490:
Under the date 4 May 1863, the record holds a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d590:
Secretary William H. Seward directed a letter to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington on 17 July 1863. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d690:
William H. Seward wrote once more to Lord Lyons on 11 November 1863. Lyons, the British minister in Washington, was his most frequent foreign contact that fall. The letter is document 690 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863.

Three notes in this run bear the same date, which tells its own story about the load of work. The Union wanted trade kept open and the South kept isolated. Britain wanted its ships and goods kept safe. Seward's mail walked that line in short, firm steps. This dispatch is one such step, and its worth lies in the full sequence it belongs to.
frus-1863p1-d90:
On 24 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is document 90 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It opens a three-day run of Seward letters in the file.

Seward's late-February sheets set the brief anew as spring neared. The war at home was stuck in winter mud, and the talks abroad moved by small steps. His letters told Adams which claims to press and which to let rest. This one begins that run, a sign that Washington meant to keep its London hand tight as the season turned.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d190:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent President Roosevelt a long personal review from Moscow on 4 November 1943, and it sums up what the foreign ministers' conference had shown him about Soviet thinking. It runs to several parts and mixes praise for new cooperation with warnings about hard issues ahead.

Harriman says the Soviet leaders had decided to try working with Britain and America on war and postwar problems. Molotov grew more open as he saw no united front against him. Their acceptance of China as a signer of the Four Nation Declaration proved the point, he argues. Against that, Moscow was stung by Western caution on Turkey and Sweden, and still awaited a firm answer on the Italian ships.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d290:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 401/1 at Cairo on 23 November 1943, on airfields for very-long-range B-29 bombers in the China-Burma-India area. It answers the American paper C.C.S. 401, after President Roosevelt's telegram to Churchill asking for help in building the bases.

The British chiefs accept the American recommendations in full and are issuing orders to their authorities. Churchill has already told the commander in chief in India to give every help with the four Indian bases. One warning is attached. If the work is to finish in time, the American units and equipment must reach Calcutta by 15 January. Otherwise the deadline of 1 April will slip. The building effort may even have to stop for the Ledo road.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d390:
Louis Dreyfus, the American minister in Iran, wrote a secret letter to General Patrick Hurley at Tehran on 29 November 1943. It reports a morning call from Iran's prime minister, Mohammad Sa'ed Soheily, about the statement the conference might issue at its close.

Soheily told Dreyfus he had seen Foreign Secretary Eden that day and raised the idea of a joint communiqué built on three lines. The Allies would recognize that Iran has given them every possible help. Iran's independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity would be confirmed, as already set out in the Tripartite Treaty. And Iran's economic needs would be considered when the peace treaty came to be negotiated. Eden agreed in principle, Soheily said, but asked him to approach the Americans and the Soviets for their agreement to go ahead.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d490:
President Roosevelt sent a message to Prime Minister Churchill on December 5, 1943, while both men were at the Second Cairo Conference. They were meeting daily, yet still exchanged written notes, which the State Department later printed in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Written messages between the two leaders matter because they fixed points that conversation left loose. Roosevelt and Churchill's wartime correspondence runs to hundreds of items, and the Cairo notes belong to its most intense stretch, right after Tehran. A reader finds the alliance's two heads communicating in their own words at the moment of decision, not filtered through staff summaries or later memoirs.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d90: John Winant, the American ambassador in London, wrote to President Roosevelt on November 2, 1943. His dispatch is Document 90 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Winant was close to Churchill's circle and reported British thinking with a sympathetic ear, which made his letters a valued channel. The record gives the date and the two men and no topic. The dispatch is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1944-quebec-d190:
For this September 14, 1944 meeting, the editors print Eden's diary. Eden and Cadogan found Churchill with Roosevelt, Morgenthau, and Cherwell conferring about lend-lease. The visitors were welcomed as an interruption, and talk ranged over Russians, Poles, and Dumbarton Oaks until it was time to dress for dinner.

White, who was not present, adds the scene's famous line. Roosevelt delayed initialing the lend-lease committee memorandum by telling stories, while Churchill grew nervous and eager. At last Churchill burst out: "What do you want me to do? Get on my hind legs and beg like Fala?" Fala was the president's dog. The anecdote survives because Morgenthau retold it to White the next day.
frus-1944-quebec-d290:
The companion message to Chiang Kai-shek, sent September 16, 1944, over Leahy's name, hastens to inform the Generalissimo of plans for the mutual effort, particularly in Southeast Asia. Roosevelt and Churchill declared themselves determined to employ all available resources toward the earliest practicable invasion of the Japanese homeland, and were expediting redeployment after Germany's defeat to that end.

Mountbatten's operations in north Burma would continue and extend, securing the Myitkyina air bases and opening overland communications between India and China. The message asks continued cooperation from Chinese troops in Burma and the Salween armies. Success by next spring would let the Ledo Road advance with its pipelines. Mountbatten was also directed to prepare a large-scale amphibious operation in the Bay of Bengal.
frus-1944-quebec-d90:
Secretary of War Stimson wrote to Secretary Hull on September 9, 1944. The State Department printed the letter in its Quebec 1944 volume. It came three days before the Quebec Conference opened. Stimson and Hull led the two great wartime departments.

Letters between cabinet secretaries settled positions before summits began. The War Department ran the armies nearing Germany's border. The State Department handled the alliance and the coming peace. For readers, Stimson's message shows those two worlds meeting on paper. Their agreement, or friction, shaped what Roosevelt could promise at Quebec. The conference opened at Quebec City on September 12.
frus-1945-50-intel-d190:
A letter dated 13 March 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg). The reader was the Chairman of the Joint Research and Development Board (Bush). It stands as document 190 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff.

Letters between senior men often carried the real weight of a matter, since a signed letter put the writer's name and office behind the words. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d290:
A memorandum dated 17 June 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan). The reader was the Under Secretary of State (Lovett) and Secretary of State Marshall. The State Department prints it as document 290 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was in its first year, and the Council was taking up covert action for the first time.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d390:
On 25 July 1949, the Executive Secretary (Souers) sent a memorandum to the National Security Council. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 390 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d90:
McCormack wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 23 April 1946, his last letter in the volume's State thread. He had led the department's intelligence office since its birth the previous September. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A last paper by a founding chief carries a summing-up quality, whether the writer intends it or not. McCormack's office had begun as the heir of the OSS analysts and the seed of a State-led intelligence system. By April, that hope had passed to the central group. Readers who have followed his thread from the first hopeful exchanges of October will find this letter a fitting close. The man who built the office writing to the chief who let it go.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d190:
The new Bonomi government took office with allied blessing, this press release announced on 14 December 1944. Reprinted in the Malta and Yalta volume, the statement closes the public phase of the Italian cabinet crisis. It speaks in the name of both wartime partners.

The American and British ambassadors in Rome, it says, have stayed in close contact through the recent developments. Ambassador Kirk reports that Italy's new government rests on a majority of the political parties, those of the Committee of National Liberation among them. It thus keeps a representative character. The United States, in accord with the British government, is happy to see the new government under Signor Bonomi take office.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d290:
The cruiser Quincy carried Roosevelt into Grand Harbor, Malta, on 2 February 1945, and the President's log records the morning by the clock. The log entry, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, comes from the official booklet of the trip. It is the plainest kind of sea record.

At midnight the ship was in the Mediterranean, steering from Gibraltar. Sicily was sighted at ten past six, and Gozo and Malta soon after. At twenty-five to ten the Quincy passed the submarine net gate into Grand Harbor at Valletta. The President stood on deck as crowds lined both sides of the channel. The ship moored at Berth 9 an hour later. The total run from Newport News stood at 4,883 miles. Churchill watched the arrival from the cruiser Sirius across the channel.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d390:
Admiral Ernest King, the Navy's chief, set down the Soviet questions put to him on February 8, 1945, with his answers. Admiral Kuznetsov had asked what had been settled about transferring ships to the Russians under the Milepost program. King answered that firm dates were hard to give. Much depended on the U-boat offensive in the Atlantic.

Deliveries, King said, could be worked out step by step, though later ones might slip. On the transfer port, Dutch Harbor might not suit. Kodiak was the second choice, and King gave his view. The memo shows sea power changing hands by schedule and training class.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d490:
Yugoslavia and Rumanian oil lead the excerpts of Grew's cable of February 10, 1945, his thirty-third message of the series. The British Foreign Office held that Subasic, rather than Tito, had opposed Simovic. Subasic would likely leave soon for Belgrade even without agreement on the regents. King Peter's approval, London felt, was essential, above all for the air and naval forces.

On oil, the Moscow embassy had been instructed to welcome the decision to stop removing equipment from Rumania. It was also to renew America's unwillingness to accept the Soviet contention on the matter. The digest shows the home department fighting Yalta's side battles in parallel.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d90:
Gromyko's mind was not closed on voting, the Secretary of State told the President in this draft memorandum of 20 January 1945. The draft, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, reports two long talks between the Soviet ambassador and Leo Pasvolsky. It was prepared for Roosevelt on the eve of his trip.

The ambassador had asked many questions and seemed to be getting the American arguments into his mind. Pasvolsky gained the firm impression that Gromyko wanted to present the matter fully to his government. Speaking personally, Gromyko had even floated a distinction between discussion in the Council and formal action by vote. The draft calls that a move in the right direction, though not enough.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d190:
Acting Secretary Grew staked out a hard line on the Balkan satellites in a telegram extract dated July 6, 1945. The extract is document 190 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full message appears later in the volume.

Winant may tell the Foreign Office that at the coming high-level talks the United States intends to press strongly for carrying out the Yalta Declaration on Liberated Europe. Washington also wants the Allied Control Commissions in all three ex-satellite states reorganized. And it will oppose proposals to establish diplomatic relations with, or conclude peace with, the present governments there. The position put Romania, Bulgaria, and Hungary near the center of the Potsdam fight over Soviet control in Eastern Europe.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d290:
Acting Secretary Grew asked the field missions to judge a British shortcut in a telegram dated June 21, 1945. The message to Maynard Barnes in Bulgaria is document 290 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The same questions went to the American representatives in Romania and Hungary.

The British Foreign Office had proposed that the two governments work for an early conclusion of peace treaties with Hungary, Bulgaria, and Romania. London's reasons follow. Moscow is not likely to give the Western members a fuller voice on the control commissions. And peace would bring the withdrawal of Soviet troops. That would free the countries to decide their own destinies. Grew asks for urgent views on two points. First, does ending the armistice early outweigh the weak Western position meanwhile? Second, what would peace with the present governments mean for free choice and for the Yalta pledges?
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d390:
German warships and merchant ships are treated separately in an extract from a State Department memorandum of June 30, 1945, later forwarded to President Truman. On the battle fleet the extract makes no recommendation at all. Disposal of the German fleet, it says, is a military problem, and one the Joint Chiefs of Staff were already considering.

Merchant ships are another matter. Subject to the military authorities' approval, the extract recommends agreeing to the Soviet claim to one-third of these ships. The short extract shows the Department leaving guns to the soldiers while it bargained over cargo hulls, the shipping Europe needed to recover and America needed against Japan.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d490:
Bierut's promises are reported in an extract of Harriman's cable from Moscow of June 26, 1945. Harriman had discussed with the Polish leader, point by point, the assurances Washington sought in its cable of June 22. Bierut said American representatives would be given every opportunity to travel within Poland and see what they wished.

Rapid communications between the Warsaw embassy and Washington mattered greatly, Harriman stressed. Bierut said his government was working on it and was anxious to establish direct radio communication with the United States. Air links could be arranged after the ambassador's arrival. Harriman closes with a doubt: he cannot predict how far the Russians will try to brake Polish desires for open contact with the West.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d590:
A top secret briefing paper of July 3, 1945, takes up military government in a beaten Japan. It is document 590 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Its central question is what the occupying forces should do about the Emperor.

One part suggests that any talk of the Emperor be sent to a Far Eastern advisory body. An appendix then gives the State Department's own approved line. On surrender, the Emperor's powers should be suspended at once. He and his close family should be held in a detached palace outside Tokyo, in seclusion. He should be made to proclaim the surrender himself and to order all forces to lay down their arms. He should also sign the surrender instrument with Japan's top commander.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d690:
Ambassador Harriman reported the Turkish ambassador's private fears from Moscow on June 25, 1945. His secret wire is document 690 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. A member of Harriman's staff had talked with Ambassador Sarper the day before.

Sarper said there were no new developments in the Soviet demands. Turkey's flat replies, he thought, had given Moscow pause. Had Turkey yielded, he believed, fresh demands on its inner affairs would soon have followed. Their aim would have been to bring Turkey, in his words, like Poland under direct Soviet sway. The rebuff had only postponed the joining of the issue, he warned. The Russians, he said, are not bluffing. Sarper saw Turkey lying in a Soviet security zone taking shape from Finland to China, and he expected the pressure to go on.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d90:
Churchill passed Stalin's answer on the conference site to President Truman on June 23, 1945. Telegram number 98, document 90 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam, repeats Stalin's reply to Churchill's proposal that each delegation run its own closed enclave, as in the Crimea.

Stalin agrees to the plan and names the ground. The delegations will be housed at Babelsberg, southeast of Potsdam, each on its own closed territory. Joint sessions will meet in a fourth building, the palace of the German Crown Prince in Potsdam. Advance parties should arrive around June 28, when Zhukov returns, and a good airfield sits at nearby Kladov. Churchill adds that he has ordered Montgomery to send his party in as soon as possible.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1090:
Acting Secretary of State Joseph Grew sent this memorandum to Potsdam on July 18, 1945. Italy's ambassador had called that morning, leaving papers for the President and Byrnes. Rome fears Britain and the Soviet Union want the harshest possible peace terms for Italy. Harsh terms, the ambassador warned, would crush Italian morale and block her recovery.

Two letters from Ambassador Tarchiani are enclosed. One thanks Washington for pledging not to sign an unfair or oppressive treaty, and for promising Italy a full hearing before any treaty is final. The other carries Foreign Minister De Gasperi's views. Italy's first need, he writes, is release from the armistice terms and standing restored among nations.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1190:
Staff of the United States Chiefs of Staff wrote this memorandum on 18 July 1945. Papers from the chiefs' staff gave the American team the armed forces' formal view of the questions at Potsdam. This one dates from the second day of the talks.

The chiefs spoke for the services that still fought Japan and now held half of Germany. Their staff work turned that weight into advice the envoys could use. A memorandum like this is the Pentagon's paper, filed for the diplomats. It shows the military house putting its knowledge on record at the start of the bargaining.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1290:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 18 July 1945. It came from the summit's second day, early in the British staff's run of papers. The note shows the military view being worked out before it hardened into stands.

London's chiefs had to weigh a shrinking purse against a world-wide set of duties. Their papers brought that hard math to the envoys' table. This memorandum is one of the early pieces. Read beside the American notes of the same date, it shows two allied staffs at work. They started their Potsdam labors in step, each in its own voice.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1390:
Instead of a memorandum, Mikołajczyk's paper of 28 July 1945 is a diary entry. The Polish deputy prime minister kept a private record beside his formal papers during the Potsdam period. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Diary entries differ from memoranda in one great way: they are written for the writer, not for a reader in office. That freedom often brings candor about moods, meetings, and men. Readers can set this entry beside Mikołajczyk's formal papers of the same days and watch the public and private voices diverge. The volume gains depth from printing both, and the diary is among its most human pages.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-90:
A second set of Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 24, 1945 survives in the Potsdam record. The chiefs met more than once that week as the conference pressed on. Each session dealt with live war business while peace terms were debated nearby. The set was printed in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Having two records for one day shows the pace of work at Potsdam. Military questions could not wait for the plenary sessions to end. The minutes let readers track what the chiefs settled among themselves. They also show what was passed up to President Truman for a final call.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d790:
Nikolai Novikov, secretary of the Soviet delegation, wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on July 25, 1945. Document 790 is a formal Soviet-American exchange inside the conference machinery. Delegation secretaries ran the paper flow between teams. Novikov later became a noted Soviet envoy. His letter entered the second Potsdam volume.

Secretaries' letters look minor and are not. They move texts, set meetings, and fix the record of what passed between sides. Readers see the conference's clerks doing the work that let leaders lead. The document also shows courtesy holding under strain. Even hard rivals kept the forms, and the forms kept the talks alive.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d890: Emilio Collado wrote to Assistant Secretary of State William Clayton on August 1, 1945, about one word in a presidential letter. The letter told the War Department its duties on German financing. Collado had spoken with Admiral Leahy, who did not know if Truman had signed it yet. Collado argues the word facilities should not appear in the first charge sentence, given the shape of the reparations deal. He prepared a substitute page without it. The editors note the swap was never made.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d990:
The American military attaché in Sweden, Kessler, cabled the War Department on July 24, 1945. His subject is a group of interned German aircraft in Sweden. The planes had come there from the German-Soviet front during the war.

A Russian delegation in Stockholm has surveyed the aircraft. The Russians propose to fly them out shortly as war booty. Their plans, Kessler reports, have been aired in the newspapers. He notes that neither Britain nor the United States has made any request about the remaining aircraft. The message reached the American delegation at Potsdam the next day, by retransmission from the War Department.
frus-1977-80v12-d90: A 1977-1980 FRUS telegram from the embassy in Afghanistan. The Soviet invasion loomed. This document preserves that cable. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
gao-gaoreports-b-296490: Johnson Controls Security Systems doubled its August 2005 protest — two case numbers, one security fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-297890: PDS Consultants took its April 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298390: Dismas Charities took its August 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Charities get the same full hearing as the corporations.
gao-gaoreports-b-298590: General Injectables & Vaccines tripled its November 2006 protest — three case numbers, one pharma fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles all three. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Triple filings get one thorough answer. Three dockets, one thorough answer.
gao-gaoreports-b-298790: SCS Refrigerated Services tripled its November 2006 protest — three case numbers, one cold-chain fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles all three. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Triple filings get one thorough answer. Three dockets, one thorough answer.
gao-gaoreports-b-310790: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by C&H SERVICE Srl. Decided February 5, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-190: Six DOE labs' personnel gripes got a GAO ear in 2005, and the report covers actions, employee concerns, and oversight. The review listens to the lab workers. The scientists' workplaces were studied. The concerns were heard. The scientists' workplaces were studied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-290: The Indian Child Welfare Act's implementation got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says existing information could target guidance and assistance. The review points the way. The Native children deserved the protection. The information had to be used. The Native children deserved the protection.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-490: D.C. charter school oversight got a GAO review in 2005, and the report examines the practices. The findings take the measure. The report shows the capital's charter schools were watched. The oversight had to be understood. The capital's charter schools were watched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-690: Tax expenditures represented a substantial commitment in 2005, and GAO's report says the breaks needed more scrutiny. The findings do the math. The report warns that the hidden spending deserved daylight. The commitment had to be understood. The hidden spending deserved daylight.
