The study included 72 adults, average age 71. They wore a ring device measuring sleep through heart and breathing signals for at least two nights. They also walked ten metres at their usual pace wearing motion sensors. Each one percent rise in sleep fragmentation raised the chance of wide step variability by six percent. Other sleep measures, including duration, efficiency, and breathing disturbance, were also examined.
pmc-13272590:
Yi Pan leads updated 2026 results from the TRAILBLAZER phase 2 trial in stage III lung cancer that could not be removed at first. The drug tested, retlirafusp alfa, blocks two signals at once, PD-L1 and TGF-beta. Patients got it before surgery or radiation, with or without chemotherapy, based on PD-L1 level.

At a median follow-up of 39.4 months, three-year event-free survival was 50.5 percent in the combined chemotherapy arms and 77.1 percent with the drug alone. Among 27 patients who had surgery, three-year survival was 84.9 percent. No new safety problems appeared, and the authors back this response-guided approach for further study.
pmc-13272890:
Ukah Cynthia Chinonso and Majani Edward present a 2026 study of midwives' knowledge of the World Health Organization Labour Care Guide in Enugu State, Nigeria. The guide, launched in 2020, replaced the older partograph for monitoring labor. Midwives are frontline maternity providers, yet uptake of the new guide is unclear.

Among 43 midwives in public facilities, 69.8 percent had heard of the guide, but 37.2 percent had poor knowledge of it. Only a third of those aware saw it as highly feasible for routine use. Almost all wrongly thought it includes alert and action lines. Barriers named included complexity, time, lack of training, and staff shortages, pointing to a need for training and curriculum change.
pmc-13272990:
Ramya Walsan leads a 2026 document analysis of what skills patients need to use virtual care well. Virtual care delivers health services by video, phone, or messaging. The team examined patient-focused documents from Australia and New Zealand, drawn from 83 government, health, private, and consumer organization websites.

They found three broad skill themes: technology and infrastructure, literacy and advocacy, and service engagement, with nine sub-themes in total. Most documents focused on technology and task steps, with less on equity, advocacy, safety, privacy, and support for priority groups. The authors call for research on how these skills play out in real care and for more inclusive design.
pmc-13273190: Retraction note for a 2025 article on an AI model for predicting diabetes stages in connected health care. The editors have retracted the article in 2026. Concerns were raised about the diabetes data set used in the study. The authors had used a public data set whose origin and validity cannot be confirmed. Since that data set trained and validated the model, the editors no longer trust the results. One author disagrees with the retraction, and others did not state a view or did not reply.
pmc-13273390:
Mohamad Behzadi leads a 2026 case report of a mature teratoma, a germ cell tumor, found in the omentum of a 65-year-old Iranian woman. Teratomas usually arise in the ovaries, and tumors outside the gonads are extremely rare. She had mild belly pain for a year and a normal physical exam.

A CT scan showed a calcified pelvic mass with fat, seeming to connect to the right fallopian tube. At surgery the mass was in the greater omentum, a fold of tissue in the abdomen, with no link to the ovaries. Tissue tests confirmed a mature, benign teratoma. Surgical removal succeeded and her recovery was smooth.
pmc-13273890:
Coffman and colleagues report a 2026 quality improvement project that used hospital stays to check care transition needs. Most transition work happens in clinics. The team worked at a large urban pediatric hospital.

Care coordinators complete an electronic assessment for admitted patients. It includes an optional item on health care transition. Completion was low at baseline. The project aimed to raise completion by 50 percent in six months. It covered patients aged 16 and older. A standard workflow set the age threshold. Staff also received interactive training. Documented completion rose from 44.0 percent to 74.4 percent. Surveyed staff reported higher confidence after training.
pmc-13274090: Adam R Aluisio and co-authors issued a 2026 correction notice for their study protocol on an HIV testing program in emergency rooms. The protocol describes a cluster randomized trial using a systems improvement method, called HEATED-SAIA. It appeared in Implementation Science Communications. The notice fixes only the competing interests statement, which wrongly said the authors had none. The corrected text states that Malabika Sarker is an editor of the journal, while the other authors report no competing interests. The notice says the original article has been corrected.
pmc-13274190:
Paulius Bucius and colleagues report a 2026 journal article comparing heart scan grades in a disease where abnormal protein clogs the heart muscle. Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy is now often diagnosed with a bone tracer scan instead of biopsy, graded by how strongly the heart lights up. Whether the two positive grades differ in severity was uncertain.

Reviewing 302 scans done from 2018 to 2025, the team found fifty-three confirmed cases, only eight at grade two and forty-five at grade three. Grade three patients walked shorter distances in six minutes and had thicker heart walls, weaker pumping, and higher troponin, a damage marker. Scan grade tracked closely with heart muscle mass on MRI.
pmc-13274590:
Xinshui Yu and colleagues present a 2026 journal article uncovering how white mulberry trees build a family of protective compounds called moracins. These benzofuran chemicals show varied biological activity, but the plant's recipe for them was unknown. The team hunted for the enzymes involved using a heat-based protein profiling method.

They found an unusual enzyme, a laccase named MaLAC, that folds a precursor called oxyresveratrol into moracin M, a shared stepping stone to the other moracins. The reaction is a copper-driven radical ring closure, the first of its kind shown for a plant laccase. The team then rebuilt the whole pathway inside a tobacco relative, pointing toward factory production of these compounds.
pmc-13275590:
Simone Bellavia and a large team report a 2026 journal article on whether adding clot-busting drugs before mechanical clot removal helps stroke patients with a blocked basilar artery and mild symptoms. This artery feeds the brainstem, and its blockage is perilous, yet mild cases are understudied. The team pooled 134 such patients from ten European stroke centers treated between 2017 and 2024, balancing groups statistically.

Adding intravenous thrombolysis before thrombectomy did not raise the risk of brain bleeding or in-hospital death, so the combined approach looked safe. But it brought no extra benefit: ninety-day function scores and successful reopening rates were no better than with thrombectomy alone. The authors conclude the drug adds safety-neutral cost and delay in this mild-symptom group.
pmc-13276090:
Feng Qianqian and co-authors report a 2026 computational study on a rose fruit extract and a kidney disease. The disease, IgA nephropathy, damages the kidney's filters and is now treated with drugs that can cause harsh side effects. The fruit of Rosa laxa, a rose from Xinjiang, has a history of use for kidney complaints.

Instead of lab tests, the team used gene databases, machine learning, and molecular simulations. They overlapped genes changed in patients with targets of the extract's ingredients and found one hundred eighteen shared targets. Three rounds of machine learning narrowed these to two core proteins, named FGR and LDHB. Three ingredients, including ellagic acid and rutin, were the likely active parts. Simulations showed these compounds bind both proteins steadily, supporting further lab work.
pmc-13276190:
Carmen Ayala-Martinez and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a quick body measure that may flag fading strength in older adults. The measure, phase angle, comes from a painless electrical test and reflects cell health and muscle quality. Whether measuring single body parts beats a whole-body reading was unclear.

Ninety-three adults aged sixty-five and older, living in their own homes in southern Spain, took the electrical test and several function tests. These covered balance and walking, grip strength, walking speed, and leg power. Phase angle in the legs linked most strongly to the combined performance score, walking speed, and leg power. Arm readings linked mainly to grip strength. Trunk readings linked to nothing. The authors say matching the body region to the task gives the sharpest signal.
pmc-13276290:
Shuqiang Cheng and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on an odd class of RNA molecules in stomach cancer. Cross-strand chimeric RNAs form when genes on opposite DNA strands fuse into one message. Their role in gastric cancer was unexplored.

Scanning three hundred seventy-two tumor samples, the team found these fused messages enriched in tumors regardless of stage or spread. A three-step machine learning pipeline picked six genomic regions that together predicted survival. Patients with high risk scores lived far shorter on average than low-risk patients. In a small separate group, high-risk tumors showed an immune-suppressing makeup, with fewer killer T cells. Lab tests confirmed one fusion message was real. Silencing it slowed cancer cell growth and spread and pushed cells toward death.
pmc-13276490:
Cameron Watson and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on mental health after encephalitis, inflammation of the brain. Survivors often report lasting psychiatric problems, but how common each symptom is was poorly mapped. The team pooled studies reporting symptoms at least three months after illness.

One hundred one studies covering about forty-seven hundred patients met the criteria. Depression affected about twenty-seven percent of survivors, and anxiety about twenty-three percent. Loss of inhibition and emotional instability each hit roughly one in five. Infectious causes carried far higher rates of mood symptoms than autoimmune causes. Symptom rates shifted with follow-up length, age, and the share of women in each study. Differences between studies were large. The authors call for standard outcome measures and forward-looking comparison studies.
pmc-13276590:
John Madias wrote a 2026 letter to the editor on two heart conditions that may cause each other. Spontaneous coronary artery dissection is a tearing of a heart artery wall. Takotsubo syndrome is a stress-triggered ballooning of the heart's main chamber. A registry study had found forty-four patients with both, without confirmatory follow-up imaging.

Madias praises the careful review of the patients' heart images by a central laboratory, which he calls crucial for telling dissection apart from ordinary heart attacks. He notes the study found few differences between patients with dissection alone and those with both conditions, apart from more procedures and in-hospital events in one group. His main point is a two-way relationship he has argued since 2015: the ballooning could set up the tear, and the tear's stress could trigger the ballooning. Timing of scans against symptom onset, he says, may reveal which came first.
pmc-13279190:
Simin Chen and colleagues give a 2026 review of Streptomyces, a group of soil germs famed for making useful natural drugs. The review covers gains from 2020 to 2025, drawn from about one hundred fifty cases. Its focus is chassis work, meaning tuning a host germ into a clean factory for a target product.

Sections cover slimming genomes, cutting side products, steering raw feed and energy, rewiring gene controls, and matching host to gene cluster. Tough growth in large tanks gets its own section. A five step loop, named the 5M plan, ties the parts in one cycle from how a path works to full scale making. The map should help labs build strains for high value goods.
pmc-13279390:
Alejandra Bravo-Balado and colleagues report a 2026 lab study that compares lasers for breaking kidney stones. Two laser types face off: thulium fiber laser and high power holmium YAG laser. The holmium tool was tried with four pulse modes that shape each burst. Fake stones made from a set powder mix stood in for real stones in the tests.

A motor arm moved the laser at a fixed speed to make fair cuts. Tests used three energy and rate settings, with five cuts each and seven hundred fifty measures in all. The thulium tool with a mid width fiber cut the most stone in most settings. Its edge was clear at mid and high rates. Pulse mode choice changed holmium yield a lot. Bench results can guide stone surgery set up, though body trials must confirm.
pmc-13279490:
Tomoki Asano and colleagues report a 2026 study of drains after hip replacement surgery. Closed suction drains are tubes that pull fluid from the wound. Surgeons use them to stop blood pools and muscle swelling, yet proof of gain is mixed. The team ask if drains change blood pools, swelling and patient results after total hip replacement.

Records held one hundred sixty eight patients who had one side, cement free hip replacement for hip wear from hip dysplasia. Sixty matched pairs, with and without drains, were picked by a score match on age, sex, weight, surgery time and stem type. CT scans before surgery and on day seven measured deep tissue area as a stand in for blood pool and swelling. Blood loss, pain scores and side effects were also tracked.
pmc-13279590:
Alexander J. Wong and Christopher C. Donnell present a 2026 scoping review of fluoride free toothpaste options. Some families shy from fluoride, a mineral that guards teeth from decay. The review maps how fluoride free pastes have been studied, what outcomes were used and what the proof means for talks with children and families. Searches covered studies from January 2020 to March 2026.

One hundred twenty two studies fit, yet most were lab or mechanism work. Just twenty studies gave direct child evidence. Fluoride free mixes showed germ kill acts, film shifts and gains on stand in measures of mineral return to teeth. Direct checks of real decay in teeth were rare. Mix types, designs and outcomes varied a lot. The map shows where proof is thin, which can guide honest family talks and new trials.
pmc-13279790:
Carlos Garcia-Lopez-de-Haro and colleagues present a 2026 tool paper on SAMJ, a plugin for fast image annotation. Marking objects in biomedical images trains AI systems for cell finds, tissue counts and disease reads. Pixel exact marks take long expert hours, which slows AI uptake. The Segment Anything Model, or SAM, can cut objects from simple clicks. Yet its use in common image tools was hard for non coders.

SAMJ puts light SAM variants in ImageJ and Fiji, the widely used free image programs. Users mark objects in large images in real time with clicks or boxes. No coding skill or special hardware is needed, and work runs on standard computers. Tests show fast, interactive and accurate marks. Easier marks can speed dataset builds for bioimage AI across many labs.
pmc-13280590:
Elliot Heward and colleagues present a 2026 multicentre retrospective cohort study of referral patterns for paediatric otorrhoea in the United Kingdom. Otorrhoea is discharge from the ear when the eardrum bursts in middle ear infection. It causes hearing loss during a critical developmental period. Children with otorrhoea were identified among two thousand one hundred paediatric ENT referrals from primary care at two hospital trusts in England in 2023.

Of the referrals, two hundred twenty eight, about eleven percent, had otorrhoea. Mean age was about six years, and one hundred ten were female. The most frequent symptom duration at referral was over three to six months, at about twenty one percent. Chi squared analysis compared referral urgency for those with or without hearing loss. Timely management matters to prevent disease repercussions, and no evidence on referral patterns existed before this count.
pmc-13280690:
Angharad N de Cates and colleagues ran a 2026 drug trial on thinking skills in people who had recovered from depression. Low mood had lifted, but slow thinking often stayed. Fifty adults who had had depression at least twice took part. Half got a drug that boosts a serotonin receptor, a switch for a brain chemical. Half got a dummy pill, for seven to ten days.

The drug group recalled more words on a memory test. They also worked faster on a hard memory task with no loss of accuracy. They read fast-shown facial feelings more correctly too. Mood scores did not drive the gains. The authors say the drug may help thinking after depression, a need few drugs now meet.
pmc-13281490:
Yi Tian and colleagues reported stomach flu outbreaks in a Guangzhou college district in a 2026 paper. The events took place from January to April 2013, during a global wave of norovirus. Norovirus spreads fast and causes vomiting and loose stools. Six hundred fifty-two people fell ill across five universities and one middle school. Labs tested close to four hundred samples, and about a third held the virus.

Gene reading pinned the strain as a new variant first seen in Sydney in 2012. The team read its full gene code and set it beside older strains. Small changes sat in spots that grip human cells and in spots the immune system reads. Tests showed the strain could grip cells from a wider range of people than older strains. The authors say that broader grip may explain its worldwide spread.
pmc-13281890:
Jing Zhou and colleagues tested a pecking order of life settings in teen mental health in a 2026 study. Classic theory says close settings, like family, should outweigh wider ones, like the neighborhood. The team used a 2019 Finnish school health survey. Nearly seventy thousand teens, averaging about fifteen and a half, took part. Their answers covered mood, anxiety, loneliness, and life satisfaction. Factors were added in blocks, from personal traits to family, school, peers, and community belonging.

Thinking troubles tied most strongly to low mood and anxiety. But community belonging broke the pecking order. It showed the largest tie to life satisfaction of any factor. It also showed the strongest guard against low mood, even after close settings were counted. Loneliness answered most to school and peer factors. Cross-setting buffering was rare; effects mostly added up. The authors urge towns to count as mental health actors.
pmc-13282890:
Fat cells hugging a breast tumor can blunt key cancer drugs, a resistance route traced in 2026 under Renhong Huang. Fat cells near tumors, called cancer-associated adipocytes, can change tumor behavior. The question is how they block drugs that target CDK4 and CDK6.

Fluid from these fat cells induced stronger resistance than fluid from normal fat cells. Screens found high IL-6, a signal that acts through STAT3 and SREBF2. That chain raised cholesterol control and cell cycle activity. Cancer cells also sent a small RNA that turned normal fat cells into tumor-linked ones. Blocking cholesterol production with simvastatin restored drug response in lab and animal tests.
pmc-13282990:
Brain infection by a drug-resistant germ after hemorrhage surgery is the emergency in a 2026 case assembled by Hao Wu's group. The germ was Acinetobacter baumannii, a drug-resistant bacterium with poor outcomes. No standard treatment plan exists for this rare and severe infection type.

Spinal fluid checks, cultures, and inflammation markers guided care for the patient. Drugs were meropenem and vancomycin given through a vein. Care also used spinal fluid replacement and drainage from the lower spine. After one week the patient improved and fluid cultures turned negative. The authors stress that one case gives early guidance only. Larger studies are needed to set a shared treatment standard.
pmc-13283190:
Arginine paste, low-level laser, or both for sensitive teeth perform alike in a 2026 trial run by Viviane Leal Barbosa's group. Tooth sensitivity causes sharp pain from air or touch at the gum line. The trial tests each method alone and combined against a control.

A total of 60 adults joined, and 54 finished the eight-week trial. Four groups got laser, arginine paste, both, or control care in the design. Pain scores fell over time in all groups by clear margins. No method beat the others at any check point in the results. Air and touch tests both showed the same broad pattern. Longer trials may be needed to split the options.
pmc-13283390:
Blood fat patterns track cataract type unevenly in Yepei Qin's 2026 Fudan clinic analysis of older patients. Cloudy lenses are the top cause of blindness in older adults worldwide. Links between high blood fats and cataract have stayed disputed for years.

A total of 384 patients at a Fudan University eye hospital took part. Cataracts were split into cortical, nuclear, and rear capsule types for analysis. High blood fats linked most clearly to severity of the rear capsule type. One fat carrier and blood triglycerides raised risk, while HDL cholesterol lowered it. Cortical severity linked to female sex and two blood markers. Nuclear type showed a distinct pattern.
pmc-13284290:
Bloodstream infection by a gut anaerobe clusters in cancer patients in a 2026 five-year review by Meliha Cagla Sonmezer and colleagues. Bacteroides fragilis causes deep and blood infections yet often escapes routine notice. Testing limits in labs leave its resistance patterns under-tracked.

Blood culture cases ran from July 2018 to January 2023 at one tertiary hospital. Cancer treatments that weaken gut defenses likely explain the cancer clustering. Hospital-acquired infection raised thirty-day death risk notably in the analysis. Lung infection as source also raised death risk in the cohort. Clindamycin resistance was substantial, while carbapenem resistance stayed uncommon but present.
pmc-13284890:
Melaku Zewdu Yehualaw and co-authors report a 2026 cross-sectional study of hepatitis B vaccination among health workers. The virus is a major job risk, above all where vaccine coverage stays low. A census-based survey covered 448 health workers in late 2025, using a pretested questionnaire and adjusted models to find linked factors.

Only about 38 percent of workers were fully vaccinated in this survey group. Knowledge and attitude scores were higher than coverage. Training in infection prevention, strong knowledge of the infection and of the vaccine, and a favorable attitude each linked to vaccination. The authors urge stronger workplace programs, free vaccine access, and better prevention training.
pmc-13285990:
Mustafa Mohammed and colleagues describe a near-collapse during a heart ultrasound exam in a 2026 case report. An 83-year-old woman with kidney failure, severe lung pressure, and a badly leaking tricuspid valve came for a probe exam through the food pipe. Standard sedation is usually safe, yet her strained right heart left almost no margin for error.

Soon after the calming drug and probe went in, her blood pressure crashed and live images showed the right ventricle ballooning with weak squeeze. Staff stopped the exam at once and gave drugs that tightened her vessels and steadied the heart. Within twenty minutes she sat back at her starting readings, awake and stable. The authors urge slow, low dosing and early vessel support for patients whose right heart already works at its limit.
pmc-13286190:
Debbie-Ann Shirley and colleagues review amebiasis as a neglected tropical disease in a 2026 survey of knowledge gaps. A gut parasite that also seeds liver abscesses still ranks among the worst causes of severe diarrhea in poor regions. The review walks through spread, testing, and treatment, with a hard look at how little has moved in five years of published work.

Gene-based tests can now tell the harmful species from harmless look-alikes, yet cost and thin labs keep them out of reach where cases cluster. One old drug family still carries nearly all treatment for invasive disease, with no approved backup if it fails or harms. No licensed vaccine exists, and work toward one crawls for lack of funds. The authors urge fresh money for tests, drugs, and prevention aimed at the places hit hardest.
pmc-13287290:
Azusa Kato and colleagues built a mouse model in 2026 of abdominal sepsis that animals can survive, by removing dead bowel tissue six hours after infection and giving antibiotics for three days. Survival reached about 90% by day fourteen, against none without that source control.

Blood infection markers fell and bacteria cleared, yet lungs stayed inflamed. Defence cells gathered in lung tissue while T and B cells dropped. One antibody type fell in airway fluid even though blood levels held, and airway lining proteins linked to antibody transport weakened. The authors offer the model for studying lasting lung harm after sepsis recovery.
pmc-13288490:
Ryan T Steele and co-authors swap one ring atom in a 2026 chemistry study. The work deals with isoindolines. Step one widens the ring. A Stevens rearrangement drives that step. The wide ring gains an aroyl group. Step two uses light to push nitrogen out. The ring then shrinks toward indene products.

Both steps can run in one pot. The net effect swaps nitrogen for carbon. The team probed what steadied the short-lived products. Those products are amino-indanes. Some were treated with anhydrides. That gave stable forms that could be kept. Such edits could tune drug scaffolds with less rebuild work.
pmc-13288690:
Junming Hu and a large team build a machine-learning screen for Alzheimer's disease risk in a 2026 UK Biobank cohort study. Drawing on 13,076 participants followed for up to 16 years, they trained an automated pipeline with a boosted-tree classifier on routine records, splitting data into training, development, and test portions.

During follow-up, 927 participants developed the disease. Selection cut 3,590 candidate variables down to 26 predictors. They spanned age, the APOE4 gene variant, and social conditions. Medical history plus routine clinical measures also counted. The finished model separated future cases well in held-out tests. It stayed calibrated there too, with similar patterns for men and women. Social factors added signal, though the authors warn those links are predictive, not proven causes.
pmc-13289090:
Kaori Baba and colleagues test home visits for young mothers in Japan. Their 2026 study copies a trial design from past data. Mothers were first-time parents aged 16 to 25. Four Tokyo areas fed the data. The program was co-designed with young mothers.

The visit group held 151 mothers. The past-care group held 158 mothers. Trained teams visited from pregnancy to one year. Most mothers stayed to 12 months in both groups. Needs felt more met in the visit group. That held at six and 12 months. Low mood scores were also lower there. Gains in well-being were less clear cut.
pmc-13289690:
Jackline A Tepson, Daniel S Agyirifo, and Lei Yuan offer a 2026 integrative review on microbial ecology where food safety meets biotechnology. Microbes in food play two roles: they spoil and sicken, yet they also ferment, preserve, and create useful products. Ecology ties these roles together through competition, stress response, and biofilm growth across farm and factory settings.

The review gathers peer work from 2015 to 2025 on interactions, contamination paths, and control mechanisms. The same ecology that spreads risk is harnessed for controlled fermentation, natural preservation, probiotics, enzymes, and engineered microbes. Gene sequencing and multi-layer molecular tools now let scientists link community patterns to outcomes. Gaps for future work close the survey.
pmc-13289890:
Diane Yirgnur Some headed a 2026 field trial in Burkina Faso on a smarter malaria test algorithm for febrile children under five. Standard rapid tests detect one parasite protein that lingers after treatment, causing false positives. The new algorithm reads two proteins in sequence and adds recent treatment history to judge whether illness is truly current malaria.

Children aged 6 to 59 months at clinics were randomized to standard testing or to algorithm arms using an electronic or paper decision path. In the algorithm, a second protein line meant positive, no lines meant negative, and a lone first line was resolved using treatment in the prior four weeks. Field accuracy was then compared fairly.
pmc-13290390:
A traditional formula, Guilu Erxian Glue, steadied the immune system of mice with aplastic anemia in a 2026 study by Song Sun and colleagues. Aplastic anemia is bone marrow failure driven in part by misdirected T-cell attack.

The team first mined patient data to find misregulated microRNAs, landing on miRNA-17-5p and miRNA-10a-5p. They then profiled the formula's chemistry and tested it in a mouse model built with irradiation and donor lymphocytes. Treated mice showed better marrow structure and restored blood counts. Harmful T-cell subsets fell while regulatory T cells rose, and the authors link the effect to the two microRNA pathways and Fas signaling. Sun and colleagues present the formula, given with standard immunosuppression, as a candidate for restoring immune balance in this disease.
pmc-13290590:
Telling three kinds of lumbar spine tumor apart before surgery is the job of an imaging nomogram built by Canghai Shen and colleagues in 2026. Benign primary tumors, malignant primary tumors, and metastases call for different plans, yet they can look alike on scans.

The retrospective study drew on 100 patients with proven lumbar tumors and pulled radiomic features from three MRI sequences. A signature of 11 stable features joined five clinical predictors in a combined nomogram. On an independent test set it separated the three classes with a macro-average AUC of 0.887, calibrated well, and promised net benefit across many decision thresholds. Shen and colleagues offer it as non-invasive support for preoperative planning.
pmc-13290890:
Young women who sell sex in Tanzania work in hiding and lean on peers to find health care, Joyce Wamoyi and colleagues report in an ethnographic study from 2026. These women face high HIV risk, yet sexual and reproductive health services remain hard for them to reach, and the team explored why from inside their world.

Thirty-eight in-depth interviews and photovoice work with workers aged 18 to 24, plus six program implementers, fed a thematic analysis. Sex work's illegality forced discretion under fear of arrest, and stigma at clinics blocked care. The women preferred differentiated services designed for them, and peers proved decisive in whether and where they sought care. Wamoyi and colleagues recommend action at every level: friendlier clinics, community stigma work, knowledge and livelihood support, and policy reform.
pmc-13290990:
Inside a Finnish trap facility, M Winter and a large physics team report a 2026 precision measurement of antimony-129 and its isomer. Mass and decay energy values for this short-lived isotope matter for tests linked to the mass of the electron antineutrino, where very low decay energies are prized.

Atoms made and separated at the IGISOL facility were weighed with the JYFLTRAP double Penning trap, giving a decay energy far sharper than the older adopted value. Five decay branches once seen as possible ultra-low cases now sit too high in energy to qualify, closing that route. A separate branch from the isomeric state lands near the ultra-low range, though its spin and parity likely block the decay in practice.
pmc-13291290:
Central lines help tiny preterm babies feed and grow. Christine Silwedel leads a 2026 study of their long-term effects. Babies born before 29 weeks often need these lines. Whether lines shape later growth or brain scores was unknown.

Network records tracked over two thousand such infants. Three quarters had a central line in early life. Those babies were born smaller and earlier. At preschool age, they weighed less on raw counts. Their test scores also ran lower before fair adjustment. Matching and risk adjustment were used to level the field. Raw gaps thus reflect birth state more than line use. Care teams get a calmer read on line safety.
pmc-13291490:
Tiny antibodies can be tuned to picomolar grip with physics-guided AI. Ning Shi leads a 2026 study designing a cancer nanobody. Such small binders clear the body too fast for therapy. Ultra-strong grip is needed to hold targets under washout.

The method pairs structure forecasts with motion simulations. Energy math spots weak points at the binding face. A focused variant library fixed those weak points. Nearly all built variants bound their target. Best grip improved about three hundred fold over the parent. Heat stability stayed strong across variants. Deep tumor entry and clear imaging are the aims. The route may speed binder design for other targets.
pmc-13291890:
Victoria J Clemett and a large team present a 2026 systematic review asking whether skin tone changes how chronic venous insufficiency gets spotted and treated. Leg vein disease shows on the skin, but signs look different across tones, and the patient journey impact was unclear. The review followed a registered PROSPERO protocol and searched six databases plus trial registries through February 2025.

Twenty-two studies covering 111,090 people qualified. Evidence suggests Black and Thai patients can show internal vein changes without the surface signs clinicians expect, which may delay care. Treatment gaps also appeared, with Black patients facing higher costs and more procedures. Because skin tone itself was seldom recorded, the reviewers used ethnicity as a stand-in and warn that this blurs the findings.
pmc-13292790:
Matteo Morello and co-authors examine, in a 2026 study, whether loss of the Y chromosome in blood cells relates to aortic valve narrowing or a wider aorta in older men. Both conditions share inflamed tissue pathways and occur more often in men.

Blood came from 64 men with moderate or worse valve narrowing and 69 men without major valve disease, matched for age. A DNA test estimated how many blood cells lacked a Y chromosome by comparing X and Y gene copies. Heart scans gave valve status and the widest aortic measure for each man. The work tests a possible link between an aging blood change and heart structure.
pmc-13292990:
Zibin Zhan and colleagues trace, in a 2026 study, how a fat-making enzyme called GPAM affects alcoholic liver disease. Fat disorder and failing cell powerhouses are both core features of the disease, yet how they connect in patients was unknown.

GPAM levels were lower in patients and fell further as disease grew worse. With less GPAM, harmful fats such as ceramide built up while a key membrane fat for cell powerhouses dropped. Powerhouses then changed shape, cleared poorly, and breathed weakly, which sparked inflammation in mouse livers. Restoring GPAM in cells, animals, and liver organoids eased the disease, marking GPAM as a possible treatment target.
pmc-13293690:
Ali Tabrizi and co-authors report, in a 2026 case study, giant recurring orf disease in a man with weak immunity. Orf is a sheep and goat virus that gives mild sores in healthy people but can grow huge and stubborn when immunity fails.

The 59-year-old man cut his left ring finger while slaughtering a sheep. He had a blood disorder under chemotherapy, which weakened his defenses. Disease spread widely over his hand and lower leg, and the report notes that dirty surgical tools during the first removal sped spread to new sites. Care of giant lesions in such hosts stays hard, with few guiding cases.
pmc-13293990:
Jenni K. Pedor and colleagues simplify production of MarathonRT in a 2026 protocol. The enzyme copies RNA into DNA for sequencing and can read through the tight folds and chemical marks on transfer RNAs that stall ordinary enzymes. Commercial rivals work but cost a lot, while the open MarathonRT version suffered precipitation and long purification.

One affinity step now yields active enzyme that stays stable over 1 year, cutting a day of work and two chromatography steps. A cheap activity assay checks each batch. In the mim-tRNAseq pipeline, the home-made enzyme matched Induro and UltraMarathonRT, widening access to accurate transfer RNA counts.
pmc-13294490:
Matteo Zannini and coauthors use transfer learning to make heart tracing AI explanations land on the right waves in a 2026 study. Their two-branch network reads ECG shape in one branch and rhythm in the other to spot atrial fibrillation. Each branch first trained on a matching narrow task, P wave spotting or interval variability, then fine-tuned with staged layer freezing.

Accuracy after tuning spanned 85.70% to 95.23% across setups, matching the base model. Explanation maps told the real story: shape pretraining pushed credit onto P waves, rhythm pretraining onto R peaks, and freezing more layers sharpened the split. Training order can teach models to explain like clinicians.
pmc-13294690:
Satoru Takahashi and colleagues present a 2026 case report about tiny fragments found in blood drawn back after a brain procedure. The patient had a grade III occipital arteriovenous malformation treated with Onyx, a liquid blocking agent. Clinicians often aspirate blood from a distal access catheter afterwards, though the reason it helps was unclear.

Scanning electron microscopy with elemental analysis found tantalum-bearing clumps matching Onyx on the catheter and in the drawn blood. The fragments measured roughly 50 to 90 micrometres, and a simple bench model also showed Onyx sticking to catheters. Whether such fragments matter for patients stays uncertain, but the findings suggest leftover material can persist inside the catheter system.
pmc-13295690:
Seda Koçak and colleagues give a hormone-like peptide to rats with low thyroid function in a 2026 study. Too little thyroid hormone disturbs reproduction, mood, movement, and memory in people and animals. Spexin, a peptide tied to energy and hormone control, was tested in a drug-induced rat model.

The team tracked two partner proteins, irisin and KISS-1, in brain cortex and testis tissue alongside blood and behaviour measures. The model itself was built with methimazole, which blocks thyroid hormone making and mimics human illness patterns. Results are framed as a step toward understanding how spexin interacts with thyroid pathways across body and brain.
pmc-13295790:
Pornchanok Yensookjai and colleagues read ancient cattle DNA in Thailand in a 2026 study. Zebu cattle dominate Southeast Asia today, while earlier Thai herds were thought to be purely taurine. Twenty-six specimens from nine dig sites, spanning 3,400 to 600 years ago, were examined for lineage clues.

Usable DNA came from remains at two sites, dated roughly 1,700 to 650 years ago. Those animals grouped with modern zebu from India, China, and Cambodia rather than with taurine lines. Zebu tied to South Asian herds therefore reached Thailand at least 1,700 years ago, revealing trade and travel links across the region.
pmc-13295890:
Ateeqa Aslam and colleagues compare two pig coronavirus strains in 2026: a brain-seeking strain from 1972 and a recent one found in nasal samples in 2020. They track how each grows in pig kidney cells, airway tissue pieces and airway lining cells.

The older strain started infections faster, while the newer one grew stronger later in kidney cells, and both behaved alike in nasal tissue. In smell-related tissue the older strain infected more support cells. Two changes in the spike protein may alter how the virus grips cells. The authors link those small genetic shifts to differing growth habits.
pmc-13296090:
Kai Shi and colleagues compare, in 2026, laying and non-laying Zhedong white geese to learn why this valued Chinese breed stops laying for long stretches each year. Blood chemistry, chemical profiles and gut microbes were measured in both groups.

Non-laying geese differed in reproductive hormones, inflammation markers and antioxidant levels, with many chemical changes centred on amino acid and steroid pathways. Gut microbe variety held steady, but helpful bacterial kinds linked to reproductive chemicals fell sharply. The authors argue that disturbed metabolism plus gut decline together drive the pause, and they flag markers that might lift egg output.
pmc-13296190:
Wei Wang and colleagues test, in 2026, a grape seed extract formula designed to deliver proanthocyanidin C1, a natural compound that clears worn-out cells, more effectively by mouth. Ageing mice in two models received the improved formula, named NSPCC1.

Treated mice absorbed the compound better, lived longer and showed fewer ageing signs. Blood-forming stem cells in bone marrow worked better, immune cell balance improved, and damage and inflammation eased in liver, kidneys and lungs. The authors suggest food-based products of this kind could support healthier ageing, though human work lies ahead.
pmc-13298990:
Learning a new motor skill briefly swells brain cells before durably rewiring their connections, show Guillermina Griffa and colleagues in a 2026 imaging study. Using ultra-high-gradient diffusion MRI with a cell-specific model, they watched the living human brain's microstructure change as people learned.

Two responses appeared on different clocks. Cell bodies expanded temporarily across every region the task engaged, a pattern the authors read as short-lived housekeeping. Meanwhile, the density of cell processes rose and stayed up, but only in key motor regions, consistent with lasting structural change. The approach gives researchers a noninvasive window on plasticity mechanisms previously visible only in animal studies.
pmc-13299190:
Osteoarthritis may start in the gut as much as in the joint, argue Ruipu Zhang and colleagues in a 2026 review of the gut-joint axis. Gut bacteria ship metabolites through the blood to synovial joints, and the balance among them may decide whether cartilage is protected or attacked.

Three metabolite classes anchor the account: short-chain fatty acids that calm inflammation, trimethylamine N-oxide that provokes it, and bile acids that regulate in either direction. The authors package this into a homeostasis imbalance framework spanning gut barrier integrity, metabolite traffic, and joint-level effects. They also assess whether exercise and probiotics can retune the axis, pointing toward precision treatment of metabolic osteoarthritis.
pmc-13305190:
Ghislaine Boungou-Tsona and co-authors study healing compounds in leaves of Vitex madiensis, a shrub used in African folk medicine for aches and pains, in a 2026 lab report. Sorting which extract parts carry the strongest effect was the goal.

Chemical profiling and step-by-step splitting of the extract isolated four steroid-like plant compounds from its most active part. One compound, 20-hydroxyecdysone, cut a key inflammation enzyme's presence by over seventy percent in provoked human blood cells. Other fractions were screened for oxidation-fighting power as well. The results back the plant's traditional use and its compound family.
pmc-13305690:
Scott and co-authors test whether machines can flag young people heading for bipolar disorder in this 2026 study. First episodes of mania or hypomania, unusually elevated mood states, often strike in youth. Family history, genes, and early symptoms each carry some signal. The team built classification models from a long running study of twins and siblings.

Of 1473 participants, 104 developed bipolar disorder type one or two. The best boosting model scored strongly overall and caught most future cases. Depressive symptoms carried the most weight, followed by psychotic symptoms, a combined genetic score, hypomanic symptoms, and family history. The model classified mania cases far better than hypomania cases. Scott calls for agreed definitions of risk factors and methods that respect how rare true cases are.
pmc-13305890:
Yu Cui re-examined trial data in 2026 to find who still worsens early after a stroke despite dual blood-thinning drugs. The source trial, ATAMIS, treated mild to moderate ischaemic stroke with clopidogrel plus aspirin.

Among 1122 treated patients, 66 people, or 5.9%, deteriorated within seven days by the study definition of a two-point rise on a standard stroke scale. Shorter delay before starting drugs and higher admission systolic pressure each linked to greater risk in adjusted models, among three factors in total. Spotting this group early could guide closer watching and targeted extra care.
pmc-13307290:
Hassanain Ali reviewed soft gel sensors from first mix to end use in a 2026 survey. Gels feel like body flesh, hold much water and react to heat and touch, which opens sense paths hard gear cannot match.

Plant and lab made gels are set side by side, with link styles that span bond, touch and mixed types in the survey. Sense modes span push, charge, heat volts, chem tests, hue and light ratio, each with score facts. New types join self power heat sense, sharp chem read and gel frames with MXene bits.
pmc-13307590:
Chen Chen and co-authors study in 2026 repeat SARS-CoV-2 infection and antibody levels in Shanghai after the zero COVID era ended in China. Their group covered 2095 people who had earlier caught the Omicron BA.2 form, with surveys on life habits and blood tests for blocking antibodies.

Meeting World Health Organization activity guidance tracked with lower odds of repeat infection, though the design cannot prove cause and effect. Every vaccinated group showed higher antibody levels than the unvaccinated group did in these tests. Older age and more months since the last immune event both tracked with lower levels. The authors call for larger forward looking studies to confirm each of these links.
pmc-13308490:
Christian J Wiedermann and co-authors check in 2026 whether strong albumin fluid raises pressure inside the skull in very ill patients with brain problems. Old trial hints blamed weak albumin for harm in head injury, yet the fault may lie with the watery mix, not the protein itself.

They mined intensive care records for 18 patients who got 25 percent albumin and had at least three pressure reads before and after the dose. Overall pressure barely moved, while blood pressure rose in a clear way after the dose. In five patients who started with high skull pressure, readings fell, though the shift was not firm at this small size.
pmc-13309190:
Hiroaki Nishioka reports in 2026 a case of purple urine bag syndrome in a woman aged 88 years who lives in a long term care home with mild dementia. A Foley catheter was placed for urine block, and two weeks later the tube and bag turned a strong purple while the urine stayed yellow.

Germs break down a food amino acid into blue and red pigments that cling to plastic, which paints the bag in this benign state. She had no fever or mind change, so no urine test or antibiotic was given at the time. A fresh tube and bag plus bowel care cleared the colour at once. Calm spotting of the sign can spare needless drugs.
pmc-13309390:
Eugenia Sly-Moore led a 2026 field study on anemia in young children in Ghana. Anemia weakens growth and health, and its causes differ from place to place. Local data from the Ejura-Sekyedumase area were needed to guide local action.

Health workers studied 476 children aged one to five in four communities during 2021, using surveys, body measures, diet records, and blood tests. About three in four children had anemia, and about half carried malaria parasites in their blood. Older age within the group linked to lower severity, while other child and household traits raised risk. The authors call for local steps against both anemia and malaria.
pmc-13310490:
Xiaofeng Jiang and co-authors use genetics to test gut microbe and immune links to insomnia in a 2026 study. The gut-brain axis may shape sleep, yet whether microbes truly cause poor sleep, and whether immune cells carry that effect, needs stronger proof than surveys give. Inherited variants offer a natural experiment route.

Large genetic data sets for gut microbes, 731 immune cell traits, and insomnia from a Finnish release were combined in a two-way causal analysis. Suggestive links tied 13 microbial groups to insomnia risk, with one Blautia species standing protectively after strict correction while sister species raised risk. Seventeen immune traits also linked to insomnia. Mediation checks traced which immune traits might carry microbe effects.
pmc-13310790:
Russell C Dale led a 2026 case report on early brain reaching immune care for a baby with Aicardi-Goutières syndrome. The rare gene disease drives excess interferon signals that harm the brain. Fast gene testing found two faults in the ADAR1 gene, and past data showed most such children face severe disability or death.

Care began at 11 months with pulsed steroid doses every three weeks plus a daily JAK blocking drug. By 24 months the child crawled and took a few steps alone, far ahead of past norms. Blood cell tests showed interferon signals reversed after three months of care. Which drug drove the change stays unclear.
pmc-13310990:
Bo Ling studies how sports education links to mind, thinking, and social outcomes in a 2026 quantitative paper. Sports teaching builds body skill, but its wider role in well being, focus, and group growth needed a joint test. Survey data were modeled with a path method that weighs direct and indirect links at once.

Sports education showed strong positive links to social growth, well being, nature awareness, focus, and planning skill. Well being lifted focus and carried part of the sports effect on focus. Planning skill lifted social growth and carried part of that link too. Emotional skill boosted well being and focus, though its direct social link was weak.
pmc-13311190:
Yueqiong Lao and colleagues build a platelet linked gene signature for bowel cancer outlook in a 2026 study. Platelets educated by tumors enter blood tests as liquid biopsy clues, yet their gene value in bowel cancer was unclear. Ten learning methods were raced to build a stable score tied to survival and drug response.

The final score beat 71 past signatures at foretelling survival. High scores marked more gene faults, weaker immune traits, pro tumor macrophage types, and more platelets in tissue maps. High score patients resisted immune therapy but answered a targeted drug in tests. One gene was confirmed as a growth driver in lab assays.
pmc-13311990:
Hidenobu Kuniyoshi and colleagues report their 2026 lab assay for testing topical antivirals against herpes simplex infection of the cornea. Few dish models exist for this eye infection, pushing work toward animal tests.

The assay uses an immortalized human corneal cell line that the virus infects readily, with damage read by a color-forming test. Most clinic antivirals worked in the model, and acyclovir matched its prodrug valaciclovir when applied directly. Vidarabine barely worked, and blocking its breakdown enzyme helped only partly. The model also handled a drug-resistant virus strain, widening its use for screening eye drugs.
pmc-13313290:
Yating Zhang and co-authors review the role of microbes in uterine cancer in a 2026 journal article. Tumors of the womb are a leading cause of cancer death in women, and the mix of cells and microbes around a tumor shapes how it starts, grows, and answers treatment.

Work on the microbe mix in cervical and womb-lining cancers is still young, yet early finds link shifts in these communities to tumor growth, escape from immune attack, spread, and drug resistance. Some shifts may also serve as signs that help doctors spot disease or judge outlook. The review gathers what is known on the landscape of these cancers and their microbe setting. It argues that tracking microbes could open new ways to prevent, detect, and treat uterine tumors.
pmc-13313690:
Lina Rodriguez-Aponte, Jorge Martin Rodriguez, and Fernando Ruiz-Vallejo study unmet need for contraception among racialized women in Colombia in a 2026 journal article. They ask which social and money factors raise the risk of wanting to avoid pregnancy yet lacking a method.

The team worked from the national demography and health survey of 2015, comparing women who claim an ethnic or racial belonging with those who do not. Multivariable regression and machine learning models were both used. Region, wealth index, schooling level, and job status of the women stood out as drivers, joined by marital status and age, as the report shows. The finds name the groups where family planning services fall shortest and where outreach in Colombia could close the gap first.
pmc-13314390:
Yun Ji Park and co-workers test a mango variety extract for calming inflammation and oxidation in a 2026 cell study. Mango is the best-known member of its genus, yet the teloor variety had barely been studied for these effects.

The extract was tried on mouse macrophage cells called RAW 264.7, stirred up with bacterial toxin. It cut nitric oxide output and the making of the enzyme that produces it, in a dose-linked way and without killing the cells. It also blocked the firing of p65, a switch for inflammation genes, and kept p65 from moving into the cell nucleus. Harmful oxygen byproducts fell, and genes for signals such as interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor alpha were dialed down. The team backs the extract as a candidate functional food material.
pmc-13314490:
J. Jeni Jovitha and Daisy Gohain read a Vietnam war novel through ideas of justice and the body in a paper from 2026. The novel is Dust Child, a 2023 work by Nguyễn Phan Quế Mai that spans generations marked by the war.

The study blends three frames: slow violence, the idea that harm seeps across bodies and land; transcorporeality, the flow between bodies and world; and restorative justice, repair through truth and witness. It follows Dan, an American veteran, Phong, an Amerasian child, and survivors Trang and Quỳnh, as named in the report. Their bodily and land-based trauma becomes a site of shared moral duty in the reading. The paper argues the novel shows slow violence crossing bodies, landscapes, and generations while pressing against the silencing of war history.
pmc-13314890:
Shao-Min Huang and colleagues pool studies of lung ultrasound for pneumonia in walk-in care, in a review from 2026. Good accuracy had been claimed for the method, but most proof came from emergency, ward, or intensive care units, and the studies assumed their reference tests never erred.

Their review, logged in PROSPERO under a code given in the report, searched standard databases for studies in ambulatory and primary care. Reference tests were chest X-ray, CT, or digital tomosynthesis. A Bayesian latent class model let both the ultrasound and the reference tests be fallible, giving a truer read on accuracy. The answer matters for front-line clinics, where a fast, radiation-free check could speed care for chest infections.
pmc-13315090:
Mauricio Sandoval Osses and colleagues report a glomus tumor far from the fingers, in a letter published in 2026. These rare benign growths spring from the glomus body, a tiny vessel knot that helps control body heat. They make under 2 percent of hand soft tissue tumors by the figure cited in the report.

Off-finger forms are rarer still and often miss the classic marks of sharp local pain worsened by cold, so they are caught late or misread. Their patient was a 76-year-old man with a left deltopectoral lesion, in the fold between chest and shoulder. He had first noted a quiet skin lesion there four years earlier. It was cut out and read as an angioma, though the old report was lost, as the letter relates. The new case adds a caution for odd skin lumps off the hand.
pmc-13316190:
Rachel L Delahunty and a very large team report the CODEC study in 2026 on circulating tumor DNA around surgery for endometrial cancer as a forecast marker. Tumor DNA in blood was checked at several points around the operation, across all disease stages and molecular subgroups.

Before surgery, DNA levels tracked tumor volume measured by MRI and PET imaging. After surgery, finding tumor DNA still present carried prognostic weight for later outcomes. Such blood checks could sharpen risk sorting after surgery, helping clinicians judge who needs closer watching or added treatment in this womb cancer.
pmc-13316290:
Arjun Neyyathala and co-authors describe, in a 2026 data article, an open dataset on a carbonylation reaction run with palladium phosphide particles held on a support. The dataset sits in the Repo4Cat repository and records both the catalyst itself and how it performed.

Files hold figures, tables, and raw plus descriptive data gathered with many lab tools, among them X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, elemental checks, and surface spectroscopy. Adding phosphorus to the metal reshapes the active sites, an idea borrowed from how ligands tune dissolved catalysts. Clear records of make-up and testing let other groups repeat the work, compare new catalysts fairly, and reuse the numbers in later studies of green chemical production.
pmc-13316390:
Gianluca Pagnoni and colleagues wrote a 2026 letter about ultrasound measures of heart and lung artery matching. The measures were read after catheter repair of a leaking tricuspid valve. They welcome the study under discussion, then caution against reading single snapshots too simply.

Such measures depend heavily on loading conditions, and repair suddenly cuts the leak, shifting the heart's fill and pressure at once. A reading taken at rest may also hide strain that only shows during effort, so stress testing could reveal hidden weakness. Later checks over time, they suggest, would better show true recovery of the heart muscle after the valve is fixed.
pmc-13317690:
