No blue dots were needed, since the wood's own scattering spreads and blends the light. A sheet just 0.6 millimeters thick passed light well, hazed it strongly for glare-free spread, and converted photons at a quantum yield of 42 percent in the reported tests. The composite also kept excellent strength. A renewable wood base for home lighting could replace plastic diffusers while storing carbon at the same time.
pmc-13318390:
Elif Görkem Bademci and colleagues present a 2026 trial on cervical screening follow-up for women whose smear looked normal but who carried high-risk human papillomavirus types other than 16 or 18. The question was whether examining the cervix right away beats waiting.

In total, 122 women were split evenly between immediate colposcopy and standard repeat testing without that first examination. Everyone had repeat smear and virus testing plus colposcopy after one year. Rates of the loop excision treatment were close between groups, at 11.5 and 8.2 percent respectively, and persistence of the virus and abnormal smears also did not differ clearly. Early examination caught high-grade lesions for treatment without adding procedures overall.
pmc-13318490:
Erica F de Oliveira and colleagues present a 2026 feeding trial testing whether added B-complex vitamins help newly weaned beef calves during a 42-day preconditioning period. Sixty-three Angus and Hereford cross calves were sorted by weight into 21 pens of three.

Pens received dried distillers grains alone, or grains carrying one gram or two grams of a vitamin blend each day. Weight, feed measures, stress hormone, and blood proteins were tracked repeatedly, and vitamin B7 levels were checked on set days. Growth did not differ between groups, but the higher dose raised blood B7 by day 14 and kept it higher at day 42 in the trial. Supplemented calves also ended with lower cortisol than controls.
pmc-13318690:
V. Dhanavarshini and Sasikumar Periyasamy present a 2026 computing study on self-driving car perception. Cars can train shared models without pooling private data through federated learning. Real driving data differ sharply between vehicles, which weakens standard methods. The authors propose a tuning framework that accounts for that variance.

Their framework, DV-FedTune, adjusts each car's contribution dynamically. Weighting reflects update consistency, diversity, and loss-based reliability. It was built around the YOLOv12 detector. Tests used the KITTI object detection dataset under varied uneven-data settings. The method beat three comparison approaches on communication cost, computing cost, and detection performance. Privacy protection also stayed stronger. The authors argue it scales well as more vehicles join.
pmc-13318790:
Jie Hu and co-authors report a 2026 retrospective cohort study of insulin resistance and fertility treatment outcomes in China. Their measure, TyG-BMI, combines triglycerides, glucose, and body mass. It is a cheap stand-in for insulin resistance. The sample came from one large reproductive hospital.

Altogether 53,393 women had assisted reproduction between January 2017 and March 2023. Women in the highest index third had lower cumulative live birth rates. Their adjusted relative risk was 0.973 against the lowest third in the analysis. Higher index values also linked to more miscarriage, later fetal loss, and preterm birth. Oversized babies were markedly commoner, with an adjusted risk of 2.352 in the top group. The authors propose the index for risk flagging.
pmc-13319090:
Domenico Mallardo, Margaret Ottaviano, Giuseppe Palmieri, and Maria Teresa Melucci wrote this 2026 editorial opening a research collection on immune biomarkers in skin and breast cancer. Melanoma anchors the piece as a model for cancer immunology. Checkpoint drugs changed its care, yet resistance and toxicity persist. No single marker captures who will respond.

The editorial surveys candidate signals, from PD-L1 and mutation load to blood markers and the microbiome. It extends the same questions to Merkel cell carcinoma and skin squamous cancers. Breast cancer adds variety, since immune-rich subtypes behave differently from hormone-driven ones. A table maps 20 collected studies to their biomarker themes. The editors argue markers must become decision tools, guiding step-ups, monitoring, and stopping rules.
pmc-13319390:
Jorge Mas-Gómez and co-authors report a 2026 study that uses light scans to speed up almond breeding for food value. Lab tests for fat, protein, and fiber in nuts are slow and costly, which limits how many trees breeders can screen. A camera that reads light past the range eyes can see was paired with a fast data routine to guess those traits.

Kernels and ground meal from 112 types were scanned, then checked in the lab to train the guessing models. Strong guesses were then used on 528 more types from collections and crosses. Traits passed from parent to seedling showed real weight, which means breeders can now screen far larger groups for better nuts.
pmc-13320290:
Dengwei Cao and co-authors trace how immune scout cells hasten a deadly aorta tear in a 2026 mouse study. A tear in the aorta wall kills fast and still lacks drug care, and wall muscle cells that switch from tight to loose form drive the tear wider. Parcels shed by angry scout cells were found to carry a gene scrap that forces that switch.

The scrap lands in wall cells, mutes a guard gene, and fires a stiffening path that flips the cells loose. Calm scout parcels were then loaded with a blocker of the scrap and given to mice prone to tears. Treated mice lived longer, tore less often, kept tighter wall cells, and showed parcels homing to the torn aorta. Engineered parcels may become drug care.
pmc-13320390:
Akkamahadevi C. Hiremath and co-authors give a 2026 account of one patient that links long term tuberculosis of the womb to an early warning change in a fallopian tube. A 29 year old woman with past treated womb tuberculosis had lasting pelvic pain and both tubes swollen with pus. Keyhole surgery found the tubes twisted and full of pus, so both were removed.

Under the scope the tube lining showed chronic grainy swelling plus a patch of odd cells. That patch held a strong fault signal in one marker and a low growth rate. The mix marks an early step toward a fast tube cancer rather than the cancer itself. Lasting infection harm may seed such early change, so careful scope checks of removed tubes matter even when infection seems the whole story.
pmc-13320490:
Jiajin Shen and co-authors describe a 2026 computer model that plans where dental implants should sit in the back lower jaw. Safe placement must respect the shape of the jaw, a hollow on the tongue side, and the nerve canal below. The team trained a deep learning system that mixes a Swin Transformer with a 3D U-Net network.

Cone beam scans of single missing teeth were used to teach and test the system in five rounds. Scores for outlining teeth and jaw parts were high across test rounds, and sorting of hollow shapes proved highly accurate as well. Planned implant spots kept a clear gap from the nerve canal and left enough bone on both sides.
pmc-13320590:
Zeyu Wu and co-authors examine a plant compound in a 2026 mouse study of kidney injury caused by the cancer drug cisplatin. Cisplatin often harms the kidneys, which limits its use, and the full chain of that harm stays unclear. Sulforaphane, found in cruciferous vegetables, switches on a defence protein called NRF2 and has calming and protective effects.

Mice given a single cisplatin dose were treated with or without sulforaphane, and blood, tissue, and cell harm marks were compared. Tests covered kidney function in blood, cell death proteins, tissue stains, swelling signals, and harmful oxygen levels. The design lets readers judge whether NRF2 linked defence can blunt drug caused kidney harm.
pmc-13322190:
YuChung Lin and co-authors borrow strength from large gene studies to sharpen risk scores for small patient groups in a 2026 study. Polygenic scores need huge data sets, which blurs fine clinical types, while small well defined cohorts alone are too weak. Their external score framework blends target cohort evidence with genetic correlation to a larger source study.

Simulations showed gains across a range of genetic links between source and target traits. Applied work refined an epilepsy score to separate juvenile myoclonic epilepsy from sister types and used a large ADHD study to predict impulsivity in that group. A cystic fibrosis cohort test predicted diabetes linked to the disease, with checks for platform artefacts.
pmc-13322390:
Jayant Raikhelkar and a large team train an AI model to spot weak heart pumping from ordinary chest scans in a 2026 study. Many people with early heart muscle weakness feel no symptoms, yet early treatment can slow decline. The model reads plain, non-contrast chest CT scans that were never meant for heart checks.

Training used 34,058 paired scans and ultrasound reports from two centres, with testing on 8110 pairs from a third centre. The model scored 0.786 on held out tests and 0.762 on outside checks for spotting an ejection fraction below 50 percent in the study. It beat expert radiologists on accuracy and speed and highlighted the image features behind its calls.
pmc-13322490:
Luciana Cássia de Jesus, Luciana Mendonça Alves, and Luciana Macedo de Resende validate an online hearing skills questionnaire for Brazilian adults in a 2026 study. The expanded EAPAC scale asks adults how well they handle central auditory processing in daily life. A total of 1274 people aged 18 to 59 answered it, with smaller groups getting full hearing and thinking tests.

Factor checks led to five questions being dropped for weak fit. Curves testing how well scores flag true processing disorder gave no clear signal, and sensitivity and specificity were judged fragile. Answers stayed stable when 63 people retook the scale later. The tool still helps surface daily hearing complaints and guide coping strategies, even if it cannot diagnose risk alone.
pmc-13322790:
Dongyan Zhang and co-authors build a light AI model to classify Alzheimer's disease from brain scans in a 2026 study. Standard networks read local detail well but miss long range links, while transformer models capture those links at heavy computing cost. Their HDFT-MViT model mixes both, using cheap early layers and dynamic filters plus a light transformer deeper in.

On two public ADNI scan sets, accuracy reached 98.85 percent for three class sorting and 98.07 percent for four class sorting, with only 3.46 million parameters in the model. Channel attention helped separate the classes. The balance of accuracy and small size suits clinics with modest computing power.
pmc-13322890:
Hongmei Wang and Xiaoou He study what teens like in art from other cultures, in a 2026 survey of 400 adolescents aged 14 to 18 years. Participants came from Chinese and Western backgrounds, judged art from both traditions, and answered measures of art exposure, openness and mental flexibility.

Teens tended to favour art from their own tradition, and cultural background strongly predicted those choices. Wider exposure to global art weakened that home bias and partly explained it, acting as a bridge in the authors' models. Teens high in openness or flexibility showed less cultural bias as well. The findings link family and school art contact with broader taste during a key stage of cultural learning.
pmc-13323490:
Şafak Yalçın Şahiner and colleagues ask Turkish university students how addiction should be fought, in a 2026 qualitative study. Their group held 119 undergraduates who answered an online form in their own words, analysed through descriptive thematic methods.

Students backed a wide mix of action, spanning structural steps and individual support. The most stressed themes were prohibitions, sanctions and monitoring on one side, and education and awareness work on the other. Knowledge of existing policy proved considerably weak, which the authors flag as a gap in current campaigns. They argue that prevention gains force when young people join the design of anti-addiction strategy rather than only receiving its messages.
pmc-13325490:
Xin Xu and colleagues link kidney lymphatic vessel growth to IgA nephropathy severity in a 2026 cohort study. The vessels may tie tissue injury to immune activity in this common kidney disease.

Biopsy samples from 127 untreated patients at Tongji Hospital in Wuhan were stained and scored for vessel density. Density ran higher than in controls and tracked with urine Gd-IgA1, complement parts, and IL-6 levels. Patients in the densest group carried more protein in urine and worse tissue scores. Over a median 93 months of follow-up, that group faced a hazard ratio of 3.67 for doubled creatinine and 19.81 for end-stage kidney disease.
pmc-13327890:
Sarah Johnston, Yu Jo Chua, and Alisha Azmir present a 2026 case series on a paradoxical gut blockage during cancer immunotherapy. About 15 percent of colorectal cancers carry mismatch repair deficiency, respond poorly to standard chemotherapy, and often shrink well on PD-1 blocking drugs such as pembrolizumab. At their center, several such patients developed bowel obstruction anyway.

Scans and course showed the blockage came from lasting narrowing at the original tumor site even while the cancer itself responded excellently. The series walks through the cases, including a 40-year-old woman with widespread disease, to sharpen recognition of this rare complication. Teams may still need surgery for the narrowed bowel despite a winning drug response.
pmc-13327990:
Huizhong Bai and co-authors present FreeMMIF, an interactive system for merging medical scans, in a 2026 article. Fusion joins functional and structural images to aid diagnosis, but older methods fix one aim and cannot adjust on the fly. Their framework pairs a vision-language model with a diffusion generator steered by text instructions.

During training, the language model picks the best outputs of older methods as stand-in targets, removing the need for reference images. A re-weighting branch then teaches the generator to balance source images against those targets, and at use time doctors type instructions to shift the blend between scan types. Tests showed fused images of diagnostic quality that matched stated clinical intent.
pmc-13328190:
Gulce Coskun Senturk, Asli Kaya, and Cagri Basbug build a scale for music exam self-belief in a 2026 study. High-stakes aptitude exams stress adolescent musicians, and what they expect of themselves beforehand may shape results. Drawing on social cognitive theory, the team developed the Music Aptitude Self-Efficacy Scale and tested it on 2,030 adolescents.

Factor work supported three parts: cognitive-auditory belief, psychomotor performance belief, and emotion regulation belief, and the scale held together reliably while matching other self-efficacy measures. In a live performance simulation judged by experts, higher pre-exam scores went with better technical playing under stress. Teachers and counselors could use the scale to spot students needing support before exam day.
pmc-13328490:
Liang Zhang and co-authors show a plant compound restoring cisplatin power in lung cancer in a 2026 study. Morusin, from mulberry plants, suppresses non-small cell lung cancer, and the team asked whether it also sensitizes tumors to cisplatin, called DDP in the study. Cell tests measured survival, drug synergy, and iron-driven death signs.

Morusin triggered ferroptosis and sharply raised cisplatin sensitivity, even in a resistant cell line, by binding the protein GDF15 and sending it for destruction. Restoring GDF15 erased those gains, while removing it made resistant cells drug-sensitive again, and tumor data linked high GDF15 to the cancer. A natural compound may thus reopen a standard drug's usefulness in stubborn lung tumors.
pmc-13329390:
Yan Li and co-authors review tiny membrane bubbles drawn from immune cells as a possible therapy for autoimmune disease in a 2026 article. Current drugs often act broadly, cause side effects, and fail to restore immune tolerance. Bubbles shed by red blood cells, platelets, neutrophils, dendritic cells, or macrophages keep surface marks from their parent cells.

Those marks can guide bubbles to swollen tissue and calm immune action. Bubbles can also carry drug cargo or added targeting tags. The review covers making and loading methods, then uses in illnesses such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, bowel disease, and type 1 diabetes. Hurdles include large-scale making, keeping membranes intact, and loading cargo well. Fixes for those hurdles will decide clinical use.
pmc-13330090:
Prince Imani-Musimwa and a large team report a maternal death in an Ebola unit in DR Congo in a 2026 case account. The patient was a pregnant teenager in her second pregnancy, admitted at 32 weeks with high virus load after vaccination and antibody treatment. Virus levels fell over the first days of care.

On day 3 she delivered a live preterm baby after efforts to halt labour failed. Heavy bleeding followed, with tears in the cervix and vagina and urine leaking through a fistula. Staff removed retained tissue and gave womb-tightening drugs, but lack of surgical gear in the unit blocked full repair. She died 14 hours after delivery from blood loss and clotting failure. The authors call the death preventable with better obstetric tools on site.
pmc-13330690:
Soudeh Ashrafipour and colleagues study whether puberty timing shapes brain network links in teens in a 2026 report. Timing was scored as a puberty age gap, the split between model-predicted puberty age and true age. Data came from the ABCD Study with about 3,500 young people, covering 12 large brain networks.

Earlier timing tied to altered resting links within and between networks in same-time checks, the authors report. Most patterns echoed normal age-related change, while some control network links looked specific to puberty. Sensorimotor, attention, and control networks featured most, in both sexes but wider in males. Later change over time showed weaker links. Timing beyond age matters for brain wiring, the authors argue.
pmc-13332390:
Marco F. Monteros and co-authors name a new orchid species from northwestern Ecuador in a 2026 taxonomy paper. Pleurothallis pembertonii grows in lower montane cloud forest inside the Dracula Reserve in Carchi Province, in the western Andean foothills, and is known from a single locality.

The species sits in a small series whose members look so alike that they are often confused, and its closest match is P. forceps-cancri. The new plant stands apart through wine-colored, oblong and slightly S-curved petals that taper to long points, plus an arrow-shaped three-lobed lip with a kidney-shaped glenion and two small spreading basal ridges. The authors note the area's many range-restricted species and the growing pressure from mining, which makes naming and mapping such plants urgent for protection.
pmc-13333590:
Xukun Liu and co-authors present a robot learning framework in 2026 for teaching two arms to work together from demonstrations. Bimanual imitation is unforgiving. The arms must stay in sync, avoid colliding, plan over long horizons, and ignore clutter. Diffusion-based policies tend to sacrifice either the long view or fine precision while latching onto background cues.

Their system, SCH-DIL, splits the diffusion process into temporal and spatial branches, so multi-scale action structure survives. It learns visual features forced to carry little information about confounding surroundings. It estimates observation uncertainty during denoising. And it adds a penalty that discourages distraction and keeps attention steady over time. On the RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark the framework beat diffusion and imitation baselines, holding success rates in clean scenes and randomized, shifted ones. The authors note the gains come at little added cost, making the approach practical for real-world deployment.
pmc-13334090:
Thomas Williams and co-authors ran a 2026 follow-on analysis of the MS-STAT2 randomized trial, asking whether treating vascular risk changes the course of secondary progressive multiple sclerosis. Blood vessel risk factors track with worse disability in MS, but whether modifying them helps was unknown.

The trial randomized 964 patients to simvastatin at 80 mg or placebo for three years, with 246 of them also getting yearly MRI scans. Vascular risks and cholesterol profiles were taken at baseline. The parent trial found no benefit of simvastatin on its main medical outcomes. This analysis tests a narrower idea: whether assignment to simvastatin weakened the link between a harmful cholesterol profile and later disease worsening, against placebo.
pmc-13334790:
Wenjing Yu and co-authors looked at the type III-A CRISPR-Cas system of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in a 2026 article, arguing it does far more than fight invading DNA. The tuberculosis bacterium keeps this system fully built yet barely collects new spacers, a hint that its job has changed.

The machinery still interferes with targets, working through transcription-dependent recognition and cyclic oligoadenylate signals that switch on the Csm6 effector. Proteins of the system also shape antibiotic susceptibility, resistance to oxidative stress, and interactions with host immunity, and some may be released to sway the host directly. The review organizes the system's genomic layout and regulatory wiring, and weighs its roles in stress coping and infection, which could matter for future tuberculosis control.
pmc-13336390:
Anastasia Shihabi and co-authors reviewed the mechanics of the egg cell in a 2026 article arguing that physical properties belong in judging oocyte quality. A good oocyte must complete two lopsided divisions that keep the mother's reserves while halving the genome.

Those divisions run on actomyosin networks at the surface and in the cytoplasm, and the remodeling of these networks sets the cell's stiffness and flow. Mechanics in turn govern cytoplasm organization, spindle placement, chromosome segregation, and the final pinch into polar bodies. Errors climb with maternal age, and fertility preservation by freezing has sharpened the hunt for quality markers beyond looks. The review covers the pathways controlling oocyte mechanics, their failure in disease, and possible clinical uses.
pmc-13336990:
Luca Zangrando, Emanuele Buratti, and Francesca Paron review the double life of the protein TDP-43 in a 2026 article. TDP-43 normally manages RNA tasks from splicing to transport, and its clumps mark diseases such as ALS and much frontotemporal degeneration. Newer work shows its self-gathering is not always harmful.

Reversible assemblies and liquid droplets help TDP-43 do its normal jobs. Mutations, altered RNA binding, chemical tags, or cutting can tip that balance into permanent toxic aggregates, much like prion proteins. The review maps the structural switches in its prion-like domain and surveys strategies to clear aggregates or steer its phase behavior. Keeping the healthy side of the balance is the therapeutic goal.
pmc-13337390:
Jia-yun Wu leads a 2026 team teaching an AI model to spot thyroid autoimmunity risk from lip gland tissue. Patients with connective tissue disease often develop autoimmune thyroiditis, flagged by thyroid antibodies. Lip gland biopsies are already common in this group, so the team asked whether their slide images hide predictive patterns.

Slides from 121 patients were split by antibody status into positive and negative groups. A pre-trained EfficientNet-B5 network extracted image features, combined with multi-instance and ensemble learning. The integrated model reached an AUC of 0.829 across internal and external validation sets in the reported evaluation, and it highlighted the tissue features tied to high risk. Slide-based screening could flag patients for earlier thyroid checks.
pmc-13337890:
Matthew J. Slarve leads a 2026 broad review of antibody drugs aimed at bacterial infections. Rising antibiotic resistance has pushed the search for other ways to treat hard infections. Antibodies built to target single bacterial features offer one such path.

Findings are sorted by bacterial species and by molecular target. Both antibodies that helped and those that failed are covered, so design lessons stand out. Biofilms that shield bacteria receive attention as well. New molecular methods that speed antibody building and tuning are also reviewed, pointing to a growing era for antibacterial antibody therapy.
pmc-13338390:
Yan Zhuang and a large team build a clinical language model centered on medical records in a 2026 study. Their system, AI4Doctor, aims to mimic how doctors reason through complex cases. General chat tools give information but rarely copy that layered judgment.

Training mixed distilled knowledge from electronic records with insights from practicing doctors during fine-tuning. A staged curriculum helped merge the two sources in order. A reward system then pushed answers toward qualities valued in doctor expertise, such as sound diagnosis. The design tries to create a realistic practice setting inside the model, so its advice follows clinical logic more closely.
pmc-13341990:
Neutrophil genes forecast pancreatic cancer outcomes, in a 2026 modeling study by Zhengrong Ou's team. Drawing candidate tumor-linked neutrophil genes from cancer genome and gene banks, the team used penalized and Cox regression to build a prognostic signature, tested in a separate expression dataset.

Four genes made the model: AIM2, PSCA, IL18BP, and LIPE. Immune infiltration and drug sensitivity guesses added background context, and protein atlas plus single-cell resources checked where the genes act. Tissue staining and PCR on patient samples confirmed expression patterns in the lab. Pancreatic cancer badly needs prognostic tools, and immune-cell genes offer an underused angle.
pmc-13342190:
Delayed brain damage after carbon monoxide poisoning gets a risk chart, in a 2026 study by Wanqiu Zhu's team. The project reviewed 200 poisoning patients admitted between 2017 and 2024, of whom 140 developed delayed brain illness and 97 severely.

Severe cases skewed older, with longer blackouts, more hypertension and high homocysteine, higher D-dimer, and lower albumin than the others. Regression distilled separate predictors into a chart checked by accuracy, calibration, and decision curves. Because severe delayed damage disables long after the emergency fades, flagging risk during the first hospital stay could change follow-up depth.
pmc-13345790:
Maryam Ali and Rebecca Brooks review treatment of returning low-grade serous ovarian cancer in 2026, a rare, slow-growing form that shrugs off chemotherapy. Unlike its high-grade cousin, this cancer often runs on the MAPK growth pathway through KRAS or BRAF changes and answers to hormones, and patients commonly live years with recurring disease.

Repeat surgery and hormone blockers such as letrozole serve many patients, while combined BRAF and MEK blocking suits the V600E mutation group. The authors center the RAMP 201 trial of MEK inhibition as the field's current test of pathway targeting. With median survival near 92 months, gentler, durable control matters more here than short bursts of harsh chemo.
pmc-13346090:
Aravindhan Manivannan and Anthoniraj Amalanathan present GeoGuard-PTI in 2026, a security framework that forecasts cyber attacks by place and time instead of waiting for them. Live intrusion signals, geofencing, and forensics feed a graph attention network plus a diffusion predictor that treats attack spread like an epidemic over a world map.

Forecast maps run from 15 minutes to a full day ahead. Tested on five public datasets with synthetic spread traces added, the system hit 96.4 percent accuracy at 15 minutes and 91.2 percent at two hours, with false alarms under 1.9 percent. Live trials cut successful intrusions by about a third and slashed blocking time, pre-arming defenses in under three milliseconds.
pmc-13347390:
Elena Bray and colleagues synthesise a brominated tryptamine and profile its biology as a base for new analogues, in a study from 2026. The compound, 4-Br-DMT, was built as a late-stage hub so palladium coupling could attach varied carbon groups at the 4-position, speeding a library of ring-swapped tryptamines for receptor studies.

Direct tests compared the new compound with psilocin and plain DMT on serotonin targets and in mice, and the profile stayed serotonergic in the reported assays. Unlike its comparators, it showed no psychedelic-like effects in mice, yet its safety margin looked weaker than both reference drugs. The route, more than this single compound, is the main offer for analogue hunters.
pmc-13349890:
Xiaoxue Ding and colleagues profiled blood chemicals in a 2026 study of two heart artery conditions. Thirty patients with chronic coronary syndrome, thirty with artery calcification, and thirty healthy people gave plasma samples for broad chemical testing.

Simple blood tests already differed between the groups. The calcification group had higher creatinine and fasting glucose. Both patient groups had higher urea nitrogen than controls. Deeper profiling found clear gaps between the two patient groups. Two fatty acids, oleic acid and arachidonic acid, helped set them apart. Markers like these could aid earlier detection of calcified disease, though the team treats the work as a first step.
pmc-13350590:
Jiankun Liao and co-authors pooled evidence in a 2026 meta-analysis on tumour deposits in stage III colorectal cancer. These separate cancer nodules near the bowel may worsen outlook independently of lymph node spread, with implications for staging and treatment.

Eighteen solid studies covering 236,867 patients were gathered from five databases through the end of 2025. Patients with both tumour deposits and positive nodes fared significantly worse on five-year overall and disease-free survival than comparison groups. If deposits carry their own risk, staging rules that treat them as an afterthought may undertreat patients who need stronger follow-up.
pmc-13351690:
Syed N Barmaver and colleagues report 2026 lab findings on KIF21A, a motor protein linked to type 2 diabetes, in pancreatic islet cells. Beta cells release insulin at set spots near blood vessels, and the cell skeleton that guides release is still unclear. The team combined large and single-cell RNA data with protein databases and detailed imaging of mouse islets.

KIF21A was lower in human islets from donors with type 2 diabetes at both RNA and protein levels. Within islets, the protein was richest in delta cells, then alpha cells, then beta cells. Levels also varied widely from cell to cell within each type. The pattern hints at specialised roles that merit further study.
pmc-13352990:
Ruihua Ma leads a 2026 study of radiation work, blood lipids, and high blood pressure risk. Two designs were paired: a cross-sectional study of 2,548 radiation workers and a follow-up cohort of 484 workers, all examined in Shijiazhuang from October 2021 to March 2025. Models tested exposure links, lipid mediation, and prediction of new hypertension.

Longer radiation work years and industrial exposure raised hypertension risk after adjustment, with all P values below 0.05. HDL cholesterol protected, while total cholesterol, triglycerides, and LDL cholesterol raised risk. Lipid ratios such as fasting glucose over HDL also mattered. The authors argue lipid checks could flag at-risk radiation workers early.
pmc-13354090:
Weifeng Guo, Long Chen, Licheng Chen, and Wanxia Zhang review animal models of diabetes-related shoulder disorders in 2026. Diabetic shoulder disease has tangled mechanisms and no unified research model. Three mainstream models are compared: diabetes with frozen shoulder, diabetes with rotator cuff injury and repair, and natural tendon degeneration in type 2 diabetes.

Each model mimics parts of human disease but misses others, such as a true type 2 metabolic background or whole-joint change over time. An ideal model would copy type 2 metabolism, progressive multi-tissue damage across tendon, capsule, and bone, and pain plus function testing. The authors urge a shift from single-disease copies toward integrated simulation.
pmc-13354590:
Réka Tóth and co-authors tested an old drug, trifluoperazine, in mice with stroke in a 2026 study. The drug is used for mental illness and can change how brain support cells handle water. After blood flow was restored in the mice, the team gave the drug and checked brain harm, blood flow, and early recovery.

Treated mice had smaller areas of brain harm and got better sooner than untreated mice. The drug also eased cell swelling, calmed harmful brain waves, and lowered a key water channel in support cells. Since the drug is already in clinic use, the authors see it as a lead for stroke care trials.
pmc-13354990:
Christen Rachul and co-authors compared two ways medical learners report mistreatment in a 2026 study at one school. One way came through end-of-rotation forms that prompt every learner, and the other was a voluntary web form learners chose to use. The team coded reports filed from 2015 to 2021 for type, place, and people involved.

The prompt forms gave 90 reports and the web form gave 240, with much overlap in mistreatment types. Web reports more often named disrespect, bias, and unfair treatment, and covered a wider range of places. The authors say running both systems gives schools a fuller picture and gives learners more choice in how to speak up.
pmc-13355690:
Zhicheng Luo writes a 2026 letter to the editor about a study testing a child kidney disease risk tool in a Korean cohort. The study was the first check of the calculator, which predicts need for kidney replacement therapy, in an East Asian group of children. Luo praises its promise but questions whether routine clinic use is justified yet.

The letter notes mismatches between the study's abstract and its results tables on sample size and accuracy values, and unclear counts of excluded children. It also notes that accuracy tests flagged poor fit, so local recalibration may be needed first. Luo asks for clarified numbers and updated performance before wider use.
pmc-13357090:
Christoph Schultheiss and co-authors reply in a 2026 letter to commentary on the FOCUS trial, which tested a cancer vaccine plus an immune drug in recurring or spread head and neck cancer. The phase 2 trial randomized 75 patients to pembrolizumab alone or with the UV1 vaccine, which targets a protein most cancer cells need. The combined arm did not meet its main goal.

Six-month progression-free survival was lower with the vaccine, at 31 percent versus 42 percent, though the vaccine was safe and sparked target-specific T cells in most patients. The authors defend the chosen dose range, citing wider trial data, and discuss why blood immune responses may not control tumors.
pmc-13358490:
Nizhen Xu and co-authors present a 2026 study on papillary thyroid cancer, the most common cancer of hormone glands. Most cases grow slowly, but some turn aggressive, and genes plus immune cells shape that path. The team joined gene data from many sources to build a model that sorts patients by risk.

They mixed gene data from six public sets with genetic study data to find genes that truly drive risk, not just track it. They also mapped the immune cells inside tumors. The model aims to flag patients who need stronger care early, and to point at new drug targets for this cancer.
pmc-13358990:
Sarah Rodriguez-Louette examines how racist ideas spread through memes in a 2026 article. On the platform X, memes that borrow the look of science revive old claims that races differ by nature. The author studied 68 viral items and four cases in depth, using a model that splits memes into content, form, and stance.

The analysis shows quick visual contrasts doing the work of argument, helped by feeds that reward fast judgment. Old hierarchies reappear in neutral words about competence. The memes travel across racist, masculinist, and tech-elite circles, reaching mainly young men. The article shows how a joke format can quietly rebuild discredited ideas.
pmc-13361290:
Jinhu Peng and co-authors tested a plant extract against eczema-like skin disease in mice in a 2026 study. Atopic dermatitis is a long-lasting skin inflammation driven by a weak skin barrier and a confused immune response. The team used an extract of Bidens bipinnata fruit in alcohol. Mice with drug-triggered dermatitis got the extract painted on their skin daily at three dose levels.

The extract eased the visible symptoms, skin thickening, and redness scores. It also improved skin moisture and helped restore two barrier proteins that the disease had lowered. A standard steroid drug, used for comparison, did little for the moisture measures. These results suggest the plant extract both calms inflammation and repairs the skin barrier, a pairing worth more study for skin care.
pmc-13362990:
Dennis Patrick Wilhelm and colleagues report a 2026 machining study on a MAX phase composite, a layered ceramic-metal material strengthened with titanium carbide. Its heat expansion can be tuned to match glass, which makes it a candidate for molds in precision glass molding, where hot glass is pressed into shape. The team ground the material at ultra-fine settings, varied the process inputs, and checked forces, surface finish, and the zone just under the surface.

Fine grinding produced sound surfaces overall, and the authors judge the method fit for making such molds. pmc-13374190:

pmc-13377790:

pmc-13379390:

pmc-13380290:

pmc-13380790:

pmc-13380890:

pmc-13381090:

pmc-13382790:

pmc-13391990:

pmc-13392190:

pmc-13392390:

pmc-13393290:

pmc-13393790:

pmc-13394590:

pmc-13395890:

pmc-13396190:

pmc-13396490:

pmc-13396890:

pmc-13398490:

pmc-13398790:

pmc-13399690:

pmc-13399890:

pmc-13400990:

pmc-13401090:

pmc-13401790:

pmc-13401990:

pmc-13402090:

pmc-13402890:

pmc-13403090:

pmc-13403590:

pmc-13404490:

pmc-13408790:

pmc-13409090:

pmc-13410090:

pmc-13411290:

A contrast study first showed normal passage, which could have falsely reassured the team. Persistent symptoms prompted a CT scan showing a swollen bowel limb and swirling mesentery, the classic hernia signs. Emergency surgery found the limb trapped through a defect above the colon; freeing it and closing the gap brought full recovery.
pmc-13412590:
Rebecca Payne and colleagues map in 2026 which Aspergillus fungi and aflatoxin types turn up across Queensland's peanut regions. Aflatoxins are cancer-causing poisons made by two soil fungi that infect crops before harvest. The team measured toxin variants in peanuts from the 2020 to 2024 seasons by liquid chromatography and surveyed post-harvest soils from four growing regions in the final season.

The G family of toxins proved most common in three of the four regions. Aspergillus parasiticus dominated soil isolates at 97 percent, while its cousin Aspergillus flavus made up just 3 percent and appeared only near Tolga. One region, the North Burnett, yielded no Aspergillus colonies that year. The authors stress strong regional patchiness in contamination risk.
pmc-13412890:
Nasong A Luginaah, Seth Climans, and Aquila Akingbade recount in 2026 a case of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, or PRES, appearing two days after a cancer drug was started. PRES is a rare brain complication linked to drugs that block blood-vessel growth signals, lenvatinib among them. Their patient, a 63-year-old woman with kidney cancer spread to the pancreas, was taking pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib.

Headaches, confusion, visual hallucinations, and a generalized seizure struck alongside severe high blood pressure. Brain imaging showed the swollen white-matter pattern typical of PRES at the back of both hemispheres. Stopping lenvatinib and treating pressure and seizures brought complete recovery within two weeks, with follow-up scans clear. Pembrolizumab alone continued without the problem returning.
pmc-13414090:
Jae-Yong Park and Sehoon Yoo age solder joints in 2026 to test whether a copper-zinc finish can outlast the industry-standard nickel-gold coating under heat. Data centre electronics bake for years, and the metal layer where solder meets pad grows brittle compounds that crack under impact. Joints on both finishes sat at 180 degrees for up to 250 hours, then faced microscopy and high-speed shear testing.

The copper-zinc interface grew a thicker compound layer than the nickel-gold one throughout ageing. Shear strength, however, matched or beat the standard finish at every time point in their tests. Cracks in the standard joints ran along a phosphorus-rich layer, driving brittle fractures to roughly 75 percent by the longest ageing, against about 47 percent for copper-zinc. The authors endorse the zinc finish.
pmc-13415290:
Howard Haonan Ho, Ebenezer Ekow Essel, and Pierre Edward Sullivan simulate a circular synthetic jet blowing into a crossflow, in a 2026 fluid mechanics study. A synthetic jet puffs and sucks through one opening, adding momentum without extra fluid supply. Nine computer cases varied blowing strength, stroke length, and the height of the surrounding boundary layer.

At low pulsing frequency the jet shed tilted vortex rings with a trailing pair. Higher frequency packed the expelled swirls closer together, while the tallest boundary layer produced hairpin shaped vortices. Jets with low to moderate strength kept extra momentum near the wall over long distances. That pattern suits control of flow separation on wings or blades.
pmc-13415490:
Yoshinori Makino and colleagues simplify a drug exposure model for the lung cancer drug amrubicin, in 2026. Amrubicin treats small cell lung cancer, yet its active breakdown product can drive steep drops in white blood cells, a harm that caps the dose. Their population model links drug levels in blood to neutrophil counts over time.

Cutting a gut loop and one gene trait made the model easier to use while keeping its fit. Checks with mock runs and retests backed the simpler form. A trial web app shows a patient's forecast white cell curve, with its doubt band. The tool marks risk; it does not set doses.
pmc-13415790:
Amira E. Abd-Elnabi and co-authors propose a six step framework for building fast multi-drug plasma assays, in 2026. Their method couples liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry. Steps run from profiling each drug's chemistry through extraction, column tuning, mobile phase choice, validation, and a greenness score.

The framework was proven on three drugs at once in spiked human plasma: rifaximin, ciprofloxacin, and fluconazole, with ibuprofen as internal standard. Liquid extraction with dichloromethane recovered the drugs well. A simple methanol and water mix separated them quickly on a standard column. Linearity was excellent, and two scoring tools rated the method's environmental footprint.
pmc-13415990:
Baojia Huang and colleagues pair a pasteurized gut bacterium with a fruit extract against diet induced obesity in mice, in 2026. The germ is Akkermansia muciniphila strain AKM Lab-01, a much watched new kind of probiotic. Garcinia cambogia extract is a popular natural weight loss ingredient. Fat mice on a rich diet got both at once.

The pair cut body weight and fat mass, raised blood scores, and calmed fat tissue swelling. Fat tissue genes shifted toward burning lipids. Gut reads showed more Lactococcus and less of two other genera. Cell tests hinted that Lactococcus itself helps steer fat handling and swelling, tying germ shifts to host effects.
pmc-13416390:
Shifa Shamim and colleagues present a giant growth hormone secreting pituitary tumor that grew for years before diagnosis, in a 2026 image case. A woman aged twenty-seven arrived after a seizure, with headache and stopped periods following six years of enlarging hands, feet, and facial features. Hormone tests confirmed acromegaly, with growth hormone and its partner marker far above normal ranges.

Brain imaging showed a multilobulated adenoma measuring about ninety-five by seventy-three by seventy-nine millimeters. Thyroid and adrenal shortfalls were replaced with daily hormones before surgery through the skull. A temporary hormone deficiency followed the operation. Giant tumors form six to ten percent of pituitary tumors.
pmc-13416590:
Enrico Paci and a team of Italian researchers pilot urine testing for fungal toxin exposure among pig farm workers, in 2026. Mycotoxins from moldy feed can ride farm dust into workers' bodies, yet Italian human data are scarce. Urine from thirty-five swine workers and thirty unexposed controls was screened for four toxin markers plus five oxidative stress markers.

Aflatoxin M1 appeared most often among workers, detectable in about twenty-three percent and quantifiable in about eleven percent. Controls showed lower detection and no quantifiable results. Mixed low dose exposure is the picture that emerges. Pairing urine results with earlier farm air and feed monitoring strengthens exposure assessment.
pmc-13417890:
Lu Shen and colleagues measure hepatitis B vaccine response in low birth weight infants after the full three dose course, in a 2026 study. Small babies were feared to respond weakly. The study enrolled 511 infants vaccinated at birth, one month, and six months, with blood drawn weeks after the last dose. Catch up growth and mother and baby traits were examined.

Protection was near universal, with about 99 percent of infants above the antibody threshold and high average levels. Catch up growth did not predict antibody strength, nor did maternal infection status. Maternal thyroid disease linked to higher infant antibodies, a surprise finding the authors say needs prospective checking.
pmc-13417990:
Thuy Thi Thanh Nguyen and colleagues blend bacterial cellulose with a common polymer and silver zinc oxide particles to make an active food film, in a 2026 study. The film aims to fight bacteria, slow oxidation, and keep fruit fresh longer. Several particle loadings were compared for strength, vapour blocking, and protective effects.

A loading of 0.20 percent by weight performed best, with the strongest antibacterial and antioxidant action plus good strength and low permeability. Wrapped Vietnamese tangerines kept well for up to 15 days at room temperature with less weight loss. The biodegradable blend is proposed as a greener wrap for fresh produce.
pmc-13420190:
Hammad surveys nurses who work in critical care units in Palestine. The study asks how their values, work setting, and job contentment link. It drew 263 nurses from fifteen hospitals in the West Bank. Nurses scored their values high. They scored their work setting and contentment at a mid level. The work setting was the strongest link to contentment.

High workload linked to lower contentment. So did plans to leave the job. Values linked to contentment through the work setting, not on their own. Hammad urges fair staffing, shared choices, and praise for good work. Those steps, the study says, help keep skilled nurses in post.
pmc-13420290:
Tuan Huynh and colleagues characterize carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii from a tertiary hospital in southern Vietnam, a germ the World Health Organization ranks as its top priority for new antibiotics. Carbapenems are last-line drugs, so resistance to them closes most treatment doors. The team re-examined 156 stored isolates with gene tests for the enzymes that break these drugs.

Resistance showed in 70.51 percent of isolates in the reported share, a heavy burden for one hospital. Two resistance genes traveled together most often, appearing in 23.64 percent of the resistant set by the count given. That pairing defeats more drugs than either gene alone. Gene maps like this one guide both bedside choices and hospital infection control in the region.
pmc-13421590:
Khalil M Abdelnaby and four colleagues propose, in a 2026 paper, an artificial intelligence framework that trims the energy use of wireless networks without surrendering performance. Traffic growth keeps raising network power bills, and in interference-heavy access schemes the choices about power and timing are tightly entangled.

Their framework first learns the interference geography with a graph neural network and the rhythm of traffic with a recurrent network. Those representations feed a multi-agent reinforcement learning controller that sets power and scheduling decisions as conditions change. In realistic simulated 5G conditions with heavy interference, the system saved up to fifteen percent of energy. The authors present adaptive, learning-based control as a route to greener networks.
pmc-13421790:
Hamilton and colleagues reflect on what happens when the public helps build a policy model, warts and all. The model in question estimates how income support policies would change population health. Their 2026 account draws in thirty two people who have lived with income insecurity and over sixty professional stakeholders. They work through three systems mapping workshops and five policy priority workshops. A poverty charity partner guides the work with trauma informed practice.

The dividends were real: a systems map, co drawn with contributors, steered the modeling strategy and shifted team choices. The disconnects were real too. Research teams split into silos struggled to turn stories into model inputs, workshop formats did not suit everyone, and paying and protecting contributors needed more thought. The authors' advice is plain: budget for involvement, build rooms where people can speak safely, and keep translators between the story side and the math side.
pmc-13423190:
Jia and colleagues present in 2026 DuSSM, a computer system that extracts drug-drug interactions from biomedical text, a backbone task for drug safety monitoring worldwide. The challenge is that local word cues can distort the long-range logic of a sentence.

The design splits the work into two parallel streams. A convolutional stream scans for local trigger patterns, while a state-space stream tracks the sentence's evolving meaning in a single efficient pass. Tested on four biomedical benchmarks, the system reached an F1 score in the low eighty percent range on the main drug interaction benchmark. An F1 score combines precision and recall, and the system scored notably well on precision for sentence pairs. Precision on cases with no interaction was especially high, which matters because false alerts tire the pharmacists who must review them.
pmc-13423490:
Kai Wang and seven colleagues hunt for the proteins that the chemotherapy drug paclitaxel touches in resistant breast cancer, using tailor-made chemical probes of the drug itself. Resistance blunts taxane treatment and drives recurrence, so knowing the drug's hidden partners could expose new targets.

Of four probes built, PTX-4, joined by a stable carbon bond, fished out binding proteins most efficiently from parent and resistant cells. The catch included AKT2, a growth-signalling protein never before tied to paclitaxel. Follow-up tests confirmed direct binding, and silencing or blocking AKT2 made resistant cells sensitive to the drug again. The team proposes AKT2 as both a driver of resistance and a target for restoring taxane power.
pmc-13424090:
Peter Pothmann and three colleagues refine a habitat model for Aedes vexans, a floodplain mosquito, showing that biased sampling data can hide what really drives the species. Records of the mosquito cluster in towns, so a first model barely credited flood hazard, even though the insect breeds in temporary flood water.

The team thinned clustered records and filtered out over-sampled environments, then compared models with and without the clean-up across several test sets. Bias correction improved accuracy more than adding the flood variable alone. The final model mapped suitability far more reliably, especially in flood-prone ground that earlier data had neglected. Their lesson reaches beyond mosquitoes: cleaning occurrence data can matter more than adding predictors.
pmc-13424190:
Shubham Vishnoi and three colleagues design, on the computer, a peptide drug meant to hit three hormone receptors at once for diabetes and obesity. Drugs like tirzepatide already pair two of these signals; adding the third receptor, GIPR, alongside GLP-1 and glucagon receptors, could tighten glucose control and weight loss in a single molecule.

The team mutated peptide sequences in software, then ran long molecular simulations to score how each design gripped the three receptors. Their candidates showed balanced, favourable binding across the trio, better than natural hormones and reference drugs in the models, with clean targeting. Weak spots where enzymes snip peptides were swapped out for stability. Lab testing is the stated next step.
pmc-13424590: Linmei Dong and five co-authors publish a correction only, fixing the record of their study on enzyme-assisted extraction of polyphyllins from Paris polyphylla rhizomes. Two sets of initials, “Y. J.” and “L. C.”, had been added to the author group by mistake as seventh and eighth authors; the notice restores the correct six-author list, running from Dong to Rui Sun. A keyword is also corrected, with its first letter now capitalised as “Pectinase-assisted extraction”. The publisher notes the original article has been updated to match.
pmc-13424790:
Fang and co-authors measure three decades of ear infection burden in American males, in this 2026 epidemiological study. They use Global Burden of Disease 2021 estimates for otitis media. That family covers middle-ear inflammation: acute infections, fluid buildup, and chronic discharging ears.

Case counts rose from roughly 4.10 million in 1990 to 4.57 million in 2021, and the age-standardized incidence rate climbed from 3,899 to 4,147 per 100,000 males across the period. Deaths fell overall, from about 32 to 21 a year in the modeled estimates, though trend analysis found mortality rising again during 2010 to 2019. Disability burden concentrated in boys aged five to nine, while deaths clustered in older adults. Tobacco use and secondhand smoke stood out as the leading attributable risks, making smoke exposure the authors' prime prevention target.
pmc-13425890:
Jiahui Fu and coworkers developed silk microneedles for sampling skin fluid in a 2026 bioengineering study modeled on plant xylem channels. Chronic inflammatory skin diseases need repeatable access to local molecules, yet biopsy is invasive and surface samples poorly reflect the skin environment. Their anisotropic porous needles use directional freezing, solvent-exchange crosslinking, and a salting-out step to form aligned channels with strong penetration.

One patch collected over 10 microliters of interstitial fluid within five minutes and recovered large molecules of at least 150 kilodaltons efficiently. Such sampling could support biomarker and protein profiling of skin disease with minimal harm. A patch that pulls this much fluid this fast could let staff track flares at home with far less pain and far less fuss for sick skin.
pmc-13426490:
Huijuan Lei and colleagues explored anxiety in early pregnancy after perinatal loss in a 2026 qualitative phenomenological study in Guangdong. Sixteen women pregnant again after losing a baby joined the study at a women and children's hospital in Guangdong. Interviews ran from December 2025 into April 2026 and followed a semi-structured guide. Transcripts were analyzed with Colaizzi's seven-step method using NVivo software.

Four themes emerged from the interviews. The earlier loss stays present in the new pregnancy, and vigilance under uncertainty intrudes on daily life. Women also hold a fragile balance through reassurance seeking and boundary control, while support expectations go unmet. Findings should inform individualized psychological support and continuity of care for this group.
pmc-13427090:
Sukhbir S. Singh and coauthors present a French-language 2026 case of deep endometriosis causing kidney shrinkage, bowel blockage, and sciatic nerve compression. Endometriosis affects about ten percent of women of reproductive age, as endometrial-like tissue grows outside the uterus and often causes disabling pelvic pain and infertility. Its deep form, the most severe, infiltrates underlying tissues, organs, muscle, and nerves and can irreversibly damage target organs.

Damage reaching kidney, intestine, and the sciatic nerve in one patient shows how far infiltrating disease can travel beyond the pelvis. Clinicians reading in French gain a stark reminder to image urinary, bowel, and nerve symptoms in known endometriosis.
pmc-13427790:
Hu and colleagues published a 2026 study on bile signals shaping immune cells in gut disease. Inflammatory bowel disease inflames the gut lining and resists full control. Helper T cells of a newer kind gather in the inflamed gut tissue. The team asked how a bile acid sensor on scout immune cells affects them.

Helper cell shares ran high in inflamed gut tissue samples from patients. Turning the bile sensor on in mice raised helper cell counts further. Scout cells lacking the sensor failed to mature and guide helper cells well. A partner signal path switched on instead, cutting a key helper signal. The work links bile chemistry to gut immune balance in new ways.
pmc-13430190:
Farahnazsadat Ahmadi, Fatemeh Nakhaei, and Mahboubeh Tajaldini study, in a 2026 Iranian cohort, whether injecting a woman's own platelet-rich plasma into the womb lifts IVF success after repeated failures. Recurrent implantation failure, where good embryos repeatedly fail to attach, has few proven fixes. The study covered 100 women aged 21 to 42 at a Gorgan infertility center in 2023. Fifty-one received the plasma injection two days before a frozen embryo transfer, while 49 had the standard transfer alone.

Clinical pregnancy occurred in about 27 percent of the treated group versus about 8 percent of controls. Implantation rates mirrored that gap. Miscarriage rates and pregnancy complications did not differ between groups, and no side effects from the injection were reported. Womb lining thickness did not explain the gain. The authors call the approach cheap and practical, while the design, a backward-looking cohort, caps the certainty.
pmc-13431590:
Katharina Kopp reviewed in 2026 how response teams should pick genome reading plans for grave RNA virus outbreaks. The fresh Bundibugyo virus outbreak in Congo and Uganda serves as the test case. Full genome reads anchor outbreak work, yet their worth hinges on sample quality, lab safety, and the tools at hand as much as on the machine used.

The virus was known from two past outbreaks, yet old genome samples stayed sparse, and past tests leaned toward its Ebola kin. Kopp sorts reading routes by how much prior knowledge of the virus each one needs, from direct reads to copy-based and trap-based routes. For like outbreaks, the review backs a staged plan. Teams start broad and cast a wide net across fever causes. They win a first genome with tolerant tools, then scale a proven route across places and weeks.
pmc-13431790:
Wang and colleagues review intron retention, a quirk of gene reading in which the segments normally cut out of a gene's RNA copy stay in. Those leftover segments were once dismissed as junk, and retained copies were thought only to mute a gene's output. Their 2026 review gathers new work on retention in health and in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the fatal disease that paralyzes by killing motor neurons.

Retained copies behave differently by location: some stay in the nucleus and some reach the cell body, with distinct jobs in each place. They can steer where RNA protein complexes gather, drain the pool of working RNA binding proteins, and shift the droplet like clumping of cell material, all themes in ALS biology. Retention itself can act as a regulatory element beyond making protein. The authors flag retained introns as drug targets and expect machine learning to speed discovery.
pmc-13431990:
Luiz and colleagues traced in 2026 how food insecurity moved over a decade in Brazilian households, sorted by the sex and race of the household head. Food insecurity means lacking steady access to enough good food, and in Brazil it falls hardest on Black families. The team compared three large national surveys, covering hundreds of thousands of homes.

Between 2013 and 2018, food security fell for every group. By 2023 it had recovered, most sharply in homes headed by Black women. Yet the worst forms of insecurity stayed concentrated in homes headed by Black and brown Brazilians, with Black women heads facing the highest rates. Models showed relative risk shrinking for severe insecurity in that group while staying well above white-headed homes. The authors call for policies aimed at the roots of racial inequality.
pmc-13435890:
Li Jiang and a large team link a simple insulin resistance score to hidden heart weakness in diabetes in 2026. Heart scans for 235 patients with type 2 diabetes measured shape, squeeze, energy yield, and blood flow. Patients split into thirds by the triglyceride glucose index.

The high score third showed more heart remodeling and weaker squeeze in all directions. Energy yield and resting flow also sagged in that group. The score held its link after matching for other risks. Energy yield and flow carried part of the score effect in path models. A cheap blood score may flag hearts that need scan follow up.
pmc-13435990:
Tharindu Wickramaarachchi and coauthors model the payoff of curbing teen pregnancy and child marriage in five Southeast Asian countries in 2026. Girls aged fifteen to nineteen were modeled by marriage, poverty, and school status. Survey and census figures drive the national level runs.

Base spending of 1.4 billion dollars over 2024 to 2030 still leaves 2.4 million unintended pregnancies and 2.1 million child marriages projected. Raising proven programs to ninety five percent cover costs five billion more. That scale up averts 1.3 million pregnancies and 1.1 million marriages. Sex education, cash aid, and life skills lead the program list.
pmc-13437390:
Yunshu Zhang and colleagues used scalp recordings to find shifting brain patterns in depressed teenagers, comparing those who lived through childhood trauma with those who did not. Their 2026 pilot study recorded resting brain waves in eighty-four adolescents: twenty-five depressed with trauma histories, twenty-seven without, and thirty-two healthy peers. Trauma and severity were scored with standard questionnaires, and the team tracked how brain networks link and unlink.

The trauma group fell ill earlier and scored more severely depressed than the other depressed group. Sorting the changing connections produced three recurring brain states. Features of those states tracked with trauma scores, which the authors read as a possible fingerprint of trauma-linked depression. They propose resting recordings, cheap and painless, might one day spot which depressed teenager carries a trauma history. That could guide trauma-focused care, though the small pilot needs larger tests.
pmc-13437490:
Jiahui Ding and Yanjuan Teng built learning models that estimate body makeup in people on long-term dialysis from a simple electrical test. Bioimpedance sends a weak current through the body and reads how tissues resist it. Muscle loss in dialysis patients predicts poor function, so tracking fat-free mass and body fat share matters. Their 2026 study trained several model types on routine test outputs and used an explanation tool to rank which inputs drove each estimate.

Grouped ensemble models beat single models across all four targets, with one method reaching near-perfect fit scores. Total body water and height dominated every prediction, followed by water inside and outside cells, minerals, and weight. Real value would come from a readable body profile flagging patients sliding toward muscle loss. They insist the models earn clinical use only after checks against measured function in larger, multi-center groups.
pmc-13437590:
Magdalena Zaniewska, writing alone in 2026, traces the two-way traffic between serotonin and alcohol use disorder. When its signaling runs low, vulnerability to heavy drinking rises, most sharply in the early-onset form marked by violence and antisocial behavior. Animal evidence runs parallel: mice bred without brain serotonin drink more, and alcohol-preferring rats show thin serotonin wiring.

Genes that build and carry serotonin, shaped by stress, help set each person's risk. That variety also explains why standard serotonin-raising antidepressants disappoint in most drinkers, helping mainly in milder, later-onset cases. Fresh interest centers on psychedelic therapies acting through a specific serotonin receptor in the prefrontal cortex. Zaniewska argues the disorder must be split into subtypes before serotonin drugs can be aimed well. Her review sets out the known links and calls for markers sorting patients by serotonin profile, so treatment can match biology rather than diagnosis alone.
pmc-13437690:
Shumin Lin and colleagues lay out a registered plan for a blinded acupuncture trial against constipation tied to Parkinson's disease. Constipation is among the most draining non-movement complaints in Parkinson's, and standard fixes often help little. Their 2026 protocol will enroll sixty-six patients, assigned by chance to real acupuncture or a sham version. Patients, assessors, and analysts will not know who got which.

Treatment runs four weeks, with four more weeks of follow-up. Weekly counts of bowel movements and stool form fill out the picture. Fluid samples will probe possible biology: short-chain fatty acids from gut microbes, an enzyme tied to gene control, and a marked form of the Parkinson's protein. The team grants sham needling can stir its own effects, so the gap between arms is the real test. Results should show whether needle treatment earns a place in gut care for Parkinson's.
pmc-13437790:
Domenico Vicari and a large team asked whether a simple maturity estimate explains power differences among young off-road cyclists. Teen athletes grow unevenly, so a stronger rider may simply be an earlier developer. Their 2026 study tested twenty-two young cyclists. Each rider's maturity offset, years from their fastest growth spurt, was estimated from body measures, then set against two lab tests: repeated six-second sprints and a rising ramp to exhaustion.

Maturity offset predicted top power in both tests with clear statistical support. The maturity measure failed to predict power relative to weight, the figure deciding climbing speed. The authors read this as maturity feeding raw output more than efficiency: bigger bodies push more watts without gaining an edge once weight is counted. They suggest coaches use the offset to read results fairly and track growth paths, rather than ranking teens on raw power and mistaking timing for talent.
pmc-13438190:
Fernández‐Lebrero and a large team test a blood marker in patients with a brain vessel disease in this 2026 study. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy deposits amyloid in brain blood vessels and often overlaps with Alzheimer's disease. The blood marker p-tau217 is a strong indicator of Alzheimer's, but whether it still works when vessel disease is present was unclear. The team studied 231 people, including 50 with the vessel disease and 154 with Alzheimer's.

Among the vessel-disease patients, 29 also met spinal fluid criteria for Alzheimer's. The blood marker separated those with and without the overlap very well. It scored a discrimination value of about 0.92 in this cohort's analysis, a strong result. The marker showed no relationship to scan measures of vessel disease severity, supporting that it reflects Alzheimer's pathology specifically. Two pre-set cut-off values both identified the overlap accurately.
pmc-13438390:
Kyle Siler replies to two critics of his study claiming a sharp post-2022 shift in words academics use, widely read as the fingerprint of large language models. In the 2026 reply, Siler grants each point, arguing they trim the edges of his claim without touching its center.

On scale, he clarifies that his statistic measures how far the word distribution moved, not a head count of AI-written papers. Read as a share, fifty-seven percent is a floor, and only under stated assumptions. On measurement, he concedes the word set was picked for its surge, so the chart alone proves nothing. Yet the words jumped when ChatGPT launched and partly fell back in 2025, timing editorial drift cannot explain. On his field and publisher breakdowns, he accepts the critics' math: those figures cannot be separately identified. The descriptive core, a rapid, patterned vocabulary change, survives intact.
pmc-13438690:
Yue Jiang led a very large team asking whether the hormone shot triggering egg release in fertility treatment leaves marks on children conceived that way. Assisted reproduction shapes chemical tags on offspring DNA, yet the trigger drug was unexamined. Their 2026 study followed a birth cohort of 365 families and 1,333 more children, then tested the chain in mice.

Higher trigger-day doses of human chorionic gonadotropin tracked with lower overall DNA methylation in the blood of assisted-reproduction children. In the larger group, higher doses also tracked with more suboptimal early development. Mice told the causal half: brief exposure dulled offspring learning behavior, cut new neuron growth in a memory region, and lowered a key methylation-guiding enzyme. Injecting that enzyme's message into exposed embryos restored neuron growth and behavior. The authors urge clinics to tune trigger doses for a child's long-term health, not only the cycle's success.
pmc-13439190:
Jingwen Yu and a large team hunt for rice genes that leave plants open to root-knot worms, publishing their findings in 2026. The worm Meloidogyne graminicola bores into rice roots and cuts yields across Asia, yet few resistant rice types are known. Genome-wide scans, multi-layer molecular data, and gene tests pointed to a factor named Rsf1, which codes a small cysteine-rich protein. A single letter change in the gene's switch region separated types by risk.

Plants with the risky letter made much more Rsf1 once worms attacked, while the safer letter kept levels low and plants held up better. A regulator called Myb44 was shown to drive Rsf1 output. Knocking the gene out in rice and in a model weed both raised resistance, pointing to a shared weakness that breeders could target.
pmc-13439690:
Ajay and colleagues built VIDEO in 2026, a web tool that layers several kinds of gene data. It shows how enhancers, the DNA switches near genes, may work in specific tissues of the fruit fly. Gene regulation studies juggle gene activity, open chromatin, and factor binding data. Few tools let researchers view them together against the binding motifs, the short DNA words a factor recognizes, in a tissue-specific gene set.

Starting from a custom gene list, VIDEO finds which switching factors are present in the tissue, locates their motifs in nearby enhancers. Overlays open chromatin maps and binding data for those factors. The team showcased it on a well-known system, the factor CrebA and the secretory pathway in the larval salivary gland, then used it to form hypotheses in the less-studied embryonic hindgut. The authors offer VIDEO as a hypothesis engine for developmental gene regulation.
pmc-13441290:
Jaime Piquero-Casals and colleagues revisit a modern skin steroid, methylprednisolone aceponate, weighing its power against its gentleness in a 2026 review. Skin steroids remain the backbone of care for inflamed skin, yet strength often trades against thinning and whole-body effects. The reviewed drug is a fourth-generation, non-halogenated steroid built for local punch with limited body exposure. A literature search spanning 1990 to 2025 gathered pharmacology and clinical studies across eczema types.

Twin ester groups and a methyl tweak in its structure drive strong local action with low thinning potential. The drug activates inside skin, then breaks down quickly once absorbed, keeping body-wide exposure small. Trials showed fast itch relief and high clearance in atopic, contact, and seborrheic eczema, usually with once-daily use. Long-term thinning and hormone-axis suppression stayed rare in the record. The authors position it for both flare control and maintenance care.
pmc-13441890:
Ifen Ayu Malinda, Imam Budi Putra, and Ariyati Yosi test whether the hormone progesterone tracks with syringoma, a benign sweat-gland growth, in a 2026 Indonesian study. Syringomas appear as small skin-coloured bumps, often around the eyes, and can trouble patients' confidence. Hormone influence has long been suspected in their origin. The cross-sectional study enrolled thirty-five patients with syringoma and thirty-five without, each examined by eye and dermoscope and tested for blood progesterone.

Most patients were women in their late twenties to mid-thirties, and the localised form was commonest, with familial cases making up a quarter. High progesterone appeared in ten patients with syringoma against only two controls, a statistically significant association with odds several times higher. Receptor staining evidence points the same way in the authors' reading. They conclude that hormonal involvement in syringoma growth deserves weight in future work on causes and care.
pmc-13442690:
Leonardo Rigon and colleagues report a rare clue to where excess beta rhythm in Parkinson disease begins in a 2026 case paper. The rhythm, a fast brain wave, runs too strong in the loop that links the cortex to deep brain hubs. A patient with a deep brain stimulator grew brief swelling on one side of the brain, which let the team watch the rhythm through the device.

The excess rhythm on the swollen side fell silent while the swelling lasted. It came back once the cortex swelling cleared, even though deep hub swelling had healed sooner. The team reads the timing as proof that a sound cortex is required for the deep rhythm to run wild. That points drug and device work at the cortex link in the loop. One case cannot settle the debate, yet the timing here is hard to explain away.
pmc-13442890:
Zhenan Ruan and colleagues review how gut microbes shape asthma through the gut-lung axis in a 2026 paper. Asthma fills lungs with chronic swelling, and standard drugs fail some hard forms. Work from 2011 to 2025 spans group studies, animal tests, clinic records, and small trials.

Gut microbes tune airway swelling by coaching immune cell growth, by sending chemical signals, and by guarding the gut wall. Microbe marks differ between allergic and plain asthma, and between child and adult forms. Cures that target microbes span live cultures, feed goods, mixed packs, waste goods, and stool swaps. Early gains look bright, yet cause proof stays weak and trial plans vary wildly. The authors ask for tighter trials before gut care joins asthma care.

Yun Wen and Pengfei Luo size up a cell enzyme, UBE2A, as a cancer mark across tumor types in a 2026 study. The enzyme tags proteins for fate calls inside cells, and its cancer role stayed blurry. Public sets from tumor banks and gene banks fed checks on levels, outlook, gene traits, and immune ties.

Single-cell reads placed the enzyme thick in fast-growing T cells. Bench tests in breast cancer cells showed that silencing UBE2A curbed growth, spread, and invasion. The authors pitch UBE2A as a broad outlook mark with immune links worth drug study.

Ling-Dong Shi and colleagues find jumbo DNA rings riding with methane-eating archaea in a 2026 study. Side DNA in archaea is the least grasped class of genetic goods, and rings past 200 kbp are rare. Their rings reach 535 kbp in Methanoperedens, microbes that burn methane without air.

The authors place the rings on a slide from plasmid-like to mini-chromosome-like.
pmc-13444490:
Hadi Koohi and colleagues report two cases where treating one giant liver hemangioma shrank its untreated kin in a 2026 paper. Hemangiomas are the most common benign liver growths, and giants past 5 cm can ache. Both patients had sore giant lumps treated by direct needle sclerotherapy with a bleomycin-lipiodol mix.

That echo hints at body-wide or inflammatory paths set off by the local fix. The authors share the pair as a hypothesis, not a rule. Planned trials must test whether one hit can calm distant lumps for real.
pmc-13445190:
David Czell and Melina Anina Brandenberger test whether a single dose of caffeine raises the rate of small muscle twitches in healthy adults, in a 2026 ultrasound study. Such twitches, called fasciculations, are often harmless, yet they can also hint at nerve disease. Knowing what caffeine does to them could sharpen how doctors read muscle scans.

Twitch rates rose in most muscles, with the largest gains in the calf and foot and the smallest in the thigh. Younger adults gained more in arm muscles, older adults more in leg muscles, so the authors advise asking about recent caffeine before muscle tests.
pmc-13445290:
Kai Wang and colleagues review a two-stage spine operation for adults whose worn spines curve sideways and tilt forward, in a 2026 records study. Side curves near the pelvis are hard to straighten, above all when the lowest curve is stiff. The staged plan first works from the side of the body, then adds screws from the back.

Charts covered fifty-one patients treated in sequence at one center. X-ray measures of side curve, trunk shift, and forward lean improved step by step after each stage, and the gains largely held at the last check. Back pain scores and daily function scores also improved. The authors read the pattern as stepwise straightening that lasts, within the limits of a single-center review.
pmc-13445490:
Annika Müller-Eigner and colleagues review the double-edged role of reactive oxygen species from mitochondria, the cell's power plants, in aging, in a 2026 paper. These reactive molecules were long cast as pure harm, waste from breathing that rusts the cell. Newer work shows they also carry signals, and effect depends on place, timing, and dose.

The review sorts output by its source inside the power plant, at three named sites of the breathing chain. From there it traces how local bursts touch each hallmark of aging, from worn gene caps to failed clean-up systems. The authors argue that blunt anti-oxidant plans miss this detail, and that future work must target the right site at the right moment.
pmc-13446190:
Ibironke W. Apata and colleagues compare infection control habits in United States dialysis centers between 2015 and 2021, in a 2026 survey study. Bloodstream infections in dialysis patients fell sharply over the late twenty-teens, after national pushes for safer catheter care. The team asked which habits spread in step with that fall.
