Use of strong skin antiseptic at catheter exit sites rose by about six points, and ointment or treated dressings rose by a like step. Alcohol care of catheter hubs jumped near ten points. Near half of centers had adopted germ-killing catheter caps, a new tool in that span. The authors urge wider uptake of the lagging habits.
pmc-13446290:
Kanta Kumaki and colleagues devise a way to measure the twist, or chirality, hidden in fine bone vessel networks, in a 2026 methods study. Bones look mirror-matched left to right, yet their tiny canals wander off true symmetry, and random noise can mask a real bias. Their bipixel rotation method turns flat images step by step and counts aligned pixel pairs at each angle.

The angle with the richest count marks a center, and the lopsided spread around it yields a bias score. Letter fonts and wallpaper patterns with known twist validated the math. Applied to pig thigh bone canals seen by nano-scale scans, the method picked out up-right against down-right leanings. The team offers it for mesh networks across the body.
pmc-13446490:
Marr and colleagues describe in 2026 an outreach model that brings crystallography, the science of crystal structure, into kindergarten classrooms, a subject usually left until graduate school. The fourth center read a new children's book the team created, a sugar crystal mystery story published in 2025 that links kitchen crystals to laboratory science. Instructors observed every child set up crystals safely and record observations, and most grasped the atom and X-ray ideas at an age-appropriate level.
pmc-13447190:
Tanmay Boob leads a 2026 study of day-long blood pressure checks before discharge after a heart failure flare in India. Risk tools at that handover point are scarce. Patterns across day and night, plus how much pressure swings, might flag who faces death or a return stay in the next three months.

Just over half showed a normal night-time dip, while smaller shares showed flat, reversed or extreme patterns. Death within three months affected a small share, yet readmission touched more than four in ten. pmc-13447290:
In Ha Kim and Jae Kwang Yun evaluate a move from many-port to single-port robot chest surgery in a 2026 weighted comparison. Lung cancer removal through one small entry promises less pain, yet surgeons need proof that a structured switch keeps patients safe. All operations in the series came from one surgeon, which sharpens the learning-curve question.

Complete tumour removal was achieved in every case, with similar drainage time, hospital stay and complication rates across groups. Single-port operations ran shorter on average, and patients reported less pain in the first two days. The authors conclude the transition proved safe and workable within their pathway.
pmc-13448190:
S Anderson leads a large team setting out a study protocol for response-adapted radiotherapy in throat cancer in a 2026 paper. Cancers of the oropharynx, the middle throat, are rising, and poor-prognosis cases often fail standard radiation. Blanket dose increases for everyone have not improved survival, so the trial instead escalates dose only for tumours that respond poorly early on.

All participants start standard radiation, with diffusion MRI scans at the first and tenth sessions measuring water movement inside tumours. Slow improvement marks a tumour as a non-responder, earning a higher total dose to the visible tumour in later sessions. Responders stay on the standard course. The main goal is feasibility, meaning whether the scan-guided adapted workflow can be delivered without treatment gaps, before any large comparison trial.
pmc-13448290:
Maia and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract TLSB-33, a Johns Hopkins study of sacituzumab govitecan. This antibody-drug conjugate is approved for later-line metastatic breast cancer. The study asks how well it controls disease inside the central nervous system versus elsewhere.

Seventy-three women, median age fifty-eight, mostly treated in the third line or later, were reviewed. Before the drug, about ten percent already had brain or spinal metastases. During treatment another ten percent developed them, and pre-existing central nervous system disease progressed in about eighteen percent. The telling contrast was timing. pmc-13449990:
Rametta and colleagues tested in 2026 whether a rare kidney cancer displays two targets used by modern antibody drugs. Collecting duct carcinoma is a rare, aggressive kidney cancer with few treatment options. It resembles bladder-lining cancer in origin, so the team checked tumour samples for two drug targets, Nectin-4 and Trop-2, used by antibody-drug conjugates proven in bladder cancer. Samples came from 59 patients in a multi-centre study and were stained in a central lab.

Nectin-4 was found in about four in ten tumours, with varied staining strength. Trop-2 was found in nearly nine in ten tumours, often with strong, widespread staining. The authors say the frequent presence of both targets supports a biological kinship with bladder-lining cancer. They stress that staining alone does not prove the drugs will work in patients.
pmc-13451890:
Habeeb Abood and Farah Hasan AlHusseini review in 2026 six studies of a curvature measure on two families of near-complex shapes. The measure in view, the conharmonic tensor, flags shape events that older measures miss.

Across the six studies, forcing the measure flat squeezed the shapes into tight classes, often the famed Einstein kind or forms that map neatly onto simpler ones. The review sets out the rules each class must meet and where point-even forms can exist. The authors offer the tensor as a sorting tool that yields fresh classes of shapes for pure math.
pmc-13452290:
Nakamura and co-authors report a spinal fluid leak pinned to a tiny bone spur in the lower back. Their 2026 case report describes a 41-year-old woman with severe headache on standing and nausea, the signature of spontaneous intracranial hypotension from leaking cerebrospinal fluid. Whole-spine MRI showed fluid collecting outside the dura, confirming a spinal leak, but not its exact source.

CT myelography spotted a small calcified spur at the first lumbar level pressing on the front of the dural sac. Digital subtraction myelography, a dynamic X-ray technique, then caught contrast actively escaping at that spot, proving a ventral dural tear from the microspur. A targeted epidural blood patch at that single level resolved symptoms rapidly, with no recurrence over eighteen months. The authors claim the first lumbar microspur case confirmed by this dynamic method, and commend it for localising elusive leaks.
pmc-13452390:
M Aldiki Febriantono and three co-authors present a photo set of Manalagi apples grown in Indonesia, built so computer models can learn to spot fruit disease. The 2026 data paper covers fruit gathered in orchards from August 2024 to June 2026. Each fruit was photographed in natural light with phone and DSLR cameras.

The team logged 1,168 distinct fruits and about 5,100 raw photos before checks for image quality began. Each kept photo was cropped to one fruit, resized to a square of 1024 by 1024 pixels, and saved as a JPEG file. The final set holds 482 labeled images in four classes: healthy fruit, anthracnose, black pox, and powdery mildew. Growers and coders can use the set to train and test tools that flag sick fruit early.
pmc-13453490:
Hao Ding and thirteen co-authors build barbed microneedle patches to treat melasma, the stubborn brown facial patches that resist creams. The patch needles copy the backward barbs of a tick's mouthpart, so they grip skin instead of slipping out. Their 2026 design loads two agents: tranexamic acid, a drug that calms pigment, and exosomes, tiny cell bubbles from fat stem cells.

The patch matrix breaks down when it meets the harmful oxygen species that crowd melasma skin, freeing both agents on demand. The exosomes mop up those oxygen species, while the drug breaks up the extra tiny blood vessels that feed the patches. Together they quiet the pigment making chain and shift immune cells toward a healing mode. In mice with hormone and light induced melasma, the patch visibly lightened the dark patches.
pmc-13454290:
Han-Lin Li and five colleagues report a 2026 brain imaging study of children with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder who had never taken medication for it. The group included 62 children with the disorder, aged 6 to 15 years, and 46 healthy peers. Scans taken at rest measured how strongly regions in the sensorimotor network connect with each other and with other large brain networks.

Children with the disorder scored worse on attention and self-control tests and showed stronger connections within the sensorimotor network. Links from that network to the default mode and salience networks were also stronger than in controls. Some stronger links tracked with lower hyperactivity scores, while others tracked with better test control. The authors say these patterns may help explain mixed past findings on brain wiring in the disorder.
pmc-13455090:
Hassani and co-authors review the search for protein biomarkers in breast cancer in this 2026 paper. Proteins measured in tissue or body fluids could in principle flag cancer early, predict its course, and track treatment, but few candidates have reached the clinic. The review covers samples from blood and saliva to urine and tiny released vesicles, and the platforms used to measure their proteins.

Modern mass spectrometry and affinity assays such as Olink and SomaScan now probe thousands of proteins at once, widening the search considerably. Still, most candidate markers stall at the discovery or early checking stage. Weak sensitivity holds them back. So do overlap with other conditions, differences between platforms, and small mixed patient groups. The authors call for standardized workflows, targeted verification, and multi-center validation before panels can guide routine care.
pmc-13456990:
Fatma Shalabi and four colleagues present, in a 2026 case series, three patients whose brains were struck by fat embolism after broken long bones. Fat entering the blood after fractures can reach the brain, with effects from mild confusion to sudden coma and death. About one in ten patients with the brain form dies.

The three cases span that range. One patient lost consciousness with startling speed. Others showed milder or slower courses, with different scan pictures and different recoveries. Diagnosis leaned on the injury story and clinical signs, since magnetic resonance imaging is not always at hand when decisions must be made. The authors walk through the symptoms, imaging, and care choices in each case. Their point is recognition: after a major fracture, a fading mind should trigger suspicion of fat in the brain, not only bleeding or swelling.
pmc-13457190: A tested blood assay — PATHFAST TB LAM Ag — for quantitatively tracking TB treatment. Yassir Adam Shuaib and Stéphane Coisne prove the plan. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is TB disease testing. It establishes a quantitative assay for tracking TB treatment response.
pmc-13457390: Nomograms to diagnose toxic blood in newborns — built and tested at a single site. Yun Yu, Huawei Wang, and others construct them. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is newborn disease testing. It builds test nomograms for newborn toxic blood retrospectively, aiding early bedside decisions.
pmc-13458390:
Lian and colleagues uncover how a tumor suppressor protein helps repair broken DNA in this 2026 study. The protein, menin, is best known because its loss causes inherited tumor syndromes. Cells repair double-strand breaks by homologous recombination, an accurate copying process. A chemical mark called H3K36me3 guides that repair. How the mark gets placed at damage sites was unclear.

Deleting the menin gene in mice caused spontaneous lung tumors and severe genome instability, the team found. Menin directly grabs the damage-marked histone at break sites and recruits SETD2, the enzyme that lays down H3K36me3 there. A reader protein then spots the mark and brings in CtIP, which trims DNA ends to start repair. A drug that restored the mark rescued repair in menin-deficient cells.
pmc-13459190:
Coffey, Simons, Taylor, and Kingston describe redesigning an evaluation of virtual reality in hand therapy in this 2026 service improvement report. Their outpatient service had adopted virtual reality to make repetitive hand exercises more engaging, but standard numerical measures did not capture why it was introduced. Seven clinicians and twelve patients answered the new questionnaires, mixing open and closed questions. The findings showed virtual reality created a low-pressure, engaging setting that encouraged participation, something the original measures would have missed entirely. Participants also flagged practical conditions for success: enough physical space, reliable technology, attention to culture and language, and continued hands-on guidance from therapists alongside the headset.
pmc-13459290:
Bo Chen and Yanbei Lin surveyed in 2026 the self-esteem of heart patients after percutaneous coronary intervention, a procedure that opens blocked arteries, often with stents. Their cross-sectional study enrolled 316 patients treated at one hospital between February 2024 and January 2025. Participants completed the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, a ten-item questionnaire where higher scores mean stronger self-worth, and shared clinical and social details.

Average scores sat at the low end of general population norms. Self-esteem ran lower in older patients and in those receiving more stents, while education, income, and longer time since diagnosis each tied to higher scores. Where a patient lived also mattered. The authors recommend psychological support aimed at the most vulnerable groups during recovery.
pmc-13460190:
Yuyan Liu and colleagues asked in 2026 whether fixing broken ribs surgically, early, helps the most severely injured patients who already need a ventilator. Their Tianjin cohort held 59 patients admitted between 2018 and 2025 with at least three rib fractures or a flail segment and breathing failure within a day of arrival. Thirty received surgical stabilization of the rib fractures and twenty-nine were managed without surgery.

Surgical patients came off the ventilator in a median of six days against seventeen for the others, left intensive care sooner, and gained far more ventilator-free days. Pneumonia, tracheostomy, and hospital death all occurred less often after surgery, with no deaths in the surgical group. Adjusted analysis confirmed the operation itself as the factor tied to faster liberation.
pmc-13461390:
Lin Gui and colleagues studied in 2026 newly diagnosed multiple myeloma patients whose disease arrived with high blood calcium, a marker of heavy tumor burden. Their two-center cohort held 82 such patients diagnosed between 2015 and 2024, compared against eighty randomly chosen myeloma patients without high calcium, with a median follow-up just over four years. By the end, fifty-nine of the eighty-two had died.

Several features predicted survival in early analysis, including chromosome abnormalities, kidney function, remaining disease after treatment, and calcium itself. In the final model, having few chromosome abnormalities and clearing residual disease protected patients. Severe calcium elevation and high ferritin, an iron storage protein rarely studied here, worsened both survival measures on their own. The group showed high early mortality overall.
pmc-13461990:
Alessandra Giannella leads a 2026 report on a structured way to read rare gene variants in patients with too many red blood cells. Targeted gene sequencing at their clinic over three years found thirty-four eligible patients.

 Each rare variant was weighed using several lenses. They included how firmly the gene links to disease, how common the variant is in the population, computer predictions, classification rules, and protein shape modeling. The structured sorting ranked which variants most likely matter. The authors stress how varied the genetic picture is under one label. Their message: finding a variant is only the first step. Careful, layered interpretation decides what it means.
pmc-13462390:
Yi Wang leads a 2026 blood study on how four subtypes of the antibody IgG relate to disease activity in pemphigus. The authors propose the two subtypes as add-on markers beside standard autoantibody tests, supporting more personal judging of disease status.
pmc-13462990:
Buianova and Pat examined in 2026 how body physiology and brain measures together relate to thinking ability in aging, using data from over 30,000 UK Biobank participants. Most of the overlap between body and cognition, about eighty-five percent, was shared with brain imaging measures, especially white matter features. Almost all of the link between age and cognition was shared with brain or body markers. The authors say the results show body and brain aging move together in explaining cognitive decline.
pmc-13463290:
Alsamani and Alsamiri published a 2026 scoping review of artificial intelligence in gifted and talented education. One covers teaching and growth, where generative AI, tutoring systems, and AI-made tools support tailored and creative learning. The other covers assessment, where machine learning helps spot gifted learners, including twice exceptional learners who also have disabilities. Reported risks include biased test data, too much trust in AI, privacy worries, and threats to fresh ideas. The authors call the evidence base early stage still.
pmc-13464090:
Xiaomin Liang and eight co-authors test a plant alkaloid, rhynchophylline, as a guard for dopamine neurons in Parkinson's disease. pmc-13464590:
Francesca Sanguedolce and three co-authors write a pathologist's guide to BRCA testing in prostate cancer. Faults in BRCA1 and BRCA2 flag harder disease and foretell response to PARP blocker drugs. As testing widens, the tissue handler's craft decides whether results can be trusted.

Fixing, storage time, tumor share in the slice, and DNA quality all bend test success before any machine runs. Bone samples need special care, since the acid baths that soften bone can shred DNA. Tumors with BRCA2 faults tend to show higher grade and stage at diagnosis. Certain growth patterns hint at gene instability yet cannot stand in for testing, so the authors press for tight teamwork.
pmc-13464790:
Elliott and colleagues review in 2026 how focused ultrasound, sound waves aimed precisely into the body, affects anti-tumor immunity across its several forms. The authors argue these immune effects may matter as much as local tumor destruction. They aim the comparison at guiding combination therapy with immunotherapy and speeding safe clinical use of the technology.
pmc-13465290:
Liu and co-authors built in 2026 a questionnaire to measure digital health equity among rural older adults in China. Scores also held steady when people retook the test two weeks later, supporting the tool for early assessment work.
pmc-13466290:

pmc-13466590:
Ryota Asahara and colleagues scan the brains of young and older adults doing a task-switching test after exercise, in a 2026 crossover study. Brain scans ran before the activity and again at two points afterward.

Switching between task rules costs speed and accuracy, and blood-flow signals mark the brain effort involved. Older adults showed stronger activation in frontal and temporal areas during the task. Mixed models compared how a single exercise bout and simple repetition each shifted those signals and the behavior, testing whether movement sharpens mental flexibility differently with age.
pmc-13467990:
Run-hua Li and nine colleagues published this 2026 study building a model predicting when endoscopic ultrasound will disagree with the pathology diagnosis in colorectal subepithelial lesions, growths beneath the bowel lining. pmc-13468690:
He Yang, Siyu Pan, and Zhaobin Qiu speed up the crystallization of a biodegradable plastic in 2026 by growing it around a pinch of talc. At 2 percent loading, the melt crystallization temperature rose from 46.1 to 58.9 degrees Celsius at the tested cooling rate, and the time to half-crystallize at 66 degrees fell from 7.69 minutes to 1.95. pmc-13468890:
Zhang introduces a journal research collection on microbial diversity in mine drainage, in a 2026 editorial surveying seven published articles. pmc-13469290:

The assay showed high sensitivity and specificity and tracked closely with neutralizing antibody titers, the functional gold standard. pmc-13470490:
Arif Ali leads a fifteen author team reporting in 2026 a set of forty chalcone compounds tested as possible diabetes helpers. The team made the series through a classic condensation reaction and confirmed structures with infrared and magnetic resonance readings.

Six members stood out, and the best one beat the standard drug acarbose by a wide margin in the dish. Hydroxy and methoxy decorations generally helped, while some ring swaps and heavy halogen patterns hurt. Computer docking placed the winner neatly in the enzyme active groove, and property forecasts looked acceptable.
pmc-13470590:
Lingayat and co-workers in India tried in 2026 a one step fix for long bone breaks that will not heal and are steeped in germs. The classic path takes two stages and months: clean out, park a drug block, then fix the bone. Their path coats a bone nail with cement laced with the right drug for each germ, and sets it in the same clean out step. Ten patients with shin, thigh, or arm breaks got the nail, with six weeks of body wide drugs on top.

At a year of checks, the plan had won most rounds. Germs were cleared in four of five patients, and bones had fused in seven of ten. Shin breaks took near half a year to fuse, thigh breaks a bit less. Two patients kept their germ load and needed more work. The authors limit the plan to small bone gaps.
pmc-13471390:
Ditta and co-authors asked health service leaders and clinicians what would help or hinder rolling out online psychological support for stroke survivors across England. Their 2026 qualitative study reports interviews with 14 professionals who commission, manage, or deliver stroke care, conducted between February and April 2024.

The program under discussion, WAterS-2, offers group therapy online based on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy and is delivered by trained staff who are not psychologists. Every participant agreed current emotional support after stroke is inadequate, especially for people with aphasia, a language disorder, and for minoritised ethnic communities. Stakeholders also pressed for proof of cost-effectiveness and suggested shorter, adapted sessions for people with communication difficulties. Their recommendations aim to keep the service equitable as it scales.
pmc-13471490:
Wang and co-authors lay out the protocol for an umbrella review, a review of reviews, on whether antibiotics and other anti-infective drugs taken in pregnancy harm the baby. Their 2026 plan searches six databases up to June 22, 2024 and adds a three-stage extraction method with software to untangle overlapping reviews.

The stakes are broad: between 63 and 97% of pregnant women take at least one drug, and 28 to 40% receive an anti-infective, yet safety findings conflict across reviews. When two meta-analyses overlap by more than a corrected threshold of 5% shared primary studies, only the newest and most complete one will be kept. Quality will be graded with standard tools so clinicians get one consolidated safety picture.
pmc-13471590:
Skweres and co-authors asked why one hippocampal neighborhood, CA2, shrugs off the excitotoxic damage that devastates its neighbor CA1. Their 2026 study stained rodent brain tissue and living slice cultures for the mitochondrial calcium uniporter, a channel that pulls calcium into mitochondria, and then blocked it during toxic NMDA exposure.

The map matched the mystery: MCU levels ran highest exactly where neurons resisted injury, and NMDA itself pushed CA2 to make even more of the channel. Blocking the uniporter sensitized CA2 neurons to damage in a dose-dependent way, while low-MCU CA1 neurons barely noticed the drug. The result flips the usual story, in which this channel is blamed for worsening excitotoxic injury, at least for this protected region.
pmc-13471990:
Zeliang Wu, Yixin Chen, Zuxin Wen, and Xianbiao Fu lay out in 2026 a strategy for cleaning nitrogen oxide exhaust from ammonia burning power systems electrochemically. Ammonia promises carbon free energy, but burning it releases NOx, and turning that NOx back into harmless nitrogen gas would close the loop. At the dilute concentrations of real exhaust, the electric route loses selectivity to side reactions that make hydrogen or hydrogenated products instead.

The mechanism, the authors argue, runs through a surface bound NO stage with nitrous oxide as a key halfway product. Sparse surface coverage starves the nitrogen pairing step that finishes the job. Their fix pairs tandem catalysis, splitting the chemistry across cooperating sites, with control of the interface microenvironment. Practical hurdles under gas phase, dilute conditions close the perspective.
pmc-13473490:
Qintao Wang and a broad team pair gene editing with rapid cell sorting in 2026 to find what drives oil-rich algae to make more carotenoids. These pigments are valued in food and health goods. The team built a library of more than three thousand edited algae strains, each missing one gene. A light-based sorter then picked out single cells rich in pigment without any labels or dyes.

Two gene hits stood out from the sorted cells. Knocking out one set of pigment-processing genes raised one pigment form, while knocking out a protein-recycling helper raised three forms at once. Gene activity data hinted at two fresh control routes for pigment making. The approach can speed gene hunts in other algae bred for fuel or food.
pmc-13473590:
Yuran Gui and colleagues trace a gene switch that guards memory in 2026 work on mouse brains. The switch, called Npas4, rises soon after blood flow to the brain is cut. It turns up two partner proteins that help nerve cells hold strong links to each other. Lowering Npas4 dropped those partners and weakened the boost in link strength seen after the injury.

In Alzheimer disease, levels of all three genes fell in both human and mouse brain tissue. Raising Npas4 in a mouse model of the disease restored the partner proteins. Memory test scores and link strength both improved in those mice. The chain from Npas4 to its partners offers a fresh lead for protecting thought and memory.
pmc-13473990:
Guan and a large team of land and climate modelers argued in 2026 that pools of ecosystem models can mislead choice makers when they are built with no firm rules. Such pools, called multi model ensembles, mix forecasts from many models to firm up a call. Land use, farm, and climate funds now ride on their word. The authors say weak pools can fake trust and steer cash and rules the wrong way.

They set two posts for sound pools. First, stiff side by side tests of the models, with shared data marks, must drive which models join and how much each counts. Weak or twin like models drag a pool down. Second, the users of the call, from farmers to fund staff, must help shape the test from the start. The authors add guides on pool size, spread, and where smart computer help fits.
pmc-13474390:
Hiroki Anzai and a wide team build tiny shark antibodies in the lab in 2026 without using live animals. Shark blood holds the smallest known natural binding units, called VNARs. The team designed a synthetic set from shark gene data and used folding software to predict shapes. A display method then fished out binders for two glowing test proteins.

Two winning binders were picked, one for each test protein, and both gripped their targets in lab checks. Grip strength ranged from strong to moderate across the pair. The work is the first to show this display route can select shark binders. Animal-free selection could speed early drug and test development.
pmc-13474590:
Yinan Chen and colleagues hunt causes of lasting severe low blood pressure during major pancreas surgery in 2026. Just over one hundred patients were split into those with the pressure problem and those without. Blood measures, monitor data, and tissue from the belly lining were compared. Tiny vessel wall cells were viewed under an electron microscope for damage signs.

Forty-four patients met the pressure problem, and they had bigger operations, more bleeding, and longer surgery times. Their vessel resistance ran low while heart output ran high. Blood calcium in arteries dropped far more in this group. Vessel wall cells looked swollen with raised internal traffic, which fits leakier vessels.
pmc-13474690:
Zhang and co-authors trained a stacking ensemble, a model that learns how to blend nine other machine learning algorithms, to predict atrial fibrillation after heart bypass surgery. Their 2026 retrospective study drew 563 bypass patients from one center, split into 394 for training and 169 for validation, with 29.5% developing the postoperative rhythm problem.

Feature selection with stability-checked elastic net kept thirteen predictors, led by age, intraoperative phenylephrine use, and prior stroke. The stack reached a validation discrimination of 0.7425 AUC with an F1 score of 0.711 on the study's metrics, barely ahead of plain logistic regression at 0.718 AUC, a gap that was not significant at p 0.09 in the comparison. The authors are candid: moderate accuracy, no external validation, and limited clinical utility until other hospitals test it.
pmc-13474790:
Zhigang Xie and co-authors compare palliative care awareness in the United States in 2026 across caregiver groups. Palliative care lifts quality of life in serious illness, yet myths about it persist. A national survey from 2024 gave data on more than five thousand adults, weighted to stand for the full adult population. Groups covered non-caregivers, paid caregivers, and unpaid family caregivers.

Awareness rose step by step across those groups, from about forty-five percent to about sixty-two percent. Care for a parent or for cancer patients marked the highest awareness of all. Paid caregivers were most likely to wrongly think palliative care means stopping all other treatment. Outreach must lift facts, not just name recognition.
pmc-13474890:
Rao and colleagues compared two mitral valve repair styles in 2026, asking whether cutting away part of a floppy leaflet or preserving it changes how the heart recovers. The Resect approach trims the leaflet, while the Respect approach keeps it and adds support cords. Their data came from the UK Mini Mitral Trial, focusing on patients with isolated prolapse of the back leaflet, scanned before surgery and again at 12 and 52 weeks.

The analysis covered 175 patients, 36 repaired with resection and 139 with preservation, drawn from the trial's 330 randomized patients overall. Both groups shrank the key heart chamber measure by 5.6 percent on average by 52 weeks, with no meaningful gap between the techniques at any point. Leak severity at one year also matched, so the authors say surgeons can choose either approach with confidence on these measures.
pmc-13477090:
Hou and colleagues pooled studies in 2026 on coronary bypass surgery for patients whose hearts pump extremely weakly, with an ejection fraction of 20 percent or less. Ejection fraction is the share of blood the heart ejects per beat, and such low values make any operation risky. The team searched three databases for trials and cohort studies published from 1995 through December 2023 on bypass outcomes in this group.

The pool covered 29 studies and 5,910 patients, and the combined death rate around surgery was 9 percent in this fragile population. Heart attack after surgery affected 2 percent and stroke 3 percent, while low cardiac output syndrome, where the heart cannot meet the body's needs, appeared in 16 percent of patients. Despite the early risk, pooled five-year survival reached 74 percent, leading the authors to argue bypass should stay on the table for selected patients.
pmc-13477390:
Sukran Erdem and colleagues report a 2026 prospective study on muscle loss in people living with Fontan circulation, a surgical heart arrangement used for single-ventricle defects. The team measured the psoas muscle at the hip two ways on magnetic resonance scans. One method used a single slice area, and the other used the full muscle volume.

Seventy patients and 51 healthy controls of similar age and sex took part. Male patients had lower muscle area and volume for their body size than healthy males, while female differences were not clear. Full volume added modest predictive value for Fontan failure beyond liver disease, protein level, and oxygen saturation, while single-slice area did not. The authors suggest volume measurement as a useful extra marker of disease burden.
pmc-13480090:
Tulay Sati Kirkan and co-authors describe a 2026 study of social media use among people with schizophrenia. Clinics often worry that online life may harm this group, yet proof stays thin. The team enrolled 222 outpatients and split them by whether they used social media, then scored symptoms, daily function, and quality of life with standard scales.

Users were younger, more often male, and better educated than non-users. Most users scored low on a scale for problem use, though a small share scored high. Users showed lower symptom scores, notably for flat affect and withdrawal, and better daily function. Quality of life scores ran higher for physical and social areas, while pain and mood areas matched. Since the study took a single snapshot, it cannot show that social media caused the gains. Follow-up over time would help sort cause from selection.
pmc-13480190:
Jing Zhu and colleagues present a 2026 survey of a gene called FGD3 across many cancer types. The gene helps control cell shape and movement switches, yet its role across cancers stayed murky. The team compared gene levels in tumour and normal tissue from large public databases, checked links to survival and immune cell mix, and ran lab tests in breast cancer cells.

Gene levels varied widely by cancer type, with survival links that flipped direction between cancers. Levels tied to immune markers and to the mix of immune cells inside tumours. In lab work, cutting the gene slowed breast cancer cell growth and movement, which hints at a brake-like role there. The authors see the gene as a candidate marker for outlook and treatment choice, though its mixed behaviour across cancers calls for type-by-type study.
pmc-13480490:
Na Jin and co-authors describe a 2026 study of a cobalt reagent that plucks hydrogen from ring compounds at one chosen spot. Rings holding nitrogen, such as pyridine, anchor many drugs and farm chemicals, yet swapping their hydrogens for metals normally needs harsh lithium reagents and deep cold. The cobalt amide reagent works by direct exchange, keeping its own oxidation state while taking the hydrogen.

Selectivity followed where the ring nitrogen could grip the cobalt, not the usual acidity ranking, giving clean single-spot products in high yield. Two rings even took cobalt at two spots under control. Watching reactions by magnetic scans and modelling backed the grip-first picture. Treating the products with iodine then swapped cobalt for a bulky nitrogen group, opening routes to crowded ring designs that older methods struggle to reach.
pmc-13481590:
Wang and co-authors identify what predicts survival when cell therapy is followed by transplant in hard-to-treat leukaemia. Their 2026 retrospective study covers 63 patients with relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia who received donor stem cell transplants after CD19 CAR-T therapy. The team modelled overall survival and the severity of graft-versus-host disease, the main transplant complication.

Two-year overall survival was about 68 percent and progression-free survival about 56 percent. A longer gap between CAR-T therapy and transplant independently worsened survival, as did high-grade graft-versus-host disease, while low-grade disease appeared protective, consistent with a graft-versus-leukaemia benefit. Longer gaps and residual disease before transplant predicted severe graft-versus-host disease. The authors built a nomogram for that risk which discriminated well internally. They present the tool for early, individualised planning of the CAR-T to transplant sequence.
pmc-13482290:
Chan and co-authors examine suicidal thinking among women in Hong Kong battered women's shelters in 2026, asking which life circumstances mark the highest risk. They analyzed clinical records for 597 women who used three major shelters between 2020 and 2024, all fleeing intimate partner violence. Suicidal ideation means thinking about ending one's own life, and the team graded its frequency over the previous year for each woman.

Almost half the women, 48.1 percent, reported suicidal thoughts, and 21.3 percent fell into the high-risk group based on how often those thoughts came during the year. High risk clustered with the woman's own burdens, lower schooling, chronic illness, being divorced or separated, and diagnosed mental illness among the strongest links found. The partner's history mattered too, including his childhood abuse, jealousy, and depression, as did illness and gambling problems elsewhere in the family.
pmc-13482590:
Lee and colleagues map a sneaky anatomical variant in 2026, an accessory branch of the temple nerve whose missed presence can leave forehead anesthesia incomplete during procedures. They dissected 36 half-faces from 20 embalmed cadavers, hunting that branch and measuring where it surfaces relative to the marginal tubercle, a bony bump clinicians can feel. Ultrasound in 23 living volunteers added the tissue depths needle users need.

The extra branch turned up in 7 of 36 sides, 19.4 percent, surfacing within a few millimeters of that bump in every positive case found by the team. Measured from the eye's outer corner, the exit point sat 22.3 millimeters to the side and 5.8 millimeters above, with modest variation between specimens. Scanning put the target fascia layer 5.92 millimeters under the skin on average, and the authors offer the combined map for safer, more complete temple blocks.
pmc-13484490:
Su and colleagues optimized the underground layout of a Serbian copper-gold mine that extracts ore by block caving, where a rock mass is undercut so ore crumbles and flows down by gravity. The bottom structure, the network of tunnels where ore is collected, must stay stable under great depth and rock pressure. Their 2026 study combined simulations and structured experiments at the Cukaru Peki mine to compare layouts and spacings.

A branching herringbone layout won, overlapping collection zones well while letting electric loaders turn and work efficiently. The best vertical gap from the extraction level down to the undercut level came out at 20 meters in their coupled analyses. Drawpoint spacing was fixed by weighing ore recovery against tunnel stability. Rock around the tunnels responded in three stages as caving advanced in simulation. Su presents the chosen geometry as a balance of recovery, safety, and machine access.
pmc-13487190:
Yang and co-authors surveyed 387 respiratory nurses across 32 Chinese hospitals about inhaler therapy, the treatment backbone for chronic airway disease. Nurses teach patients inhaler technique, so gaps in nurses' own knowledge pass straight to patients. Their 2026 questionnaire of 61 items scored knowledge, attitude, and practice, and asked what training each nurse had actually received.

Only about half the nurses reached a good level of theoretical knowledge on the scoring used in this survey. Practice tracked attitudes much more strongly than it tracked knowledge, suggesting motivation moves bedside behavior more than facts alone. Hands-on workshops, specialist training, and teaching videos each linked to better knowledge or practice scores. Specialty experience mattered as well. Yang recommends practice-focused training formats over lectures to close the knowing-doing gap for inhaler education.
pmc-13487390:
Junjie Ma layers four data types to compare champion and poor egg layers across the gut-liver-fat axis in hens. Published in 2026, 180 Hy-Line Brown hens are production-tracked for six weeks, then ranked so the top fifteen and bottom fourteen at fifty weeks form contrast groups of nearly equal body weight. Gene activity, general and bile-acid chemistry, and gut microbes are profiled together.

Egg laying demands relentless yolk precursor production, which loads the liver heavily in every hen. High producers therefore differ from low producers in coordination across organs rather than in size. The integrated design catches changes that any single data layer would miss, from microbial shifts to bile acid routing. Findings feed breeding and feeding strategies for an industry where small per-hen gains multiply across billions of birds.
pmc-13488190:
Martin J. Batty and colleagues ask whether drugs can prevent chronic Chagas disease in a 2026 review. The parasite infection, spread by insects in the Americas, can damage the heart years after a silent start. Two old drugs kill the parasite early, yet their benefit once the disease turns chronic stays debated. The review weighs trials and cohort studies of treatment at different disease stages.

Treatment cleared the parasite from blood in many studies, while gains in heart outcomes were slower and less certain. Side effects often stopped courses early. Newer drug candidates aim for shorter, gentler treatment. The authors call for trials with heart outcomes, not blood tests alone, to settle who benefits from treatment.
pmc-13488290:
Shreyas Hulusemane Karunakara and colleagues study a silenced microRNA cluster in liver cancer in a 2026 laboratory and data analysis. The cluster, called C14MC, holds many tiny RNAs that normally restrain growth genes, and it was switched off in liver cancer cell lines and in a large public tumor cohort. Chemical marks called methylation, which attach to DNA and mute nearby genes, covered the cluster's start region in cancer cells.

Restoring two cluster members with synthetic copies shut down several cancer-driving genes and slowed cell movement and invasion in dish tests. Cluster levels and target gene patterns also tracked with patient survival in the cohort data. The authors propose the cluster and its targets for early detection, prognosis, and treatment design.
pmc-13488590:
Hailemichael Mulugeta and colleagues describe work injuries reaching emergency departments in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, in a 2026 prospective study at three public hospitals. Over five months, 868 injured workers aged eighteen to sixty took part through interviews and chart review, drawn from more than five thousand injury patients seen. Severity followed World Health Organization surveillance guidance, and statistical models hunted for factors tied to severe injury.

Work cases made up about eighteen percent of injury visits. Manufacturing and construction dominated, young men were the typical patients, and hands and arms were hurt most often, mainly by cuts from sharp objects. About one fifth of injuries counted as severe. Low education, fall mechanisms, and no fixed work area linked with severity in the reported models.
pmc-13490590:
Gulyás and team pooled outcome studies of blood markers in melanoma, the deadliest skin cancer, to judge which markers genuinely forecast death or spread. Clinics measure many candidates, but single studies disagree. Their 2026 meta-analysis followed registered protocol and reporting guidelines across three databases, combining hazard ratios, the standard measure of risk over time, for each marker on its own and in fuller models.

Five markers tied clearly to worse overall outcomes in the pooled single-variable checks reported. IL-6 carried the highest pooled hazard, at about three times the death risk for elevated levels in those checks. Lactate enzyme marker, tumor DNA in blood, and an inflammation ratio from blood counts predicted shorter progression-free time as well. The same core markers survived adjustment for other factors. Gulyás concludes a small panel, not the whole catalog, deserves routine forecast use.
pmc-13490890:
Halvaeezadeh and colleagues compared the enzyme arsenals of Aspergillus flavus fungi taken from human ear infections with species collected from the environment. Their 2026 study ran in Ahvaz, Iran. The fungus secretes enzymes that double as weapons for invading tissue, so clinical strains might be more armed. The team confirmed eighty-one isolates using a marker gene and measured their enzyme output on culture media.

Halvaeezadeh found every isolate producing phospholipase and urease, enzymes that attack cell membranes and handle nitrogen waste. Ear-infection isolates outgunned environmental ones on two fronts, producing esterase, a fat-splitting enzyme, in ninety percent of cases against about sixty percent. They produced hemolysin in nearly all cases against about seventy percent. The isolates showed catalase activity, which neutralizes the bursts immune cells use to kill fungi. The pattern supports the idea that enzyme output helps separate fungi from invasive ones.
pmc-13493990:
Jian, Wu, and Xiao improve a nature-inspired search method called the parrot optimisation algorithm, which imitates how green-cheeked conures flock, forage, and stay alert. Such methods hunt for the best solution to hard problems by trial and adjustment. The original parrot method, though, slows down and gets stuck on merely good answers in high-dimensional problems. Their 2026 upgrade, named STPO, borrows a danger-alert trick from a sparrow algorithm, adds experience sharing, and jitters the worst performers elsewhere.

On the standard CEC2017 and CEC2022 benchmark suites, STPO earned the best average rankings against twelve rival algorithms in most dimension settings. It sat near the top from ten dimensions up to one hundred. Statistical checks and component-removal experiments backed each added strategy's contribution. The team also ran five classic engineering design problems through the method successfully. They caution that no optimiser suits every problem shape.
pmc-13495090:
Mączka and colleagues presented a biographical-narrative toolkit for studying anxieties and coping strategies across countries, developed in research in Poland, Ukraine, and Hungary, in a 2026 methods article. Anxiety is hard to study because worries span health, family, and the environment and are entangled with language and local context. Their approach uses life-story interviews that place each anxiety within a person's life course.

Mączka situates environmental anxieties beside the other anxieties participants report. lets researchers see how climate or nature worries compete with everyday fears and reduces the bias of asking about one topic alone. The toolkit standardizes the hardest parts of qualitative work: building the codebook in stages, training coders uniformly, paired review of coding, and harmonizing codes across the three countries. The authors offer the framework as transferable to other topics needing context-sensitive, comparable qualitative evidence for policy and practice.
pmc-13499890:
Hussain Ahmad Bhatti reports in 2026 a case of severe muscle disease linked to rosuvastatin, a cholesterol-lowering statin drug, first recognised in an outpatient clinic. Statin muscle complaints range from mild aches to rare immune-driven muscle destruction. His patient was a 62-year-old woman who had taken the drug daily for about four months. She arrived with four weeks of worsening fatigue, widespread muscle pain, weakness near the trunk, and trouble walking.

Blood tests showed a muscle enzyme level many times above normal, raised inflammation markers, and liver enzyme changes, while kidney function held. The drug was stopped at once, she was sent urgently to emergency care, and family reports described a four-day hospital stay whose records the author could not obtain. Enzyme levels available through day 54 peaked higher before easing downward, and the case warns that liver enzyme rises here may signal muscle injury, not liver disease.
pmc-13500090:
Kei U Wong and Harsh Sule describe in 2026 a training innovation that folds brief child emergency drills into the daily morning case conference of an emergency medicine residency. Residents get limited exposure to high-risk child emergencies, and standard simulation is squeezed by space, scheduling, and cost. From September 2021 to May 2025 their four-year programme ran 27 paediatric simulation sessions inside weekly morning reports. Sessions used basic mannequins, a portable setup, and scripted or web-based cases with evolving data, followed by guided debriefing.

Post-session surveys drew replies from most participants, mainly residents alongside students, attending physicians, and other staff. Respondents generally agreed the sessions improved their knowledge, comfort, and teamwork for child emergencies in the reported survey. Because the format reuses existing conference time and cheap equipment, the authors present it as a route to repeated practice that scales and sidesteps the usual barriers to such training.
pmc-13500390:
Yoshimichi Goda and colleagues report in 2026 a brain form of feline infectious peritonitis, a fatal viral disease of young cats, that appeared on scans as a single tumour-like mass. Their patient was an 11-month-old neutered male mixed-breed cat brought in with worsening loss of coordination. MRI revealed a well-defined, egg-shaped solitary mass on the fourth ventricle's left side, a fluid cavity deep in the brainstem region.

Staining of the surgically removed tissue identified the viral disease, settling a diagnosis that is notoriously hard to prove before death. The authors state this is the first report of the central nervous system form presenting as a solitary fourth-ventricle mass on MRI. They urge clinicians to include this disease among the possibilities when a young cat shows such a lesion, since its usual scan patterns look quite different from a discrete mass.
pmc-13501690:
Yasaman Sadat Nabipour leads a five-author team with a 2026 study of green-made quantum dots against drug-resistant wound infections. Using extract from Quercus brantii acorns, the team synthesized silver, copper, and zinc oxide quantum dots by a hydrothermal route, then verified their quantum behaviour with light spectroscopy. The dots were tested against multidrug-resistant clinical isolates of four problem bacteria, including MRSA and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and for safety on human skin cells.

Silver dots, averaging 7.2 nanometres, performed best: they killed bacteria at concentrations from 4.5 to 18.1 micrograms per millilitre and blocked up to 85 percent of biofilm growth at half that dose. Radical-trapping tests supported oxidative stress as the killing route, and the effective doses spared human keratinocytes and fibroblasts. In infected mouse wounds, a silver-dot hydrogel closed 95.3 percent of the wound by day 14 and cut bacterial load by more than four orders of magnitude.
pmc-13503790:
Siva Shanmukha Anjaneya Babu Padavala leads a team testing two waste powders as partial cement swaps in concrete, in a 2026 study. Cement making drives a large share of world carbon output. Silica fume and Alccofine are fine powders that can fill some of that role while raising strength.

Trials first set silica fume at three swap levels, then varied Alccofine on top of the best one. A blend with set shares of both raised crush strength by about a third over plain concrete. Bend and split strength rose by about a sixth. Water uptake and salt passage both fell by more than two fifths. Smart models predicted crush strength well. A life-cycle check found the best blend cut warming impact by about a tenth.
pmc-13503890:
Zhigao Zhang leads a team charting plant growth change in China's Taihang Mountains from 2000 to 2024, in a 2026 study. The range shields the North China Plain and holds key ecosystems. Knowing what drives greening or loss guides land care in the region.

Satellite greenness data rose steadily over the period, with gains across most of the range. High values sat in the south, and low values in the northwest. A persistence test hints that much of the area may slip back toward decline. Splitting the drivers, the team credits human action for about 86 percent of the change, far above climate. Pines gained most under human care, while farm and mixed plots lost the most.
pmc-13503990:
Humaid Sadiq and four colleagues recount a case of a massive lung artery clot that struck without the usual warning signs, in a 2026 report. The patient, a woman in her early forties, came in with dizziness, racing heart feelings, and deep tiredness rather than chest pain or breathlessness.

Scans confirmed a huge clot blocking flow from the heart to the lungs. Her heart stopped, and clot-busting drugs given during resuscitation brought her back. The same drugs then caused severe belly bleeding that needed emergency surgery. More clots formed in an arm artery and in the lungs' blood circuit during her stay. That pattern raised suspicion of a clotting disorder. She recovered after 33 days and went home on blood thinners.
pmc-13504290:
Catley and colleagues produced the first direct images of two DNA molecules recognizing and pairing with each other in the presence of doubly charged metal ions. Their 2026 biophysics study combines high-resolution atomic force microscopy with atomistic computer simulations. How matching DNA sequences find each other underpins recombination and genome packing, yet the structural basis of the pairing has never been seen.

Catley found strongly paired DNA duplexes often settle into groove-to-groove alignment. In that arrangement the helical groove of one molecule faces the other's, held by ionic bridges in which the metal ions link the minor grooves of both partners. Sequence-specific contacts added further stability, and their strength and specificity varied with which ion was used. The authors argue this ion-mediated groove alignment supplies the molecular mechanism behind a long-standing helical alignment model of homology recognition, with implications for chromosome condensation and genome organization.
pmc-13506190:
Ramesh Nadarajah leads a wide international team behind FIND-AF 2.0, a machine-learning model that reads routine health records to flag people likely to develop atrial fibrillation within six months. The model uses only age, sex, and ten common conditions, so it can run inside ordinary record systems. Training and checks drew on millions of records from the United Kingdom, Japan, Israel, Canada, and China.

Prediction quality ranged from good to excellent across all five countries, beating two established risk scores. In a prospective test, 1,923 volunteers wore a handheld heart recorder four times daily for three weeks. New atrial fibrillation appeared in about five percent of the high-risk group but well under one percent of the low-risk group, and nearly all detected cases started blood-thinning treatment. Registry data showed untreated high-risk patients faced a notable stroke rate, strengthening the case for risk-guided screening.
pmc-13507090:
Rachel Lau and colleagues present, in 2026 work, cellGeometry, a very fast tool that estimates cell mixes in bulk gene samples from single-cell references. Bulk samples blend signals from many cells, and older unmixing tools struggle as reference atlases grow to millions of cells. Their method projects bulk signals onto cell group directions in gene space, with rules that bar negative shares.

In tests built from datasets with over three million cells, the tool proved more accurate than leading rivals and steadier under noise. It also flags odd genes that may reveal disease shifts or missing cell types. Checks on real blood and tissue samples gave more realistic mixes. Speed plus accuracy suits large clinical studies.
pmc-13508190:
Zebedee Kerry leads a twelve-author team asking people in Papua New Guinea how they view new tools against malaria-carrying mosquitoes, in 2026 work. Malaria has resurged in the country since 2015, partly as bed nets lose strength against insects. Extra tools under study include indoor spraying, devices that release repellent vapor, and draining or treating mosquito breeding sites. The team ran interviews and group talks in four coastal villages in Madang Province. Transcripts were coded for shared themes.

Villagers showed a strong grasp of malaria risk, seasons, and where mosquitoes breed. They mixed traditional steps with program tools already in use. Views on bringing back indoor spraying depended on past practice and local context, the team found. Health system readiness was also part of the picture. The study gives planners a ground-level read on what communities will accept before new tools roll out.
pmc-13508290:
Hafsa Kanwal and six co-authors run a trial testing whether pharmacist-led care improves outcomes for lung disease patients who also carry other illnesses, in 2026 work. The disease, COPD, blocks airflow and often travels with heart disease and diabetes. The trial placed 120 patients into three groups at random: standard care, pharmacist counselling, or full pharmaceutical care guided by treatment rules. Care ran for 24 weeks. Scores tracked symptoms, breathlessness, lung function, flare-ups, and quality of life.

The full pharmaceutical care group improved most. Symptom scores dropped far below the standard care group, and breathlessness eased more as well. Lung function declined least in that group over the study span. Flare-ups that did occur were shorter, and disease progression scores were lower. Quality of life rose more with pharmacist-led care. The authors argue pharmacists should sit inside the care team for such patients, not at its edge.
pmc-13509990:
Michele Gottardi and eleven co-authors review how the bone marrow setting shapes acute myeloid leukemia, in 2026 work. Leukemia stem cells live inside marrow niches that send survival signals, and the review argues the setting does more than host the disease. Rare cases of leukemia arising in donor cells after transplant, plus lab models where faulty niche cells trigger blood disease, suggest a damaged setting can help start the cancer in some cases.

In settled disease, niche signals keep leukemia cells lodged, quiet, and tolerant of chemotherapy, while leukemia cells reshape the marrow to suppress normal blood making. Resistance to a key modern drug combo is tied to these exchanges, through shifts in cell death controls and fuel use. Trials aiming to break niche protection show early activity in some groups, yet firm randomized proof remains scarce.
pmc-13510590:
Anastassiya Ganina and seven co-authors review stem cell therapy for recovery after stroke, with a focus on cells taken from the jelly of the umbilical cord, in 2026 work. Cells from bone marrow and fat are used more often, yet those sources carry a more mature state that limits growth and repair power. Cord jelly cells are younger, grow readily, and stir less immune trouble.

Many animal studies and early human trials support a repair potential for these cells after stroke. A newer line uses only what the cells release, in tiny packets and fluids, which may aid recovery at cell and molecule level with few side effects. The authors argue that cell-free products could serve as an add-on for chosen patients, especially after strokes from blocked vessels. Such care would join clot drugs, vessel procedures, therapy exercises, and digital tools over long recovery periods.
pmc-13510690:
Mariela Alpizar-Rojas and co-authors review in 2026 a decade of artificial intelligence in nuclear medicine, the field that images body function with radioactive tracers. Their critical overview covers clinical uses from 2015 to 2025, plus rules, ethics, and drug-related questions.

Searching five major databases and regulator websites, they found deep learning now rebuilds and cleans scans while preserving the numbers doctors rely on. Uses span cancer, brain, and heart care, along with paired diagnosis-and-therapy approaches. Yet most studies were small, single-center, and retrospective, with little outside validation and thin coverage of Latin America. The authors call for multicenter testing, open standards, and a clear seat for radiopharmacists in oversight.
pmc-13512090:
Molly J. Taylor, Tait D. Shanafelt, and Lisa G. Williams review burnout among biomedical scientists in academic medicine, a group the authors call overlooked beside frontline clinicians, in 2026 work. Research faculty and staff keep the discovery engine of health systems running, yet their exhaustion is rarely measured and still more rarely addressed. Reported burnout rates in this group rival those of physicians, with fewer support resources in reach.

Drivers include grant pressure, publication demands, and thin control over time, while the fallout reaches staffing, discovery pace, and the wider care system. The authors urge institutions to build collegial ties on purpose, guard teaching time, renew a sense of meaning in the work, and back autonomy for lab leaders. They also call for research and intervention effort to stop lagging so far behind the clinician side, starting by asking scientists themselves what would help.
pmc-13513490:
Muhammad Aljukhadar explores how sleep broke down under stress during COVID-19 lockdown in a mixed-methods study, in 2026 work. Open responses from 59 participants were mined for patterns in what changed and why. Three disturbance forms stood out: drifting to later sleep schedules, sleeping longer overall, and getting too little sleep.

Emotional arousal, mental overload, and shattered daily routines fed all three forms. Two kinds of bedtime thinking mattered most, one pressing and worried, the other comforting, and they pushed sleep in opposite directions. Sleep apps and guided meditation tools were widely available, yet most participants never took them up, citing doubt or plain inertia. The proposed model ties personal traits, pre-sleep habits, and stress response into one loop. The author urges public health programs to offer simple, trusted sleep help during large crises.
pmc-13517090:
Roberta Perego, Giada Giuliani, Eva Spada, and Daniela Proverbio count skin yeasts on healthy dogs in a 2026 survey. Malassezia yeasts live harmlessly on dog skin and in ear canals, but overgrowth triggers itchy skin and ear disease, and vets judge cases by yeast counts. What counts as normal is unsettled. The team swabbed multiple skin sites and ear canals of healthy Golden Retrievers and Bernese Mountain Dogs and tallied the yeasts under the microscope.

Golden Retrievers carried clearly more yeasts than Bernese at several sites. Counts in many plainly healthy dogs from both breeds topped the reference limits published earlier. Perego's team therefore warns that the usual cut-offs cannot be applied blindly: breed and body site shift what normal looks like. Their numbers give clinics a breed-aware yardstick for reading skin cytology, so healthy dogs are not misread as infected and medicated without cause.
pmc-13518090:
Yang and colleagues hunt for gene clues to a childhood kidney illness that answers well to steroids. In the illness, filters in the kidney leak protein into urine. Past gene hunts were small, so much of the inherited risk stayed hidden.

The team scanned genomes of children in China, then pooled data across world groups. Two new risk spots stood out near genes tied to immune system jobs. One spot links to a gene that, when more active in immune cells, raised risk. The other links to a gene where more activity cut risk. A combined gene score also tied to illness starting at a younger age.
pmc-13518790:
Sona Ayadi Hassan, Leila Rezaei Somee, Parinaz Ghadam, and Ahya Abdi Ali describe in 2026 a green way to make silver-copper nanozymes using extract from walnut green husks. These tiny particles act like enzymes. The husks are a plentiful farm by-product. Drug-resistant microbes, oxidative stress, and metal pollution all motivate the search for new materials.

Plant chemicals in the extract formed and coated spherical particles averaging about 17 nanometers across. Laboratory tests showed strong enzyme-like activity, killing of both major bacterial groups including resistant strains, action against Candida albicans fungus and mature biofilms, and free-radical scavenging. The paired metals outperformed single-metal versions, pointing toward medical and cleanup uses.
pmc-13520290:
Mine Esen Baris and three colleagues test in 2026 whether phenylephrine eye drops, the standard pupil dilator, quietly alter front-of-eye structures in healthy adults. Twenty volunteers received three doses of the 2.5 percent drop in the right eye, with the untreated left eye as control. Scleral thickness was imaged at three depths, and protein haze in the front chamber was measured by laser photometry 45 minutes later.

The white wall thickened significantly right at the scleral spur on both sides of the eye, while thinning occurred one millimeter behind the spur on the temple side. Chamber haze drifted upward without reaching significance. Baris and colleagues conclude the drops reshape the sclera locally yet leave inflammation essentially untouched.
pmc-13521290:
Poirier and Aparicio Chacón review the PHO1 protein family in this 2026 plant biology paper. PHO1 was first found in the plant Arabidopsis thaliana as an exporter that moves inorganic phosphate, a key nutrient, out of cells and into the root's water-carrying tissue. Related proteins appear across many living groups, in both plants and animals.

Recent cryo-electron microscopy images, which freeze proteins to reveal their shape, show these proteins act as channels with two gates controlled by inositol polyphosphate signals. The parts that bind phosphate and work the gates are nearly unchanged across species, suggesting an ancient shared job. The review also covers puzzles. The proteins sit mostly on inner cell compartments rather than the surface. The plant version also shapes responses to the stress hormone abscisic acid in seeds and leaf pores.
pmc-13521890:
Keshab Raj Paudel and colleagues link in 2026 national drug exam scores with school scores for 290 medical students. The classes graduated from 2019 to 2023. Schools want to know if in-house teaching tracks board-style skill in drug knowledge. Entry scores were part of the check.

School drug scores tracked national scores strongly. Entry test scores tracked at a mid level. Grade averages tracked weakly but still clearly. Joint models kept school scores and entry scores as predictors. The model explained just over half of score spread. Overlap checks showed no bad redundancy. In-house exams mirror national hopes fairly well, the team concludes.
pmc-13522490:
Lei Wang and colleagues introduce a new laboratory method for making circular RNA in a 2026 study. Circular RNA forms a closed loop, which makes it more stable than straight RNA and appealing for future medicines. Existing enzyme-based methods use each helper enzyme at most once and leave cleaning difficult, limiting scale and options.

The new design separates the ribozyme, a catalytic RNA, from the material it acts on, so one ribozyme can be reused many times. The system produced both plain and chemically modified circular RNA, and fixing the ribozyme in place reduced impurities and improved yield. The authors argue the approach could support wider variety and larger-scale production of circular RNA treatments.
pmc-13522590:
Peishen Li and co-authors show how to reshape a confined light wave into a flat-topped profile in a 2026 photonics study. Waves trapped in a finite space normally form uneven standing patterns with peaks and dips. The team used spatial phase engineering, which acts like an artificial gauge field, to tune the trapped modes in a photonic crystal slab.

Adjusting the accumulated phase drove a flow in the mode spectrum and morphed ordinary oscillating profiles continuously into a uniform, nonzero flat-top state. Measurements of near and far fields during single-mode lasing confirmed the transition. Such uniform states could benefit quantum emitters, optical antennas, and lasers, where even coverage matters more than peaked intensity.
pmc-13523490:
Helene Smith and colleagues present a 2026 qualitative study on contraception access for women in prison in New South Wales, Australia. Justice-involved women show high unmet need for contraception, shaped by violence, unstable housing, substance use, and poor mental health. Little Australian research had asked incarcerated women about their own experience of family planning services.

Seventeen women aged 19 to 45 from two correctional centers gave semi-structured interviews within a larger prisoner health study. Access problems stemmed less from mistrust of providers than from an unreliable system, with unanswered requests, long delays, and unsafe attempts to remove implants themselves. Time in custody also prompted reflection on readiness for motherhood. Limited method choices and side effects pushed some women toward sterilization, which some later regretted.
pmc-13524690:
Teresa K. Chen leads a large team in a 2026 prospective cohort study mapping metabolomic signs of inflammation in chronic kidney disease. Inflammation predicts kidney decline, cardiovascular events, and death, and the chemical environment of the blood may reveal why. The team linked hundreds of small molecules to a panel of inflammatory proteins.

The main cohort held 491 people from a kidney disease study in African American adults, with replication in two further cohorts. Among 718 metabolites tested, hundreds of cross-sectional links survived correction, mostly positive for two tumor necrosis factor receptors and mostly negative for uromodulin and epidermal growth factor. Distinct pathways appeared for distinct proteins, and 45 links predicted two-year change in inflammatory markers. Replication was strong for the receptor proteins and poor for one interleukin.
pmc-13525890:
Kassandra M. Jade leads a large team in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on how life-context factors shape sinonasal outcome scores in chronic rhinosinusitis, a long-lasting sinus inflammation. Social conditions, demographics, and health behaviors were suspected influences, yet their effects on the standard 22-item symptom score were unclear.

Searches of four databases through December 2024 produced sixty-one eligible studies from over three thousand records. Women scored worse at baseline but improved similarly after surgery. Younger patients often started worse, and race and ethnicity data were limited with no clear differences. Medicaid and privately insured patients started worse than Medicare patients, while smokers scored worse than nonsmokers. Education, income, and environmental effects were inconsistent. Standardized collection of context data is urged.
pmc-13526690:
Huidong Guo and Xiao-Jun Huang review, in a 2026 paper, bone marrow transplantation as an immune reset rather than simple cell replacement. Transplantation has long been framed as a cure for blood cancers through swapping a diseased blood-forming system for a healthy donor one. The authors argue the process runs deeper, collapsing and rebuilding immunity itself.

After transplant, immunity does not return to its former state. Instead it settles at a new equilibrium shaped by conditioning injury, donor-recipient immune interactions, regrowth of supporting stroma, and ongoing treatments. The review gathers evidence on how tolerance is reinstalled and stability maintained under those forces. By treating transplantation as a human model of immune reprogramming, the authors extract principles that may guide therapies for autoimmunity, immune aging, and other immune diseases.
pmc-13526790:
Yahan Qin and colleagues identify, in a 2026 study, an enzyme called PARP10 as a driver of lung cancer spread to bone, a complication marked by resistance and severe illness. Sequencing of bone metastases across cancers found PARP10 consistently raised, and high levels in primary tumors tracked with poor survival. The team probed how it works.

Removing PARP10 damaged tumor DNA, raised oxidative stress, and switched on a second enzyme, BCAT2, under control of the MYC regulator, boosting breakdown of branched-chain amino acids. That shift fed tumor energy production yet starved the bone environment of those amino acids, suppressing the bone-eating cells that metastasis needs. A PARP10-blocking drug shrank bone metastatic burden in mice without visible toxicity, attacking tumor cells and their niche together.
pmc-13526890:
Saranya Matta and Sambhudutta Nanda present a 2026 antenna design for sub-6 GHz wireless services, combining a slotted bowtie radiator with dual polarization in a compact form. Access points and small cells need antennas with strong isolation between channels, clean radiation patterns, and good forward gain. Bowtie shapes are simple to build and suit polarization diversity.

The design arranges slot-cut bowtie elements at right angles on a common circuit board material, fed in a balanced configuration, then adds a metal reflector plate set behind them to sharpen performance. Measured operation centers near 2.52 and 4.42 gigahertz with usable bandwidths around 220 and 420 megahertz. Isolation stayed above thirty decibels, cross-polarization stayed low, and the reflector lifted gain from about two to over seven decibels on average.
pmc-13527990:
Lin Liu and eight colleagues describe a 2026 biodegradable implant for internal radiation therapy. The device is a calcium-based reservoir labeled with radioactive iodine-131. It is built to break down inside tumors rather than stay in the body forever. Once there, it slowly releases hydrogen peroxide, oxygen, and calcium ions. Those releases stay minimal in normal tissue because breakdown speeds up in acid conditions.

The oxygen eases tumor hypoxia, a state that helps cancers resist treatment. Extra peroxide and oxygen boost radiation damage. Calcium overload disrupts cell power plants and triggers a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis. Oxygen also lowers PD-L1, a shield tumors use against immune attack. In the team's models the implant cleared both treated and distant tumors. The authors pitch it as internal radiotherapy and immune therapy in one.
pmc-13528090:
Yuhan Zhang, Jianquan Cheng, and Lian Duan review how health appears in city master plans across China in a 2026 study. The team read the Territorial Spatial Planning 2035 schemes of thirty-six major cities. A framework built from global writing and policy sorted the health content. Word networks and gap measures compared the cities.

All thirty-six plans mention healthy city goals. Eight themes appear, led by green open space and disaster readiness. Sports facilities, pollution control, and medical services follow. Equity gets the least attention in most plans. Higher-rank cities wrote broader and richer health sections. Lower-tier cities often stayed thin and generic. The authors place China at a middle stage of health planning. They recommend stronger laws, open plan texts, and tailored support for smaller cities.
pmc-13529890:
Pecoraro and colleagues reviewed in 2026 treatments aimed at a protein called DLL3 in advanced prostate cancer. Some prostate cancers stop responding to hormone-blocking therapy and take on nerve-like features, a state called neuroendocrine prostate cancer. These cancers grow fast, spread widely, and respond poorly to standard chemotherapy. DLL3 sits on the surface of such tumour cells but is rare in healthy adult tissue, making it a target.

DLL3 was found in about three in four resistant neuroendocrine tumours but only about one in eight ordinary resistant tumours. Early trials suggest benefit mainly in tumours that carry DLL3, echoing success in a similar lung cancer. The authors stress that picking patients by DLL3 testing will decide whether these drugs help. They urge prostate-specific trial designs as the field moves forward.
pmc-13530590:
Tokish, Iturregui, and Lai present in 2026, as conference poster 245, animal experiments on improving rotator cuff repair with bioengineered patches and biologic materials. The repairs were tested biomechanically, genetically, and under the microscope at eight weeks after surgery.

Four augmentations were compared against traditional repair, alongside sham controls in the rat model used for this work. They were an electrospun synthetic patch mimicking the tendon-to-bone junction, a sheet of amnion membrane from the placenta, and a combination of the two. Breaking strength ran higher on average in every patch group than in traditional repair, and the yield loads showed the same ordering. The combination patch's tissue maturity score matched traditional repair. However, the electrospun products provoked an exaggerated immune reaction with giant cells and fibrotic growth, a warning the authors say warrants further investigation before clinical enthusiasm.
pmc-13531590:
Helen Leach and co-authors warn in a 2026 essay that general practice reforms in Britain must be tested against rural reality. Current policy prizes same-day appointments and digital access. Rural patients, older and spread over wide areas, face distance, thin staffing, and transport limits that city-focused plans overlook.

Access in the countryside also means continuity with a clinician who knows local life, a bond tied to better outcomes and fewer hospital stays. Speed-first reforms risk trading that relationship away. The authors propose routine rural-proofing, a systematic check of every policy for geographic fairness before rollout.
pmc-13531790:
Seok Joo Chae and colleagues build in 2026 a screening model that flags South Korean firefighters at risk of post-traumatic stress. Stigma keeps reported rates low in this workforce, so indirect signals matter. Records covered 52,428 firefighters, of whom 2,305 had probable disorder on a standard checklist.

Seven features carried the model: poor concentration, appetite change, guilt feelings, sleep trouble, work pressure, poor adaptability, and doubts about seeking help for others. The gradient-boosting model classified risk with strong accuracy, and a fresh year of data confirmed the performance. A short flagged list could steer early support toward hidden cases.
pmc-13534690:
Nureeda Che-alee, Ninadia Jitprasitporn, and Lakkhana Kanhayuwa Wingfield study in 2026 pigments from a fungus living inside healthy plant leaves for textile dyeing. Natural dyes face low yields and seasonal limits, while synthetic dyes raise health and pollution concerns. The strain made a vivid red pigment in liquid culture.

Chemical analysis named oosporein as the main pigment compound. The colour held up well under heat and light, shifted with acidity, and showed low harm to human skin cells in tests. Cotton took the dye strongly with alum, and the pigment blocked one common skin bacterium.
pmc-13536690:
