Johan Diaz and colleagues present a 2026 case report of synovial sarcoma, a rare and aggressive soft tissue cancer that can grow slowly and look harmless at first. The patient was a 43-year-old man with leg pain and chest pain who had a large, tender calf mass. Earlier visits had treated the mass as benign. New scans and lung biopsies changed that view and pointed to cancer that had already spread.

Imaging showed a large lobulated mass inside the calf muscle with calcium deposits, plus many lung nodules suggesting spread. Lung tissue showed markers consistent with the monophasic form of the disease, though a confirmatory gene test was not obtained. Combination chemotherapy was planned, yet the patient declined further care and died about six months later from lung complications. The authors urge prompt workup of slow-growing soft tissue lumps.
pmc-13538490:
Ayush Mahanta and colleagues propose a quantum-inspired hybrid optimizer for clustering and routing in wireless sensor networks in a 2026 study. Battery limits dominate sensor network life, while separate handling of grouping and routing wastes energy. The framework fuses swarm search with genetic search and scores options on leftover energy, crowding, distance, and stability. Simulations ran one thousand rounds on hundred-node layouts against five rival protocols.

The hybrid outlasted every rival, with first-node-death gains ranging widely over classic protocols and a clear edge over the strongest hybrid rival. Total energy use fell, high-delivery operation lengthened, and delays dropped, with tight repeatability across thirty runs. The authors present the method as ready support for industrial sensing, environment watching, and smart city systems.
pmc-13538690:
Rukiye Sumeyye Bakici and colleagues compare outer ear shape among young adults from ten countries in a 2026 morphology study. Photographs of 1,351 ears from 676 student volunteers aged 16 to 30 years at a Turkish university were scored for shape, folds, lobes, and small landmarks. Participants hailed from countries across Africa, the Middle East, and Central Asia.

Overall ear shape differed sharply by country, with round forms leading in one nation, triangular in two others, and oval in three more. Helix form also varied significantly across groups. The authors present the dataset as a standardized reference for forensic identification, anthropology, and ear reconstruction planning, noting ears vary by population much like other facial traits.
pmc-13542090:
Zhen Wen and colleagues propose a tuning method in a 2026 study. The setting is electric vehicle energy systems. Each system pairs a battery with a supercapacitor. The supercapacitor handles power bursts. That spares the battery and slows its ageing. The gain hinges on how control settings split the work.

Their method is called Decision-Flux Optimization. It searches settings by simulation. It accepts only changes that keep every trace inside safe limits. The limits cover charge, voltage, and power. On a standard driving cycle, battery stress came out lowest. Eight rival strategies scored worse. Modelling projected about 3,720 cycles before the battery faded to eighty percent.
pmc-13542590:
Ilaria Mancini and colleagues published a 2026 genetic study of early-onset coronary artery disease in Iranians, a population largely missing from research dominated by European and East Asian samples. The case-control study enrolled 697 patients whose artery disease was confirmed by angiography at young ages, alongside 911 matched controls. Twenty-four gene variants were tested: twelve already linked to coronary disease elsewhere, and twelve candidates from genes governing blood clotting.

Only some known variants replicated in this population, and several effects appeared only within particular ethnic groups, underlining how ancestry shapes genetic risk. A six-variant risk score separated people clearly, with each extra risk allele raising odds by about a fifth. Genetic burden also multiplied the danger from metabolic conditions far beyond simple addition. The authors argue that risk tools built on other populations cannot simply be imported into Iranian care.
pmc-13543390:
In 2026, Yang Liu and colleagues published a study of a new Trichoderma asperellum strain, called M2. It fights root rot in Angelica sinensis, a medicinal plant grown mainly in China's Gansu province. Root rot is a destructive soil disease cutting yield and quality. The fungus was tested against the Fusarium pathogen in dishes and on seedlings, and its broth was checked for destroying neosolaniol, a toxin the pathogen leaves behind.

Under the microscope, M2 hyphae wrapped around and parasitised the pathogen, whose threads collapsed and shrivelled. Applied before the pathogen, it blocked growth by up to about fifty-eight percent. Treated seedlings grew taller and heavier, with root length up about sixty-seven percent, and their defence enzymes rose sharply. The broth degraded about eighty-seven percent of the toxin in eleven days. One microbe thus offers disease control, growth promotion, and toxin cleanup together.
pmc-13543590:
Vivian Salama and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review of artificial intelligence for predicting and imaging heart damage caused by radiotherapy. Radiation to the chest can injure the heart years later, and AI promises earlier warnings. Searching four databases to October 2025, the reviewers included sixty-five human studies and graded prediction work and imaging work with separate quality frameworks, pooling performance figures where that was defensible.

Thirty-one studies built risk predictors and thirty-four worked on cardiac imaging; deep learning dominated both. Predictive models reached a median accuracy measure of 0.82, and imaging models traced large heart structures well, though coronary arteries stayed hard to segment. The weaknesses were glaring: only a tenth of prediction studies checked calibration, a fifth validated externally, and most studies in both camps carried high risk of bias. Promise is real, the authors conclude, but clinical readiness is not.
pmc-13543890:
Xiang Zhang and colleagues published a 2026 study of how a gut bacterium, Bacteroides acidifaciens, protects the liver from immune-driven injury by reshaping bile acids. Mice were fed the bacterium and then challenged with concanavalin A, a standard trigger of liver hepatitis. Bile acid profiles in the liver shifted, and one acid, glycocholic acid, was pursued through cell experiments using receptor blockers and gene deletion to find its route of action.

The bacterium raised hepatic glycocholic acid, which lowered the death receptor CD95 on liver cells at both the gene and surface-protein levels. Blocking or deleting its receptor, TGR5, abolished that protection, and a transcription factor called FOSL1 carried the signal onward. Mice given the acid in drinking water for thirty-five days resisted the hepatitis with less cell death. A gut microbe's bile-acid messenger, the authors show, can disarm a liver death pathway.
pmc-13544190:
Paolo Reho and seven colleagues published this 2026 study searching for early-pregnancy epigenetic marks linked to small for gestational age births among Black women in the United States. About a tenth of American infants are born small for their stage, with doubled risk in babies of Black mothers, and the biology behind the gap is poorly understood. Using the nuMoM2b cohort from eight centres, the team scanned DNA methylation, chemical tags on DNA, in blood taken at 6 to 13 weeks of pregnancy.

The analysis covered 931 non-Hispanic Black women, 133 who delivered small babies and 798 whose babies were grown. Fourteen methylation sites differed, mapping to genes involved in placental development, blood vessel remodelling and fetal growth control. Enrichment analysis highlighted pathways for embryonic and placental function. The authors propose that methylation patterns in early pregnancy could become a biomarker for SGA risk, and a window into how the disparity arises.
pmc-13544790:
Alaa Eid Alfarhan and colleagues published a 2026 case report of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, a throat cancer behind the nose, already spread to bone in an eight-year-old girl. The disease is exceptionally rare under age ten, and metastatic presentation rarer still. She arrived after eight months of a growing neck mass with fever, weight loss, night sweats, bone pain, and exhaustion. The mass measured ten by eight centimetres, with enlarged nodes on both sides of the neck.

Scans showed the primary tumour with extensive nodal disease and bone metastases confirmed on bone scan, and biopsy proved non-keratinising nasopharyngeal carcinoma. She received three cycles of cisplatin and fluorouracil, then chemotherapy delivered alongside radiotherapy, and the combined approach brought the disease under control despite its advanced stage. A persistent neck lump with systemic symptoms in a child, the authors stress, should trigger consideration of this cancer.
pmc-13546590:
Jiyang Li and colleagues used a national cancer registry in 2026 to study mucinous adenocarcinoma of the colon and rectum. They asked whether this mucus-producing subtype carries a worse outlook than the conventional form after curative surgery. Their cohort held 69,335 patients with stage I to III disease treated between 2010 and 2022. At first glance the mucinous group survived less well, yet the detailed breakdown changed the picture.

The disadvantage held only in stage III disease, and only among patients who received chemotherapy, suggesting these tumors benefit less from standard drug treatment. Stage I and II patients showed no independent difference. In rectal cancer at stage III, patients given chemotherapy both before and after surgery lost the disadvantage entirely, which points to treatment planning rather than biology alone.
pmc-13547190:
Hang Ruan and co-authors reviewed in 2026 the double-edged role of GRP78, a helper protein that manages stressed cells, in viral pneumonia caused by influenza, RSV, and coronaviruses. Where the protein sits in the cell changes what it does. On the cell surface it helps viruses attach and enter, while inside the cell's protein factory it supports viral copying and can worsen lung inflammation.

The same protein also protects lung tissue by limiting cell death and calming overload in that factory. Drug strategies under study include small molecules that block it, larger biological drugs, indirect regulators, and natural products. The authors map these approaches and their early evidence, aiming to guide precise treatments that blunt the viral help without losing the protection.
pmc-13547290:
Sivasundaram Karnan and a large team screened 1,374 compounds in 2026 looking for something that slows cancers driven by mutant KRAS, a growth switch long considered hard to drug. The standout was nintedanib, a drug known for blocking vessel growth receptors. It killed KRAS-mutant cells more selectively than its peers and shrank such tumors in mice.

Inside the cells, the drug quieted the VEGFR2 receptor and the growth signals running beneath it. Removing that receptor exposed a chain in which KRAS activity itself depends partly on the receptor's signals, and mutant KRAS in turn raises receptor levels, forming a self-feeding loop. Pancreatic tumor samples showed the receptor abundant in most cases. The authors propose it as a fresh target for these cancers.
pmc-13548490:
Yufeng Luo and a large team built in 2026 living tumor clusters grown from oral cancer patients' own tissue. The aim is to test drugs on a faithful copy of each person's cancer before choosing treatment. The clusters keep the tumor's immune surroundings, appearance, and genetics, and need only about ten milligrams of tissue. Success in growing them topped ninety-seven percent across 165 attempts.

In 42 patients with advanced oral cancer, cluster drug testing for a three-drug chemotherapy combination matched the patients' actual outcomes about ninety percent of the time. The platform also screened more than a hundred compounds within two weeks, and gene analysis flagged one protein, MMP13, as strongly tied to resistance. The authors present the system as precision medicine infrastructure for oral cancer.
pmc-13548590:
Xingcheng Zhou and colleagues package bee venom peptide into metal-linked nanoparticles to fight crop disease, in a 2026 study on rice bacterial blight. The peptide melittin kills bacteria and breaks their protective biofilms, yet it degrades quickly outdoors and harms other cells. Adding a histidine tag let the peptide self-assemble around zinc ions into uniform particles the team calls NanoMel.

The packaged peptide killed two rice blight bacteria at lower doses than the free peptide and destroyed most of a mature biofilm within a day at moderate strength. Sprayed on rice plants, it cured and protected against blight better than a commercial copper bactericide. Tests in zebrafish showed the packaging softened melittin's inherent toxicity. The authors offer the approach as a general recipe for turning fragile antimicrobial peptides into practical, gentler farm sprays.
pmc-13550490:
Changzhi Yu and colleagues reconstruct moving images from a trickle of photons by teaching a network to borrow information across time, in a 2026 imaging paper. At a few photons per pixel, ordinary reconstructions lose contrast, detail, and steadiness. Their PhotonST-Net architecture watches frame-to-frame differences to enforce temporal coherence while restoring fine structure, and it carries a module that can separate two overlapping moving targets even through scattering.

Working at sampling ratios as low as one in five hundred twelve, the system produced square movies of two hundred fifty-six pixels. They ran at two hundred frames per second with under two photons per pixel. Quality scores beat conventional compressive imaging by a wide margin and a standard U-Net clearly under photon starvation. The authors target remote sensing, fleeting event capture, and traffic monitoring.
pmc-13551690:
Wen Yang, with eight colleagues, published a 2026 brain scan study of men who had quit methamphetamine. Thinking problems often persist after use stops. The team scanned 25 men in abstinence and 29 healthy men at rest. All took a standard test of thinking. Four methods probed local activity, links from the hippocampus, and large brain networks.

The patient group showed lower activity in some frontal and visual areas. Links from the right hippocampus ran stronger than normal. Networks for rest, hearing, and movement also behaved oddly. The hippocampus pattern tied to thinking scores in the reported links. The team says using several scan measures at once gives a fuller picture of change in abstinence.
pmc-13551790:
In 2026, Mauro Martínez-Moré and eight colleagues looked at how soybeans that fix their own nitrogen handle drought differently from fertilizer-fed plants. Soybean roots host bacteria that supply nitrogen, and water shortage limits yield worldwide. The team compared both the full message pool and the actively translated messages in roots of nodulated and nitrogen-fed plants under water restriction.

Nitrogen-fixing plants under drought showed more complex changes at both levels, including transcription factors not previously tied to this response in such plants. Network analysis grouped genes into modules, with one enriched for protein-building and energy genes. Control of translation for those genes emerged as a central response, and the authors name candidate genes, including uncharacterized hubs, for breeding drought-tolerant soybean.
pmc-13553590:
Zhang and colleagues publish a cleaned-up record of how the built environment changed across the Global South. Their 2026 dataset covers 130 low- and middle-income countries from 2016 to 2023 at roughly hundred-metre grid resolution. It derives from Google's temporal building data, which suffer year-to-year flicker from uneven satellite imagery, and provides three measures per cell and year: building count, surface area, and volume.

To fix the flicker, the team built a deterministic smoother that borrows the logic of Kalman updating without being a formal filter. Years that jump implausibly from a cell's own trajectory get downweighted against a spatially smoothed baseline. Validation showed the harmonisation cut implausible oscillations and zigzag swings while keeping high rank correlation with the raw layers, preserving the broad geography. City examples show the method bridging years with missing observations.
pmc-13554090:
Si Wu leads a fourteen-author team linking the spleen to brain swelling after stroke in a 2026 study. Records from seventy-six patients with a blocked large brain vessel showed that spleen shrinkage after stroke marked a strong risk for worse brain swelling. Falling counts of immune cells in blood partly explained that link. The team then tested stem cells from deer antlers in rats with a blocked brain vessel.

Rats given antler cells moved better and showed less swelling and smaller dead brain areas than rats given standard marrow stem cells. Removing the spleen erased much of that gain. Treated spleens kept their weight and cell balance, and fewer immune cells marched into the brain. A signal guiding that march was turned down, pointing to a fresh drug target.
pmc-13554890:
Sapna Kumari leads a ten-author team unravelling clotting chaos after heart bypass surgery in a sixty-eight-year-old man in a 2026 case report. After surgery his arteries kept clotting while his platelet count plunged, a pattern suggesting a reaction to the blood thinner heparin. One lab test supported that diagnosis, while a functional test stayed negative during strong antiplatelet treatment. Doctors judged the reaction probable despite the split results.

Genetic testing then revealed a mutation behind essential thrombocythemia, a marrow disorder that overproduces platelets and favours clots. His long record of high platelets and past clots fitted that hidden diagnosis. The authors warn that both conditions together raise clotting risk sharply, and that functional tests can mislead under strong antiplatelet drugs.
pmc-13556090:
Yasuhiro Onishi and twelve colleagues evaluated in 2026 a hands-on kidney biopsy workshop for medical students at Okayama University. Kidney biopsy is essential for diagnosing kidney disease, but it is invasive, so practising on simulators protects patients while skills form. Most earlier studies involved trainee doctors rather than students. The workshop joined a short lecture, peer practice with ultrasound, and guided work on a biopsy simulator during the nephrology clerkship.

One hundred thirteen fifth-year students took part, and almost none had even watched a real biopsy beforehand. Afterwards, students said they understood the procedure far better: the share of the procedure they felt able to perform jumped from near zero to about seventy percent at the median. Satisfaction ran high, and motivation to learn rose. The authors support bringing simulation into undergraduate teaching for invasive skills.
pmc-13558990:
Mariana Loezar-Hernández and four colleagues set out a 2026 protocol for a systematic review of how informal caregivers experience programs meant to ease their load. The caregivers in view are unpaid family members, friends, or neighbors looking after dependent people aged 60 and over. Earlier work judged support programs mostly by numbers, so the voices of caregivers themselves remain largely unsynthesised.

The planned search covers five databases plus grey literature, taking in English and Spanish publications from 2014 onward. Eligible work must report qualitative findings from caregivers who received an intervention aimed at burden or well-being. Two reviewers will extract data on their own, and the team will build themes following the method of Thomas and Harden. Study quality will be checked with the CASP checklist, and confidence in each finding rated through GRADE-CERQual.
pmc-13560290:
Jie Zou and colleagues examine a simple insulin sensitivity estimator against future cardiovascular disease in people with early-stage cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome. Their 2026 prospective study uses 391,793 UK Biobank participants at stages zero through three, followed for a median of 7.6 years. The index needs only HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, and body mass index, skipping any insulin measurement.

About seventeen percent of participants developed cardiovascular disease during follow-up. The relationship bent into an L shape: risk fell steeply as the index rose to a turning point near 5.81 in the spline analysis, then leveled. The highest third of the index carried thirty-one percent lower cardiovascular risk than the lowest third, and nearly half the coronary risk in the reported hazard ratios. Benefits looked stronger in participants under forty-five. The authors propose the cheap index for early risk stratification in this syndrome.
pmc-13563790:
Hailong Dou and five colleagues chart the microsatellite landscape, the short repeating stutters scattered through DNA, across the genomes of thirteen cat species. These repeats steer gene activity and chromosome behaviour, and their patterns can expose how relatives diverged. Working from genome assemblies, the 2026 team counted every repeat class, mapped where each kind settles, and compared the Felidae family member by member. Abundance fell as repeat length grew, and single-letter repeats outnumbered all others, in a ranking that ran from one-letter units down to six.

Repeats crowded the stretches between genes most densely. Inside coding regions, three-letter and six-letter repeats ruled, a bias that keeps reading frames intact. Genes carrying such repeats worked mainly in transcription and translation, the cell's protein-making core. The authors offer the atlas as a foundation for building genetic markers for breeding and conservation work across the cat family.
pmc-13563890:
Carmen D'Amore and ten colleagues chart seven years of drug-resistant bacteria in an Italian children's hospital, where the youngest patients face the resistance risk. Their 2026 study pulled blood and spinal-fluid cultures from inpatients and the emergency department between 2017 and 2023. Attention centred on the ESKAPE pathogen group plus E. coli. Resistance was tracked per organism, and models linked resistant infections to year, ward, and patient traits.

Of 51,886 cultures, 1,528 grew an organism and 211 of those, 13.8 percent, were resistant to many drugs. Carbapenem-proof Pseudomonas topped the table at 52.8 percent, with MRSA next at 36.7 percent. Two trends improved: MRSA fell from 43.5 to 25.7 percent across the period, and resistant Pseudomonas dropped steeply, especially in 2020 and 2021. Klebsiella and vancomycin-resistant enterococci held steady. Newborn and intensive care wards carried MRSA risk, while cancer wards tripled the odds of VRE. Maps like this, the authors argue, are what empirical prescribing should follow.
pmc-13569090:
Sayra M. Cristancho argues, in a 2026 commentary on medical training, that uneven supervision of doctors in postgraduate programs should be read as evidence about work systems rather than as failure by individual supervisors. Feedback, observation, and trust decisions appear in every setting, yet the learning they produce varies widely.

Continuity, workload, team structure, and local culture decide how those practices combine, and the resulting patterns cap what supervision can achieve. Seen that way, familiar complaints about supervision become clues about the system itself. Educators are urged to redesign conditions, not only to retrain supervisors, when learning falls short across a program.
pmc-13570590:
Hongping Liu leads a 2026 chemistry study on pyrene, a flat carbon molecule that glows. The study asks how the position of an added group changes reactivity and light output. Groups can sit at a node, where electron density vanishes, or at an anti-node, where it peaks. Coupling reactions and detailed light measurements compared the two placements directly.

Coupling at the node gave lower yields, matching the weaker electron presence there. Node-substituted versions kept their orbital symmetry and formed twisted charge-transfer states that switched on room-temperature phosphorescence, a long-lived glow. Anti-node versions broke symmetry and fluoresced faster. The rules give chemists a design handle for glowing materials used in displays and sensors.
pmc-13572390:
Juraj Litavský, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 field study of road edges as homes for ground-living invertebrates. The site was the Nitra-Selenec expressway junction in Slovakia. Roads split up wild land, yet their edges can shelter beetles and harvestmen if managed well. The team asked which care style helps most.

Pitfall traps at ten sites over two years caught 1,416 ground beetles from 50 species and 1,409 harvestmen from six species. Sites were left alone, seeded with a shop-bought grass mix, or mulched only. The seeded sites held poorer mixes of species. Thick herb cover and rich shrub layers drew more kinds, and distance from the road shaped where species sat. Harvestmen fell over time. The authors urge less seeding with shop mixes and more light-touch care.
pmc-13573490:
Mahdi Mollazadeh and Sara Ramezanpour present a 2026 pooled review of mild brain stimulation and the minds of athletes. The method, tDCS, runs a weak current through scalp pads and can nudge brain activity up or down. Coaches and researchers alike wonder whether it sharpens focus and cuts mental fatigue in sport.

Four databases were searched to February 2026, and 14 studies with 376 athletes made the cut. Pooled results showed clear gains in attention and in wider thinking skills. Mental fatigue fell, and reaction times sped up as well. Effect sizes sat in the large range for each outcome. The authors cast the method as a promising aid for the mental side of sport. They also note the field is young, with varied setups across studies.
pmc-13574890:
F Feliziani and six co-authors model why soft rock cliffs on the coast slowly fall back, using the tuff cliffs of Ventotene Island in Italy for their 2026 study. Their computer framework joins fluid flow modelling with a method that tracks how rock breaks apart. They tested gravity, sea erosion, wave hits, heat, and slow loss of rock strength.

Gravity or base erosion alone failed to produce realistic failures in the runs. Collapse patterns emerged only when erosion at the base was paired with strength loss moving inward over time. Waves and heat mostly caused small, elastic responses, though waves did concentrate movement in cracked zones. The authors frame the tool as a way to study how forces combine, not as a direct forecast of collapse.
pmc-13576790:
Ivan Pradilla leads a 2026 case series of three meningiomas, tumours of the membranes around the brain and spine, carrying faults in the BAP1 gene. This subgroup behaves aggressively in ways the standard grade may miss. The series covers both faults arising in the tumour and one inherited through a family.

The first patient, a 44-year-old woman, had a tumour fault that cut the protein short; her grade 1 spinal disease kept returning and needed repeated surgery, radiation, and drug therapy. The second, a 22-year-old man with an inherited fault, had a grade 3 tumour yet stayed free of progression 24 months after surgery and radiation. The third man, with a low-share missense fault and grade 2 disease, did well after full removal alone. The authors argue fault type and share should guide risk calls.
pmc-13578690:
Wei Wei and colleagues model a keyhole spine operation in healthy and weakened bone, in a 2026 computer study. The surgery opens a small window on one side of the spine to free nerves on both sides, easing leg pain while sparing tissue. Their virtual spine covered two lower back bones, and the weakened version mimicked bone softened by age related loss, without claiming to copy the full disease.

After the virtual cut, joint motion rose only modestly under bends and twists in both models. Stress on the disc rose somewhat, more in healthy bone by share. Stress on the bone end plates climbed most in the weak model, a hint of fracture risk the authors flag for real world checks. Motion stayed well within safe bounds in both.
pmc-13579990:
Patrick Weldon and colleagues chart who survives thyroid cancer at an urban safety net hospital, in a 2026 study. Registry records covered 336 patients diagnosed from 2000 to 2023, most of them women and most under fifty five. The well differentiated form of this cancer usually carries a good outlook, which makes survival gaps stand out.

Five year survival ran worse for patients over fifty five, for White patients, and for those on Medicaid. Death risk also ran higher for men. The White patient result cuts against national patterns, a surprise the authors flag plainly. Coverage type split the group into rough thirds across Medicaid, private, and public plans. The team calls for a closer look at what drives the local gap, so fixes can target the right group.
pmc-13582790:
Bin Ke and colleagues present a 2026 study of a long RNA strand called LINC00323 in non-small cell lung cancer, the most common form of lung cancer. The strand is found at high levels in tumors, and patients with more of it tend to do worse. The group asked how it helps tumors grow and form new blood vessels, a process tumors need to feed themselves.

Tests on tumor tissue and on lung cancer cells showed that raising LINC00323 sped up cell growth and vessel growth, while lowering it slowed both. The strand works by holding on to a protein named CDC5L and keeping it stable, which switches on two growth pathways. Tiny parcels sent out by cancer cells also carried the strand to vessel-lining cells.
pmc-13584290:
Minxuan Hu and colleagues uncover a self-feeding loop that fuels asthma in this 2026 study. Asthma involves long-term airway inflammation, and the cells lining the airways help drive it. The team focused on lactylation, a chemical mark placed on histone proteins when cells burn sugar quickly and release lactate, a waste product of that burning.

Samples from patients and cell studies showed both sugar burning and the mark, called H3K18la, running high in asthma airways. The mark sat on the control region of a gene named CSF1R and switched it on harder, which set off a signaling loop that kept inflammation going. Blocking sugar burning or the mark-making step calmed the response, while adding lactate made it worse. The authors name this loop a fresh drug target.
pmc-13585890:
Eric Luiz Domingos and colleagues build a fast test for a fungal skin disease in cats in this 2026 study. The disease, sporotrichosis, spreads to people and is common in Brazil, while standard lab checks are slow and costly. The team read blood plasma with an infrared light method that leaves a chemical fingerprint, then trained computer models to sort infected from healthy cats.

Seventy-five cats took part, sorted by fungal culture as the trusted standard. Several models sorted the training cats almost perfectly, and the toughest checks, leaving one cat out at a time or testing a fresh set, still scored well. The telling parts of the fingerprint sat in zones tied to sugars and fats, which mirror the body's response to infection. The authors see a quick, low-harm test that fits a One Health view of animal and human care.
pmc-13587190:
Jiwon Jung writes on forecasting the future of children born with malformed kidneys or urinary tracts in this 2026 piece. Such defects, grouped under the name CAKUT, are the top cause of long-term kidney disease in children in rich countries. Pregnancy scans can spot them from about the middle of pregnancy, yet a scan picture alone predicts a child's kidney future poorly.

Jung discusses a study of 55 infants followed from before birth through their first year, and sets it against larger cohorts. Kidney tissue defects, where the filtering units form badly, carried far higher rates of chronic disease than defects in the drainage plumbing alone. Early warning signs across studies included small kidneys, extra defects, early birth, and low birth weight. The message is that risk sorting must blend the scan with what follows after birth.
pmc-13592390:
Wioleta Kitowska leads an evaluation of Koronavilkku, Finland's COVID-19 exposure notification app, against a set of performance marks. The study mixed system records with a survey of more than 4,000 people from April 2022. At its peak the app reached about half of active smartphone users. Men, people over 34, and those living alone used it less, while parents and the highly educated used it more.

Over half of users who got a code from health staff entered it, keeping alerts flowing. Yet about seven in ten positive users said no code ever reached them, a bottleneck the team flags hard. Users followed pandemic guidance more than nonusers. Kitowska and the team urge automated code delivery and steady public engagement in future outbreaks.
pmc-13592490:
Florent J M Boyer-Aymé leads a 2026 study of brief slow wave bursts on brain recordings as a signpost of hidden seizure networks. Scalp EEG often looks normal between seizures, which stalls diagnosis. The team tracked these bursts in a rat model of temporal lobe epilepsy and in patients under long term monitoring, some with electrodes inside the brain. Bursts clustered in temporal frontal networks and rose around seizures.

In rats the bursts marched in step with deep temporal discharges and answered to drugs that raise or lower seizure risk. In patients, scalp bursts mirrored spike and wave activity in the hippocampus. A look back over 137 seizures in 18 patients confirmed the rise before and during events. The team offers the marker for spotting silent deep foci.
pmc-13592790:
Kamenski-Rathmanner and colleagues report a 2026 study of pulmonary hypertension, high pressure in the lung arteries, in people with hypersensitivity pneumonitis, a lung disease triggered by inhaled allergens. The team studied two groups: patients with severe lung scarring awaiting transplant, and patients with mild disease at a rehabilitation program, who were screened on purpose. Ultrasound and catheter pressure checks tested for it.

In the severe group, ultrasound pressures ran high, and half of those measured crossed the line for likely pulmonary hypertension. In the mild group, screening confirmed the condition in only about one in twenty patients, and every confirmed case had another plausible cause. In advanced disease the pressure deserves close attention; in mild disease, a positive screen should prompt a search for other causes.
pmc-13596790:
Pia Pennekamp and colleagues used eye tracking to test a theory of how eyewitnesses decide in police lineups. Diagnostic feature detection theory holds that witnesses compare faces. They lean on features only one person has, since shared features cannot distinguish anyone. The team checked whether gaze behavior actually follows that logic.

One hundred participants memorized twelve faces, then viewed lineups in which one feature, the nose, eyes, or mouth, had been digitally copied onto every member, making it useless for telling them apart. Eye movements showed no extra attention to the genuinely distinguishing features, and viewing patterns did not differ between lineup types or between accurate and mistaken witnesses. The authors conclude that whatever witnesses do with shared features, they do not appear to do it through overt visual attention, which trims one proposed mechanism of the theory.
pmc-13597090:
Serap Öner and Eylül Tutar surveyed 253 midwifery students about how they perceive accreditation, the outside quality stamp on their degree program, and what shapes their view. Students filled in forms on their knowledge of quality checks and accreditation, and a scale for how favorably they view it.

Views sat at the middle. Two factors did the real work. Students who knew more about accreditation viewed it more positively. Those willing to take part in the process viewed it more positively still. Together the pair explained about seventeen percent of the differences between students. Year of study and joining research events made no difference. The authors conclude that goodwill toward accreditation grows from understanding and involvement rather than seniority. They urge weaving structured teaching on quality systems into the course plan. That would build a lasting quality culture.
pmc-13599090:
Qi Wu and co-authors sequenced the complete chloroplast genomes of twenty-three Gastrochilus orchids, a genus prized in gardens and traditional medicine, to chart how these compact genomes evolve. Their 2026 comparative study describes each genome's structure, gene content, and repeat landscape in detail.

Every genome kept the classic four-part layout and the same 120 genes. Yet a set of ndh genes kept decaying. They turned into pseudogenes or vanished across species. The authors link the pattern to life in dim forest understory. There, those photosynthesis helpers matter less. Ten highly variable regions and eight genes stood out as candidate identification markers, and two genes carried marks of positive selection. Family trees built from the full genomes split the genus into four well-supported branches. The authors call the framework the most complete yet for Gastrochilus, while noting the adaptive story needs experimental proof.
pmc-13599690:
Cory Shulman, Danielle Bitton, and Zili Nir study 110 autistic children in 2026. They ask how daily living skills and sensory responses relate to behavior problems, and whether those links differ for girls and boys. Parents and caregivers rated each child's adaptive functioning, meaning everyday skills like communication and self-care, plus sensory processing and emotional or behavioral difficulties. The children averaged about 86 months old: 50 boys and 60 girls.

Girls showed more behavior problems, both inward kinds like anxiety and outward kinds like acting out. Boys showed larger sensory processing differences. The patterns of association split by gender: among girls, stronger adaptive skills tied to fewer behavior problems, while among boys, sensory differences tied to behavior problems instead. Formal moderation tests confirmed gender changed the adaptive-skills link. Support plans, the authors argue, should weigh these different pathways for girls and boys.
pmc-13608290:
Luyi Xu leads a nine-author team studying how fear of progression moves through couples after a stroke. Self-care after stroke is often poor, and spouses carry much of it, so the team treated recovery as a two-person system. Between August 2024 and March 2025, 384 patient-spouse pairs completed questionnaires on fear of progression, daily self-care, and the spouse's contribution. A moderated network analysis mapped how each dimension pushed on the others, and whether the patient's sex changed the wiring.

Fear dimensions within each partner, and self-care dimensions across the pair, pulled positively together. Fear and self-care pulled negatively on each other in both directions. Sex mattered: male patients' fear related negatively to their wives' fear, while female patients' fear rose with their husbands'. Wives' fear damaged their caregiving contribution more than husbands' fear did. The authors translate this into tailored advice for each couple type.
pmc-13612390:
Jason Smucny and colleagues compared resting brain scans of people with early psychosis against healthy controls from a large brain project. They measured how strong the slow natural fluctuations are in each brain area, a signal tied to local activity.

The study covered 109 people with early psychosis and 55 healthy controls, all scanned while resting. Fluctuation strength ran clearly lower in the movement and touch cortex of the psychosis group. Weaker signal there matched poorer hand dexterity and weaker thinking scores in the same patients. That quiet area also linked more strongly than usual to the cerebellum, the anterior cingulate, and the insula, Smucny reports.
pmc-13614990:
Emma McCarthy leads a team reviewing in 2026 how diet and supplements affect iron status in active women of reproductive age. Iron shortage affects an estimated 15 to 35 percent of female athletes, draining energy and performance. Searching five databases through March 2026, the team gathered intervention trials that tested food-based plans or supplements and measured at least one iron marker in the blood.

Pooling the trials showed that iron pills in the form of ferrous sulfate raised blood iron stores in a clear way. The review also weighed other diet routes and tracked effects on performance and inflammation marks. For coaches and clinicians, the combined results sort which eating strategies genuinely move iron levels and which rest on habit, helping active women treat a common and fixable problem.
pmc-13616090:
Ouso and Pollastri build in 2026 SCL2205, a benchmark dataset for predicting where inside a cell a protein ends up, a task called subcellular localization. They argue that flashy scores in this field partly rest on data leaking between training and testing sets.

Built from the UniProt protein knowledgebase with careful preprocessing, manual label mapping, and strict separation of similar sequences, the dataset targets trustworthy evaluation. On independent test sets, models trained on SCL2205 beat state-of-the-art baselines by up to about eleven percentage points on a precision-recall measure. The largest gains came beside modern protein language models. The team also measured the hidden problem directly: standard similarity-based expansion of training data leaked at a rate of roughly five percent. The dataset is openly licensed.
pmc-13616290:
Shujuan Cao, Chunping Ren, Jing Qin, Xiujuan Wang, and Xiaoming He show how the choice of linker in an organic battery cathode can unlock a second electron per unit and lift performance. Their cathodes build on phenothiazine, a molecule that gives up electrons at a high voltage, prized for lithium-organic batteries. Single-electron use caps the stored charge, and the small molecules tend to dissolve into the battery fluid, shortening life.

Chaining the units into three polyamide polymers fixed the dissolving problem and turned the linker into a design lever for light, charge, and ion flow. The benzene-bridged version balanced those traits best and ran two reversible electron steps. Smarter links, the study shows, can matter as much as the active molecule itself in organic battery design.
pmc-13616590:
Kryštof Prášil and colleagues test how often the automatic control of the heart and blood vessels fails in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, an inherited nerve disorder best known for weak hands and feet. They studied 36 patients with the CMT1A gene duplication, 24 with the CMTX1 mutation, and 62 matched controls. Tests covered reflex heart responses to breathing and standing, blood pressure on standing, and heart rate patterns over ten minutes lying and standing.

Autonomic failure of the heart appeared in 30.6 percent of the first group and 33.3 percent of the second, against 10.0 percent of controls. Only the duplication group had definite cases, at 11.1 percent, though the gap between disease types was not firm. Linking failure rates with neuropathy severity scores helps clinics decide which patients need heart monitoring alongside nerve care.
pmc-13618390:
Mugheesa Rab and five colleagues report an eighteen-year-old man whose new diabetes and pancreatitis traced to being born with most of his pancreas missing. He arrived with eight weeks of stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, excessive thirst and urination, and four kilograms of weight loss. Blood tests showed high glucose with ketones and mild acidosis, fitting mild diabetic ketoacidosis, alongside enzyme levels showing pancreatic inflammation.

CT imaging showed the neck, body, and tail of the pancreas were absent while the head was enlarged. A later duct study confirmed complete dorsal pancreatic agenesis, the failure of one early bud to develop. Insulin production ran extremely low three months on, while the usual autoimmune diabetes markers were negative, pointing to the malformed pancreas as the cause, though antibody-negative type 1 diabetes cannot be excluded. The authors advise suspecting this anomaly in young patients with unexplained pancreatitis plus insulin-poor diabetes.
pmc-13618690:
Shuangshuang Zhang and two colleagues sort nurses by their health resources and compare compassion fatigue, the emotional exhaustion of caring work, across the groups. Drawing on the salutogenic model, which asks what keeps people well, they profiled five hundred sixteen nurses by sense of coherence, perceived organizational support, and mindfulness. Latent profile analysis found natural groupings rather than imposing cutoffs.

Two profiles emerged. Just under half the nurses fell into a low-resource profile, below average on all three resources, while the rest formed a high-resource group above average on each. Compassion fatigue was twice as high in the low-resource group, roughly sixty-three against thirty-one on the scale used. Within the low-resource group, working more than four night shifts a month added to fatigue, while no job or demographic factor mattered inside the high-resource group. The authors suggest tailoring support to these profiles.
pmc-13618890:
Lei Zhu and twelve colleagues expose how circoviruses, the smallest known mammalian viruses and costly livestock pathogens, steal the host's DNA copying machinery. Their own replication protein cannot build DNA, so the team screened host polymerases and found the workhorse is POLD1, the catalytic core of DNA polymerase delta. Infection even boosts the cell's production of this enzyme.

The viral protein grabs PCNA, the sliding clamp that organizes replication, through a short motif at its tip that matches a motif on the clamp. Thereby it drags POLD1 into viral replication centers indirectly. A screened small molecule, R428, blocks this handshake for the pig virus PCV2. In cells it stopped complex formation, and in mice and piglets it suppressed viral replication and eased tissue damage. The authors propose the mechanism as a general antiviral target for circovirus diseases that vaccines cannot fully prevent.
pmc-13620190:
Kim and colleagues used machine learning in 2026 to sort blood pressure patterns during dialysis sessions and link them to body makeup in long-term dialysis patients. Pressure often swings during treatment. The team recorded pressure every thirty minutes across 928 sessions from 179 patients and let a clustering algorithm find natural groups, alongside body composition scans.

Three patterns emerged: a steep fall, a mild fall, and a rise during treatment, covering roughly a sixth, just under half, and a bit over a third of sessions. Body weight index did not differ between groups, but muscle measures rose steadily from the falling groups to the rising group, while body fat fell. The rising group carried the most extra water between cells. The links held after adjustment, suggesting pressure patterns could guide fluid targets.
pmc-13620290:
Nana Wang, Manrong Li, and Guozhen Zhang ran a randomized trial on waking patients from coma after severe traumatic brain injury. Eighty-six patients received one of three four-week treatments: magnetic stimulation of the scalp, electrical stimulation of a wrist nerve, or both together. The team tracked awakening rates, brainwave grades, blood flow in the head, consciousness scores, and safety.

The combined group woke at a far higher rate than either single-treatment group, with about nine in ten patients awakening. Consciousness scores climbed most in the combined group, brainwave patterns normalized most often there, and blood flow measures improved most strongly. Thinking scores among patients awake enough to test also favored the combination, though the authors flag that comparison as biased by who could take the test. No seizures occurred, and side effects were least common in the combined group.
pmc-13621390:
Thomas T Livecchi, Mark C Pierce, and Steven L Jacques released an open-source Python tool that predicts how light spreads through layered tissue, a calculation at the heart of optical diagnosis. Shining light on skin and reading the glow back can reveal blood, pigment, and water levels, but only if a model translates the signal. Gold-standard simulations crawl, while simple formulas pretend tissue has one uniform layer.

Their implementation solves the diffusion approximation for any number of layers with a fast banded-matrix method. Four hundred randomized comparisons against heavy simulations, covering one to eight layers, showed the fast model's spectra hugging the reference closely. Calculation time dropped by more than five orders of magnitude, to a tiny fraction of a second per spectrum, and error did not grow with extra layers. The authors offer the code freely for real-time tissue profiling work.
pmc-13623090:
Ghada Elhadari and four co-authors review what helps or blocks the setup of triage systems in hospitals across low- and middle-income countries. Triage means sorting arriving patients by urgency so the sickest are treated first. Good emergency care could prevent many deaths in these countries, yet triage often fails to take hold.

The team searched eight databases and kept fifty-seven studies that named barriers or supports. Each factor was mapped onto a standard framework for putting new practices into place. Reports clustered most around how programmes are run day to day, the traits of the people involved, and the inner life of each facility, such as staffing, space, and leadership. Features of the triage tools themselves also mattered. The authors offer the map as a planning guide for emergency care leaders who want triage to last, not just launch.
pmc-13623390:
Beatriz Caroline Leão Lima leads a time-series study of violence by neglect or abandonment against older women in Brazil from 2009 to 2022. Neglect here means failing to give needed care, and it is among the most common yet least reported forms of elder abuse. Data came from the national notifiable diseases reporting system.

The study counted 34,860 reported cases in women aged sixty or more. The Southeast region recorded the most cases, while the Northeast showed the fastest proportional growth, rising by roughly a third each year on the trend measure used. Eight in ten episodes happened at home, and in about two thirds the offender was a family member, the very person expected to give care. Two in five victims reported repeated violence. The authors describe a rising, uneven pattern and urge stronger protection and reporting routes for older women.
pmc-13626190:
Ritika Kamlesh Patel and colleagues work with family doctors in Alberta to build a care pathway for gut infections that keep coming back. Clostridioides difficile causes the most common hospital-linked infectious diarrhea, and its recurrences are hard to manage, partly because stool transplant therapy, though guideline-backed, is unfamiliar to many primary care doctors. The team of specialists first drafted a pathway, then refined it with its future users.

Family doctors joined two rounds of long video interviews, thinking aloud while they worked through staged cases with the draft in hand. Their struggles with test reading, drug choice, and referral timing surfaced as barriers and helpers, which fed straight back into the design. Building the tool with its users, the authors argue, is how a pathway earns trust and real use.
pmc-13628190:
Akin, Özgen, and Cesur follow up girls with early periods in this 2026 single-centre retrospective study, asking what early menarche costs in height, gynecological health, and mental health. The cohort comprised 58 patients whose first periods arrived between 9.5 and 10.75 years of age, unusually early, with adult outcomes gathered from records and questionnaires.

Final adult height averaged 157.71 centimeters against a predicted target of 159.27 centimeters from parental heights, a significant shortfall at p equals 0.029 in the analysis, concentrated in girls who also had chronic illness, especially asthma. Half the group reported painful periods, about 15 percent were diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome, and 22.4 percent had psychological problems, with 15.5 percent receiving treatment for them. The authors conclude early menarche travels with more PCOS and psychiatric difficulty than peers typically report.
pmc-13628290:
Sara Cignola and two colleagues translated the Anticipated Turnover Scale, a twelve-item questionnaire measuring nurses' intention to leave their jobs, into Italian and checked whether the adapted version still measures soundly. Their test group was 168 nurses at a public university hospital in northeastern Italy.

Expert review and statistical checks supported the scale's content, and the full version held together reliably, though its content validity score was modest. A trimmed ten-item version performed better on both content coverage and internal consistency, settling into two underlying factors. Even so, the authors judge the Italian scale promising rather than finished, calling for confirmatory testing, stability checks over time, and a cut-off score before managers use it to plan retention work.
pmc-13629790:
Miranda Hendry and two colleagues tracked how overweight and obesity spread among South Asian women of childbearing age. Their analysis pooled survey data for over one and a half million women. The women were aged fifteen to forty-nine. They lived in Bangladesh, India, Nepal, the Maldives, and Pakistan. The years ran from 2000 to 2022.

Rates climbed clearly everywhere except the Maldives. The condition clustered among urban and wealthier women. In many places it also clustered among less schooled women. National rates spanned from single digits to well over a third. Some of the fastest growth appeared among the poorest women in Bangladesh. The authors describe a marked shift in disease patterns. It carries direct weight for pregnancy health and chronic disease policy in the region.
pmc-13633690:
Rui Zeng and five colleagues ran a randomized trial on the timing of a nerve block for older hip fracture patients. Confusion after surgery, called delirium, is a feared outcome in this group. The block numbs the front hip region through a space near a deep muscle. Seventy-nine patients aged sixty-five and over, all set for hip replacement after fracture, received the block either the day before surgery or one hour before.

Seventy-six patients finished as planned. Delirium appeared in a small share of both groups, slightly fewer with earlier timing, yet the gap was well within chance. Early pain scores looked better with the earlier block, but that edge faded once the many comparisons were properly corrected. One inflammation marker hinted at a calmer stress response, a lead the authors flag as exploratory. They call for larger trials before timing becomes standard practice.
pmc-13645590:
Zhanying Lin and six colleagues pool trial evidence on acupuncture for swallowing problems after radiation treatment for nasopharyngeal cancer, a cancer behind the nose. Radiation for this cancer often leaves patients struggling to swallow safely. The team searched eight databases through March 2026 for randomized trials. Twelve trials with 863 patients met their rules.

Patients who received acupuncture scored better on a standard water swallowing test than control groups. More of them reached a favorable swallowing status, and imaging-based swallowing scores also improved. Quality of life and nutrition measures moved in the same direction. Safety was poorly reported, so firm claims about harm are not possible. The authors describe acupuncture as a possible add-on therapy, while noting the trials were small and their methods uneven.
pmc-13645690:
Junmei Zhang and four colleagues describe seven breast cancer patients whose cancer spread to the membranes around the brain and spinal cord, a complication with a very poor outlook. All seven received an antibody-drug treatment called trastuzumab deruxtecan together with whole-brain radiation. Four also received a blood-vessel drug and chemotherapy placed into the spinal fluid. The paper pairs the case series with a review of the wider literature.

In the four patients who got the fuller combination, brain and nerve symptoms eased fast, and survival ran longer than older reports suggest for this condition. No severe or fatal side effects appeared in the group. The authors are careful to frame this as early experience from very few patients. Still, the cases give other cancer teams a concrete regimen to consider where no standard treatment exists.
pmc-13645890:
Dongha Lee and nine colleagues describe, in a 2026 case report, how a drainage shunt rescued a fifty-five-year-old woman from stubborn fluid buildup after pancreatic cancer surgery. Her cancer had first been judged inoperable, then shrank enough for surgery that removed part of the pancreas and nearby vessels. Six months later, milky lymph fluid began filling her abdomen, a problem called chylous ascites. Diet measures, drainage procedures, and repeated needle removal all failed.

After checks ruled out infection and leftover cancer cells in the fluid, surgeons placed a Denver shunt to move the fluid back into a neck vein. The buildup cleared quickly, her weight and blood protein recovered, and she left hospital safely. The shunt came out twenty-nine months later over a vein clot, yet the fluid never returned. Five years after the cancer surgery she remained alive with no recurrence, a notable salvage success.
pmc-13647090:
Laura Schellhas and nine colleagues search for chemical marks on DNA that track with young children's inward-turning symptoms, such as anxiety and withdrawal, in a 2026 study. Three European birth cohorts supplied blood DNA data at birth and at age six, plus mother-reported behavior at ages three and six. The analysis was run within a large pregnancy and childhood epigenetics consortium. Sample sizes ran above one thousand per analysis.

No single DNA site linked reliably with symptoms at either age. Looking at whole regions instead, the team found a handful of stretches in newborn blood tied to symptoms at three and at six, and two more in blood taken at age six. Some nearby genes had prior links to depression, including one already tied to teenage depression. The authors say bigger samples and sharper symptom measures are needed to judge whether these marks truly matter.
pmc-13647990:
Li Hong and seven colleagues report a national cross-sectional study of complementary feeding and growth among children aged zero to thirty-six months in China. Their work asks whether eating a wider range of solid foods alongside milk relates to length, weight, and weight for height in very young children.

The sample held 26,266 children from thirty-three provinces, with parents answering questionnaires posted through a maternal and child health association. Greater food diversity was linked with better linear growth in every age group, while diversity was linked with lower weight for height after six months. Iron-rich foods such as liver were rarely used, and many parents favoured supplements over varied meals, so the authors call for clearer feeding guidance.
pmc-13649290:
Tillis and co-authors study dropout in this 2026 mixed-methods study of a telehealth trial. The trial coached parents to deliver behavioral therapy to toddlers with tuberous sclerosis complex. That genetic disorder causes seizures and developmental delay. Fifty-nine children aged 12 to 39 months joined the randomized waitlist trial. The team modeled which parents did fewer sessions. They also interviewed them about why.

The models found no dominant factor. Two exploratory signals emerged, though. Children with more severe seizures did sessions at a rate ratio of 0.95 per severity step in the model. Parents who joined during the COVID era came in at 0.77 against other periods in the regression. Distance from the hospital and socioeconomic risk, classic dropout drivers, showed no link under telehealth. Interviews filled the gaps. Medical crises, competing demands, and doubts about fit or benefit drove quitting more than logistics.
pmc-13649490:
Erxinxian Bei and four colleagues asked if leg vein clots after stroke raise the risk of later seizures. Both problems strike stroke patients, and they share roots in weak limbs, swelling, and thick blood. The team reused data from more than 21,000 patients at many centres, tracked for one year after an artery-block stroke.

At first pass, patients with a leg clot had near double the odds of seizures. Once stroke severity and the brain areas hit were taken into account, the link all but vanished. Adding clot status to a risk model did not sharpen its calls at all. The authors read a leg clot as a sign of a harder stroke case, not a cause of seizures in its own right.
pmc-13649990:
Feng Yang and six colleagues show how stress inside a dangerous yeast can breed resistance to the drugs used against it. The yeast, Candida auris, spreads in hospitals and already resists many treatments. When the team exposed it to a chemical that stresses the cell's protein-folding compartment, the survivors that grew back had gained resistance to a common antifungal.

Gene activity readings showed the stressed parent cells turning up wall-building, transport, and cleanup genes while turning down protein production and energy use. Resistant survivors leaned on a pump that pushes drug out of the cell, and one isolate also raised a drug-target gene. A smaller set of survivors tolerated a second drug by thickening the cell wall with extra chitin, a wall material, through a separate route involving two well-known stress proteins.
pmc-13650490:
David Haynes and nine colleagues build a public dataset estimating, neighborhood by neighborhood, how many Americans qualify for lung cancer screening. Screening with low-dose scans saves lives, yet fewer than a fifth of eligible people get it, partly because eligibility hinges on a detailed smoking history that records and surveys usually lack.

A tool called the Smoking History Generator was woven into national surveys. It reconstructs how much and how long older adults smoked, letting the team count those who cross the twenty pack-year threshold at census tract level. The dataset can be grouped by county or state and filtered by age, sex, race and ethnicity, and current or former smoking. Health programs can use it to aim outreach where eligible people actually live, rather than guessing from clinic records alone.
pmc-13651490:
Brianna Murray and four colleagues track atrial fibrillation and blood-thinning treatment in British patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a pairing where an irregular heartbeat raises stroke risk against fragile lungs. Their primary care cohort ran from 2010 to 2022 through a national research database.

Over four hundred forty thousand patients contributed more than two million person-years, and close to thirty-eight thousand developed atrial fibrillation. Its incidence rose by roughly thirty percent across the period, running higher in men, white patients, the over-eighties, and severe lung disease. Only about two thirds of new cases started an anticoagulant within a year, although prescribing nearly tripled over the study years. The oldest and youngest age bands, non-white patients, and severe COPD cases lagged furthest behind. The authors call the gaps a target for stroke prevention research in this high-risk group.
pmc-3047790:
Coutinho and Chapman review the anti-inflammatory and immune-suppressing effects of glucocorticoids. These steroid drugs were discovered in the 1940s and quickly recognised for calming inflammation. Since then they have ranked among the most widely used and effective treatments for inflammatory and autoimmune disease.

Their clinical power, though, is compromised by side effects with long use. The authors gather recent developments and mechanistic insight into how the drugs act on immune cells. Better understanding of those pathways points toward safer steroids that keep the benefit while shedding harm.  Dose and duration limits in clinics reflect exactly this balance of effects.
pmc-3882890:
Proctor, Powell, and McMillen offer advice for naming and reporting rollout strategies. Such strategies are the how-to part of changing healthcare practice, and they carry central importance in this field. Yet researchers and others involved could not fully use study findings about them.

The problem is vague reporting: strategies are named without saying who acts, on what, and how often. The authors propose a reporting framework covering those elements. Precise detail lets others copy what worked and lets reviewers compare strategies across studies honestly.  Checklists in the paper name the information each rollout report should always contain.
pmc-4103590:
Bolger, Lohse, and Usadel introduced Trimmomatic in 2014, a tool that cleans raw sequencing reads. Before analysis, reads from Illumina machines often need trimming to remove adapter pieces and low-quality ends. Many tools existed, but the authors found none that met all their needs at once.

Trimmomatic was built to be flexible, fast, and correct with paired-end data, where two reads come from the same DNA piece. It chains trimming steps in the order the user chooses. Clean input reads improve every later step, from genome assembly to variant calling. The tool became a standard first pass in sequencing pipelines worldwide.
pmc-4167990:
Geeleher, Cox, and Huang presented pRRophetic in 2014, an R package that predicts how tumors will respond to chemotherapy. The team had earlier shown that response could be predicted in several separate clinical trials. Their method was trained on gene and drug response data from hundreds of cancer cell lines.

For each cell line, the method uses gene expression data paired with measured drug sensitivity. It then applies those models to a patient's tumor gene profile to forecast response. Such forecasts could help doctors choose the drug most likely to work for a given patient. The package made the method open for other cancer groups to test.
pmc-5624990:
Shaffer and Ginsberg gave an overview in 2017 of heart rate variability metrics and norms. Healthy living systems vary in complex patterns, the kind that chaos mathematics describes. Heart rate variability, or HRV, is the pattern of gaps between one heartbeat and the next, called interbeat intervals.

A healthy heart is not a metronome; its timing varies in rich patterns that reflect nervous system control. The overview explains the main HRV metrics, in time, frequency, and nonlinear forms, and gives normative values for each. Norms let clinicians and researchers judge whether a recording is unusual. HRV is used in cardiology, stress research, and biofeedback, so shared references matter.
pmc-5753190:
Simon Harding and many coauthors reported the 2018 update of the IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology. The guide collects expert-checked facts about drug targets and the chemicals that act on them. It has grown from a database first built in the early two thousands.

The update adds new targets and drugs and launches a companion guide on immune pharmacology. Each entry links targets to ligands with data drawn from key papers. Drug hunters use the guide to check what is known before planning experiments. Because experts curate it by hand, users treat it as a reliable first source.
pmc-6292890:
Pramod Darvin, Salman Toor, Varun Sasidharan Nair, and coauthors reviewed immune checkpoint inhibitors in 2018. Tumors survive partly by switching on brakes that quiet immune attack. Antibodies that block those brakes produced a breakthrough in cancer care.

The review covers recent trial progress across cancer types and the uneven pattern of response. Only some patients gain lasting benefit, so markers that predict response are badly needed. The authors survey candidate markers, including tumor mutation load and immune cell patterns. Their survey helps readers see both the real gains and the open search for better selection.
pmc-6872490:
The One Thousand Plant Transcriptomes Initiative published this green plant study in 2019. Green plants number near half a million species and shape land and water ecosystems. Their family tree still had many unresolved branches.

The team sequenced the active genes of more than a thousand species chosen across the whole group. Comparing those data rebuilt relationships among algae, mosses, ferns, and flowering plants. Several long-debated splits gained strong support. The shared data set gives plant science a backbone tree for studying how traits like flowers and wood evolved. All sequence data were released openly for reuse by the wider plant science community.
pmc-6889290:
Mark Pittenger, Dennis Discher, Bruno Péault, and coauthors gave a perspective on mesenchymal stem cells in 2019. These cells, also called mesenchymal stromal cells, can form bone, cartilage, and fat. They are found in marrow and many other tissues.

The authors trace the field from early marrow studies to today's clinical trials. They stress that the cells' healing power may come more from signals they release than from rebuilding tissue directly. Naming confusion and uneven trial quality get frank treatment. The piece helps readers judge bold stem cell claims against the evidence.
pmc-7005290:
Reed Sutton, David Pincock, Daniel Baumgart, and coauthors gave an overview of clinical decision support systems in 2020. These computer systems help clinicians with complex choices at the point of care. They have evolved fast since their first use decades ago.

Modern systems are woven into electronic records and can warn, suggest, and order on the spot. Benefits include fewer errors and more uniform care. Risks include alert fatigue and blind trust in bad advice. The authors offer strategies for design and rollout that keep clinicians in charge, which decides whether such systems help or hinder.
pmc-7144090:
Richard Challis, Edward Richards, Sujai Kumar, and coauthors presented BlobToolKit for genome assembly checks in 2020. Assembling a genome from mixed DNA is confounded by contaminants. Foreign DNA can sneak in during sampling or lab processing.

BlobToolKit plots each assembled piece by its composition and likely species of origin. Contaminant pieces stand out as separate blobs that users can inspect and remove. Interactive views suit the huge assemblies of biodiversity projects. The toolkit became part of the quality routine for the Darwin Tree of Life and similar efforts. Case studies show the plots catching contamination that standard summary statistics had missed entirely.
pmc-7164390:
Jianzhong Shi, Zhiyuan Wen, Gongxun Zhong, and coauthors tested animal susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 in 2020. The pandemic virus likely came from bats, but its route into humans was unknown. Knowing which animals it infects helps science and farming alike.

The team exposed ferrets, cats, dogs, pigs, chickens, and ducks to the virus under lab conditions. Ferrets and cats caught and spread it readily, while dogs were poor hosts and farm birds resisted it. The results picked ferrets and cats as models for vaccine tests. They also warned that pets and farmed animals needed watching.
pmc-8280690:
Hannah Davis and co-authors, several of them patients themselves, characterized long COVID in 2021 by studying an international group of people still ill months after infection. Many patients with COVID-19 go on to suffer prolonged symptoms, yet few systematic studies had examined them, especially people never admitted to hospital. The team surveyed patients about the full course of their illness over about seven months.

They catalog which symptoms appear, how they ebb and return, and how deeply they cut into work and daily life. Memory problems, exhaustion after effort, and relapses triggered by exertion feature strongly in their account. The study gave early, detailed shape to a condition patients had been reporting long before medicine had a name or a plan for it.
podcast-powerfuljre-33Fc_mLqY90:
Jesse Michels returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2545, filed here under the PowerfulJRE channel. Michels hosts American Alchemy, where he interviews scientists and witnesses at the edge of accepted knowledge. His repeat visits show how central that fringe beat is to Rogan's show.

Michels digs into his latest cases, from UFO reports to inventors he says history ignored. He argues that curiosity, not credentials, should drive hard questions. Rogan compares his stories with years of similar guests and claims. The curious get another long-form trip along science's edge with a practiced guide.
podcast-tuckercarlson-sO-sy5ut490:
Car builder Casey Putsch tells Tucker Carlson why he believes the EPA wants to destroy his custom-made car. Putsch built a one-off vehicle by hand, then ran into federal rules on emissions and safety. The fight became his gearhead grievance against the regulatory state.

Putsch explains the rules he says make small builders' work nearly impossible. He argues the agencies crush craft and choice in the name of standards big makers helped write. Carlson frames it as the builder versus the bureaucrats, the state versus speed. Car lovers and libertarians get a craftsman's case in full.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-the-christ:
Readers of Punch, the London comic weekly, got a special Christmas number for 1890, opened by a picture of Mr. Punch among the planets. In the opening tale, Father Time sits in his observatory tower on a clear, starry night as the old year nears its close.

Mr. Punch enters with his dog Tobias and finds Time at work on his reminiscences, a vast work running to thousands of volumes. Their talk mixes greeting, teasing, and talk of publishers. Holiday readers get a fanciful frame tale in the paper's usual playful voice, made for the season.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-99-:
Punch for August 16, 1890, volume 99, leads with "Modern Types," number seventeen in a series drawn by the magazine's own type writer, on the Spurious Sportsman. The essay picks apart a familiar figure of clubs and country houses in late Victorian Britain.

Such a man longs to seem a great hunter, fisher, and shot, though his real trips were few and bare of success. He reads widely, listens to other men's tales, and slowly turns their feats into his own, building a bright suit of false sporting deeds. The piece grants him one excuse: few men tell of their longest shot without adding a foot or two.

Volume 99 of Punch for August 2, 1890 opens with a Highland cartoon. A beaten husband still defies his wife from under the bed. A verse address to a battalion of Guards bound for Bermuda follows. The poem scolds soldiers who had shamed their name in a row.

Quoting Juvenal on who guards the guards, the verses grant that harsh officers may have driven the men too far, yet insist that British redcoats must not copy street mobs. Discipline, called a parent who must not spare the rod, closes the appeal. A piece called "Robert's American Acquaintance" follows.

Punch dated August 23, 1890, volume 99, leads with "Novelty Up to Date," a short Scots play printed in full to test a charge of copying. The new Adelphi play The English Rose had been called unoriginal, so the magazine answers with a drama of its own, Telmah, in three short acts.

Telmah is Hamlet in Scots dress, set at the Horse Guards Parade, Elsinore, near Edinburgh. MacClaudius and MacGertrude greet the moody prince, the colours are trooped, and the ghost of Telmah's father walks on cue. The joke rests on how well readers know the source play, line by line.

Punch for August 30, 1890, volume 99, leads with a set of mock letters under the heading "Why Not Live Out of London?" a subject lately raised in the Daily Telegraph. Each writer answers the question in a way that serves his own comfort first.

One husband, signing himself One in a Thousand, urges that his wife and family move to the country. He, the bread-winner, would keep a club and a room in town. He would visit now and then. A cheesemonger named Charles Cheddar replies that he lives out of London and makes a good living out of it too. A third writer wishes everyone he dislikes would leave town.

Volume 99 of Punch for August 9, 1890 opens with "First Aid to Tommy Atkins," a letter from a former Yeomanry man who visited the Military Exhibition in London. Lame and leaning on a young friend, he asks to be taken to the battle pictures and lands instead in the open arena.

There, detachments of citizen soldiers run through ambulance drill with stretchers and simple kits, ten groups in all. The sight moves even his scoffing friend. Wishing the scene had cannon fire and bursting shells, the writer supplies them in fancy and begins a mock battle account, with a sergeant dressing the ranks and calling on Jenkins.

Punch dated December 13, 1890, volume 99, leads with number nine of Mr. Punch's Prize Novels, "The Curse of Cognac," credited to a parody author called Water Decant. His note to the editor praises the tale as a cure for too much Christmas cheer, fit to read aloud in small groups.

Chapter one finds George Ginsling alone in his rooms at Christ's College, Cambridge, after his friends have gone. Stung by a question about refusing a seat in the Trial Eights, he paces the room. He sips his seventh tumbler of neat brandy. The nightly habit, he claims, steadies him for his Greek verse.

For December 20, 1890, Punch in volume 99 offers a Voces Populi piece, "The Riding-Class," set in a bare, gas-lit riding school on a raw afternoon. Mothers and friends watch from an alcove while grown pupils wait on the tan for their horses.

Mrs. Bilbow-Kay explains that her son Robert rode well as a boy but needs lessons again, on doctor's orders for exercise. The riding master then pairs each man with a mount: the lively Shar for Bilbow-Kay, Lady Loo for Mr. Tongs, Kangaroo for Mr. Joggles, the Artful Dodger for Mr. Bumpas, and a bucking starter called Frar Diavolo for Mr. Sniggers.

Punch for December 27, 1890, volume 99, leads with "Our Booking-Office," the magazine's chatty column of book notes for the Christmas season. The Baron, its reviewer in chief, moves from French duelling terms to ghost tales and Cambridge letters in a few pages.

He praises the tale of the phrase Le Coup de Jarnac in Macmillan's Magazine. He notes two seasonable ghost stories in The Argosy under Charles Wood. He also enjoys Harry Fludyer at Cambridge. Those letters were first printed in The Granta and issued by Chatto and Windus. One novel, The Missing Member, he calls muddle-headed, and French picture books go up to the nursery.

Volume 99 of Punch for December 6, 1890 leads with "Modern Types," number twenty-two, on the Manly Maiden, drawn by the magazine's own type writer. The essay takes aim at a young woman who tries to win the title of good fellow by copying men's rough ways.

She swears, slaps backs, and scorns peril, hoping for the praise men give bluff, strong men.
