The piece argues that men in fact prize softness and calm in women, and that her act costs her the courtesy she might have claimed. Born to rich town parents, she meets country life at about fourteen, and the sketch follows from there.

Punch dated July 12, 1890, volume 99, opens with a Voces Populi sketch, "At the Military Exhibition," set in an avenue facing the arena. An unreasonable old lady arrives breathless with her grandson and her niece Maria, sure that a balloon is about to go up from that very spot.

No balloon can be seen, since leaves block the view, yet the crowd is proof enough for her. Maria slips away and returns with word of a fine open view elsewhere. The old lady, who had sworn she would not move to fare worse, at once agrees to go, saying it is all the same to her.

For July 19, 1890, Punch in volume 99 leads with "Our Booking-Office," where the Baron reviews Oscar Wilde's Dorian Gray, printed whole in one number of Lippincott's Magazine. A cartoon pairs Wilde's hero with the fat boy from Pickwick, each startling a respectable lady.

The Baron calls the romance weird and sensational, fit to be read in one late sitting by those who love dark tales, and in small doses by day for the rest. He sums up its plot of a portrait that bears the marks of sin while its sitter stays young. He faults the ending. He quotes Wilde's claim that the book is poisonous yet perfect.

Punch for July 26, 1890, volume 99, leads with "Modern Types," number sixteen, on the Hurlingham Girl, a portrait of a young woman of the smart London set. Her spirits, the essay says, run higher than her aims, which have drifted off almost out of sight.

She has been taught to scorn school learning: history, geography, classics, maths, and tongues all bore her. In their place she knows the season's fixtures by heart, from Sandown and Ascot to Hurlingham and Ranelagh. Rich parents help but are not required; what counts is a place in the world that thinks itself good, and a mother long used to being thwarted.

Volume 99 of Punch for July 5, 1890 opens with "Week by Week," a column of comic notes on Parliament, weather, and plain speech. The House of Commons had been restless for three weeks, and the column hunts for wild causes.

One politician hints at cave-men living in barrows under the House. The weather report dissolves into mock sums involving an earl's hat, a costermonger's buttons, and street cries in the Old Kent Road. A vestryman who voted down a pay rise is told by a road sweeper that his head would fetch twopence, a breach, the column notes, in that trade's usual fine manners.

Punch dated November 1, 1890, volume 99, leads with "Modern Types," number twenty-one, on the Average Undergraduate. The essay answers older men who claim that the young have lost all courtesy, modesty, and respect since their own golden youth.

Every age, it argues, finds its young men selfish and slangy, and the charge is at best half true. Follies exist, yet the mass of students at Oxford and Cambridge match their fathers in manliness and modesty. London shows youth at its worst, the piece warns, so the fair test is the average undergraduate at either university, not the loud few in town.

For November 15, 1890, Punch in volume 99 offers number six of Mr. Punch's Prize Novels, "Thrums on the Auld String," credited to the parody name J. Muir Kirrie. A note explains that the tale came with a glossary of Scots words that the magazine has no room to print.

Chapter one gathers its cast on a pig-sty at T'nowhead's farm, the old sow listening within and grunting now and then. The narrator, a dominie, drifts into memories of childhood on the brae. He recalls thick bread and thin butter. He tells how the balance shifts with age. All this comes before any plot has had time to start.

Punch for November 22, 1890, volume 99, opens with a cartoon of the actor-manager Bancroft, retired from the stage, tempted by General Booth's relief scheme after offering a thousand pounds to it. Short comic pieces follow, each built on a newspaper item.

One piece praises a kind storm off Beachy Head that broke men's ribs yet kindly landed them at Dover Hospital. Another marvels at a schoolmaster's advertisement: a teacher aged three, with ten years of practice, offers maths, science, French, drawing, piano, organ, and singing for twenty pounds a year, without a house.

Volume 99 of Punch for November 29, 1890 leads with number eight of Mr. Punch's Prize Novels, "Jonnie," credited to Dick Dody and written in French. The tale mashes two famous Dickens figures into one small hero, Jonnie Dombey, brought to Paris by a pretty Madame Copperfield.

She begs a Paris school head to take her son, whose banker father made giant deals and looked down on the Rothschilds as newcomers. The head asks one test question: is the boy noble? He is not, and the most fashionable school in Paris shuts its doors, crown on the visiting card or nothing.

Punch dated November 8, 1890, volume 99, leads with number five of Mr. Punch's Prize Novels, "Mignon's Mess-Room," by the parody author Tom Rum Summer. His note calls it a true tale of soldiers and children, and warns that he charges extra for pathos.

Chapter one gathers the officers of the Purple Dragoons in their ante-room, all tall, broad, and good as gold, which soon grows dull. Relief comes from Gavor, a downright villain marked to break his neck. Captain Emily, called the biggest fool in the service, trusts all he is told and twists his tongue on the words he tries to repeat.

For October 11, 1890, Punch in volume 99 leads with "Modern Types," number twenty, on the Divorcée. The essay opens in the court of Sir James Hannen, where ill-matched couples could at last be parted without great cost or an act of Parliament.

The rules, it notes, favor men: a wife's straying alone ends a marriage, while a husband must add cruelty or desertion to his own. Women's wit answers with sworn tales that swell a pinch into a mountain of ill use, until a wife plants her flag of freedom on top. Divorce, once suspect, now counts as a settled part of national life.

Punch for October 18, 1890, volume 99, leads with "How It's Done," a handbook to honesty, number eleven, on the straight "tip." The scene is the private room of a large wholesale house, where a pompous principal leans on his head of department, Mr. Scroop.

Profits in Scroop's branch have fallen short, and cuts must be made somewhere, though the principal will not say where. He hints that Puddicombe, a new supplier, charges too much and should lower his lines. Scroop, aside, reads the game at once: the old man wants extra pounds squeezed from a small trader for his own use.

Volume 99 of Punch for October 25, 1890 leads with number four of Mr. Punch's Prize Novels, "Bob Sillimere," by a parody author named Mrs. Humphry John Ward Preacher. A note wrapped round the manuscript calls it a highly religious story fit for a bishop's study table.

Chapter one lingers over an Oxford evening, its grey courts, pealing organs, and chapel services, before a tall youth in an oversized surplice dashes into St. Boniface's as the porter shuts the door. This is Robert, called Bob Sillimere, whose Irish mother, the narrator warns, will die in the eleventh chapter once she proves surplus to the plot.

Punch dated October 4, 1890, volume 99, opens with an announcement for a new series of Mr. Punch's Prize Novels. The age, it argues, is an age of prizes, in which solvers of puzzles, dressers of dolls, and tellers of tales have all been richly paid.

Novelists alone had won nothing as novelists, until a newspaper editor offered a thousand pounds for the best novel, with only the winner's name to be told. Punch claims powers to seize every entry sent in, winners or not. It vows to print a choice of them. The authors' names will be told. Its own kind notes will be added, with pruning where it must.

For September 13, 1890, Punch in volume 99 prints "Out for a Holiday," a comic travel piece by its self-styled impartial critic. He sets out for St. Margaret's Bay, between Deal and Dover, a spot praised as lovely beyond compare and used as a summer base by the painter Alma Tadema.

The train leaves him at Martin's Mill, a mile and a half from the village by a dusty road of endless hills. In the village there is still no sea; a young woman directs him a mile farther on. Stone eagles guard a boarding house, cottages built like upturned boats offer rooms to let, and a Marine Lodge stands far from any water.

Punch for September 20, 1890, volume 99, follows its impartial critic "Out for Another Holiday," this time to Ostend in Belgium, praised to him as a town of palaces. He leaves Dover by steamer and tells tales of the cross-Channel boats and their pranks.

One mail boat lately left early, smashed a gangway, and dropped a bag in the sea. His own crossing runs on time. The food list fails him, though. Both cutlets and cold roast beef are off. Ostend offers a Kursaal, a Casino, and grand hotels, plus furnished flats let at prices that suggest the tenants, not the rooms, are being taken in.

Volume 99 of Punch for September 27, 1890 leads with "Modern Types," number nineteen, on the Servant of Society. He is the tuft-hunter who gives up all thought of his own and hangs on the coats of the great, living as an extra in the houses of the rich.

The essay warns that such men are not all low-born or crude. New wealth is often courted by men fit only to serve it, and even royalty accepts a willing helper. The true servant, though, comes from good family, with a small income, and learns his trade early as a fag to a big school athlete.

Punch dated September 6, 1890, volume 99, leads with "Modern Types," number eighteen, on the Undomestic Daughter. Most daughters, the essay says, pass their seasons and then settle into quiet use at home while they wait for marriage, yet no one quite agrees what daughters are for.

One sort comforts her mother, plans dinners, writes invites, and pours the tea. Another backs her brothers in their scrapes and wishes she had been born a boy. Against both stands the undomestic kind. She is marked from childhood by romantic leanings. Her plain brothers mock them. Her plain sisters envy them. She will not live the calm life set out for her.
regius-manuscript-c1390:
The Regius Manuscript, written around 1390, is the oldest known Masonic document. Its Middle English poem renders the Old Charges of operative masonry, the legendary history and rules of the working stonemasons. Every later Masonic tradition descends, in part, from texts of this family.

The poem tells how the craft began, naming Euclid and the masons of ancient lands. It then sets rules for masters, fellows, and apprentices at work and at table. Morals and manners matter as much as geometry in its charges. Scholars call it the root text of the speculative tradition. To read it is to stand at the head of the lodge's own river of memory.
schiller-thirty-years-war-1790:
Schiller's History of the Thirty Years' War appeared in 1790, in A. J. W. Morrison's English translation of 1846. The war began in 1618 as a clash over faith in the German lands. It grew into a thirty-year struggle that drew in Sweden, France, and Spain and left whole regions wasted.

Schiller follows Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden and the imperial general Wallenstein as the war's twin giants. Battles, sieges, and shifting leagues fill his clear, dramatic narrative. The history won Schiller his professorship at Jena. It also supplied the research behind his Wallenstein plays. For a century it stood as the standard account of the war in English homes.
sherman-antitrust-act-1890:
Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act in 1890, the first law of its kind. Every pact in restraint of trade is declared illegal by its terms. Trusts and monopolies had grown vast in the age of rail and oil.

The act lay quiet for years, then woke as a mighty weapon. Courts used it to break Standard Oil and the railroad combines. Its short, broad clauses still anchor American competition law today. Judges and lawyers argue its reach in case after famous case. The statute stands as the founding charter of fair markets in America.
sibly-illustration-of-the-celestial-scie:
Ebenezer Sibly published his New and Complete Illustration of the Celestial Science of Astrology around 1790, in four parts. Sibly was an English astrologer who aimed to give his art a full, grand system. Plates, charts, and worked examples filled the large pages.

Readers learned how to cast a birth chart, judge planets and houses, and answer questions by the stars. Sibly also treated weather, nations, and the fates of kings by the same rules. He claimed astrology rested on nature and long practice, not mere fortune telling. The work stands as the most ambitious English astrology of the eighteenth century.
smith-theory-moral-sentiments-1790:
Adam Smith published The Theory of Moral Sentiments in 1790 in its final form, the sixth edition of a work first issued in 1759. Smith was a professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow before he wrote on wealth. This book, his first, sets out how humans judge right and wrong.

Smith held that sympathy, our power to feel with others, grounds moral judgment. Each person carries an impartial spectator, an imagined fair witness who checks our acts. From such checks come conscience, rules of justice, and social order. The book is the moral philosophy behind the Wealth of Nations, and Smith kept revising it to the end of his life.
spenser-faerie-queene-vol1-1590:
Edmund Spenser planned The Faerie Queene as a huge poem of twelve books, each following a knight who embodied one virtue. He served the English crown in Ireland and wrote for Queen Elizabeth's court. The first installment, Books One through Three, appeared in 1590 and made his fame.

Book One sends the Red Cross Knight, patron of Holiness, against dragons and deceivers with the lady Una. Book Two tests Temperance in Guyon's journey, and Book Three follows Chastity in the lady knight Britomart. Spenser invented his own nine-line stanza for the poem and filled it with allegory. Every adventure carries a moral meaning beneath its pageantry.
spr-proceedings-vol6-1889-1890:
Volume six, covering 1889 and 1890, binds parts fifteen through seventeen of the Proceedings. The Society for Psychical Research was then near the height of its early energy. Its census of hallucinations, a vast survey of waking visions, nears report stage. Telepathy trials continue under fresh safeguards against leakage and luck.

Trance mediumship, above all the sittings with Mrs. Piper, draws long reports. Thompson's case and other trance studies of the day appear in the mix. Physical phenomena receive cooler, shorter treatment than mental ones. The society prints its doubts in the same type as its wonders. Volume six shows a research program maturing. Its files anchor histories of the field.
strong-exhaustive-concordance-bible-1890:
James Strong published his Exhaustive Concordance of the Bible in 1890, after decades of work with a team of helpers. Strong was a Methodist scholar and professor. His book indexes every word of the King James Bible with its verse references.

For each Hebrew or Greek original, Strong assigns a number, and those numbers became a worldwide standard. Two dictionaries at the back give the meanings of every Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek word in the text. Preachers and students without the ancient languages could now trace a word through the whole Bible. Strong's numbers still anchor Bible software today.
stubbe-peeter-werewolf-1590:
Printed in London in 1590, this English pamphlet retells the case of Stubbe Peeter, a farmer near Cologne who was put to death in 1589. No author is named. Crowds heard that Peeter had confessed, under torment, to murders, witchcraft, and turning into a wolf by means of a magic belt given by the Devil.

The tale piles horror on horror, then ends with his gruesome execution and warnings to the reader. Such cheap pamphlets fed a hungry market for crime and wonder news. This one fixed the werewolf in English print and shaped how later writers told such tales, so it is read now as both news and folklore.
stumpp-true-discourse-bedburg-1590:
Peter Stumpp farmed near Bedburg in Germany and died on the wheel in 1589 after a trial for murder and sorcery. A True Discourse, printed in English in 1590, carried his tale across the Channel. Stumpp is the famed Werewolf of Bedburg, the best-known such case in print.

The pamphlet says he confessed to killings done, by his own claim, in wolf form by means of a magic girdle. It dwells on his crimes, his pact with the Devil, and his hard death. English readers took the tale as true news from abroad. The print fixed Stumpp in folklore as the werewolf above all others.
taylor-eleusinian-bacchic-mysteries-1790:
Thomas Taylor wrote his Dissertation on the Eleusinian and Bacchic Mysteries in 1790. Taylor was the great English voice for Greek thought of the old world. The work was the first to lay the Greek rites bare for English eyes. It helped found the grave study of pagan rites in the West.

Taylor tells of the rites at Eleusis, where men sought a blest fate past death. He reads the myths of Demeter and Dionysus as signs of the soul's path. Old Greek and Latin texts give the sparse facts he works from. The book still shapes how the rites are read today.
the-american-missionary-volume-44-no-01-: Volume 44 begins with January 1890: New Year greetings, a lesson on the collection drawn from the Corinthian church, and Africa in shadow and sunshine. President Eaton's address is printed, along with word of meetings held by colored people. The Reverend F. E. Jenkins sends Southern field notes, Washington, D.C. reports a revival, and Straight University and Tillotson Institute appear. Dakota missionary life, a new church at Fort Yates, and a cry of China for Christ fill the last field pages.
the-american-missionary-volume-44-no-02-: February 1890 prints a full roll of field workers and an address by Bishop H. B. Whipple, with a letter from Miss Collins and a report from Grand View, Tennessee. Editors honor the Reverend Frank E. Jenkins and the Reverend W. W. Patton, note a revival at Straight University, and call one gift beautiful. Women's pages explain how one mission band raised its money and list the state groups, before receipts end the number.
the-american-missionary-volume-44-no-03-: Removal notices and a call for half a million dollars to fund growth open March 1890, under a motto about keeping at the work. Two watch night meetings are told in the South, one plain and one very different. The Ramona School represents the Indian field. A Chinese item treats an unbelieving wife, and C. H. Richards gives an address on the future of the Negro in this country. Women's pages mix state reports with a humble life of faith.
the-american-missionary-volume-44-no-04-: April 1890 marks a removal and the passing of the Reverend Frank P. Woodbury, then turns to Indian civilization and the movement of colored people to new homes. An enterprising woman and the stereopticon in New England also get space. Chandler Normal Institute is dedicated in the South, churches report around Paris, Texas, and Berea's temperance fight brings the cry that Becca must go. Streaks of light and an exemplary mother fill the Indian pages, and two Chinese anniversaries are kept.
the-american-missionary-volume-44-no-05-: Ballard Normal School at Macon, Georgia, dominates May 1890: facts about the school, its church, an industrial building's interior, and a teachers' home and girls' dormitory are all set out. Editors also announce a removal, discuss money, and open a mission in Alaska. Southern notes ride in the saddle, Tougaloo University reports, teachers meet as a group of educators, and the death of Eli Tapley closes the field news.
the-american-missionary-volume-44-no-06-: June 1890 hears Dr. Storrs on the Negro problem and sends missionaries to Alaska, while editors sum up higher schooling for colored people in a nutshell. Spring conferences, Mississippi newcomers, and the mission of music get brief items. Southern pages split work into school and church reports. They note a revival at Wilmington, North Carolina, and more news from Ballard School. A dreary picture of one place and its people follows. Mountain school reports and the King's Daughters Society close the section.
the-american-missionary-volume-44-no-10-: October 1890, now printed from the Bible House at Ninth Street and Fourth Avenue, sets the annual meeting beside the Federal Election Bill and the Mississippi Convention. Southern readers ride out to Rockhold, Kentucky, check church work and Straight University, and note a better class of students and temperance gains in Tennessee. Mr. Shelton reports from Northfield for the Indian field, a widow's mite is praised, and the Chinese section runs under the head Pictures: Lights and Shadows.
the-people-s-handbook-of-phrenology-comp: The People's Handbook of Phrenology, 1890. The people's handbook. This book preserves that manual. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
the-phrenological-magazine-volume-6-new-: The Phrenological Magazine, volume 6, new series, 1890. Another volume. This book preserves that periodical. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
tob-0190:
Sir Edwin Arnold's translation The Song Celestial carries his preferred subtitle, the Bhagavad-Gita from the Mahabharata. Krishna's teaching unfolds on the field of Kurukshetra, where the warrior Arjuna's duty to fight collides with despair at killing his kin. Arnold's blank verse made Hinduism's central scripture sing for English readers when it appeared in the 1880s.

Duty, devotion, and the deathless self are expounded as Krishna reveals progressively deeper views of action and reality, culminating in a vision of his universal form. Arnold shapes the dialogue as poetry first, and generations read the Gita through his music. Poetry as philosophy and philosophy as devotion meet in his version.
tob-10790:
Hereward Carrington, better known for writings on psychic research, opened the laboratory door for novices in Chemistry for Beginners. The primer assumes no prior training. Plain language and constant attention to the beginner's confusion guide every chapter.

Elements and their combinations come first, followed by simple experiments that reveal chemistry's basic laws in action. Readers learn what acids, gases, and compounds do by watching described reactions rather than memorizing formulas alone. The book preserves a first step into science from an age when chemistry still felt like licensed magic, and it shows how popular science writing taught ordinary readers.
tob-11490:
Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection was a seventeenth-century Carmelite lay brother in Paris who washed dishes and mended sandals for his community. The Practice of the Presence of God gathers his letters and recorded conversations, assembled by others from his teaching and example. His rule was simple: do everything with continual, loving attention to God.

Lawrence claimed no raptures or learning, only a habit of returning his mind to God in the kitchen as faithfully as in chapel. That humility made the little book a classic across churches that agree on little else. Readers get proof, in one obscure life, that holiness was said to need no monastery.
tob-4090:
Legge also translated the Yi King, the Book of Changes, for volume sixteen of the Sacred Books of China. China's oldest classic builds its counsel from sixty-four hexagrams, figures of broken and unbroken lines. Legge prints the judgments and lines with the long train of Chinese commentary.

Emperors and farmers alike consulted the book as an oracle, casting stalks or coins to choose a figure. Its wisdom concerns timing: when to advance, when to wait, when to yield. Legge doubted the divination but honored the philosophy. Verified from the 1919 edition, his version remains a standard door into the Changes.
tob-4190:
Arthur W. Ryder's 1925 translation of the Panchatantra is the liveliest English form of India's ancient book of animal fables. A sage frames the tales as lessons for young princes who must learn the world fast. The lion and the bull, and the cunning jackal between them, open the teaching.

Stories breed inside stories: a tale told to prove a point contains three more. The morals are worldly, about friends, enemies, and the uses of wit. No storybook has traveled farther, through Persia and Arabia into Europe's nursery classics. The evidence notes Ryder's version is not on Gutenberg and no text is attached here.
tob-4290:
Hans Sloane sailed to Jamaica in 1687 as physician to its governor, and his Voyage to the Island of Jamaica, issued across 1707 to 1725, reported the island whole. Plants, animals, weather, diseases, and the peoples of Jamaica, enslaved Africans among them, fill his pages. Hundreds of plates picture the natural world he found.

Sloane came home with a vast collection that later formed the founding stock of the British Museum. His notes on enslaved people's music and medicine preserve voices heard nowhere else so early. Verified from the 1919 edition, the Voyage remains a founding text of Caribbean natural history.
un-sc-res-1090:
Security Council Resolution 1090, adopted on December 13, 1996, recommended Kofi Annan as the next Secretary-General of the United Nations. The catalog year simply repeats the resolution number and is wrong. Annan, a Ghanaian who had served the UN for decades, was the council's choice to succeed Boutros Boutros-Ghali, whose second term the United States had blocked.

The General Assembly confirmed the pick days later, and Annan took office on January 1, 1997. He led the UN for ten years, through wars in Kosovo and Iraq and a push to reform the world body. The brief formal text is the legal hinge of that change at the top.
un-sc-res-1390:
Sanctions on the Taliban and Al-Qaida were tightened months after the September 2001 attacks. On 16 January 2002 the Security Council kept the arms and money measures in force. It reshaped them to follow the Taliban's fall from power in Afghanistan. The measures now targeted named people and groups wherever they were. A Council list identified them. Usama bin Laden headed that list.

All states had to freeze the funds of those listed. They had to bar their travel and block arms sales to them. The measures would be reviewed in twelve months. The Council could then continue or improve them. The text turned a country-based sanction into a global list system. That system still anchors counter-terrorism sanctions today.
un-sc-res-1490:
Voting on 3 July 2003, the Council unanimously adopted Resolution 1490 on the Iraq-Kuwait border. The observer mission there, called UNIKOM, had watched the border since 1991. The 2003 war had changed the facts on the ground. The Council judged the mission and its buffer zone no longer needed.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council grants UNIKOM one final period, ending 6 October 2003. The demilitarized zone along the border ends the same day. Mission property that cannot be moved will pass to Kuwait and Iraq as fitting. The text praises the mission's twelve years of work and thanks Kuwait, which had paid two thirds of its cost since 1993.
un-sc-res-1590: Resolution 1590 is a formal act of the fifteen-member Security Council, kept here through a Wikisource transcription of the record. Its opening clauses set out what the members believed was happening; its numbered clauses then act on that belief. Together with the surrounding numbers in the 1500s run, it documents the Council's steady written output.
un-sc-res-1690:
Timor-Leste's United Nations office gained two more months in June 2006. Violence had swept the young country that spring. Foreign troops from Australia, New Zealand, Portugal, and Malaysia had come at Dili's request. On 20 June 2006 the Council extended UNOTIL until 20 August. The time would be used to plan the United Nations role after the office closed. The Secretary-General's envoy had assessed the crisis on the ground.

The Council thanked the four governments for their security forces. Those forces had to work closely with Timor-Leste's government and UNOTIL. All parties in the country had to shun violence and join the democratic process. Within weeks the Council built a much larger mission for the country.
un-sc-res-1790: Resolution 1790, adopted in 2007, is an act of the Security Council kept here as a copy of the official record. Fifteen member states stand behind the text, five of them permanent members of the Council. The entry holds their findings and their decisions together, complete and in the order the members approved when they adopted the text.
un-sc-res-1890:
Afghanistan led to a Council vote: Resolution 1890, adopted on 8 October 2009. Violence by the Taliban, Al-Qaida, and drug-linked groups had grown worse. Civilian deaths ran high, and bombs and suicide attacks struck often. Afghans had just run their own 2009 elections, with 2010 polls ahead.

The Council extends the International Security Assistance Force for twelve months beyond 13 October 2009. States in the force may take all necessary measures to do the job. Members are urged to send more troops, gear, and funds. Training Afghan soldiers and police matters most, so Afghan forces can grow, act with skill, and answer for their conduct. Reports on the mission are due every three months.
un-sc-res-190:
Resolution 190, adopted on 9 June 1964, though the catalog record gives 1963, concerns South Africa and the Rivonia trial. Leaders of the anti-apartheid movement were on trial under laws that allowed long prison terms and the death sentence. The verdict was near, and the Council feared very serious results.

The Council recalls Assembly Resolution 1881 of 1963, which condemned South Africa for ignoring repeated UN resolutions and asked it to drop the trial and free all political prisoners. It notes that its own Resolutions 181 and 182 had called on South Africa to free people jailed, interned, or restricted for opposing apartheid. South Africa had rejected the appeal, a fact the Council records with regret.
un-sc-res-1990: Resolution 1990, from 2011, is a formal Security Council decision kept here through a Wikisource transcription of the record. Its number places it near the end of the 1900s run in this collection's sequence. The text at that place is complete: findings in the preamble, decisions in the operative clauses, preserved exactly as issued.
un-sc-res-290:
Portugal's invasion of Guinea was condemned on 8 December 1970. A Council mission sent under resolution 289 (1970) had reported on the raid. Portuguese naval and army units from Guinea-Bissau had struck on 22 and 23 November 1970. A further armed attack followed on 27 and 28 November. Life was lost and damage was wide.

The Council endorsed the mission's conclusions in full. It strongly condemned Portugal for the invasion of the Republic of Guinea. Portugal had to pay full compensation for the damage done to life and property. All states were appealed to for moral support and goods so Guinea could defend its independence and territory. The Council declared that Portuguese colonialism in Africa was itself a grave threat to the continent's peace. States were urged to give Lisbon no arms help for its repression, and Portugal was called to grant self-determination to its territories without further delay.
un-sc-res-390: Formal action by the Council in its numbered series produced Resolution 390, which the catalog dates to 1923. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-990:
Croatia's new peace operation took shape in the spring of 1995. On 28 April 1995 the Security Council approved the plans for UNCRO. That was the United Nations Confidence Restoration Operation in Croatia. The Secretary-General had set out the arrangements in his April report. The Council authorized the deployment he described. The mission replaced a wider force as the Yugoslav wars were reshaped.

Croatia's government and the local Serb authorities had to cooperate fully with UNCRO. The Council voiced concern that no status-of-forces deal had yet been signed. It pressed Croatia to conclude one quickly. The Secretary-General had to report on progress soon after. UNCRO's task was to build confidence and hold a fragile ceasefire line.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Resolution 1090, adopted at a closed meeting on 13 December 1996, names the Council's choice for the UN's top job. The Council recommends to the General Assembly that Kofi Annan be appointed Secretary-General of the United Nations for a term from 1 January 1997 to 31 December 2001. The Charter gives the Council this recommending role, and the Assembly appoints from its choice.

The Taliban fell in late 2001, but the sanctions built to squeeze them lived on. Bin Laden was still free. His Al-Qaida web still struck at the world. The old bans had to be re-aimed at men and groups, not a regime. Resolution 1390 passed with no dissent on 16 January 2002.

Cash and goods of listed names froze at once. Travel by those names was barred. Arms sales to them were banned in full. The list came from the 1999 and 2000 texts, kept fresh by the sanctions team. One old ban died: the bar on Taliban flights, from 1999, was struck off. A watch team would track the bans for twelve months. States had ninety days to tell what steps they had taken.

A quiet border mission reached its end with Resolution 1490. The text was adopted unanimously on 3 July 2003, not in 1993 as some summaries claim. UNIKOM had watched the Iraq-Kuwait frontier since the 1991 Gulf War. Kuwait paid two thirds of its costs. After the 2003 invasion, members judged the mission no longer needed.

UNIKOM received one final stretch, ending on 6 October 2003. Then the demilitarized zone along the border would close too. That zone reached ten kilometres into Iraq and five into Kuwait. The Secretary-General was told to hand over the mission's property to Kuwait and Iraq. The Council praised twelve years of successful observation work.

The Comprehensive Peace Agreement signed in Nairobi on 9 January 2005 had ended Sudan's long north-south civil war. On 24 March 2005 a large mission, UNMIS, is established to help carry it out. The separate conflict in Darfur still burned.

UNMIS is created with a mandate to support the peace deal's implementation, watch compliance, and help protect civilians and aid operations. The mission would work closely with the parties and coordinate with other United Nations actors across Sudan. The Secretary-General had to report within 30 days on deployment progress, and all parties are called on to cooperate fully with the new mission's arrival and work.

Timor-Leste fell back into strife in the spring of 2006. Gangs fought in Dili. Homes burned. Crowds fled to camps. The small UN office there, UNOTIL, was set to close. Its host state begged the world not to leave. Three top Timorese chiefs wrote on 11 June. Resolution 1690 passed on 20 June 2006.

UNOTIL won a stay to 20 August 2006. The pause was for plans, not drift. The chief owed a report by 7 August on the UN's next role. Troops sent by four states won warm thanks. Australia, New Zealand, Malaysia, and Portugal had rushed men in. An inquiry into the strife's roots would be led by the UN rights chief. Donors were told to meet a flash plea for aid, sent on 12 June.

The multinational force in Iraq is extended for a final year on 18 December 2007. Iraqi forces had taken command of all army divisions, and security responsibility for nine provinces had passed to Iraq's government. Ahead lay Iraqi forces holding full responsibility, allowing the foreign force's mandate to end.

The force's mandate is extended, with the same review and early-end terms as before, and the oil-revenue arrangements are extended until 31 December 2008. Those rules channel export income into the Development Fund for Iraq under world monitoring. The United States is to keep reporting for the force. This renewal was understood to be the last, and the force's presence in Iraq ended with its expiry.

Afghanistan's international force is renewed in Resolution 1890, adopted on 8 October 2009. Violence by the Taliban, Al-Qaida, and drug-linked armed groups was rising, civilian casualties were high, and suicide and roadside bomb attacks targeted civilians and soldiers alike. The NATO Training Mission had just been set up, and Afghan-led preparations for the 2010 elections were under way.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the authorization of the International Security Assistance Force, ISAF, for 12 months beyond 13 October 2009. It authorizes its member states to take all necessary measures. It calls for more troops, equipment, and resources, and presses ISAF and its partners to train, mentor, and expand the Afghan National Army and Police toward self-sufficient, accountable forces. ISAF must work closely with the Afghan government and report to the Council quarterly through the Secretary-General.

South Africa is urged to halt the Rivonia trial in this text of 9 June 1964. Leaders of the anti-apartheid movement were on trial under laws carrying long prison terms, and a verdict was near. The General Assembly had condemned South Africa the year before for defying repeated calls to free political prisoners and end such trials.

South Africa is urged to abandon the trial and to grant unconditional release to all political prisoners and everyone jailed, interned, or restricted for opposing apartheid. Earlier calls are repeated. Member states are also invited to use their influence to bring South Africa into line with the Charter. The vote was seven in favour, none against, with four abstentions.

Abyei is an oil-rich area claimed by both Sudan and South Sudan, which was about to become independent. Fighting there had killed people and driven many from their homes. On 27 June 2011 the Council adopted Resolution 1990 and created a new force for the area. Days earlier, Sudan and the Sudan People's Liberation Movement had agreed on temporary security arrangements, and Ethiopia had offered troops.

The new force, the United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei, was set up for six months. It could have up to 4,200 soldiers and 50 police. It had to watch both armies pull out of the area. Abyei was to stay free of armed forces, apart from the new force and a local police service. The force also had to protect civilians under threat and help aid deliveries reach people in need.

Resolution 290, adopted on 8 December 1970, answers Portugal's invasion of the Republic of Guinea. Portuguese naval and military units from Guinea-Bissau had invaded Guinea on 22 and 23 November 1970, and more attacks followed days later. A Council mission sent to Guinea reported on the loss of life and the wide damage done.

The Council strongly condemns Portugal for the invasion and demands full payment for the damage to life and property. It appeals to states to help Guinea defend its freedom and land. It declares Portuguese colonial rule in Africa a grave threat to peace, urges states to stop giving Portugal military help, and warns that any repeat attack will bring fresh Council action. It also backs freedom for the peoples of Angola, Mozambique, and Guinea-Bissau.

Six more months for the Golan Heights observer force were granted on 28 May 1976, with tension still in the air. The force, called UNDOF, watches the separation of Israeli and Syrian forces. The Council noted the efforts made toward a durable and just peace. It also noted the strain that still prevailed in the area. Resolution 390 records the renewal.

The parties were called on to carry out Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. That text had demanded a cease-fire and peace talks after the October war. The observer force's mandate was renewed for another six months. At the end of that period, the Secretary-General had to report on developments. His report also had to cover the measures taken to put Resolution 338 into effect. Texts like this one kept the observer force in place, term after term, while no final peace was reached.

The Korean War was raging when the Council tidied its own agenda. Resolution 90 was adopted unanimously on 31 January 1951. The war had begun with North Korea's invasion of the South in June 1950. The Council had condemned that attack in its first debates. The item stayed on its formal list of seized matters.

The resolution removes that item, titled the complaint of aggression upon the Republic of Korea. The step was procedural, not a judgment on the war. Fighting continued for two more years. Members simply judged the listing no longer useful. The one-line text shows how the Council manages its docket even mid-war, closing files whose work has moved elsewhere.

A new name, UNCRO, marked the Croatia mission's relaunch in 1995. On 28 April, the Council adopted Resolution 990 without dissent. It acted under Chapter VII. The wars of Yugoslavia's breakup still raged at the time. A month before, the Council had split the Croatia force from the Bosnia and Macedonia ones. The Secretary-General's April report set out how the new force would work.

The text welcomes that report and backs its plan for the mandate. The deployment itself is cleared as proposed. Zagreb and the local Serb leaders must work with UNCRO in full. One sore point is flagged in plain terms. No status-of-forces deal has been signed yet. Croatia must close one fast, and a progress report is due by 15 May 1995.
una-canzone-capodistriana-del-secolo-xiv: Una canzone capodistriana del secolo XIV sulla pietra filosofale, 1890. The Capodistrian song. This book preserves that work. Later readers can locate it. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
verga-house-by-medlar-tree-craig-1890:
Giovanni Verga published I Malavoglia in Italian in 1881, and Mary A. Craig Englished it in 1890 as The House by the Medlar-Tree. W. D. Howells wrote the introduction to her edition. The Malavoglia are a Sicilian fishing family ruled by old Padron 'Ntoni and his faith in work and the house.

A wrecked cargo, debts, war, and jail strip the family member by member. Verga tells the tale in the voice of the village itself, proverbs and all. The book founded the verismo school, Italy's answer to French naturalism. Its power lies in patience: small blows, plainly told, until a world sinks. Howells championed it as a model of honest fiction.
weishaupt-pythagoras-1790:
Pythagoras is the full statement of Adam Weishaupt's thought after the fall of his order. The Bavarian state banned the Illuminati in the mid 1780s and drove its founder into exile. In this first volume, printed at Frankfurt and Leipzig in 1790, he sets his ideas out as a system.

The title names the Greek sage Pythagoras, a model for a wise and hidden teacher. Weishaupt argues that a quiet circle of trained men could steer rulers toward reason and mild reform. He treats rule itself as a craft that can be studied and taught. Later writers on secret rule still treat the book as the core text of his thought.
wollstonecraft-vindication-rights-men-17:
Mary Wollstonecraft published A Vindication of the Rights of Men in 1790. She wrote in hot reply to Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, which had defended the old order against the French Revolution. Wollstonecraft's answer was among the first and sharpest in the pamphlet war.

She attacked hereditary rank and wealth as corruptions that make men servile or tyrannical by turns. True rights, she argued, rest on reason and apply to all, not on birth or custom. The pamphlet sold fast and made her name as a political writer. Two years later she extended the same logic to women. The work is her first feminist intervention in the Revolution debate.
worcester-witches-tryals-1690:
Four people faced the Worcester assizes in 1690 on charges of witchcraft, and The Full Tryals tells their story in full. The pamphlet prints their trials with their confessions and their last speeches on the scaffold. By 1690 such trials had grown rare in England.

The dying speeches give the book its human weight, as the condemned speak in their own voice at the end. Belief in witchcraft was fraying, yet courts could still hang for it. The record shows both facts at once: doubt in the air, death on the ground. Few late Stuart prints hold that clash so plainly.
zola-monomaniac-1890:
Hutchinson issued The Monomaniac in 1901, translated and edited by Edward Vizetelly. The French title is La Bete Humaine, the human beast. A picture up front shows Severine crying out while Roubaud turns round in terror.

Jacques Lantier, a railway man, carries a dreadful family taint. Sudden murderous urges seize a man who is otherwise decent and kind. His struggle plays out in the iron world of locomotives and rushing trains. A runaway engine becomes the image of blind human appetite. Part thriller and part tragedy, the 1890 novel grips from its first chapter to its grim and famous close.
